s: three hundred thousand years in twelve plates
x: Before any close look, this chapter tells the whole human story once, from far away. Every later chapter is a slower walk along one stretch of it. Seen from far enough away, the story has a simple shape. For almost all of it, people lived in small bands as hunters and gatherers. Then, within a few thousand years of each other, people in several parts of the world began to farm. Farming fed villages, villages grew into cities, and cities into states and empires. Each change came faster than the one before. People spread out of Africa c. 60,000–50,000 years ago 1.2 Farming begins from c. 11,500 years ago 1.3 Cities and writing cities c. 3500 BCE, writing c. 3200 BCE 1.4 The world joined by sea from 1492 1.7 Machines and fossil fuel from c. 1760 1.8 Three threads run through every page. Connection: as regions joined, goods, ideas and diseases moved along the same roads. Scale: more people, living in larger and more complex societies. Evidence: how we know any of this, and how sure we can be. On the right is a plate. Click anything on it to learn more. The small labels after a sentence mark claims that are approximate, debated or traditional; click one to see the evidence and the sources.

s: three hundred thousand years, drawn to scale
x: Our species is about 300,000 years old. For about 98 percent of that time, no one wrote anything down. Homo sapiens evolved in Africa. The oldest fossils some experts assign to our lineage, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are about 315,000 years old, though whether they are fully our species is debated. Against that span, the events most people call history are recent. People began to cultivate wild cereals about 11,500 years ago, and the first writing appears at Uruk around 3200 BCE, about 5,200 years ago. So roughly 98 percent of the human story came before writing, and 96 percent before farming. Homo sapiens appears 00:00 farming begins about 23:05 writing begins about 23:35 1 CE about 23:50 1800 about 23:58:55 today 24:00 The long stretch before writing is not empty. In it people crossed oceans, painted caves, buried their dead and reached every continent but Antarctica. It is known from bones, tools, ancient DNA and dated layers of earth rather than from texts; page 1.11 shows how. Keep this scale in mind as the chapters zoom in: the whole of Volume I after Chapter 2 fits inside the last half hour of the day.

s: how one African species reached every continent
x: Almost everyone alive outside Africa descends mainly from people who left it about 60,000 to 50,000 years ago. Their descendants reached every habitable continent; the last large places to be settled were islands in the Pacific, less than a thousand years ago. Small groups had left Africa earlier: our species was in the Levant by about 190,000 years ago. But those early groups left no detectable trace in the ancestry of people living today. Outside Africa, the newcomers met other humans. Interbreeding with Neanderthals, mostly between about 50,500 and 43,500 years ago, left about 2 percent Neanderthal DNA in people outside Africa today. Some peoples of Oceania also carry up to 3.5 percent from the Denisovans, a group known mostly from their genes. Levant (early groups) c. 194,000–90,000 years ago Australia and New Guinea c. 65,000 or c. 50,000 years ago [[c-sahul]] Europe c. 45,000 years ago (Bacho Kiro, Bulgaria) The Americas before c. 15,000 years ago [[c-americas]] Remote Pacific c. 1025–1290 CE Two arrival dates are hotly argued. In Australia, excavators date the oldest tools at Madjedbebe to about 65,000 years ago; critics, partly on genetic grounds, put arrival nearer 50,000. In the Americas, footprints at White Sands in New Mexico have been dated to about 23,000–21,000 years ago, which would put people there during the coldest part of the last Ice Age; others think the dates are too old. The last great migration was across the open Pacific. Polynesian voyagers reached the Society Islands around 1025–1120 CE and then, within two centuries, Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and New Zealand.

s: at least eleven beginnings after the Ice Age
x: Farming was not invented once and passed around. People in many separate regions domesticated their own plants and animals, starting in several regions within a few thousand years of the end of the last Ice Age, and in others later. Domestication was slow. In Southwest Asia, people were tending wild cereals about 11,500 years ago, but it took another thousand years or more before wheat changed into a fully domestic form. People there domesticated wheat, barley and lentils, and sheep, goats, cattle and pigs; some animals, such as pigs, were also domesticated independently elsewhere. Southwest Asia wheat, barley, lentils; sheep, goats, cattle, pigs c. 11,500 years ago China millet (north), rice (south) c. 10,000–9,400 years ago [[c-china-farm]] New Guinea taro, bananas c. 10,000 years ago Mexico squash, then maize c. 10,000 and 8,700 years ago Andes potatoes; llamas, alpacas over 7,000 years ago Eastern North America squash, sunflower, goosefoot c. 5,000–3,800 years ago Sudan and the Sahel sorghum, pearl millet c. 3500–2000 BCE How many independent beginnings there were depends on definitions: at least 11, and perhaps more than 20. What matters is the pattern. Farming arose on its own in places that had no contact with each other, which suggests that the changed climate after the Ice Age made it possible in many places at once. Farming fed more people from the same land. World population rose about tenfold between 10,000 and 3000 BCE. Dense, settled populations with stored food are the precondition for everything on the next page. Compare 1.2: the spread across the world was the work of hunter-gatherers. Farming spread later, mostly by farmers moving into new land and by neighbours adopting it.

In a handful of river valleys, farming villages grew into cities ruled by kings and run by scribes. In Mesopotamia, writing began not as literature but as bookkeeping. Around 3200 BCE Uruk in southern Mesopotamia was the largest settlement in the region, perhaps in the world. Its earliest tablets record rations, grain and livestock for the temple economy. At about the same time, Egypt was unified under a single king, with its capital at Memphis. Further east, the cities of the Indus valley, such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, flourished from about 2600 BCE, with planned streets and drains; their script is still undeciphered. In China, Erlitou was a major centre from about 1750 BCE, and the Shang kings at Anyang left the earliest Chinese writing, questions to their ancestors carved on bone and shell. The Americas followed their own path. Caral in Peru had platform mounds and plazas by about 3000 BCE but no writing, though a khipu, a knotted-cord record, was reported there. The Olmec of Mexico's Gulf coast flourished from about 1200 BCE. Mesopotamia (Uruk) from c. 3500 BCE yes, c. 3200 BCE Egypt unified c. 3100 BCE yes, at about the same time Indus valley c. 2600 BCE onward undeciphered script China (Shang) c. 1600 (traditional)–1046 BCE yes, by c. 1250 BCE Peru (Caral) c. 3000–1800 BCE none known Mexico (Olmec) c. 1200–400 BCE perhaps, c. 900 BCE Writing was invented independently at least three times, in Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, and probably in Egypt as well. Caral shows that a large, organised society did not strictly need it. Chapters 3 to 6 slow down here: Mesopotamia and Egypt each get a chapter, the Indus and early China share Chapter 5, and Chapter 6 follows the Late Bronze Age world, from Greece to Mesopotamia, that linked Egypt with its neighbours.

s: c. 600 BCE to 600 CE, from the Mediterranean to China
x: In a few centuries much of Eurasia came under a handful of very large states, and several of the world's great traditions of thought took shape at about the same time. Persia came first. Cyrus II founded the Achaemenid empire around 550 BCE; at its height it ran from Macedonia and Libya to the borderlands of the Indus. Alexander of Macedon ended it in 330 BCE. In India, Chandragupta founded the Maurya empire around 321 BCE. His grandson Ashoka turned away from conquest after the bloody Kalinga war and had his principles of dharma carved on rocks and pillars across the subcontinent. In China, Qin unified the warring states in 221 BCE, and the Han ruled from 206 BCE to 220 CE. In the West, Rome became an empire under Augustus in 27 BCE. At their height, in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE, Han China and Rome may each have held about 60 million people: perhaps a third to a half of humanity between them. Isaiah Jerusalem 8th century BCE [[c-isaiah]] Zoroaster Iran uncertain [[c-zoroaster]] Confucius Lu (Qufu), China 551–479 BCE The Buddha Lumbini, Ganges plain died c. 480 or c. 400 BCE [[c-buddha]] Socrates Athens c. 470–399 BCE Plato Athens 428/427–348/347 BCE In 1949 the philosopher Karl Jaspers called these centuries the Axial Age, a turning point in human thought in several places at once. Many historians are wary of the idea, which may turn a loose coincidence into a single breakthrough. The traditions travelled with empires and traders. Buddhism reached China by the 1st century CE, and in 380 the emperor Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the Roman empire's official faith. Empires of this size kept returning in the same places: Persia, India, China and the Mediterranean each saw a long run of successor states. Chapters 8 and 9 follow them.

s: c. 600 to 1450: deserts, steppes and seas
x: After 600 the regions of Afro-Eurasia were tied together more tightly than ever, by trade routes across deserts, steppes and seas, and by a new faith that spread along them. Islam began in Arabia. By tradition, Muhammad left Mecca for Medina in 622, the hijra, and he died in 632. Within little more than a century, Muslim rule ran from Iberia, invaded in 711, to Central Asia and the Indus. Overland, the routes later called the Silk Roads linked China to the Mediterranean, some 6,400 km end to end. Silk went west; gold, silver and wool came east. The geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen popularised the name in 1877. At sea, the monsoon set the calendar. Its winds blow from the southwest in summer and from the northeast in winter, so ships sailed out on one monsoon and home on the next. Across the Sahara, caravans carried West African gold north and salt south. Mali's ruler Mansa Musa made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 and spent so much gold in Cairo that its value there fell for years. Tang and Song China produced inventions that later travelled along these webs: printed books by the 9th century, government paper money in the 1020s and the oldest known recipe for gunpowder, from 1044. Two catastrophes closed the age. The Mongols, united under Chinggis Khan in 1206, built the largest contiguous land empire in history. Then plague, the Black Death, crossed the same connected world. In Europe (1347–51) it killed perhaps a third to over half of the people, with large differences between regions. The connections that carried silk and ideas also carried disease. The same pattern returns after 1492, when Old World diseases devastated the Americas (1.7).

Within a single lifetime, sailors linked Europe, Africa, Asia and the Americas by sea, and the exchange that followed remade diets, populations and labour around the globe. In 1492 Columbus crossed the Atlantic to the Caribbean. In 1498 Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa to Calicut in India. In 1522 the survivors of Magellan's fleet completed the first voyage around the world. The historian Alfred Crosby named what followed the Columbian Exchange. Maize, potatoes and cassava crossed to Africa, Europe and Asia; wheat, sugar, horses and cattle came to the Americas. So did smallpox, measles and influenza, against which the peoples of the Americas had no immunity. Within about a century and a half their numbers fell by perhaps 80 to 95 percent. How many people lived in the Americas in 1492 is still argued, from about 8 million to more than 100 million. Epidemics did most of the killing, but war, enslavement and forced labour made them deadlier. Europeans forced Indigenous people to work mines and estates, and to work sugar and other plantations they turned increasingly to enslaved Africans. embarked in Africa c. 12.5 million survived the crossing c. 10.7 million landed directly in North America c. 388,000 On land, the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires, and Ming and then Qing China, remained the world's great powers. Historians sometimes call the first three 'gunpowder empires', though the label is debated.

In about a century and a half, revolutions changed who ruled, in whose name, and how almost everything was made. The American colonies declared independence in 1776. The French Revolution began in 1789; in July crowds stormed the Bastille. In Saint-Domingue, enslaved people rose in 1791 and founded Haiti in 1804, the first country created by former slaves. Napoleon's seizure of the Spanish crown in 1808 opened the way for Spanish America: Venezuela declared independence in 1811, and by 1826 Spain had lost the mainland. Meanwhile Britain began to industrialise. In the classic dating, 1760 to 1840, machines driven first by water and then by coal-fired steam multiplied what a worker could make. James Watt patented his separate condenser, which made steam engines far more efficient, in 1769. 1 CE c. 1,100 1000 c. 1,100 1500 c. 1,300 1820 c. 1,500 1900 c. 3,100 1950 c. 4,600 2025 c. 21,900 Why Britain, and why then? Kenneth Pomeranz argued that the richest regions of China and Europe were comparable until about 1800, and that coal and New World resources tipped the balance. Others date the gap earlier.

The twentieth century brought the deadliest wars in history, the end of most empires and a long confrontation between two superpowers. The First World War (1914–18) killed about 8.5 million soldiers and perhaps as many as 13 million civilians. In 1917, two revolutions in Russia ended the monarchy and brought the Bolsheviks to power. The Second World War (1939–45) was far deadlier: estimates run from about 35 million to 60 million dead or more, most of them civilians. Nazi Germany murdered about six million Jews in the Holocaust. Germany surrendered in May 1945. Japan surrendered in August, after the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet Union declared war on Japan. In 1945 nearly a third of the world's people still lived in colonies. Independence came in waves: India and Pakistan in 1947, Ghana in 1957, Angola in 1975. 1945 51 1960 99 1970 127 1980 154 1990 159 2000 189 2011 to today 193 From 1947–48 the United States and the Soviet Union faced each other in the Cold War, armed with nuclear weapons but never fighting each other directly. It ended when the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

For nearly all of history the world's population grew so slowly that no one alive could have noticed. In the last two centuries it rose eightfold. Around 10,000 BCE there were perhaps 4.5 million people. By 1 CE there were about 230 million, and by 1800 about one billion. Since then the number has risen eightfold, to 8.09 billion in 2023. It was not that people had more children; they stopped dying so young. Life expectancy at birth was under 30 in 1800 and is over 73 today. Most of that change came from children surviving. people c. 1 billion 8.09 billion (2023) life expectancy at birth 28.5 years 73.2 years (2023) share in extreme poverty c. 76% (1820) c. 10% (2018) primary energy used c. 5,650 TWh c. 176,000 TWh (2024) Behind every line of that table is energy. In 1800 almost all of it came from wood and other biomass. Today the world uses about 31 times as much, most of it from fossil fuels, which is why the same two centuries also changed the climate. This is why the industrial revolutions of 1.8 matter so much: they are the hinge of the whole chart.

s: texts, things, trees, atoms and genes
x: Every date in this book rests on evidence, and each kind of evidence reaches only so far back and answers only certain questions. Written records begin at Uruk at the end of the 4th millennium BCE. They give names, events and beliefs, but only of the few who could write, and only about what they chose to record. Tree rings give an exact, year-by-year calendar reaching back about 12,400 years, where suitable wood survives. Radiocarbon dating, developed by Willard Libby in 1949, measures the decay of carbon-14 in anything that once lived. It works back to about 50,000 years and must be calibrated against tree rings and, further back, other records such as lake sediments and corals. Beyond that, luminescence, uranium-series and potassium-argon methods date the sediments, cave deposits and volcanic layers around a find. Ancient DNA shows ancestry, mixing and migration. The oldest human-lineage DNA yet read is about 430,000 years old; the Neanderthal genome, published in 2010, showed that many living people carry Neanderthal ancestry. DNA rarely survives in hot climates and says little about culture. Ice cores record 800,000 years of climate, and their recent layers also hold traces of human activity, such as lead from Roman mining (8.0), though they name no events. Historical linguistics reconstructs lost languages, and with them the things their speakers had words for, but its dates depend on its models. When sources disagree, this book says so. The small labels after sentences mark claims that are approximate, debated or a traditional account; click one to see the evidence and its sources. Unlabelled statements are well established or close to it, and their sources are on the plates.

The rest of Volume I travels the same road as this chapter, slowly: each era gets one or more chapters, and each chapter one subject seen from many sides. The chart on the right is the main road. Each band is an era; the numbers above it are the chapters that cover it. Era boundaries are conventions, not facts of nature: standard courses place them differently, though breaks near 1450 or 1500, 1750, and 1900 or 1914 recur in most; later breaks vary between 1945 and 1991. The bands are drawn equal, though the eras are not: the first covers hundreds of thousands of years, the last only a few decades. Later eras get more chapters because far more evidence survives from them, not because they mattered more. The contents page shows which chapters are written so far. s: foragers, and the turn to farming
x: For almost the whole human story, people lived by gathering, hunting and fishing, in small groups that moved with the seasons. This chapter follows that world and the slow turn, in a few places, to farming. No one wrote any of it down. What we know comes from bones, tools, hearths, art, ancient DNA and, with care, from foragers who lived recently enough to be studied. Those recent foragers suggest how such societies worked. Hadza camps in Tanzania hold about 30 people and move every few weeks. Bands were not simply families: in a sample of 32 forager societies, most band members were not close relatives, and people moved between camps through wide networks of friends and in-laws. Two old ideas about foragers are still argued over. One is that men hunted and women gathered: a 2023 study said women hunt in most forager societies, and a 2024 reply said the division of labour by sex is still real. The other is that foragers were the 'original affluent society', working only a few hours a day; critics counter that once food processing and chores are counted, the working week was about as long as ours. share of the time since 190,000 BCE about 95% about 5% people born about 9 billion about 108 billion One number puts this in proportion. About 117 billion people have ever been born, but because forager populations were tiny, only about 9 billion of them lived before 8000 BCE. Foraging fills most of the human timeline, yet most humans were born after farming took hold. Chapter 1 showed this span from far away (1.1). Here we walk through it: the human family (2.1), minds and art (2.2), the Ice Age (2.3), and then the turn to farming (2.5-2.10).

s: many kinds of human, one survivor
x: For most of the last few million years, several kinds of human lived on Earth at once. We are the last of a large and branching family. The oldest members of the family in this chart, such as Australopithecus afarensis, walked upright more than three million years ago but had brains not much larger than a chimpanzee's. Stone tools are older than any known fossil of our own genus, Homo: the Lomekwi tools from Kenya are about 3.3 million years old. The oldest tools of the long-lived Oldowan tradition, about 2.9 million years old, were found beside teeth of Paranthropus, a different branch altogether. The family was bushy, not a ladder. Around 2.6-2.8 million years ago, early Homo and at least one kind of Australopithecus lived in the same part of Ethiopia. Homo erectus, which appeared about 1.9 million years ago, was the first known species to spread far beyond Africa and survived in Asia until about 110,000 years ago. Fire changed what people could eat and where they could live. Burned material shows fire in use about a million years ago, and in 2025 a site in England gave the first evidence of fire being made, with flint and iron pyrite, about 400,000 years ago. Homo sapiens Africa, spreading to Asia and Australia fossils, DNA, tools Neanderthals Europe, western and central Asia hundreds of fossils, genomes Denisovans Siberia to Tibet and the Taiwan Strait a few bones, DNA, proteins Homo floresiensis Flores, Indonesia fossils; dying out by about then Neanderthals buried their dead, controlled fire and made refined tools. The Denisovans are known mostly from DNA, but in 2025 proteins and DNA linked a skull from Harbin in China to them, giving the group its first known face. Our ancestors met and had children with both groups: their DNA survives in billions of people today.

Long before writing, people marked themselves and their world with symbols: beads, engraved patterns, paintings and carvings. When this began, and how suddenly, is one of the great questions about the human mind. The oldest known ornaments are shell beads from Bizmoune Cave in Morocco, about 142,000-150,000 years old. At Blombos Cave in South Africa, people engraved patterns on lumps of ochre about 75,000 years ago, drew a crosshatched design on stone about 73,000 years ago and strung shell beads. The oldest known paintings are not in Europe. In January 2026, a hand stencil in a cave on Muna, an island off Sulawesi in Indonesia, was dated to at least 67,800 years ago; elsewhere on Sulawesi, a painted scene of human figures with a pig is at least 51,200 years old. Paintings in Spanish caves have been dated to about 65,000 years ago, which would make them the work of Neanderthals; the method behind those dates is disputed. Shell beads Bizmoune, Morocco 142,000-150,000 Engraved ochre, drawing Blombos, South Africa c. 75,000-73,000 Hand stencil Liang Metanduno, Sulawesi at least 67,800 Flutes, Lion-man Swabian Jura, Germany c. 43,000-40,000 Cave paintings Chauvet, France c. 37,000-28,000 Cave paintings Lascaux, France c. 17,000 [[c-lascaux]] In Europe, the ivory Lion-man and flutes of bird bone from the caves of the Swabian Jura are 40,000-43,000 years old, among the oldest known figurative carvings and musical instruments. The great painted caves come later: Chauvet about 37,000-28,000 years ago, Lascaux about 17,000. These finds have shifted an old argument. Some scholars held that modern behaviour appeared suddenly about 50,000 years ago; beads and engraved ochre from Africa tens of thousands of years earlier support the view that it was assembled gradually.

s: a colder planet, with more land
x: Twenty thousand years ago, ice two or three kilometres thick covered much of North America and northern Europe, and the seas were so low that people could walk from Siberia to Alaska. The ice sheets were at their largest between about 26,500 and 20,000 years ago, the Last Glacial Maximum. The Laurentide ice sheet covered more than 13 million km² of North America and reached south to about 39° N, near today's Cincinnati; the Scandinavian ice sheet merged with British ice over the North Sea and reached Germany and Poland. So much water was locked in ice that sea level was about 120-134 metres lower than today. Continental shelves became plains. Beringia joined Siberia to Alaska; Sunda joined Sumatra, Java and Borneo to Asia; Sahul joined Australia to New Guinea and Tasmania; and Doggerland joined Britain to Europe. A 2022 study argues the Bering land bridge appeared only about 35,700 years ago. People adapted. Eyed needles appear about 40,000 years ago, perhaps evidence of layered or decorated clothing. At Sunghir in Russia, about 34,000 years ago, people were buried with thousands of beads, and their genomes show they were not close kin. At Kostenki, about 25,000 years ago, people built a ring of the bones of at least 60 mammoths, whether as a house, a store or a ritual place. sea level about 120-134 m lower 0 Laurentide ice > 13 million km² gone Scandinavian ice c. 6.6 million km² gone Britain joined to Europe an island Then the ice melted. Between about 16,500 and 8,200 years ago, the seas rose roughly 12 metres every thousand years, drowning the coasts where many people had lived. Doggerland shrank to an island and was gone by about 7,000 years ago. Much of the archaeology of the Ice Age now lies under the sea.

Fifty thousand years ago the world was full of giants: mammoths, giant ground sloths, wombat-like beasts the size of a car. Most were gone by the end of the Ice Age. Whether people or climate killed them is one of the long arguments of science. The losses were heaviest on continents whose animals had never met earlier kinds of human. Australia lost about 88 percent of its genera of large mammals, the Americas 72-83 percent; Africa, where people had lived alongside large animals for hundreds of thousands of years, lost about 21 percent. The timing differed from continent to continent, and in several places it followed soon after people arrived: in Australia, mostly before about 40,000 years ago; in North America, mostly between 13,500 and 11,500 years ago. In southwest Australia the die-off came within about 2,000 years of human arrival, though some giants, such as Diprotodon, seem to have lived alongside people far longer. Diprotodon Australia c. 25,000 years ago Woolly rhinoceros northern Eurasia c. 14,000 (fossils); perhaps 9,800 [[c-rhino]] Woolly mammoth Wrangel Island c. 4,000 years ago Moa New Zealand c. 1400 CE Islands give the sharpest cases. In New Zealand, all moa were gone within about 120 years of the first Polynesian settlers. The last woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island, off Siberia, until about 4,000 years ago, when the pyramids of Egypt were already standing. The argument goes on. Some researchers blame people almost entirely, others point to the changing climate, and many now think it was both: climate stressed the animals and hunting finished them.

t: Warming, and people who settled down
s: the end of the Ice Age in the Levant
x: As the Ice Age ended, the climate lurched between warm and cold. In the Levant, some foragers stopped moving: they built houses, buried their dead beside them and harvested wild grain, thousands of years before anyone farmed. The end of the Ice Age was not smooth. About 14,700 years ago, Greenland warmed abruptly. Then, about 12,900 years ago, the cold returned for some twelve centuries, the Younger Dryas, before the warm, stable Holocene began 11,700 years ago. In the warm interval, the Natufian people of the Levant began to stay put for much of the year. At 'Ain Mallaha in Galilee they built round houses sunk into the ground and buried their dead among them; one person was buried with a puppy, wolf or dog. At Hilazon Tachtit, an elderly woman was buried with 50 tortoise shells, a grave often read as a shaman's. They ate wild cereals, and did more than boil them. At Shubayqa 1 in Jordan, people baked a flatbread from wild einkorn and tubers about 14,400 years ago, some 3,000 years before people began to cultivate cereals (1.3) and at least 4,000 years before farming became a way of life. At Raqefet Cave, residues in stone mortars have even been read as beer. Did the Younger Dryas cold push them to cultivate, as wild foods failed? The idea is attractive and contested: some evidence suggests the cold brought little cultural change, and that it was the stable warmth afterwards that made farming possible. Settling down came first; farming came later. Sedentary foragers like the Natufians show that villages did not need farming, though farming made villages much larger (2.8).

Eleven and a half thousand years ago, on a hill in southeastern Turkey, people who still lived by hunting and gathering raised circles of carved stone pillars taller than a person. It changed what archaeologists thought foragers could do. Göbekli Tepe was built from about 9600 to 8200 BCE. Its round and rectangular enclosures hold T-shaped limestone pillars up to 5.5 metres tall. Many have carved arms, hands and belts, so they are stylised human figures, and they are covered with foxes, boars, snakes, vultures and scorpions. Every animal bone found there comes from a wild species. Its excavator, Klaus Schmidt, saw it as a sanctuary that hunter-gatherers gathered to build: 'First the temple, then the city.' The idea was irresistible to the press. But excavations between 2015 and 2019 found ordinary houses with hearths, a large rock-cut basin that may have stored water, and channels to fill it. More than 7,000 grinding stones show wild cereals were processed on a large scale, perhaps to feed work parties. what it was a sanctuary, 'the first temple' special buildings within a settlement who lived there no one; people gathered to build people lived there the fill deliberate ritual burial partly slope slides; how much was deliberate is debated Göbekli Tepe is not alone. Nearby Karahan Tepe has similar pillars and more than 30 houses, and about a dozen sites of the same culture are now being explored, the Taş Tepeler, 'stone hills'. Popular claims that its carvings record a comet strike or a calendar have been rejected by the excavators. What stays remarkable is the order of events. Monumental building, carving and large gatherings came before domesticated crops and animals, not after. Whatever the pillars meant, the effort of building them may have been one of the things that drew people into more settled lives.

s: plants and animals that changed with us
x: Domestication was not a single invention. Over centuries and millennia, by harvesting, sowing and herding, people changed the plants and animals they lived with until some could no longer live without them. Wild wheat scatters its seeds as soon as they ripen; domestic wheat holds them until a person harvests them. Domestic cereals also have bigger seeds that sprout as soon as they are sown. Each trait spread because people unknowingly favoured it: they harvested the ears that had not yet shattered and sowed some of that grain the next year. The change was slow. At early sites in Turkey and Syria, the share of non-shattering wheat rose over some 3,000 years, though a minority of scholars argue for a short, deliberate domestication. The 'founder crops' of Southwest Asia were wheat (einkorn and emmer), barley, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch and flax. Dog western Eurasia (origin unknown) by c. 15,800 Goat, sheep Southwest Asia c. 11,000-10,000 Founder crops Southwest Asia c. 11,000-10,000 Cattle Near East c. 10,500 Pig Near East by c. 10,500 Cat (tamed?) Cyprus c. 9,500 Goats and sheep were domesticated about 11,000-10,000 years ago, cattle and pigs soon after. All taurine (humpless) cattle descend from perhaps 80 wild aurochs; humped zebu cattle were domesticated separately in South Asia. Within a few centuries farmers carried all four to Cyprus by boat. The dog came first, long before farming. Genomes published in 2026 show dogs living with hunter-gatherers in Turkey, Britain and Switzerland 15,800-14,200 years ago; where wolves first became dogs is still unknown. Cats have a different story: a cat was buried beside a person on Cyprus 9,500 years ago, but domestic cats reached Europe only about 2,000 years ago.

As farming took hold, some settlements grew into places of thousands of people. They were not yet cities: no kings, no writing and, at the largest, no streets. At Jericho, by a spring in the Jordan valley, people built a stone wall and a tower about 8.5 metres high roughly 11,000 years ago, before pottery and before fully domesticated crops. Why they built it is still argued: defence, a flood barrier, a statement of the village's standing, or a monument aligned with the midsummer sunset that bound the community together. Across the Jordan, 'Ain Ghazal grew to about 10-12 hectares, and its people buried caches of plaster statues with staring eyes, some of the oldest large human figures known. Then, after about 8,900 years ago, it shrank, perhaps as the climate dried. Çatalhöyük, on the plain of central Turkey, was occupied for more than a thousand years, from about 7100 to 5950 BCE. Its houses were packed wall to wall with no streets; people walked across the rooftops and climbed down ladders into their homes, and buried their dead under the floors. At its height it held perhaps 3,500-8,000 people. Jericho tower c. 11,000 years ago a village of round mud-brick houses 'Ain Ghazal from c. 10,200 years ago; shrank after c. 8,900 about 10-12 ha Çatalhöyük c. 7100-5950 BCE 13.5 ha; perhaps 3,500-8,000 people No palace or temple has been found there, and men and women ate much the same food. Ancient DNA published in 2025 shows that where people buried in the same house were related, the links ran mainly through mothers; in later phases many were not related at all. Life was not easy: about 10-13 percent of adult teeth had cavities, infection was common, and healed head injuries became more frequent as the town grew more crowded.

Farming fed more people from the same land, and farming communities grew. But by many measures, early farmers were often shorter, sicker and harder-worked than the foragers before them. The clearest gain was in numbers. Cemeteries of the first farmers hold a much larger share of children than those of foragers, a sign that birth rates rose: the Neolithic Demographic Transition. Settled women could have children more often, and grain could feed them. The costs show in bones and teeth. Most studies find that adult height fell as people came to rely on farming, and grain-rich diets brought tooth decay. Living close to herds and to each other brought new diseases: in ancient genomes, diseases caught from animals appear about 6,500 years ago and are widespread by 5,000. In 1987 Jared Diamond called farming 'the worst mistake in the history of the human race'. Few specialists put it so starkly. A 2023 study of 3,507 skeletons found that in most regions height had begun to fall before farming appeared, so farming was not the only cause. more food from less land longer, harder work for many more children, faster growth shorter adults in most regions stored surplus tooth decay from grain settled villages crowding and infection animals for milk, wool, traction diseases caught from animals If it was such a mixed bargain, why did people farm? The answers are debated: a warmer and more stable climate after the Ice Age, growing populations, feasts that rewarded those who could produce a surplus, and new ideas of property. Perhaps the simplest answer is demographic: farmers had more children, and in time there were simply more of them.

Farming did not spread across Europe mainly as an idea. Ancient DNA shows it travelled with people: farmers whose ancestors came from Anatolia and the Aegean. Farmers reached Greece about 8,500 years ago, central Europe about 7,500 and Britain about 6,000. Their descendants carried the same ancestry, traceable back to the Aegean, all the way. Averaged over the continent, the frontier moved at roughly a kilometre a year. They came by two routes. One followed the Danube into central Europe, where the Linear Pottery farmers built long timber houses on the fertile loess soils. The other followed the Mediterranean coast to Italy, southern France and Iberia, and from there, eventually, to Britain. Greece c. 6500 BCE low Central Europe (LBK) c. 5500 BCE about 3% Southern France c. 5400 BCE about 31% Iberia after 5500 BCE about 13% Britain c. 4000 BCE small In much of western Europe the newcomers almost entirely replaced the earlier hunter-gatherer population, though the two mixed to different degrees along the way. Farming spread with migrating farmers elsewhere too, later than this chapter: Bantu-speaking farmers across much of Africa, and Austronesian-speaking farmers from Taiwan out into the Pacific.

t: Copper, horses and the eve of cities
x: In the last two thousand years before writing, people learned to smelt metal, buried their chiefs in gold, and put wheels under carts. Then, in southern Mesopotamia, the first city rose. People had hammered native copper for thousands of years. Smelting it from ore was new: the earliest securely dated evidence comes from Belovode in Serbia, about 5000 BCE. At Varna on the Black Sea, about 4500 BCE, a few graves held most of some 3,000 gold objects, the oldest worked-gold treasure known, and a sign that some people now held far more than others. Ötzi, the 'Iceman', died high in the Alps around 3250 BCE carrying a copper-bladed axe, a bow and a flint dagger; an arrow in his shoulder probably killed him. His genome shows he descended mainly from Anatolian farmers, with no ancestry from the steppe. Wheels appear around 3500 BCE; where they were invented is uncertain. People at Botai in Kazakhstan relied heavily on horses about 3500 BCE and may have tamed them, but those horses were not the ancestors of today's: modern domestic horses spread only after about 2200 BCE. On the steppe, the Yamnaya herders appeared about 3300 BCE, and their descendants changed the ancestry of most of Europe within a thousand years. They may have spread the Indo-European languages; where those languages began is still argued. Copper smelted from ore Belovode, Serbia c. 5000 BCE Gold treasure Varna, Bulgaria c. 4500 BCE Wheel uncertain; oldest surviving in Slovenia c. 3500 BCE Ötzi Ötztal Alps c. 3250 BCE First city Uruk, Mesopotamia c. 3200 BCE Meanwhile, on the floodplain of southern Mesopotamia, Uruk was growing into the largest settlement in the region, perhaps in the world. There, around 3200 BCE, someone began to keep accounts on clay. History, in the narrow sense, was about to begin. Chapter 3 begins here, at Uruk.

s: the first cities, between two rivers
x: Mesopotamia means 'between the rivers'. On the flat, dry plain of the Tigris and Euphrates, in what is now Iraq, people built the first cities, wrote the first texts and founded the first empire. It was an unlikely place for it. In the south it hardly rains, usually less than 200 mm a year, so nothing grows without water brought from the rivers. There was no stone worth building with, no timber and no metal: only mud, reeds, bitumen and date palms. Everything else had to be traded for. But the soil was rich and the rivers rose every spring. In the 4th millennium BCE the Gulf reached far further inland than today, and the cities stood beside freshwater marshes. A 2025 study argues that tides once pushed river water into the fields twice a day, and that when this ended people turned to great canals. Around Eridu, a 2025 survey traced more than 200 primary and secondary canals and thousands of smaller ones. rain usually under 200 mm a year water from the Tigris and Euphrates, by canal staple crops barley, dates lacked stone, timber, metal building material mud brick, reeds, bitumen Irrigation had a cost. Water evaporating from the fields leaves salt behind, and over centuries Sumerian farmers grew less wheat and more salt-tolerant barley; how much salt hurt their harvests is debated. The map on the right shows the cities of this chapter. Some are famous, such as Uruk, Ur and Babylon; one, Akkad, the capital of the first empire, has never been found. This chapter is Chapter 1.4 seen up close: from the first city (3.1) and the invention of writing (3.2) to Hammurabi's Babylon (3.8), about 3500 to 1600 BCE.

Around 3200 BCE, Uruk was the largest settlement in its world, perhaps anywhere: a city of canals, temples and workshops, many times larger than any town around it. In the late 4th millennium BCE Uruk covered about 250 hectares; the next-largest town in its region covered about 15. By about 3000 BCE a wall about 11 km long enclosed some 5 km², home perhaps to 40,000 people, though that number is an estimate built on assumptions. Magnetic surveys have mapped a canal about 10 metres wide running through the city, with branches and a harbour. At its heart stood the temple precinct of Eanna, the house of Inanna, goddess of love and war, and the district of An, the sky god. The Warka Vase shows the order of this world in bands: water and plants, then flocks, then naked men carrying produce, and at the top the goddess receiving a ruler. That ruler, a bearded man in a net skirt, appears on many works of the period; scholars call him the 'priest-king', without knowing what he was called. Uruk ran on organised labour. Hundreds of thousands of crude, mass-produced bowls with bevelled rims have been found; they have long been read as measures for workers' rations, though some held stews. And from about 3400 BCE, Uruk-style towns appeared far up the Euphrates, in Syria and Turkey. Whether these were colonies or trading communities living among local people is debated. Uruk period c. 4000-3100 BCE Jemdet Nasr period c. 3100-2900 BCE Early Dynastic period c. 2900-2350 BCE Later Mesopotamians remembered Uruk as the city of Gilgamesh, who was said to have built its wall. We meet him again on page 3.10.

Some of the earliest known writing comes from Uruk, where it kept track of grain, beer, animals and workers. Over a thousand years it became a full script that could record any word in two languages. Before writing, people counted goods with small clay tokens; Denise Schmandt-Besserat argued that writing grew directly out of them. Many scholars accept that tokens were used for counting but doubt the detailed link between token shapes and written signs. The earliest tablets, from about 3300-3000 BCE, are overwhelmingly accounts: of about 4,900 tablets of the Uruk III and Jemdet Nasr phases (about 3100-3000 BCE), some 85 percent record goods, rations and labour, and most of the rest are lists of words used to train scribes. The signs began as pictures drawn in clay, and the system used well over a thousand of them, though a couple of hundred did most of the work. Two changes made it a true script. Scribes stopped drawing and began pressing a reed stylus into the clay, making wedge-shaped marks: cuneiform, from the Latin for 'wedge'. And they began using signs for their sounds rather than their meanings, the rebus principle: the sign for 'arrow', pronounced ti, could also write ti, 'life'. Once signs could stand for syllables, they could spell names and grammar, and later write Akkadian, a language unrelated to Sumerian. used for accounts, word lists letters, laws, literature, science signs pictures drawn in clay wedges pressed with a reed reads objects and numbers words and syllables languages Sumerian (probably) Sumerian, Akkadian and others Scribes trained for years, copying Sumerian even after it had died as a spoken language, much as Latin was copied in medieval Europe. The script was forgotten for nearly two thousand years and deciphered in the 19th century; in 1857 four scholars translated the same text independently to prove it could really be read. About half a million tablets are known, most still unpublished, and since 2023 machine-learning tools have begun to help read them.

s: every city belonged to a god
x: Sumerians believed each city was the household of a god, and that people had been made to do the gods' work. The temple was the god's house, and also one of the largest employers in the land. Each city had its divine owner: An, the sky, and Inanna, goddess of love and war, at Uruk; Enki, god of fresh water and wisdom, at Eridu; Nanna, the moon, at Ur. An was formally the father of the gods, but in practice the most powerful was Enlil, whose temple at Nippur made that city the religious centre of Sumer: it was Enlil who decreed fates and granted kingship. Temples were economic as well as religious centres. They owned fields, herds and workshops and fed hundreds of workers; scholars once thought they owned almost all the land. Texts now show temple estates alongside land held by kings, nobles and families. An the sky; father of the gods Uruk Enlil air; decrees fates, grants kingship Nippur Enki fresh water, wisdom, crafts Eridu Inanna love and war; the planet Venus Uruk Nanna the moon Ur The most visible temples stood on ziggurats, stepped platforms of mud brick. The ziggurat of Ur, built by King Ur-Nammu about 2100 BCE, rose on a base about 64 by 46 metres. From Sargon's time a king's daughter served as high priestess of the moon god there; the first was Enheduanna (page 3.6). The myths explain why. In 'Enki and Ninmah', the gods tire of digging canals, and Enki has a creature made from clay, shaped by his mother Namma and the birth goddesses, to carry their baskets for them. Death offered little comfort: the dead lived in a dim underworld, drinking muddy water, and fared best if their descendants kept bringing offerings. Compare Genesis 2, where God forms the first man from the earth and puts him in the garden 'to till it and keep it'. Page 3.10 compares Mesopotamian and biblical flood stories.

s: the Early Dynastic period, c. 2900 to 2350 BCE
x: For five centuries Sumer was a land of rival cities, each with its own god, ruler and army, fighting over water and farmland. Historians call this the Early Dynastic period. Its best-documented quarrel ran for generations between Lagash and its neighbour Umma over a strip of fertile border land. Mesilim, king of Kish, once marked the boundary between them, and 'king of Kish' became a title meaning overlord of the whole land. About 2450 BCE, Eannatum of Lagash defeated Umma and celebrated with the Stele of the Vultures, which shows his soldiers marching in a tight phalanx over the bodies of the enemy, and vultures carrying off heads. A later ruler of Lagash, Uruinimgina, proclaimed that he had freed the people from greedy officials and heavy taxes, often called the first reform in history; whether it was reform or propaganda is debated. Alulim (before the flood) Eridu 28,800 years Etana Kish 1,500 years Gilgamesh Uruk 126 years Sargon Akkad 56 years Later scribes told this history differently. The Sumerian King List says that kingship 'descended from heaven' to Eridu, that eight kings ruled for 241,200 years before a great flood, and that afterwards kingship passed from city to city, one at a time. In fact many of its dynasties ruled at the same time; the list was a political document, written to show that there had always been one rightful king. Rival cities made the land rich in temples and quarrels but weak against an outsider. In the 24th century BCE, one ruler conquered them all (page 3.6).

s: gold, music and death, c. 2600-2400 BCE
x: In the 1920s, digging at Ur, Leonard Woolley found graves full of gold and lapis lazuli, and pits filled with the bodies of attendants who had died with their rulers. Woolley excavated Ur from 1922 to 1934. Among about 1,800 graves he found 16 he called 'royal tombs', built of stone, crowded with bodies and furnished with treasure; the richest date to about 2600-2500 BCE. In one, never robbed, lay Puabi, wearing a headdress of gold leaves, lapis and carnelian; her seal calls her 'queen' and names no husband. The tombs held music and display: lyres with bulls' heads of gold and lapis lazuli, and the Standard of Ur, a box inlaid with scenes of war on one side and a banquet on the other, whose purpose is still unknown. And they held the dead who went with their rulers. The 'Great Death Pit' contained 74 attendants, many adorned with gold and lapis. Woolley imagined them drinking poison and lying down peacefully. CT scans in 2009 told a different story for the two skulls examined: each had been struck a fatal blow to the head. Further study found the bodies had then been heated and treated with mercury to preserve them during long rites. how the attendants died poison, willingly blows to the head (two skulls) what happened next buried at once bodies heated and preserved Why rulers took people with them to death is debated. Some see loyalty and belief; others see public violence staged by rulers trying to impose their power.

About 2334 BCE a man who called himself Sargon, 'the true king', conquered the city-states of Sumer and much beyond. His dynasty ruled what is usually called the first empire, from a capital that has never been found. Sargon came from the north, from Kish. He defeated Lugalzagesi of Uruk and brought him in a neck-stock to Nippur, and claimed that Enlil had given him the land 'from the Upper Sea to the Lower Sea', from the Mediterranean to the Gulf. He ruled in Akkadian, a Semitic language, which now became a language of government written in cuneiform. Later generations told stories about him. A legend copied in the 7th century BCE says his mother set him adrift on the river in a reed basket sealed with bitumen, and that a water-drawer pulled him out and raised him. Readers of Exodus will recognise the motif. Sargon made his daughter Enheduanna high priestess of the moon god at Ur. Hymns to Inanna and 42 temple hymns are credited to her, which would make her the first author known by name, though whether she wrote them is debated. His grandson Naram-Sin went further: he called himself 'god of Akkad' and 'king of the four quarters' of the world, and had himself carved in a god's horned helmet. Tablets found at Girsu in 2024 show the empire's officials at work in a conquered city. Sargon c. 2334-2279 Naram-Sin c. 2254-2218 end of the dynasty c. 2154 The empire collapsed within two centuries. A later poem blames Naram-Sin's sacrilege and the Gutians, mountain people 'with canine instincts'. Some scientists blame a sudden drought about 2200 BCE; others see mostly a political crisis.

After the Akkadians, the kings of Ur built the most bureaucratic state the ancient world had seen. They left behind more than 100,000 tablets counting sheep, barley and days of labour. The Third Dynasty of Ur ruled the south for about a century under five kings. Its founder, Ur-Nammu, built the great ziggurat of Ur (3.3), and the oldest surviving law collection bears his name. Unlike Hammurabi's later laws, it punished injuries with fines in silver: knocking out a man's eye cost half a mina of silver. His son Shulgi reigned for nearly fifty years, was worshipped as a god in his lifetime, and is credited with standard weights and measures, a state calendar and roads with way-stations. In a hymn he boasts of running from Nippur to Ur and back in a day. The state counted everything. At Puzrish-Dagan near Nippur, a central office recorded the animals flowing to the gods and the court; more than 13,500 of its tablets survive, and recent study suggests most of the animals they record never physically passed through it. Workers were paid monthly in barley, with wool once a year. Over 100,000 Ur III administrative tablets are now catalogued, some 70,000 of them fully published. A 2025 study argues that some workers formed a serf-like class, free in law but bound to year-round labour. man about 60 woman about 30-40 child about 10-20 It ended suddenly. Famine and revolt weakened Ur, and about 2004 BCE an army from Elam sacked the city and took its last king captive. Poets wrote laments in which the gods themselves abandon their cities.

Hammurabi turned Babylon from one city among many into the capital of Mesopotamia. His laws, carved on a black stone pillar, are the most famous text of the ancient Near East, and one of the most misunderstood. Hammurabi reigned about 1792-1750 BCE. Late in his reign he conquered Larsa, turned on his former ally Mari, and destroyed Eshnunna, uniting southern and central Mesopotamia under Babylon. His letters show him managing canals, taxes and lawsuits in person. His laws survive on a stele 2.25 metres tall, with the sun god Shamash, god of justice, before the king at the top. It was found at Susa in Iran in 1901-02, where an Elamite king had carried it as plunder. It holds about 282 laws, framed by a prologue declaring that the gods called Hammurabi 'so that the strong should not harm the weak'. The laws divide people into free men, commoners and slaves. 'An eye for an eye' applied only between equals: if a man put out the eye of another free man, his own eye was put out, but blinding a commoner cost a fine in silver, and blinding a slave half the slave's price. free man (awilum) the offender's eye is put out commoner (mushkenum) one mina of silver another man's slave half the slave's value Were these laws actually used? Surviving court records almost never cite them. Many scholars now read the stele as a monument to a just king and as a work of scribal learning, copied in schools for more than a thousand years. Hammurabi's dynasty lasted until 1595 BCE, when the Hittite king Mursili I raided Babylon; Kassite kings then ruled for some 400 years. Compare Exodus 21:23-25, 'eye for eye, tooth for tooth'. The biblical laws share the principle, and also include protections for slaves (Exodus 21:26-27).

Most Mesopotamians were farmers, herders and workers paid in grain. Their lives survive in an unusual way: in contracts, loans, letters and ration lists. Barley was everything: bread, gruel and beer, the everyday drink. People also ate dates, onions, garlic, leeks, fish and mutton. Workers for the state were paid in barley; under the kings of Ur a working man typically received about 60 litres a month, a woman 30-40. Value was measured in silver, weighed on a balance rather than coined: a shekel was about 8 grams, and sixty made a mina. The Laws of Eshnunna price one shekel of silver at 300 litres of barley. Loans were common, at 20 percent for silver and 33⅓ for barley, and debt was a constant danger: a man could sell his wife or children into service to pay what he owed. From time to time kings cancelled debts and freed debt slaves by royal edict. 1 shekel of silver (c. 8 g) 300 sila (about 300 litres) of barley interest on silver 20% a year interest on barley 33⅓% a man's monthly ration (Ur III) about 60 sila of barley Trade reached far. At Kanesh in central Anatolia, merchants from Ashur left more than 23,000 tablets: they brought tin and textiles by donkey caravan and sent silver and gold home. Their wives in Ashur wove the textiles, invested and lent money, and wrote to their husbands on business. At Sippar, women dedicated to the sun god lived in a cloister and managed land and loans in their own names. Slavery existed, through debt and war, but historians now stress the many statuses between slave and free.

The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the oldest great works of literature to survive: the story of a king who loses his friend and goes to the ends of the earth in search of life without death. On its eleventh tablet is a flood story strikingly like Noah's. Gilgamesh may have been a real king of Uruk around 2700 BCE, but nothing from his lifetime survives. The epic grew over a thousand years: Sumerian poems about him, probably composed for the kings of Ur; an Akkadian epic of the 18th century BCE; and a standard version credited to the scholar Sîn-lēqi-unninni late in the 2nd millennium BCE. Its fullest copy comes from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh, of the 7th century BCE. In Tablet XI, Gilgamesh meets Utnapishtim, the one man who survived the flood. The god Ea warned him; he built a great boat, sealed it with pitch, and took his family and animals aboard. When the waters fell he sent out birds, and when one did not return he offered a sacrifice, and the gods gathered 'like flies' to its smell. In 1872 George Smith of the British Museum read this tablet and announced a Babylonian flood story older than any copy of Genesis; it was a sensation. An older poem, Atrahasis, tells the same flood at greater length. There the gods send it because humans have become too noisy, and afterwards they limit human numbers. Genesis gives a moral reason, human violence and wickedness, and ends with God's blessing, 'be fruitful and multiply'. How are the stories related? The shared details are many, down to the word for pitch. Most biblical scholars think the Genesis account draws in some way on Mesopotamian tradition, while differing over how and when; others see common models rather than borrowing. Either way, Genesis tells the story around one God and a moral cause. A tablet published in 2014 even describes Atrahasis's ark as a giant round coracle. Readers of the Hebrew Bible will meet Mesopotamia again in Chapter 7: the Assyrian kings of 2 Kings, Nebuchadnezzar, and the exile in Babylon.

Every time you read a clock you use Babylonian mathematics. Mesopotamian scribes counted in sixties, solved problems in geometry, and kept the longest series of astronomical records of the ancient world. The Babylonians counted in base 60, inherited from the Sumerians; nobody knows why, though 60 can be divided evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30. They wrote numbers by place value, as we do, so the same sign could mean 1, 60 or 3,600 depending on its position. Through Greek astronomers, who divided each degree into 60 parts and each part into 60 again, their system gave us minutes and seconds. Their mathematics was practical and surprisingly advanced. A school tablet gives the square root of 2 correct to five decimal places, an error of less than one part in a million. Plimpton 322, of about 1800 BCE, lists 15 rows of numbers describing right triangles, more than a thousand years before Pythagoras. In 2017 it was called the oldest trigonometric table; most historians of mathematics think it was a teacher's aid. YBC 7289 c. 1800-1600 BCE √2 to five decimal places Plimpton 322 c. 1800 BCE numbers for right triangles Venus tablet observations c. 1640 BCE a key to dating Astronomical Diaries 652-61 BCE monthly sky, weather and prices Jupiter tablets c. 350-50 BCE area under a graph The sky was read for omens: tablets published in 2024 predict a king's death from eclipses of the moon. Observations of Venus made under King Ammi-saduqa survive and are still used, with difficulty, to date the period. From 652 BCE astronomers kept monthly diaries of the moon and planets, with weather, prices and news, for six centuries. They developed the twelve-sign zodiac in the 5th century BCE, and late tablets compute Jupiter's motion from the area under a graph, a method Europeans rediscovered only in the 14th century CE.

s: buried cities, a lost script and an uncertain calendar
x: For two thousand years Mesopotamia was known mostly from the Bible and Greek writers. In the 19th century its cities, its libraries and its script came back to light, and with them a problem: exactly when everything happened. In the 1840s, Paul-Émile Botta for France and Austen Henry Layard for Britain dug into the mounds of northern Iraq and found the palaces of the Assyrian kings, with their great stone reliefs. At Nineveh, Layard and Hormuzd Rassam found the library of King Ashurbanipal, over 30,000 tablets and fragments, many hardened by the fire that destroyed the city in 612 BCE. Among them, George Smith would find the flood story (3.10). Reading the tablets took decades. The key was a cliff inscription of the Persian king Darius I at Bisotun in Iran, carved in three languages, which Henry Rawlinson copied at great risk. By the 1850s scholars could read Akkadian, and in 1857 four of them translated the same text independently to prove it (3.2). Even now, dates before about 1500 BCE are uncertain. Records give the order of kings and the length of reigns, but tying them to our calendar depends on astronomy and other evidence. The main chronologies put Hammurabi's accession anywhere from 1848 to 1728 BCE. Tree rings and radiocarbon have narrowed the choice to the 'Middle Chronology' used in this book or a date about eight years later. High 1848 BCE 1651 BCE Middle (used here) 1792 BCE 1595 BCE Low Middle 1784 BCE 1587 BCE Low 1728 BCE 1531 BCE The rediscovery continues, and so does the loss. After 2003 looters dug over more of southern Iraq's ancient sites than archaeologists ever had, and in 2015 extremists blew up much of the palace at Nimrud. The later Assyrian and Babylonian empires, the exile of the Jews to Babylon and the conquest of Babylon by Cyrus of Persia in 539 BCE come in Chapter 7.

Egypt is a long green ribbon in a desert. The Nile watered it, fed it, carried its trade and set its calendar, and for three thousand years it held one of the most stable civilizations in history. Herodotus, visiting in the 5th century BCE, wrote that Egypt was land 'acquired by the Egyptians, given them by the river', built up from its mud: the origin of 'the gift of the Nile'. The Nile is about 6,650 km long, and almost none of Egypt's water fell on Egypt. Each summer, heavy rains on the Ethiopian highlands swelled the Blue Nile and the Atbara, and the flood reached Aswan in July and peaked near Cairo in October. The flood laid down fresh black silt. Egyptians called their country Kemet, 'the black land', and the desert beyond it Deshret, 'the red land'. Everything depended on the height of the water: a Roman writer recorded that a low flood meant famine and a high one 'unbounded transports of joy'. rain almost none water the Nile flood, July-October the flood's source summer rain in Ethiopia (c. 90%) farmland a strip along the river, and the Delta population perhaps 1-3 million, some say up to 5 (estimates differ) Egypt had two halves: Upper Egypt, the narrow valley in the south, and Lower Egypt, the broad Delta in the north. They had distinct cultures before they were united, and the king remained 'Lord of the Two Lands'. How many people lived there is uncertain: one estimate rises from under a million at unification to about three million under Ramesses II. Compare Mesopotamia (3.0): two rivers, irrigation, little rain. But the Nile flood came at the right time of year for crops and was far more predictable than the Tigris and Euphrates.

Before there were pharaohs there were chiefs, cemeteries and rival centres along the Nile. Within a few centuries they became a single kingdom, with writing, a capital and a king who was buried with his servants. The Naqada culture of Upper Egypt, from about 4000 to 3000 BCE, saw growing towns, rich graves and trade. Radiocarbon dates show the Egyptian state formed quickly: the first king of the 1st Dynasty, Aha, came to the throne about 3100 BCE. Writing appeared at about the same time as in Mesopotamia. In a tomb at Abydos of about 3200 BCE, archaeologists found small bone and ivory labels with signs recording goods and places. On the Narmer Palette, about 3100 BCE, the king wears the white crown of the south on one side, striking down an enemy, and the red crown of the north on the other. Whether it records an actual conquest or a statement of royal power is debated; unification probably took several reigns. Later Egyptians credited it to a king called Menes, whose identity is unknown. Naqada I c. 4000-3500 Naqada II c. 3500-3200 Naqada III ('Dynasty 0') c. 3200-3000 Early Dynastic (Dynasties 1-2) c. 3000-2686 The first kings were buried at Abydos, ringed by the graves of servants. A 2026 study found that many of their skulls bear injuries from the time of death: they were killed to serve the king in the afterlife. The practice seems to have ended with the 1st Dynasty. In 2025 geneticists published the first complete genome from an ancient Egyptian, a man buried around the start of the pyramid age: mostly North African ancestry, with about a fifth from the eastern Fertile Crescent. Compare the royal tombs of Ur (3.5), where attendants died with their rulers some four centuries later.

s: kingship and the order of the world
x: The Egyptian king stood between the gods and humanity. His task was to keep maat, the right order of the universe, against the chaos that always threatened it. Egyptians did not call their king 'pharaoh' until the New Kingdom. The word comes from per-aa, 'great house', the palace, much as people today say 'the White House'. The king had five official names, and was identified in life with Horus, the falcon god of kingship, and in death with Osiris. His central duty was maat: the order of the universe established at creation, and also truth and justice among people. By building temples, making offerings, judging fairly and defeating Egypt's enemies, he held back chaos. How divine was he? Egyptians spoke of him as a god and depicted him among the gods, but scholars debate how literally they meant it: one influential view sees the king as the manifestation of Horus in the palace, a role that made a mortal man more than human while he held it. After about thirty years on the throne, and then every few years, a king might hold a Sed festival to renew his powers. Compare Naram-Sin and Shulgi in Mesopotamia (3.6, 3.7), who claimed divinity in their lifetimes, and the Hebrew Bible's very different picture of kingship (5.9).

In less than a century, Egyptian kings went from the first stone building to the largest stone structure on Earth. The pyramids are monuments to an idea of kingship, and to a state that could organise labour on an enormous scale. Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara, about 2650 BCE, is the first pyramid and the first large stone building in Egypt; his official Imhotep is remembered as its architect. Sneferu built three pyramids, learning as he went: at Dahshur the Bent Pyramid changes angle halfway up, and the Red Pyramid became the first true pyramid completed. His son Khufu built the Great Pyramid at Giza, about 146 metres high, its sides over 230 metres long and almost perfectly equal, made of an estimated 2.3 million blocks. It remained the tallest structure people had built for more than three thousand years. Khufu's son Khafre, who followed the short reign of Djedefre, added a second pyramid and, probably, the Great Sphinx. Who built them? Herodotus said Khufu forced 100,000 Egyptians at a time to labour on it. Archaeology tells a different story: a town of workers south of the Sphinx with bakeries, grain stores and barracks, and a logbook kept by an official named Merer, who shipped limestone by boat from the quarries at Tura to Giza. The workers were not slaves but organised, fed and rotated, though their labour was hardly voluntary. Step Pyramid, Saqqara Djoser about 61 m Bent Pyramid, Dahshur Sneferu about 101 m Great Pyramid, Giza Khufu about 146 m Mysteries remain. How the blocks were raised is still argued. A 2024 study mapped a lost branch of the Nile that may have brought boats close to the pyramid fields, and in 2023 cosmic-ray imaging found a hidden corridor inside the Great Pyramid.

s: Osiris, mummies and the weighing of the heart
x: Egyptians invested more in death than almost any people in history. Their religion promised that the dead, properly prepared and judged worthy, could live for ever. Egypt had hundreds of gods, many linked with animals: Horus with the falcon, Hathor with the cow, Thoth with the ibis, Amun with the ram. Priests at Heliopolis taught that from the creator Atum came eight further gods, among them Osiris, Isis and Seth. Osiris was murdered by his brother Seth, restored by his wife Isis and became king of the dead; but no full Egyptian telling survives, and the fullest version is by the Greek writer Plutarch, about 120 CE. A person had several spiritual parts, including the ka, a life-force that received food offerings, and the ba, shown as a bird with a human head that could leave the tomb by day. Both needed the body, so it was preserved. Embalming took about 70 days, and its quality depended on what a family could afford. Millions of animals were mummified too, as offerings to gods; many wrappings, scans show, contain no animal at all. Pyramid Texts royal pyramids Unas, c. 2350 BCE Coffin Texts coffins of officials First Intermediate Period and Middle Kingdom Book of the Dead papyrus scrolls New Kingdom The texts that guided the dead changed over time. In the Book of the Dead, the dead person declares before the gods the sins they have not committed, and their heart is weighed against the feather of Maat; a heavy heart is devoured. Scholars once thought the afterlife began as a privilege of kings and was 'democratised' after the Old Kingdom; many now argue that elites already hoped for it, and what changed was the practice of writing it down. Compare the bleak Mesopotamian underworld (3.3), where the dead drank muddy water whoever they had been.

s: hieroglyphs, and how they were read again
x: Egyptian writing was beautiful, complex and, for most of history, the possession of a tiny elite. For fourteen centuries after its last use no one could read it, until the Rosetta Stone. Hieroglyphs combined three kinds of sign: signs for sounds, signs for whole words, and 'determinatives', silent signs that showed what kind of thing a word meant. Vowels were not written. Scribes of the Old Kingdom used over a thousand signs, those of the Middle Kingdom about 750, and Ptolemaic priests thousands. Hieroglyphs were for monuments. For daily use scribes wrote hieratic, a flowing hand, and from about 700 BCE demotic, a still faster script. Writing was rare: perhaps 1 percent of Egyptians could read in the third millennium BCE, though some communities did far better. A Middle Kingdom school text, the 'Satire of the Trades', urged boys to become scribes and escape the miseries of every other job. hieroglyphic monuments, sacred texts c. 3200 BCE-394 CE hieratic handwriting on papyrus from c. 3200-3000 BCE demotic everyday documents c. 700 BCE-5th century CE Coptic Greek letters plus 7 signs from the 2nd century CE In 1799 French soldiers found a stone at Rosetta carrying a decree of 196 BCE in hieroglyphic, demotic and Greek: three scripts, two languages. Thomas Young showed that hieroglyphs could spell foreign royal names by sound; in 1822 Jean-François Champollion showed how sound-signs and word-signs worked together, and the script could be read again. Compare the decipherment of cuneiform (3.2, 3.12), which also depended on a trilingual inscription, at Bisotun.

s: the First Intermediate Period and the Middle Kingdom
x: After the pyramid age, Egypt fell apart into rival kingdoms for about a century. When it was reunited, its rulers and writers looked back on the collapse as a warning, and produced the classics of Egyptian literature. The Old Kingdom ended after the unusually long reign of Pepi II; contemporary texts record his 62nd and 65th years. In the First Intermediate Period, rival kings ruled from Herakleopolis in the north and Thebes in the south. Was drought to blame? Barbara Bell argued in 1971 that the Nile floods failed; Nadine Moeller has argued that the famine texts in tombs are largely boasts of good governance, and that the climate dried gradually. Today she sees drought as one factor among several. A poem, the 'Admonitions of Ipuwer', describes Egypt turned upside down: the poor grow rich, the river is blood. It was long read as an eyewitness account of the collapse, and some popular writers read it as a record of the Exodus plagues. Most Egyptologists now date it later and read it as literature. Mentuhotep II of Thebes, king from about 2055 BCE, reunited Egypt during his long reign. The Middle Kingdom's kings developed the Faiyum basin, and Senusret III fixed the southern border at Semna, guarded by mud-brick fortresses against Kush. Old Kingdom 2686-2160 Memphis First Intermediate 2160-2055 Herakleopolis and Thebes Middle Kingdom 2055-1650 Thebes, then Itjtawy near the Faiyum The Middle Kingdom's language, Middle Egyptian, became the classical tongue that scribes copied for the rest of Egyptian history. Its literature includes the Story of Sinuhe, an official who flees to Canaan and longs to be buried in Egypt, and the Eloquent Peasant, who demands justice from officials.

t: The Hyksos and the New Kingdom
s: from foreign rule to empire, c. 1650-1350 BCE
x: For about a century, kings of Levantine origin ruled northern Egypt. When the Thebans drove them out, Egypt built an empire that reached from Syria to the heart of Sudan. The Hyksos, 'rulers of foreign lands', governed from Avaris in the eastern Delta. People from the Levant had lived there for generations, many in royal service, and under the Hyksos the town grew to about 250 hectares. A 2020 study of tooth enamel found that many of its people had grown up outside Egypt before the Hyksos took power, suggesting they rose from within rather than invading. The period is usually credited with bringing the horse and chariot to Egypt. Ahmose of Thebes, king from about 1550 BCE, took Avaris and drove the Hyksos out, beginning the New Kingdom. His successors turned outward. In his 23rd year Thutmose III defeated a coalition of Canaanite and Syrian rulers at Megiddo after leading his army through a narrow pass; his annals at Karnak tell the story in detail. At its height the empire reached beyond the Euphrates and south past the Fourth Cataract. Ahmose c. 1550-1525 expelled the Hyksos Thutmose I c. 1504-1492 reached the Euphrates and Kurgus Hatshepsut c. 1473-1458 Punt; Deir el-Bahri (4.8) Thutmose III c. 1479-1425 Megiddo; widest empire Much later, the Egyptian priest Manetho, quoted by the Jewish historian Josephus, claimed that the expelled Hyksos founded Jerusalem, and Josephus called them 'our forefathers'. Most scholars do not equate the two, though some think distant memories of these movements may echo in the Exodus story.

s: a woman king and a religious revolution
x: Two rulers of the 18th Dynasty broke the rules in different ways: Hatshepsut ruled as king, and Akhenaten tried to replace Egypt's gods with one. Hatshepsut, widow of Thutmose II, first acted for her young stepson Thutmose III and then took the full titles of a king, ruling from about 1473 to 1458 BCE. She built the terraced temple at Deir el-Bahri. Its walls show an expedition to the land of Punt bringing back myrrh trees, incense, gold and ebony; Punt probably lay in the region of Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia. Thutmose III later had her images removed, but some twenty years after her death, which makes simple revenge unlikely. About a century later Amenhotep IV renamed himself Akhenaten, made the Aten, the disk of the sun, the centre of worship, closed the temples of other gods, and built a new capital at Amarna. Whether this was monotheism is debated: the king and queen Nefertiti shared in the cult as the Aten's only intermediaries. His Great Hymn to the Aten praises the sun as creator of all life, and it has striking parallels with Psalm 104 (compare the plate on the right). Some scholars think the psalmist knew the hymn; others see a shared tradition of praise. Clay tablets found at Amarna, mostly letters in Akkadian, record Egypt's dealings with great kings and with vassal rulers in Canaan. The ruler of Jerusalem complained of raids by the Habiru, outlaws and mercenaries; whether the name is linked to 'Hebrew' is debated. After Akhenaten's death the court left Amarna, and under Tutankhamun the old gods returned.

t: Ramesses, Kadesh and the Exodus question
x: Ramesses II ruled for 66 years, built on a colossal scale and fought the Hittites to a standstill. His son's reign gives the earliest secure mention of Israel, and his own is often linked with the Exodus. Ramesses II reigned from 1279 to 1213 BCE. He built a new capital in the eastern Delta, Pi-Ramesses, and covered Egypt with temples. Around 1274 BCE he marched north and met the Hittite king Muwatalli II at Kadesh in Syria. His temples proclaim a great victory; in fact the Hittites kept Kadesh, and historians judge the battle a draw. About fifteen years later Ramesses and the Hittite king Hattusili III made a treaty of peace and alliance, preserved in both Egyptian and Akkadian. It is often called the first peace treaty in history; older ones are known. About 1208 BCE, his son Merneptah set up a stele boasting of victories in Canaan, naming places such as Ashkelon and Gezer, and declaring: 'Israel is wasted, bare of seed.' Israel is written with the sign for a people, not a city or land. It is generally regarded as the earliest secure mention of Israel outside the Bible. What about the Exodus? No Egyptian text mentions it, or Israelites in Egypt. Scholars read that silence very differently. Some argue the Egyptian background of the story is authentic; some that a smaller group, perhaps the Levites, came out of Egypt; others that the story was composed much later. Even the places named are disputed: one candidate for Pithom, Tell el-Maskhuta, was unoccupied from about 1500 BCE until it was refounded about 600 BCE, while Raamses (Exodus 1:11) matches Ramesses II's capital Pi-Ramesses, occupied in the 13th century. Those who accept a historical Exodus disagree on its date. early date c. 1446 BCE (1 Kings 6:1) Bryant Wood late date 13th century, under Ramesses II many scholars who accept a historical core smaller exodus a group such as the Levites Richard Elliott Friedman later composition no mass departure Finkelstein and Silberman Egypt's past keeps resurfacing: Tutankhamun's tomb was found in 1922, the tomb of Thutmose II in 2025, and in November 2025 the Grand Egyptian Museum opened near Giza.

Most Egyptians were farmers whose year followed the river. The best window on ordinary lives, though, is a village of craftsmen who built the royal tombs and wrote down almost everything. The year had three seasons of four months each, Akhet, Peret and Shemu, plus five extra days at the end. Wages were paid in kind: grain, bread and beer, scaled by rank. Deir el-Medina, near the Valley of the Kings, was home to the workmen who cut and painted the royal tombs. They left tens of thousands of notes on potsherds and flakes of limestone: letters, accounts, laundry lists, love poems and court records. In some periods most of the village men could read, against perhaps 1-2 percent of Egyptians as a whole, so the village was not typical. When their rations were late in year 29 of Ramesses III, about 1156 BCE, they put down their tools, sat behind a temple and shouted 'We are hungry': the first recorded strike. Egyptian women had unusual legal rights for the ancient world: they could own and sell property, make contracts, go to court and divorce. An elderly villager named Naunakhte made a will before a court of her neighbours and cut out the children who had not looked after her. year 3 seasons x 4 months x 30 days, + 5 days wages grain, bread and beer literacy perhaps 1-2%; most men at Deir el-Medina women could own property, sue and divorce medicine Edwin Smith and Ebers papyri Medicine mixed close observation with magic.
