The Edwin Smith Papyrus works through 48 injuries from head to foot, judging which to treat; the Ebers Papyrus lists about 700 remedies. Lives were short: at one Delta town, almost a third of those buried died by the age of six.

s: an African rival, and a Kushite dynasty
x: South of the First Cataract lay Nubia, home to kingdoms that traded with Egypt, fought it, were conquered by it and, in the 8th century BCE, conquered Egypt in turn. Kerma, in what is now Sudan, was the capital of the kingdom of Kush from about 2500 to 1500 BCE, a planned city of more than 30 hectares. The first excavator, George Reisner, took it for an Egyptian trading post; from 1977 Charles Bonnet's excavations showed it was the capital of a powerful African state. Its kings were buried under great earth mounds with rows of cattle skulls, and many people were sacrificed beside them. Egypt's Middle Kingdom built a chain of forts on the Nile to hold Kush back (4.6). In the New Kingdom, Egypt struck back. Thutmose I pushed beyond the Fourth Cataract and carved a boundary inscription at Kurgus; Nubian gold paid for much of Egypt's empire. Egyptian temples rose in Nubia, and the mountain of Gebel Barkal became a seat of Amun. Then the tables turned. About 728 BCE the Kushite king Piye marched north and conquered Egypt, founding the 25th Dynasty. Piye's son Taharqa (about 690-664 BCE), 'King Tirhakah of Cush' in 2 Kings 19:9 (the King James Version has 'Tirhakah king of Ethiopia'), backed the kingdoms of the Levant against Assyria. The Assyrians took Memphis in 671 and sacked Thebes in 664-663, and the Kushites withdrew south. Kerma kingdom c. 2500-1500 BCE Kerma under Egyptian rule c. 1500-1070 BCE (Egyptian viceroys) Napatan kingdom c. 900-270 BCE Napata 25th Dynasty in Egypt c. 747-656 BCE Napata and Memphis Meroitic kingdom c. 270 BCE-350 CE Meroë Kush endured for another thousand years at Napata and then Meroë, where its kings were buried under steep pyramids. Its heritage is at risk again: since 2023 the Sudan National Museum has been looted during the civil war.

s: Persians, Greeks, Romans, and how we date it all
x: Pharaonic Egypt lasted three thousand years, and it did not end with a single fall. Persians, Greeks and Romans ruled it in turn, its last pharaohs were Greek, and its language survives in a church liturgy today. After the Kushites, a native dynasty ruled from Sais (664-525 BCE) until the Persians conquered Egypt in 525 BCE. Alexander the Great took it in 332 BCE and founded Alexandria, and his general Ptolemy made himself king. For three centuries Greek-speaking Ptolemies ruled as pharaohs. They founded the Library of Alexandria and built the great lighthouse, whose blocks archaeologists are still raising from the harbour. The last, Cleopatra VII, was, Plutarch says, the only one of her line to learn Egyptian; at her death in 30 BCE Egypt became a Roman province. Hieroglyphs were carved for the last known time in 394 CE. The language lived on as Coptic, written in Greek letters, and is still used in the liturgy of the Coptic Church. How do we date all this? Egyptologists divide this history into kingdoms and intermediate periods (see the plate). To date them they combine king lists such as the Palermo Stone and the Turin papyrus, the history Manetho wrote in Greek for Ptolemy II, which gave us the 'dynasties', and records of the stars. In 2010 a radiocarbon study of 211 samples from dated objects broadly confirmed the conventional dates. Djoser 2667 BCE 2691-2625 BCE Mentuhotep II 2055 BCE 2064-2019 BCE Ahmose 1550 BCE 1570-1544 BCE Egypt's story runs on through this volume: the Persians in Chapter 7; Greeks, Romans and the first Christians in Chapter 8; the Christian empire and Islam in Chapter 10.

s: two river civilizations, one still unread
x: While Sumerians and Egyptians were building the first cities, a third urban civilization rose along the Indus. A thousand years later, a fourth took shape on the Yellow River. The first left writing nobody can read; the second, writing still in use today. This chapter takes them in turn. Pages 5.0 to 5.3 cover the Indus, or Harappan, civilization, named after Harappa, the first city found. Pages 5.4 to 5.10 cover early China, from Neolithic towns to the Zhou kings, and page 5.11 compares all four river civilizations. The Indus civilization was the most extensive of the early civilizations, spread across what is now Pakistan and north-west India, with several hundred known sites. Its roots lie in farming villages such as Mehrgarh, settled from about 6500 BCE. Its heartland had two river systems: the Indus, fed by Himalayan snow and the monsoon, and to the east the Ghaggar-Hakra, now mostly dry. A 2012 study found that the rivers there were fed by the monsoon rather than by glaciers, and when the Ghaggar-Hakra last carried Himalayan water is debated. The question matters because many cities stood along it. Ravi phase (first village) c. 3300-2800 Early Harappan 2800-2600 Mature Harappan (the cities) 2600-1900 Transitional 1900-1800 Late Harappan 1800 to before 1300 Compare the Tigris and Euphrates (3.0) and the Nile (4.0).

Indus cities were laid out on grids, built of standard-sized bricks, and served by drains in nearly every street. What they lack is just as striking: no building clearly a palace, no royal tomb, no image of a king. Harappa was excavated from 1921 and Mohenjo-daro from 1922, and in 1924 John Marshall announced to the world a civilization nobody had known existed. Mohenjo-daro covered about 240 hectares. A raised mound on the west, called the 'citadel', overlooked a lower town of right-angled streets with covered drains. It may have held 35,000 to 41,000 people, Harappa somewhat fewer. On the citadel stands the Great Bath, a brick tank sealed with bitumen, probably used for ritual washing. Other cities had their own character. Dholavira, in the salt flats of Kutch, stored water in large reservoirs. Rakhigarhi, in Haryana, may have been the largest of all. At Lothal in Gujarat a long brick basin has been read both as a dock and as a reservoir. No building in these cities has been clearly identified as a palace, and there are no royal tombs or monuments to rulers. Even the famous bust called the 'Priest-King' is named only by convention. Some archaeologists think power was shared among many groups; others think the elite simply did not display itself in the ways Sumerian and Egyptian rulers did. Compare the royal tombs of Ur (3.5) and the pyramids (4.3). In Mesopotamia and Egypt, power is written into the landscape; on the Indus, it is hard to see at all.

Indus merchants traded by sea with the Gulf and Mesopotamia, where texts call their land Meluhha. They stamped goods with small seals carrying a script that, after a century of attempts, nobody can read. Weights across the whole civilization followed one standard: small weights doubled from about 0.86 grams, larger ones went up by tens. Weights of the same standard turn up in Bahrain, ancient Dilmun. Mesopotamian texts speak of a distant land called Meluhha. Sargon of Akkad boasted that its ships moored at his capital, a seal names a man as an interpreter of Meluhhan, and there was a 'Meluhha village' in Akkad. Indus seals and beads have been found at Ur, and Indus objects in Oman, ancient Magan. Seals were carved in soft stone, usually with an animal, most often the one-horned 'unicorn', and a short line of signs. About 4,000 inscriptions are known, but they average only about five signs. With texts so short and no bilingual inscription, the script cannot be cracked by the methods that worked for Egyptian and Mesopotamian scripts. Is it writing? most say yes; some argue it is a non-linguistic symbol system [[c-is-writing]] Which language? Dravidian (Parpola), others proposed; none accepted [[c-dravidian]] Why unread? short texts, no bilingual [[c-no-bilingual]] The search goes on. In 2025 the state government of Tamil Nadu offered a million-dollar prize for a convincing decipherment. Compare the Rosetta Stone and the decipherment of hieroglyphs (4.5), and the decipherment of cuneiform (3.2). Both depended on long texts and bilinguals.

s: and what happened to their cities
x: Without readable texts, the Harappans' identity has to be pieced together from bones, genes and settlement patterns. The questions are scientific, but in India and Pakistan they are also political. In 2019 geneticists published the first and still the only genome from a Harappan city, from a burial at Rakhigarhi. It mixes ancestry related to ancient Iranians with that of South Asian hunter-gatherers, and has little or no ancestry from the Eurasian steppe. Its Iranian-related line separated before farming began, so the authors argue South Asians largely took up farming themselves. The same ancestry appears among migrants at sites in Iran and Turkmenistan, and is the largest source of ancestry in South Asians today. Steppe ancestry arrived later, about 2000-1500 BCE, and most specialists link it to the arrival of Indo-European languages, including the Sanskrit of the Rigveda. A rival view, that these languages spread out of India, has little support among specialists and is caught up in nationalist politics. The cities did not fall in a day. From about 1900 BCE they shrank, and people moved east into smaller villages and grew a wider range of crops. Climate is one likely cause: the monsoons weakened about 4,100 years ago, and a 2025 study found long river droughts in this period. An older theory, that invading Aryans massacred the people of Mohenjo-daro, has been abandoned. Rakhigarhi genome local and Iranian-related ancestry; no steppe Later South Asian genomes steppe ancestry arrives c. 2000-1500 BCE Settlement surveys gradual shift east, smaller sites Climate records weaker monsoons; long droughts Compare the steppe herders of 2.11, whose ancestry also spread into Europe, and the droughts around 2200 BCE in Mesopotamia (3.6) and Egypt (4.6).

Long before any dynasty, farmers along the Yellow River and the Yangzi built villages, then walled towns, then cities. Some of the largest lay far from the region later histories called the centre of China. Farming villages of the Yangshao culture, about 5000-3000 BCE, grew millet along the Yellow River and made painted pottery; Banpo near Xi'an is the best known. In the lower Yangzi, Liangzhu (about 3300-2300 BCE) was a walled city of some 300 hectares, with dams in the hills beyond that controlled flooding and water supply, one of the oldest large water-management systems in the world. Its elite were buried with jade discs and square jade tubes whose meaning is unknown. Some archaeologists call it East Asia's first state. In the north, the Longshan culture built rammed-earth walls and divined the future by cracking heated bones, a practice the Shang would make famous. Taosi in Shanxi grew to a walled town of nearly 3 km², with a platform that some interpret as a solar observatory. Shimao, on the loess plateau, was a stone-walled city of some 400 hectares with a terraced core about 70 metres high and pits of skulls at its gate. Genomes from Shimao published in 2025 show family lines traced through men, and that the victims at its gate were mostly men, not women as once thought. Banpo Wei valley (Xi'an) Yangshao culture painted pottery village Liangzhu lower Yangzi c. 3300-2300 dams, jade Taosi Shanxi c. 2300-1900 walled town; 'observatory' Shimao northern Shaanxi c. 2300-1800 stone walls, sacrifice These finds have changed how Chinese civilization's origins are told. The old story began in the Central Plains of the middle Yellow River; many archaeologists now see several regional centres, like 'stars in the sky', that later came together.

Chinese tradition says the first dynasty was the Xia, founded by Yu the Great after he tamed a flood. Archaeology has found an impressive early city at Erlitou. Whether the two are the same is one of the most charged questions in Chinese history. Erlitou, near Luoyang, was a planned centre with walled palaces, roads and bronze workshops that made some of China's earliest bronze ritual vessels. In an elite grave, archaeologists found a dragon made of more than 2,000 pieces of turquoise. Chinese historical tradition, written down more than a thousand years later, makes the Xia the first dynasty; modern Chinese chronology dates it about 2070-1600 BCE. Most archaeologists in China identify Erlitou as a Xia capital. Many scholars elsewhere are more cautious: no writing from the period names the Xia, and newer radiocarbon dates put Erlitou's start about 1750 BCE, well after the traditional beginning of the Xia. The tradition says Yu earned his throne by controlling a great flood. In 2016 a team of geologists argued that a landslide that dammed the Yellow River about 1920 BCE, and then burst, could be the historical kernel of that story; others replied that the evidence cannot support the claim. first dynasty Xia, founded by Yu Erlitou culture (name of a site) dates c. 2070-1600 BCE (modern reckoning) c. 1750 BCE onward writing later texts (e.g. Sima Qian) none found at Erlitou capital several, named in texts planned palace centre Compare the Sumerian King List (3.4): later texts can preserve real memories and also shape them for political purposes. Page 5.10 looks at how China's early chronology was built.

s: bronze, ancestors and sacrifice, c. 1600 to 1046 BCE
x: The Shang are the first Chinese dynasty confirmed by their own writing. Their kings ruled through ancestors and divination, cast bronze on a colossal scale, and sacrificed people by the thousand. The Shang are conventionally dated about 1600-1046 BCE. Their early cities at Zhengzhou and Yanshi had massive walls of rammed earth. Their last capital, at Anyang, called Yinxu ('the ruins of Yin'), has more than 80 palace and temple foundations and China's first great royal cemetery. Shang religion centred on the dead. The king sacrificed to his ancestors. Above them stood Di, a supreme deity who governed weather, harvests and war but had no cult of his own and was thought too remote to be swayed by mortals. Offerings were made in bronze vessels, cast in sectioned clay moulds; the largest known weighs about 833 kg. Sacrifice included people. More than 13,000 may have been killed at Anyang over about two centuries, often 50 and sometimes 300 at a time; isotopes suggest many came from elsewhere, perhaps as captives. One tomb, found intact in 1976, belonged to Fu Hao, a royal consort who, oracle bones say, led armies in battle. Horse-drawn chariots appear at Anyang about 1200 BCE, a technology that came from the steppe. bronze objects 468 jades 755 cowrie shells about 6,900 human victims 16 dogs 6 Compare the royal tombs of Ur (3.5) and the 1st-Dynasty kings of Egypt (4.1), also buried with people killed to accompany them.

The Shang kings asked their ancestors about everything: rain, harvests, war, childbirth, toothache. The answers, cut into bone and shell, are the oldest Chinese writing, and the ancestor of the characters used by over a billion people today. The story goes that in 1899 a scholar, Wang Yirong, noticed writing on 'dragon bones' sold as medicine; in 1908 another scholar, Luo Zhenyu, traced them to Anyang. About 150,000 inscribed fragments are now known. Diviners drilled hollows in an ox shoulder blade or a turtle shell, applied heat until it cracked, and read the cracks as the ancestors' answer. Then a scribe carved the record: the date and the diviner, the question, the king's reading of the cracks, and sometimes what actually happened. The questions concern weather, harvests, war, illness, childbirth and sacrifices. One shell asks whether Fu Hao's childbirth will go well. Because many records note the outcome, the oracle bones are a dated archive of events, and they confirmed the list of Shang kings preserved by later historians (5.10). preface the day and the diviner's name charge 'It will rain' prognostication the king reads the cracks verification what happened afterwards The script already looks mature, which suggests writing began earlier, perhaps on materials that have not survived; signs carved on shells at Jiahu thousands of years before are probably symbols, not writing. About 4,500 distinct oracle-bone characters are known, and about a third have been matched to modern ones. Since 2024, AI tools have been suggesting matches for the rest. The writing system is continuous: these characters are the direct ancestors of Chinese characters today. Compare cuneiform (3.2) and hieroglyphs (4.5), which died out and had to be deciphered. Chinese writing never stopped being used.

s: a Bronze Age kingdom nobody expected
x: In 1986, workers digging clay in Sichuan found two pits full of bronze heads, gold masks and elephant tusks, broken and burned. Nothing in Chinese texts had prepared anyone for them. Sanxingdui lies on the Chengdu plain, far south-west of the Shang heartland. It became a walled Bronze Age centre about 1800 BCE. The 1986 pits held hundreds of objects of bronze, gold, jade and ivory, many deliberately smashed and burned before they were buried. Six more pits, found from 2019, held still more, including a gold mask. None held human remains, so these were ritual deposits, not graves. The bronzes are like nothing from the Shang: a standing figure over 2.5 metres tall, a bronze tree almost 4 metres high, and a mask more than a metre wide with eyes that stick out on stalks. Some scholars connect those eyes with Cancong, a legendary first king of Shu. The pits were filled late in the Shang period. Sanxingdui traded with the Central Plains and borrowed some vessel types, but its art and religion were its own. No writing has been found there, which is why its people's beliefs remain a mystery, and why the site has attracted wild theories of aliens or migrants from the Middle East. Those have no evidence behind them. A few objects may hint at contact farther west, but that too is uncertain. The culture continued at Jinsha, in modern Chengdu, until about 650 BCE, and the kingdom of Shu survived until Qin conquered it in 316 BCE. Compare Liangzhu and Shimao (5.4): Sanxingdui is more evidence that early China had many centres, not one.

t: The Zhou and the Mandate of Heaven
x: About 1046 BCE the Zhou, from the Wei valley in the west, overthrew the Shang. To explain why they deserved to rule, they offered an idea that lasted three thousand years: Heaven gives power to the virtuous, and takes it away from the wicked. A bronze vessel cast soon after the event, the Li gui, records that King Wu attacked the Shang on a jiazi day, in the morning. The year is less certain: it is usually given as 1046 BCE, and the arguments for it draw on astronomy as well as texts. The Zhou claimed that Heaven (tian) had given them its mandate because the last Shang king was cruel and the Zhou were virtuous. The idea already appears in early Zhou bronzes and texts. It cut both ways: if Heaven could transfer the mandate to the Zhou, it could transfer it again. A bronze of the early Zhou, the He zun, also contains the earliest known use of zhongguo, 'the central lands', today the Chinese name for China. The Zhou ruled by granting lands to relatives and allies, whose lords owed loyalty and military service. Whether to call this 'feudalism' is disputed. In 771 BCE attackers from the west sacked the capital and killed King You, and the court moved east to Luoyi. The Zhou kings reigned for five more centuries, but the real power passed to the lords of the states. homeland middle Yellow River Wei valley, to the west source of royal power ancestors, divination the mandate of Heaven supreme power Di Heaven (tian) main written records oracle bones bronze inscriptions, later texts The Mandate became one of the great political ideas of world history: floods, famines and rebellions could be read as signs that Heaven had withdrawn its favour, until the last dynasty fell in the revolution of 1911-12. Compare the Bible's account of kings raised up and brought down by God, as with Saul and David (1 Samuel 15-16), and Egypt's idea of maat (4.2). Each makes a ruler answerable to a higher order.

Early Chinese history rests on three kinds of evidence: histories written down centuries later, oracle bones and bronzes from the time, and archaeology. Where they meet, history becomes firm. Where they do not, it becomes contested, and sometimes political. The great early history is the Shiji of Sima Qian, written about 100 BCE. It gives year-by-year dates only from 841 BCE; before that it offers lists of rulers. For the Shang, those lists were dramatically confirmed. The oracle bones showed the Shang existed, and the line of kings reconstructed from them matches Sima Qian's list, written about a thousand years later, with only minor differences. Radiocarbon dates on the bones themselves now place King Wu Ding about 1254-1197 BCE. For the Xia, no such confirmation exists (5.5). In the late 1990s the Chinese state sponsored the Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project, about 200 scholars led by Li Xueqin, to fix the dates before 841. It placed the Xia about 2070-1600 BCE and the Zhou conquest in 1046. Critics outside China called its precision unjustified, and some saw nationalist motives. A second project, on the origins of Chinese civilization, announced in 2018 that regional civilizations existed by about 5,300 years ago, at sites such as Liangzhu. In 2022 Xi Jinping spoke of China's 'more than 5,000 years of civilization', linking the research to national rejuvenation. Some scholars worry that archaeology is being drawn into a national story. Shiji and other histories c. 100 BCE and later king lists, stories; dates only from 841 BCE Oracle bones c. 1250-1046 BCE Shang kings, rituals, events Bronze inscriptions Shang and Zhou grants, wars, dates within reigns Archaeology and radiocarbon not written cities, burials, dates in ranges Compare the Sumerian King List (3.4), the Egyptian king lists (4.12) and the debates over the Bible's early history (4.9). In each case a later written tradition meets archaeology, and the questions are much the same.

s: Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus and early China
x: The first four civilizations arose on great rivers, separately and in different ways. Set side by side, they show what early states had in common, and how differently they could be organised. All four grew from farming villages along rivers that flooded, and all built cities, specialised crafts and long-distance trade. Three developed writing early; China's earliest surviving writing comes almost two thousand years after Mesopotamia's. first cities 4th millennium BCE (3.1) Memphis, c. 3000 BCE (4.1) c. 2600 BCE Liangzhu, c. 3300 BCE (5.4) earliest writing c. 3300-3000 BCE [[c-cmp-meso]] c. 3200 BCE [[c-cmp-uj]] signs from c. 3300? [[c-cmp-indus-early]] oracle bones, c. 1250 BCE can we read it? yes yes no [[c-no-bilingual]] yes; still in use [[c-continuity]] largest city Uruk, c. 250 ha (c. 3200 BCE); c. 500 ha by 3000 BCE (3.1) uncertain Mohenjo-daro c. 240 ha; Rakhigarhi larger? Yinxu (Anyang): a scattered site zone of c. 30 km², not comparable with walled-city areas [[c-yinxu-size]] visible kings yes: palaces, inscriptions yes: pharaohs none identified [[c-no-palaces]] yes: Shang kings people killed at rulers' burials yes, at Ur (3.5) yes, in the 1st Dynasty (4.1) none known yes, at Anyang (5.6) end of the early phase Akkad and after (3.6) Old Kingdom collapse (4.6) gradual decline, from c. 1900 BCE Zhou conquest, c. 1046 BCE The biggest contrast is the Indus. The other three left kings everywhere: in palaces, tombs, statues and inscriptions. The Indus, with cities as large and as planned, left no image anyone can identify as a ruler. Whether that reflects a different kind of society or only what survives is one of archaeology's great open questions. The second contrast is writing. Cuneiform and hieroglyphs died out and had to be deciphered in modern times; the Indus script has never been read; Chinese writing has been in continuous use for more than three thousand years. Chapter 6 turns to what happened next: the Late Bronze Age, when Egypt, the Hittites, Babylon and their neighbours formed a club of great powers, and then collapsed together.

s: a club of great powers, and its collapse
x: Between about 1600 and 1200 BCE, a handful of kingdoms from Greece to Mesopotamia formed the first international system: rulers who wrote to each other as 'brothers', traded gold for horses, married each other's daughters and fought by agreed rules. Then, within a few decades after 1200, most of it fell apart. Egypt (Chapter 4) was one member of this club. The others were the Hittites of Anatolia, Mitanni in northern Syria, Kassite Babylon, a rising Assyria, and, on the edges, Mycenaean Greece and Alashiya on Cyprus. They shared a diplomatic language: Akkadian written in cuneiform, which scribes from Egypt to Anatolia learned for the purpose. Great kings called one another 'brother'; smaller rulers were 'servants'. Gold, horses, chariots and princesses moved between courts. And they shared a way of war, built on the horse-drawn chariot. Pages 6.1 to 6.3 meet the great kingdoms of Anatolia and Mesopotamia and the letters they sent; 6.4 to 6.7 the Aegean and the Levant; 6.8 the trade that bound them; and 6.9 to 6.11 the collapse and what came after. Egypt (New Kingdom) Thebes, Memphis, Amarna c. 1550-1069 (4.7) Hatti (Hittites) Hattusa c. 1400-1200 Mitanni Washukanni c. 1500 to mid-14th century Babylonia (Kassites) Babylon c. 1595-1155 Assyria Ashur from c. 1365 Mycenaean Greece Mycenae, Pylos and others c. 1500-1100 Compare the first empire, Akkad (3.6), which tried to rule everyone. This was a different idea: several great powers recognising one another as equals.

A century and a half ago the Hittites were a name in the Bible and little more. Excavation at a Turkish village revealed the capital of an empire that had sacked Babylon, fought Egypt to a standstill, and written in the oldest recorded Indo-European language. The Hittites ruled central Anatolia from Hattusa from about 1650 BCE. From 1906 Hugo Winckler dug there and found thousands of tablets, including the Akkadian text of the treaty with Ramesses II (4.9). Almost 30,000 tablets and fragments are now known, in at least half a dozen languages. In 1915 Bedřich Hrozný worked out that Hittite was Indo-European, related to Latin, Greek and Sanskrit. The early kings were aggressive. About 1595 BCE Mursili I raided far down the Euphrates to Babylon and sacked it, ending the dynasty of Hammurabi (3.8). Murders in the royal family followed, until Telipinu laid down rules for the succession. Under Suppiluliuma I in the 14th century the Hittites destroyed Mitanni and took northern Syria. Hittite religion collected gods: the texts speak of the 'thousand gods' of Hatti. Their laws are notable for replacing many death penalties and mutilations with fines. The capital was ringed by more than 8 km of walls, and at the nearby rock sanctuary of Yazılıkaya processions of gods are carved in stone. The end was strange. Early in the 12th century the court left Hattusa, emptying its official buildings; the excavators find no sign of a battle. Tree rings show a severe drought just before. The Bible's 'Hittites', such as Ephron in Genesis 23 or Uriah in 2 Samuel 11, are probably a different group from this empire.

In 1887 several hundred clay tablets came to light at Amarna, Akhenaten's short-lived capital. They are the pharaoh's foreign correspondence: letters from the great kings of the age, and from the anxious rulers of Canaan. The tablets were found in 1887, in circumstances that remain unclear. 382 are known, about 350 of them letters, chiefly from the reigns of Amenhotep III and Akhenaten; they are the only royal archive known from New Kingdom Egypt. Almost all are in Akkadian. The great kings' letters read like family quarrels about money. Burna-Buriash of Babylon complained that his gifts were meagre, and objected that the pharaoh had received envoys from Assyria, whose king he called his vassal. Tushratta of Mitanni, whose daughter married into the Egyptian royal family, demanded the statues of solid gold he had been promised, and complained bitterly when gold-plated wood arrived instead. The vassal letters are different in tone. Abdi-Heba, ruler of Jerusalem, protests his loyalty, accuses his neighbours and begs for troops: 'all of the lands of the king, my lord, are lost'. Several rulers complain of the 'Apiru, uprooted people who worked as mercenaries or raiders. Because the word resembles 'Hebrew', some scholars have linked the two; others reject the link. Burna-Buriash II Babylon gifts; Assyria's rise Tushratta Mitanni gold statues; marriage Ashur-uballit I Assyria recognition as a great king Abdi-Heba Jerusalem loyalty; troops; the 'Apiru Jerusalem appears here some 350 years before the time usually assigned to David, about 1000 BCE (1 Samuel to 1 Kings), as the seat of a minor ruler loyal to Egypt.

East of the Hittites lay three more members of the club: Mitanni, a kingdom whose kings swore by Vedic gods; Assyria, which rose on Mitanni's ruins; and Babylon, ruled for four centuries by a dynasty from the mountains. Mitanni was a Hurrian-speaking kingdom of northern Syria whose kings bore Indo-Aryan names. In a treaty with the Hittites its king swore by Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatyas, gods of the Rigveda, and a horse-training manual by a Mitanni trainer called Kikkuli uses Indo-Aryan terms. Its capital has never been securely found; in 2018 a drought exposed one of its palaces on the Tigris. Mitanni was destroyed in stages by the Hittites and the Assyrians. Assyria, centred on the city of Ashur, broke free of Mitanni under Ashur-uballit I, who wrote to the pharaoh as a great king. A century later Tukulti-Ninurta I conquered Babylon and built himself a new capital, before his own son murdered him. Babylon, after the Hittite raid of 1595, was taken over by the Kassites, a people from the Zagros mountains, who ruled for over four centuries. They kept Babylonian culture alive, and left a new kind of monument, the kudurru, a carved stone recording a royal land grant, guarded by the symbols of the gods and by curses on anyone who removed it. Tushratta Mitanni c. 1365-1330 Ashur-uballit I Assyria c. 1365-1330 Burna-Buriash II Babylon (Kassite) 14th century Tukulti-Ninurta I Assyria c. 1243-1207 Compare the Rakhigarhi genome and the arrival of steppe ancestry in South Asia (5.3). The Mitanni treaty is the earliest dated written record of Indo-Aryan gods, far to the west of India.

On Crete, Europe's first palace civilization built great courtyard complexes, painted bright frescoes of bulls and dolphins, and wrote in a script nobody can read. In the middle of its history, a volcano 110 km to the north blew apart. The Minoans, named by Arthur Evans after the legendary King Minos, flourished on Crete for most of the Bronze Age. Evans began digging Knossos in 1900, and in 2025 Knossos and five other palace sites became a World Heritage Site. The Minoans wrote in Linear A, whose language is still unknown. Their art is full of bulls, snakes and young people leaping over charging bulls, scenes that probably had a religious meaning. Evans imagined a gentle society ruled by priest-kings; scholars still argue about how peaceful it really was. Sometime between about 1610 and 1540 BCE the volcano of Thera (Santorini) erupted. It buried the town of Akrotiri, with its frescoed houses, under ash. A 2025 study places it before the reign of Ahmose in Egypt. It did not end Minoan civilization by itself, but by the 15th century Greek-speaking Mycenaeans ruled Knossos. Pottery and Egyptian links (older view) c. 1570-1500 Tree-ring radiocarbon (Pearson et al. 2018) 1600-1525 Bayesian model (Manning 2022) 1609-1560 Buried olive shrub (Pearson et al. 2023) mid-16th century Compare the debate over Mesopotamian chronologies (3.12): an exact date for one event can anchor or overturn a whole timeline.

s: Linear B and the first Greeks
x: On the Greek mainland, warrior kings built citadels of colossal stones and buried their dead in gold. Their scribes kept accounts in a script that, when it was finally read in 1952, turned out to be Greek. Mycenae, Tiryns and Pylos were the centres of small kingdoms, ringed by walls of huge stones. The earliest rulers of Mycenae were buried in shaft graves with gold masks, weapons and treasure. A grave found near Pylos in 2015, the 'Griffin Warrior', held Minoan-made masterpieces, a sign of how much the mainland took from Crete. Their script, Linear B, was deciphered in 1952 by the young architect Michael Ventris, with the philologist John Chadwick: it wrote Greek, centuries older than Homer. Alice Kober's patient work had shown the way. The tablets are bureaucratic: land, rations, taxes, offerings, bronze issued to smiths. But they also name gods the later Greeks knew: Zeus, Poseidon, even Dionysus. Ancient DNA shows Minoans and Mycenaeans were close relatives, both descended mostly from early farmers; the Mycenaeans had some extra ancestry, perhaps from the steppe. Elites were not genetically different from commoners, and marriage between first cousins was common. script Linear A (unread) Linear B (Greek) centres palaces with open courts walled citadels art bulls, sea creatures, nature warriors, chariots, hunting fate taken over by Mycenaeans palaces destroyed c. 1200 (6.9) Compare the decipherment of Hittite (6.1) and the still-unread Indus script (5.2). Linear B was cracked without a bilingual inscription, by working out the structure of the language first.

Homer's Iliad tells of a ten-year Greek siege of Troy. Archaeologists have dug at Troy for 150 years, and Hittite archives have added letters about a western kingdom called Wilusa. Did the war happen? The honest answer is: perhaps something like it. Troy is the mound of Hisarlık near the Dardanelles, with nine main layers of settlement. Two layers are candidates for Homer's city. Troy VI, a large fortified city, was badly damaged by an earthquake about 1300 BCE. Troy VIIa was destroyed by fire with signs of violence, about 1250 BCE on Carl Blegen's dating and about 1200-1180 on more recent work. Manfred Korfmann argued that the city was much larger than its citadel, a claim that drew fierce criticism. Hittite texts add a voice from outside Greece. They mention Wilusa, a vassal kingdom in north-west Anatolia that most scholars identify with Troy (Greek Ilios, earlier Wilios). They also mention Ahhiyawa, a power across the sea, most likely the Mycenaean Greeks, that clashed with the Hittites over the region. One king of Wilusa was called Alaksandu, a name some compare with Paris's other name, Alexandros. None of this proves a Trojan War. Some scholars think the epic preserves real memories; others see no evidence for a Greek attack at all. A common middle view is that raids and conflicts were later magnified into an epic. The Iliad itself was composed about five centuries after the events. Troy VI large city; earthquake c. 1300 BCE Troy VIIa burned, with signs of violence Hittite texts Wilusa a vassal; disputes with Ahhiyawa Homer composed c. 8th century BCE Compare the debate over the Exodus (4.9) and over Erlitou and the Xia (5.5): a later literary tradition, some archaeology, and the question of what kind of memory the tradition preserves.

In 1928 a farmer's plough opened a tomb on the Syrian coast. Beneath lay Ugarit, a trading city whose archives preserve the myths of the Canaanite gods, in a language close to Hebrew. No discovery has done more to show the religious world in which the Hebrew Bible took shape. Ugarit was found in 1928 and excavated from 1929. A rich port, it became a Hittite vassal about 1350 BCE. Its archives hold more than 5,000 tablets in five writing systems and eight languages, including its own: a 30-letter alphabet written in cuneiform wedges. The alphabet itself had been invented centuries earlier, by people adapting Egyptian hieroglyphs. A recent claim pushes it back further, but is contested. The religious texts tell of El, the aged father of the gods, and his consort Asherah; of Baal, the storm god, who defeats Yam (Sea) and is swallowed by Mot (Death), and of his sister Anat, who rescues him. Older accounts made Baal a crude fertility god; recent scholars argue that picture came from the Bible's polemic. Before Ugarit, Canaanite religion was known mainly from its enemies. The parallels with the Hebrew Bible are real but must be weighed one by one. El is a Hebrew word for God. Isaiah 27:1's 'Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent' is Ugarit's Lotan. Psalm 82 pictures God in 'the divine council', like El among the gods. More debated are whether Psalm 29 adapts a Baal hymn, whether Yahweh was once distinct from El, and whether Asherah was worshipped in Israel. Ugarit was destroyed early in the 12th century BCE. Its fall is part of the collapse described on page 6.9. Compare the Hymn to the Aten and Psalm 104 (4.8), and the flood stories of Mesopotamia and Genesis (3.10). In each case, Israel's scriptures share language and images with their neighbours while reshaping them.

s: the Uluburun ship, copper and tin
x: Bronze is copper alloyed with a little tin, and the two metals are almost never found together. The great powers' armies, tools and temples therefore depended on long trade routes. A ship that sank about 1300 BCE shows what moved along them. In 1982 a sponge diver off southern Turkey reported strange metal objects on the sea floor. They were copper ingots from the Uluburun wreck, excavated over eleven seasons. Tree rings and radiocarbon date the sinking to about 1300 BCE. The ship carried about 10 tons of Cypriot copper and about a ton of tin, enough for some 11 tons of bronze. It also held glass ingots, jars of resin, African ebony, ivory, and a gold scarab with the name of Nefertiti. It was probably sailing west from Canaan toward the Aegean. A smaller wreck at Cape Gelidonya, about a century later, carried scrap bronze for recycling. Copper came mainly from Cyprus, the Alashiya of the Amarna letters (6.0). Tin is harder. Recent studies trace Bronze Age tin to Anatolia, Central Asia or even Britain, and dispute each other's results. Either way, tin came from a few scattered sources, and bronze tied the great powers to long and fragile supply lines. copper c. 10 tons Cyprus tin c. 1 ton disputed glass ingots c. 175 Egypt and the Near East resin in Canaanite jars c. 0.5 ton Canaan ebony; ivory logs; tusk, hippo teeth Africa; Africa or the Levant Compare the sea trade between the Indus, the Gulf and Mesopotamia (5.2), a thousand years earlier.

Within about fifty years after 1200 BCE, the Hittite empire vanished, Ugarit was destroyed, the Mycenaean palaces burned, and Egypt fought off invaders by land and sea. Writing disappeared from Greece for four centuries. The Hittite court abandoned Hattusa early in the 12th century. Ugarit was destroyed soon after an eclipse of 1192 BCE, and nearby Tell Tweini at almost the same time. Emar fell about 1185. But Carchemish survived, and its king called himself Great King. In Greece, fires ended the palaces of Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos and Thebes around 1200. In Canaan, Hazor burned and Lachish fell decades later. Egypt left the most famous account. Merneptah had already fought a Libyan invasion joined by groups from the sea. About 1177 BCE, in his 8th year, Ramesses III fought them again. His temple at Medinet Habu says 'the foreign countries made a conspiracy in their islands' and that 'no land could stand before their arms'. Modern historians call them the 'Sea Peoples'. The firmest identification is the Peleset, the Philistines. The destructions were spread over decades, some cities survived, and some were abandoned rather than sacked. That is why most historians no longer think one wave of invaders destroyed the system. Hattusa abandoned early 12th century Ugarit destroyed soon after 1192 Emar destroyed c. 1185 Mycenae, Pylos palaces burned c. 1200 Carchemish survived - Egypt repelled invaders c. 1177 Compare the end of Akkad and the crises around 2200 BCE (3.6, 4.6): another moment when several societies failed at once.

s: drought, earthquakes, raiders and a fragile system
x: Few questions in ancient history have attracted so many answers. The evidence now points less to one cause than to several shocks hitting an interconnected world at once. Climate is the strongest new evidence. Pollen cores from the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea suggest repeated drought in the southern Levant, and a core from Cyprus a long dry period beginning about 1200. Critics said such records were too loosely dated, but in 2023 tree rings from Gordion pinned three years of severe drought to about 1198-1196 BCE, just before the Hittite collapse. A 2026 climate model points the same way. Other factors were in play. Earthquakes may have damaged several cities, and raiders struck the Levantine coast. Inside the kingdoms, revolt, elite rivalry or brittle palace economies may have turned shocks into collapse. Eric Cline argues that these causes interacted, and that the powers' dependence on one another let failure spread. Not everyone collapsed. Egypt survived, though weakened; Assyria recovered and marched to the Mediterranean; Carchemish and Cyprus carried on. In his 2024 sequel Cline asks why some societies adapted while others vanished. drought pollen cores; Gordion tree rings timing in some records is loose earthquakes damaged walls and buildings hard to prove; cities recover from quakes invasion and raids Medinet Habu; Ugarit letters no evidence of raiders in the Aegean internal revolt fragile palace economies hard to test systems collapse everything above, interacting can explain almost anything Compare the debate over the end of the Indus cities (5.3): there too, drought is now the leading suspect, but rarely the only one.

s: iron, Philistines, Phoenicians and the first Israel
x: Out of the ruins of the Bronze Age came a new world of smaller states: Philistine cities on the coast, Phoenician merchants in the north, Neo-Hittite kingdoms in Syria, and in the hills of Canaan a new people whom an Egyptian king had already called Israel. Iron objects became more common from the 12th century BCE, first in Cyprus and the Levant, though the old idea that a shortage of tin forced the change finds little support. The Peleset of Medinet Habu settled the southern coast as the Philistines, in five cities. DNA from Ashkelon shows newcomers with European-related ancestry who soon mixed with locals; the Bible remembers them as coming from Caphtor. To the north, the Phoenician cities grew rich on trade, and spread the alphabet that the Greeks would adopt. Neo-Hittite kingdoms kept Hittite traditions alive in Syria. In the hill country, about 250 small villages appeared from about 1200 BCE. They were unfortified, simple, and nearly free of pig bones. Most archaeologists connect them with the Israel named on the Merneptah Stele (4.9), but disagree about who the settlers were: mostly local pastoralists settling down, a group deliberately marking itself off from its neighbours, or a mixed confederation. Chapter 7 takes up the story in the Iron Age, as Assyria rises again and the kingdoms of Israel and Judah take shape. Philistines southern coast of Canaan five cities; Aegean-style pottery Phoenicians Tyre, Sidon, Byblos trade, the alphabet Neo-Hittites northern Syria, south-east Anatolia Hittite traditions Highland villagers hill country of Canaan early Israel Compare the Bible's books of Joshua and Judges, which tell of conquest and of tribes living among Canaanites and Philistines. The archaeology of the highland villages shows no sign of a violent invasion; it fits better with gradual settlement.

t: Iron, empire and the Axial Age
x: After the Bronze Age collapse, the Near East rebuilt itself around a new kind of power: empire on a scale never seen before, first Assyrian, then Babylonian, then Persian. In the same centuries, small peoples on the edges of these empires, Israel among them, produced ideas that would outlast them all. From about 900 BCE Assyria built the largest empire yet seen, ruled from a series of capitals in northern Iraq. Around it lay other kingdoms: Urartu in the mountains to the north, Phrygia and Lydia in Anatolia, Media in Iran, and Egypt, which revived under its Saite kings. Assyria fell in 612-609 BCE to Babylon and the Medes; Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar inherited its western empire, and in 539 fell to Cyrus of Persia (7.8). Pages 7.1 to 7.4 follow the kingdoms of Israel and Judah through these empires, using inscriptions, archaeology and the Bible side by side. Pages 7.5 and 7.6 turn west, to Phoenicians and Greeks. Pages 7.7 to 7.11 look at the 'Axial Age': the prophets of Israel, Zoroaster, the Buddha and Confucius. Assyria Kalhu, then Nineveh c. 912-609 Babylonia Babylon 626-539 Egypt (Saite dynasty) Sais 664-525 Urartu Tushpa (Van) 9th-7th century Lydia Sardis 7th century-c. 546 Media Ecbatana 7th century-550 Persia Pasargadae from 550 Compare the 'club of great powers' of the Late Bronze Age (6.0). Then several kingdoms balanced each other; now one empire at a time dominated the whole region.

The Bible tells of a united kingdom under David and Solomon that split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Inscriptions from Israel's neighbours, and Assyria, name its kings from the 9th century onward. Before that, the evidence becomes thin and fiercely debated. Several inscriptions from the 9th century BCE name Israel's kings. An Assyrian stela lists 'Ahab the Israelite' with 2,000 chariots at the battle of Qarqar in 853; the Moabite king Mesha remembers that 'Omri, king of Israel, oppressed Moab for a long time'; and the Black Obelisk shows Jehu bowing to the Assyrian king. Omri founded Samaria as his capital. The Tel Dan stele, found in 1993-94, gives the earliest generally accepted mention of the 'House of David', Judah's dynasty, in a king of Damascus's boast of victory. The Bible tells the same events differently, crediting the deaths to Jehu. Whether the Mesha stele also mentions David is disputed. David and Solomon themselves are not named in any inscription of their time, and how large their kingdom was is hotly debated. The fortified town of Khirbet Qeiyafa, about 1000 BCE, is a key piece of evidence for both sides. Jerusalem was small in the 10th century and grew greatly in the 8th; new radiocarbon dates suggest more early occupation than once thought. By about 600 BCE, writing was spreading: soldiers at the fort of Arad wrote to one another, and a tomb in Jerusalem held silver amulets with the priestly blessing, the oldest known texts that match a passage of the Hebrew Bible. Kurkh stela (Assyrian) 853 Ahab of Israel Mesha stele (Moabite) later 9th century Omri; Yahweh Tel Dan stele (Aramaic) 9th century 'House of David' Black Obelisk (Assyrian) c. 841 Jehu, 'House of Omri' Ketef Hinnom amulets (Hebrew) c. 600 the priestly blessing (Numbers 6) Compare the Merneptah Stele (4.9), which names a people called Israel about 1208 BCE, and the highland villages of 6.11.

s: the first great empire of the Iron Age
x: Assyrian kings boasted of their cruelty, and their palace walls showed it. But their empire was also an administrative achievement: provinces, governors, roads and couriers, and the deliberate movement of whole peoples. Tiglath-pileser III, who seized the throne in 745 BCE, transformed Assyria. He broke the empire into smaller provinces under governors answerable to him, built a standing army, and made deportation a tool of government. Conquered peoples were moved across the empire to break resistance and to settle land; one estimate puts the total at over four million people. A network of relay stations carried royal letters across the empire in days. Assyria's kings built palaces at Kalhu and Nineveh lined with carved reliefs. The last great king, Ashurbanipal, collected texts, and more than 30,000 tablets and fragments from Nineveh are now in the British Museum, including the Epic of Gilgamesh (3.10). Then, within a few years, the empire vanished. In 612 BCE the Babylonians and Medes took Nineveh, and by 609 Assyria was gone. Historians have blamed civil war and overextension; a 2019 study adds drought. Tiglath-pileser III 745-727 reforms; mass deportation Sargon II 721-705 new capital; Samaria (7.3) Sennacherib 704-681 Nineveh; campaign against Judah, 701 Ashurbanipal 668-c. 631 library at Nineveh Compare Akkad (3.6), the first empire: Assyria's kings saw themselves as Sargon's heirs, and one of them took his name.

For the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, Assyria was catastrophe. Israel disappeared in 722 BCE. Judah survived Sennacherib's invasion of 701, and for once we have the invader's own account to set beside the Bible's. Samaria fell after a three-year siege in 722 BCE, and many Israelites were deported to Assyria (2 Kings 17); Sargon II claimed 27,280. Which Assyrian king took the city is debated. The kingdom of Israel was never restored; its exiles are the 'lost tribes' of later legend. In 701 Sennacherib invaded Judah. His annals boast of 46 towns besieged and Hezekiah shut up in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage'. 2 Kings agrees that Hezekiah paid tribute, but tells of an angel who struck down 185,000 Assyrians. Neither source says Jerusalem fell. Sennacherib chose to celebrate Lachish instead, in reliefs for his palace, and the Assyrian siege ramp still stands there. In Jerusalem, a tunnel cut through rock brought the Gihon spring inside the walls, traditionally credited to Hezekiah, though its date is debated. Jars stamped 'belonging to the king' show a royal supply system at work. An impression of Hezekiah's own seal was announced in 2015, and in 2025 the first Assyrian document from Jerusalem. towns of Judah 46 besieged and taken 'all the fortified cities' captured Hezekiah's tribute 30 talents of gold, 800 of silver 30 talents of gold, 300 of silver Jerusalem Hezekiah shut in 'like a bird in a cage' saved; 185,000 Assyrians struck down Outcome Assyrian victory Sennacherib returns to Nineveh Compare Ramesses II's account of Kadesh (4.9): royal inscriptions record victories, and leave out what did not go to plan.

In 587 or 586 BCE Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and its temple and carried its leaders into exile. Out of that disaster, many scholars think, came much of the Hebrew Bible as we have it, and a religion that could survive without a land. Nebuchadnezzar first took Jerusalem in March 597 BCE, a date fixed by a Babylonian chronicle, and carried King Jehoiachin to Babylon. Babylonian ration lists name 'Ya'u-kinu, king of the land of Yahudu'. After a revolt, Jerusalem and its temple were destroyed in 587 or 586. Letters from Lachish catch the last months before the end. The Bible's own figures for the deportations differ. How many stayed, and how empty the land became, is debated. In Babylonia, tablets from a village called 'Judahtown' show exiled families farming, marrying and paying taxes for generations. In 539 Cyrus of Persia took Babylon. His cylinder says he restored temples and returned deported peoples to their homes, and Ezra 1 says he let the Judeans rebuild their temple; how far the two fit together is debated. The Second Temple was completed, by the traditional date, in 515 BCE. Many exiles stayed in Babylonia, where a Jewish community lasted until modern times. 597 Jerusalem taken; Jehoiachin exiled 587/586 Jerusalem and the temple destroyed 582 a further deportation (Jeremiah 52:30) 539 Cyrus takes Babylon c. 515 Second Temple completed (traditional) Psalm 137, 'By the rivers of Babylon', and Second Isaiah (7.11) both speak from the exile. Isaiah 45:1 calls Cyrus the Lord's 'anointed'.

From their narrow strip of coast, the merchants of Tyre sailed the length of the Mediterranean and out past Gibraltar, to the silver of southern Spain. Their colonies, above all Carthage, carried the culture of the Levant to Africa, Sicily and Iberia. Tyre, Sidon, Byblos and Arwad were rival trading cities, famous for purple dye. From the 9th century BCE, Tyre led a push west, drawn above all by the silver of southern Spain. By the late 8th century, Phoenician trading posts ringed the Mediterranean, from Kition on Cyprus to Motya in Sicily. In Spain, later tradition dated Gadir (Cádiz) to about 1100 BCE, but radiocarbon places the first Phoenician quarter at Huelva in the late 9th century, with Gadir just after. The meeting of traders and local people produced the culture the Greeks called Tartessos, which may be the Bible's Tarshish. New finds keep changing the picture: in 2023 and 2024 excavators at Casas del Turuñuelo uncovered carved faces and a slate showing warriors. Carthage, traditionally founded in 814 BCE, has early radiocarbon dates that broadly fit, though its oldest pottery suggests about half a century later. It became the greatest Phoenician city in the west. Its tophet, a burial ground for the cremated remains of infants, is the subject of one of archaeology's hardest debates: sacrifice or cemetery. DNA published in 2025 shows the people of Carthage and other Punic cities had almost no ancestry from the Levant: their culture spread by adoption, not migration. Gadir (Cádiz) c. 1100 BCE end of the 9th century Huelva - second half of the 9th century Carthage 814 BCE late 9th to early 8th century Motya (Sicily) - c. 775-750 BCE The Bible speaks of 'Topheth' in the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where people would 'make a son or a daughter pass through fire' (2 Kings 23:10); Jeremiah 7:31 condemns burning children there. Whether the phrase always meant sacrifice is also debated.

s: the polis, colonies and the alphabet
x: After the palaces fell, Greece became a land of small, independent communities. Between about 800 and 500 BCE they invented the polis, sent colonies across the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, adopted the alphabet, and in Athens began to experiment with rule by citizens. The centuries after the collapse were long called a 'Dark Age', but finds at Lefkandi, including a great building of about 950 BCE, show wealth and contact abroad. By the 8th century Greeks lived in hundreds of poleis, self-governing communities of citizens. They borrowed the Phoenician alphabet and added vowels; the earliest inscriptions date from about 740-700 BCE, though when the borrowing happened is debated. Greeks founded colonies from Spain to the Black Sea: Pithekoussai in the bay of Naples, Syracuse and Naxos in Sicily, Massalia in France, and dozens of cities round the Black Sea. At home, citizens fought as hoplites in close formation, which may or may not have shifted power toward ordinary farmers. Ambitious men seized power as 'tyrants'. At Athens, Solon cancelled debts and based rights on wealth rather than birth, and Cleisthenes created the institutions of democracy in 508/507 BCE. The poet Hesiod praised honest work and justice. The Olympic Games, by tradition, began in 776 BCE. c. 950 great building at Lefkandi 776 first Olympic Games (traditional) c. 770-750 Pithekoussai founded c. 733 Syracuse founded (traditional) c. 594 (trad.) Solon's reforms in Athens 508/507 Cleisthenes' reforms Compare the Phoenician colonies (7.5), founded at the same time and often in the same places: Greeks and Phoenicians competed, and traded, across the whole Mediterranean.

s: a big idea and its critics
x: Between about 800 and 200 BCE, from China to Greece, thinkers taught ideas that still shape billions of lives. Was this one great turning point in human thought, or a coincidence that a big theory has made too much of? In 1949 the philosopher Karl Jaspers named the centuries from about 800 to 200 BCE the 'Axial Age', grouping Confucius, the Buddha, the Hebrew prophets, Zoroaster and the Greek philosophers. In his view they all turned from myth and ritual toward reflection, ethics and a transcendent order. The idea was revived by sociologists and popular writers. Critics raise strong objections. The figures were not truly contemporary, other civilizations are left out, and coincidence is treated as a cause. Researchers have also tested the idea with data. One study linked new moral teachings to rising prosperity; another, using a large historical database, found 'axial' features in many places long before 800 BCE. What survives? Several literate traditions across Eurasia did, in the 1st millennium BCE, produce texts and ideas that became the core of later religions and philosophies. Pages 7.8 to 7.11 look at four of them in turn. Whether they belong to one 'age' with a single cause is far less certain. Israel Amos, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Second Isaiah 8th-6th century (7.11) Persia Zoroaster uncertain; scholars suggest c. 1000, tradition the 6th century (7.8) India the Upanishads, the Buddha, Mahavira c. 600-400 (7.9) China Confucius, Laozi 6th-5th century (7.10) Greece Socrates, Plato 5th-4th century (8.3) For a student of politics, the question matters: if these traditions arose independently, ideas of justice and human dignity have many roots, not one.

s: the first world empire and an ancient prophet
x: In little more than a decade Cyrus of Persia conquered the Medes, Lydia and Babylon, creating the largest empire the world had yet seen. Its kings worshipped Ahura Mazda, the Wise Lord, the god of a prophet named Zoroaster, whose ideas some scholars think shaped Judaism and, through it, Christianity and Islam. The Medes of north-western Iran helped destroy Assyria in 612 BCE. Their Persian neighbour Cyrus II overthrew the Median king about 550, took Lydia about 547/546, and Babylon in 539 (7.4). His son Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525. Darius I, after seizing the throne, carved his story on a cliff at Bisotun in three languages. Zoroaster, or Zarathustra, is far harder to place: many specialists now date him to about 1000 BCE, but proposals range across a thousand years. His hymns, the Gathas, praise Ahura Mazda and call each person to choose between two spirits, good and evil. The Persian kings worshipped Ahuramazda, but whether they were Zoroastrians is debated. Did Persian religion influence Judaism? Some scholars argue that ideas of angels, demons, the end of the world and the resurrection of the dead came partly from Persia. Others point out that the clearest biblical text on resurrection, Daniel 12:2, is late, and the Zoroastrian texts were written down later still. What is certain is that the Bible praises Cyrus as the Lord's 'anointed' (Isaiah 45:1). c. 1750-1500 BCE language of the Gathas, close to the Rigveda c. 1000 BCE closest to a consensus 6th century BCE later Zoroastrian tradition; generally doubted Compare the debate over Ugarit and the Bible (6.7): sharing ideas with neighbours is not the same as borrowing them, and the direction of influence is often hard to prove.

t: India: from the Vedas to the Buddha
s: rebirth, renunciation and the middle way
x: In the Ganges valley, as new cities and kingdoms rose, teachers asked what the self is and how to escape an endless cycle of rebirth. Their answers became Hinduism's Upanishads, Jainism and Buddhism. The Vedas, hymns and rituals composed in Sanskrit from about 1500 BCE, were followed by prose ritual texts, the Brahmanas. One tells of the sacred fire being carried east into the Ganges plain, where iron, cities and coins appeared: India's 'second urbanisation'. Sixteen 'great states' competed for power, Magadha and Kosala chief among them. Vedic texts divided society into four classes, though the model was more ideal than real. The Upanishads taught that the self (atman) is one with brahman, the reality behind all things, and that deeds shape rebirth. Wandering ascetics rejected the priests' authority. One was Mahavira, who taught strict non-violence and gave Jainism its classic form. Another was Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, 'the awakened one'. The Buddha's dates are uncertain by a century. Tradition places his life in a few sites of the middle Ganges, and excavations at Lumbini in 2013 found an early shrine whose date and meaning are debated. His teaching starts from the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its cause in craving, its end, and the path to that end. long chronology c. 566-486 Pali texts of Sri Lanka Richard Gombrich c. 484-404 re-analysis of the long chronology short chronology death c. 370 Sanskrit texts preserved in East Asia Compare the debate over the Rigveda and steppe ancestry (5.3), and the Mitanni treaty's Vedic gods (6.3).

s: the Spring and Autumn period, 770-476 BCE
x: After 770 BCE the Zhou kings (5.9) reigned but no longer ruled. Rival states fought for supremacy, and in that disorder Confucius taught that society could be restored through virtue, ritual and right relationships. The Spring and Autumn period, 770 to about 476 BCE, takes its name from the annals of the small state of Lu. Powerful lords, the 'hegemons', kept a fragile order in the king's name. By the end, the great states of Jin, Qi, Chu, Qin, Wu and Yue were fighting for survival. Confucius, a teacher from Lu, by tradition lived 551-479 BCE. He held that rulers should govern by moral example, that ritual expresses and shapes respect, and that names should match reality: 'let the ruler be a ruler'. His key ideas are ren, humaneness, and li, ritual propriety, embodied in the junzi, the exemplary person. His sayings, the Analects, were gathered after his death; how early the collection took shape is debated. Daoism traces itself to Laozi, a shadowy figure whom tradition makes an older contemporary of Confucius. Many scholars think the Daodejing, with its teaching of the Way (dao) and effortless action, grew out of sayings circulating in the 4th century BCE and settled into roughly its final form in the 3rd. The Art of War, attributed to Sunzi, belongs to the same world of states at war. Confucius 551-479 Analects virtue, ritual, right relationships Laozi 6th century (legendary) Daodejing the Way; non-action Sunzi 6th-5th century (legendary) Art of War winning without fighting Compare the Mandate of Heaven (5.9): Confucius looked back to the early Zhou as a golden age of virtuous rule.

Between the 8th and 6th centuries BCE, Israel's prophets denounced injustice in the name of their God, and by the end of the exile one of them proclaimed that there is no other god at all. How and when Israel's religion became monotheism is one of the great questions of religious history. Amos, a shepherd from Judah, preached in the northern kingdom in the 8th century. He and his successors put justice above ritual: Amos has God reject the festivals of those who 'sell the righteous for silver', and Micah sums up what God requires: 'to do justice and to love kindness and to walk humbly with your God'. The book of Isaiah probably holds the words of more than one prophet. Popular religion was more varied than the prophets wished. Inscriptions from about 800 BCE bless 'by Yahweh of Samaria and by his asherah'. About 621, King Josiah, according to 2 Kings, purged the temple of objects made for Baal and Asherah after a 'book of the law' was found, often identified with Deuteronomy. Many scholars think the history from Deuteronomy to Kings was edited in this period and during the exile. In the exile, Second Isaiah declared: 'I am the Lord, and there is no other; besides me there is no god'. Many critical scholars see full monotheism emerging only then, out of earlier religion that knew other gods. Others find the denial of other gods much earlier, or question whether the modern word fits. Evidence from Elephantine in Egypt shows Judean soldiers keeping their own temple of YHW in the 5th century, with no clear sign of a written Torah. Many scholars think the Torah took final shape in the Persian period, and one argues that ordinary Judeans observed it widely only centuries later. Amos, Micah, Isaiah biblical text justice above ritual Kuntillet 'Ajrud, c. 800 inscription 'Yahweh ... and his asherah' 2 Kings 22-23 biblical text Josiah's reform Isaiah 45:5 biblical text 'besides me there is no god' Elephantine papyri, 5th century documents a Judean temple in Egypt Compare Akhenaten's Aten (4.8) and the Ugaritic gods El and Baal (6.7). Israel's monotheism grew in a world full of gods, and in argument with it.

s: the classical Mediterranean, c. 500 BCE to 250 CE
x: In 500 BCE the largest state on earth was Persia, and the Greeks were a scatter of quarrelling cities on its western edge. By 150 CE one empire, Rome, ruled every shore of the Mediterranean. This chapter follows that shift, and the ideas that came out of it: democracy, the republic, history-writing, rabbinic Judaism and Christianity. The story has four acts. First the Greek cities beat off Persia, and Athens built a democracy and an empire. Then Alexander of Macedon conquered Persia itself, and his generals' kingdoms spread Greek language and cities from Egypt to Afghanistan. Meanwhile Rome conquered Italy, destroyed Carthage and absorbed the Greek kingdoms one by one. Finally the Roman Republic gave way to emperors, whose peace lasted, with interruptions, into the 2nd century CE. This is the first period in this book for which we have real historians. Herodotus wrote the history of the Persian Wars a generation after them; Thucydides wrote about a war he fought in, and told his readers how he composed his speeches. Polybius explained Rome's rise to the Greeks, Livy told Rome's story to the Romans, and Josephus, a Jewish general who changed sides, wrote the history of his own people's war with Rome. All of them had views and loyalties, and all of them made up speeches. So historians test the texts against other evidence. Inscriptions preserve official records that the writers never quote. Shipwrecks map the rise and fall of seaborne trade, though not perfectly. And the Greenland ice sheet holds a year-by-year record of Roman mining and smelting, written in lead. And new texts are still appearing: scrolls burned by Vesuvius are being read by X-ray and machine learning. Herodotus c. 430s-420s BCE the Persian Wars numbers inflated; speeches invented Thucydides from 431 BCE the Peloponnesian War speeches give 'the general sense' Polybius 2nd century BCE Rome's rise, 220-146 BCE admirer of Rome and of his patrons Livy late 1st century BCE Rome from its founding early books mostly legend; 35 of 142 books survive Josephus 70s-90s CE Judea and the Jewish War a participant, writing under Roman patrons Greenland ice 1100 BCE-800 CE, year by year lead from mining and smelting a proxy, not a measure of the whole economy

Twice in ten years the largest empire on earth sent forces against a scatter of small Greek cities, and twice it went home. The Greeks made the story into the founding legend of the West; the Persian records show how small a frontier war it was from the other side. The Greek cities of the Anatolian coast had lived under Persia since Cyrus (see 7.8). Around 499 BCE they rose in revolt, and Athens and Eretria sent ships to help. The revolt was crushed by 494, and Darius sent a punitive force across the Aegean. At Marathon in 490 the Athenians and their Plataean allies beat it on the beach. A Persian administrative tablet places a man named Datiya, probably the Persian commander Datis, carrying royal documents in the west four years earlier. Ten years later Xerxes came himself, with an army that crossed the Hellespont on a bridge of boats and a fleet that was spared the storms off Mount Athos by a canal cut across the peninsula. Leonidas held Thermopylae for two days in August 480, the Persians burned an empty Athens, and in September the Greek fleet trapped the Persian ships in the strait of Salamis. In 479 the Greeks won on land at Plataea and destroyed the remaining Persian fleet at Mycale. Almost all we know comes from Herodotus, writing a generation later. His numbers cannot be right: an army of millions could not have been fed. His speeches and his scenes at the Persian court are reconstructions. Yet the Athos canal is real, and so are the burned layers of Athens. The Persian side survives only in administrative tablets from Persepolis, and in royal inscriptions that call the Greeks Yaunā, the Ionians. Marathon 490 BCE Athenian victory Herodotus: 192 Greek and 6,400 Persian dead Thermopylae August 480 Persians force the pass 300 Spartans among several thousand Greeks Salamis September 480 Greek naval victory about 370 Greek ships against perhaps 800 Plataea 479 Greek victory on land one modern estimate: 200,000 men in all Mycale 479 Persian fleet destroyed - The Book of Esther is set in Susa at the court of King Ahasuerus (Esther 1:1-2), the Hebrew form of the name the Greeks wrote as Xerxes. Most scholars read it as a story rather than a chronicle. No Persian record mentions Esther; Persepolis tablets name officials called Marduka, but whether one of them is Mordecai is disputed.

s: how it worked, and who it left out
x: For almost two centuries the citizens of one Greek city governed themselves directly: they voted on war and peace in person, filled most offices by lottery and sat by the hundred on juries. It was the most radical democracy in history, and most of the people who lived under it had no vote. The system began with Cleisthenes, who in 508/7 BCE broke the power of the old aristocratic clans by mixing the population into ten new tribes. Each tribe sent 50 men, chosen by lot, to a Council of 500, which prepared business for the Assembly of all citizens on the Pnyx hill. The lottery was the point: it gave every citizen an equal chance at office. The great exception was the generals, who were elected, because a city at war could not leave command to luck. The Athenians invented ostracism to guard against tyranny. Each year they could vote to send one leading man into exile for ten years, without a trial; he kept his property and came back afterwards. Thousands of the potsherd ballots survive, many of them with the names of famous politicians scratched on them. Under Pericles, from the 450s, Athens began to pay citizens for jury service, so that poor men could afford to take part; juries of hundreds of citizens, 201 for small private suits and 501 or more for public cases, decided them with no professional judges. The same Pericles narrowed who counted as a citizen: from about 451 BCE, both parents had to be Athenian. Women, slaves and resident foreigners could not vote at all. A rough reconstruction makes the voters about a quarter of the population. The number of slaves is one of the most disputed figures in ancient history. Democracy at home went with empire abroad. The Delian League, formed in 478 to keep fighting Persia, turned into an Athenian empire; in 454/3 its treasury moved to Athens, and the allies' contributions became tribute recorded on stone. Some of that money paid for the Parthenon and for the jurors' wages. Historians still argue over which Athenians gained most. Assembly every adult male citizen who came 6,000 needed for some votes 1 obol, then 2, then 3, in the 390s Council lot, 50 per tribe, aged 30 or more 500 paid Law courts lot juries of 201 to 1,500 3 obols a day Generals election 10 - Ostracism Assembly vote with potsherds one man exiled for 10 years -

For twenty-seven years the two greatest Greek powers, Athens at sea and Sparta on land, fought a war that neither could win quickly. Its historian, an Athenian general exiled for failing to save a city, wrote the first analysis of power politics, and students of international relations still read him. Thucydides looked past the quarrels that started the war to a deeper cause: Athens was growing, and Sparta was afraid. Athens had money, a navy and walls that ran down to its harbour; Pericles' plan was to abandon the countryside to Spartan raids, shelter the people inside the walls and fight at sea. The plan collided with disease. In 430 BCE a plague broke out in the crowded city. Thucydides caught it and survived, and his description of the symptoms is the earliest of its kind; perhaps up to a third of the people died, Pericles among them. DNA from a mass grave of the plague years pointed to typhoid fever, but the result was challenged at once and the disease is still unidentified. The war went on through a peace in 421, a catastrophic invasion of Sicily that destroyed an Athenian army and fleet in 413, and Sparta's final naval victory in 405, won with Persian gold. Its most famous passage concerns the small island of Melos, which wanted to stay neutral. Thucydides gives the Athenian envoys the bluntest statement of power politics in ancient literature, and then records what Athens did to Melos. He wrote as an exile, having lost Amphipolis as a general in 424. Defeat brought a pro-Spartan oligarchy, the Thirty, and a year of terror before the democracy was restored in 403. Four years later a jury of citizens condemned the philosopher Socrates to death for impiety and for corrupting the young. His pupil Plato drew the lesson that the crowd should not rule, and the case against democracy has been argued from his books ever since. 431-421 Archidamian War Spartan raids on Attica; plague in Athens (430-426); Pericles dies 421 Peace of Nicias a truce that lasted six years 416 Melos the island is conquered; its men killed, women and children enslaved 415-413 Sicilian expedition an Athenian army and fleet destroyed at Syracuse 411 Oligarchic coup democracy suspended for a few months 405-404 Aegospotami; surrender Sparta, with Persian money, wins at sea; the Thirty take power

In eleven years a Macedonian king conquered the Persian empire and marched to India. He left no working state behind him, but the kingdoms his generals carved out spread Greek language and cities from Egypt to Afghanistan for three centuries. Macedonia, on the northern edge of the Greek world, became its master under Philip II. His son Alexander inherited the army and a planned war on Persia in 336 BCE. He crossed into Asia in 334, took Egypt, where he founded Alexandria, and broke Darius III at Gaugamela in 331. He pushed on through Iran and Central Asia to the Indus, where his army finally refused to go further. He died at Babylon in 323, and his generals fought over the empire for a generation. What emerged was a world of Greek-speaking dynasties ruling non-Greek majorities: the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Seleucids in Syria, Mesopotamia and Iran, the Antigonids in Macedonia. Greek cities were planted as far east as the Oxus, where the French excavators of Aï Khanoum found a gymnasium, a theatre and the maxims of Delphi carved in stone. The Ptolemies made Alexandria the intellectual capital of the age. Their Library is the most famous lost institution of antiquity, but the figures for its size come from late writers, and one leading papyrologist thinks they are ten times too large. Its end is equally uncertain. For readers of the Bible, the great Hellenistic event is the Septuagint. Alexandria had a large Jewish community whose language was Greek, and in the mid-3rd century BCE the Torah was translated for them. A later legend has 72 elders do it at the king's request. The Septuagint became the Bible of the early Christians, which is why the Old Testament of many churches follows its order and contents. Antigonids Macedonia Pella 168 BCE Attalids western Anatolia Pergamon 133 BCE, by bequest Seleucids Syria, Mesopotamia, Iran Antioch 64 BCE Ptolemies Egypt Alexandria 30 BCE, the last The Septuagint's books and order differ from the Hebrew Bible: it includes works such as 1 and 2 Maccabees, Tobit and Judith. Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments keep many of them; Protestant Bibles follow the shorter Hebrew canon and print them, if at all, as the Apocrypha.

Under Alexander's successors the small temple-state of Judea was fought over by Egypt and Syria, revolted against a king who outlawed its religion, won some eighty years of independence, and fell to Rome. In these centuries Judaism took the forms, and split into the parties, that the New Testament knows. After Antiochus III's victory at Panium in 200 BCE, Judea belonged to the Seleucid kings in Antioch. In 168 Antiochus IV was turned back from Egypt by a Roman envoy, and the next year he garrisoned Jerusalem, outlawed the Sabbath and circumcision and set up an altar to Zeus in the Temple. 1 Maccabees, written from the rebels' side, calls it 'a desolating sacrilege'. A priestly family, the Maccabees, led a guerrilla revolt. In December 164 BCE they retook and rededicated the Temple, and the eight-day festival they founded is Hanukkah. The familiar story of the oil comes from a much later source. Judas' brother Simon won full independence in 142, and his descendants, the Hasmoneans, ruled as high priests and then kings until the Roman general Pompey took Jerusalem in 63. Rome then ruled through Herod, who rebuilt the Temple on a vast new platform. Josephus describes three 'philosophies' among the Jews. The Sadducees were the priestly elite; the Pharisees, ancestors of rabbinic Judaism, added an oral law to the written one; the Essenes lived apart under strict rules. In 1947 shepherds found the first of the Dead Sea Scrolls near Qumran: the oldest surviving manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible, along with rules, hymns and commentaries of a separatist group. Most scholars think that group was Essene, but not all. A 2025 study combining radiocarbon with AI analysis of handwriting has pushed many dates earlier, including a copy of Daniel made perhaps within a lifetime of the book's composition. Sadducees priestly elite; written Torah only; no resurrection known mainly from opponents; vanish after 70 CE Pharisees oral tradition alongside the Torah; resurrection described by Josephus, a Pharisee sympathiser, and by the Gospels Essenes communal life, strict purity; about 4,000 (Philo, Josephus) never named in the New Testament Qumran community the scrolls' rule books Essene identity is the majority view, not certain 1 Maccabees 1:54 calls Antiochus' altar 'a desolating sacrilege', and Daniel uses the same words for what is set up in the Temple: 'the desolating sacrilege' (Daniel 11:31; 12:11). The echo is one reason critical scholars date Daniel's visions to these years, 167-164 BCE; traditional readers take them as prophecy from the 6th century.

Rome began as a village of huts and became master of Italy under a constitution with no single ruler. A Greek hostage who watched it work thought its secret was that every part of the state could block every other, and the framers of the American Constitution read him. Archaeology finds a cluster of huts on Rome's hills by the 10th century BCE. The Romans' own story, of seven kings and a republic founded in 509, survives in writers of the 1st century BCE, and only scraps of early evidence back it. Historians now argue about how much of Livy's early Rome to keep at all, and new excavations, such as the city centre of nearby Gabii, keep adding to the picture. By the 3rd century BCE the system had a clear shape. Two consuls, elected for a year, commanded the armies. The Senate of former magistrates had no formal power to legislate, but controlled money and foreign policy. Assemblies of citizens elected magistrates, declared war and passed laws. The plebeians, the mass of ordinary citizens, had won their own officers, the tribunes, and a written code by a long struggle that ended in 287 BCE. Polybius, writing in the 2nd century BCE, explained Rome's success by its 'mixed constitution'.
