It is the ancestor of the idea of checks and balances; whether it describes how Rome really worked, where wealthy families dominated every office, is another question. The Republic conquered Italy by war and by alliance. A Greek king, Pyrrhus, came to stop it and won battles he could not afford. Rome bound the defeated as allies who supplied soldiers but could not vote. When they demanded citizenship and were refused, they rebelled in 91 BCE, and Rome conceded what they had asked for. Consuls 2, elected 1 year command armies; preside over Senate and assemblies Senate about 300 former magistrates for life finance, foreign policy, advice Tribunes of the plebs 10, elected by plebeians 1 year veto; protect citizens; propose laws Assemblies adult male citizens - elect magistrates, declare war, pass laws

Rome and Carthage fought three wars over a century for the western Mediterranean, and much of the second was fought in and for Spain. Rome needed nearly two centuries to conquer the peninsula; in the process it left Spain its language, its towns and a layer of lead in the Greenland ice. The first war, fought over Sicily, ended in 241 BCE with Carthage's defeat at sea. Carthage looked west for compensation. The Barcid family built a power base in southern and eastern Spain, with silver mines that paid for armies, and a new capital at Cartagena, still called after Carthage today. From Spain Hannibal launched the second war. He besieged Saguntum in 219, crossed the Pyrenees and the Alps with elephants, and destroyed three Roman armies in three years. At Cannae in 216 more Romans died in one afternoon than in almost any battle in history. Rome refused to make peace. Scipio cut off Hannibal's Spanish base by taking Cartagena in 209 and beat him in Africa at Zama in 202. Half a century later, in 146, Rome razed Carthage. Rome stayed in Spain, organising two provinces in 197 BCE. The conquest was long and brutal: the Celtiberian town of Numantia held out until 133, when its starving people surrendered, and the north was subdued only under Augustus. By then southern Spain was among the most Roman places outside Italy. Spanish descends from the Latin spoken there. The Romans also mined Spain on an industrial scale: gold at Las Médulas, where they washed away mountains, and silver at Riotinto. Smelting released lead that drifted to Greenland and fell in the snow, so the ice cores carry a year-by-year record of Iberian mining. 264-241 First Punic War; Carthage loses Sicily 237 Hamilcar Barca begins a Carthaginian domain in Spain 218-201 Second Punic War: Hannibal in Italy, Scipio in Spain and Africa 209 Scipio takes Cartagena 197 Nearer and Further Spain become Roman provinces 146 Carthage destroyed 133 Numantia falls 19 Cantabrian Wars end the conquest of Iberia

In a hundred years the Roman Republic went from reforming tribunes to rival generals, civil wars and finally one man's rule, dressed up as a republic restored. It is the most studied case in history of how a republic dies, and the arguments about why have never stopped. Conquest flooded Italy with slaves and wealth, and many small farmers lost their land. In 133 BCE the tribune Tiberius Gracchus pushed through a land reform and was clubbed to death by senators and their followers; his brother Gaius died in a similar outbreak of violence in 121. For the first time, Roman politics had been settled by killing. Then came the generals. Marius won seven consulships and showed what a general's veterans could do for him in politics. Textbooks credit him with a reform that gave Rome armies loyal to their commanders, though that story has recently been attacked. In 88 BCE Sulla became the first Roman to march an army on Rome, made himself dictator and killed his enemies from published lists. Caesar did it again in 49, crossing the Rubicon. Caesar's murder in 44 BCE did not restore the Republic. His adopted son Octavian won the next round of civil wars at Actium in 31 and became Augustus. His genius was to rule as a monarch while claiming to have handed the state back to the Senate and people. Historians still argue over whether the Republic was doomed, or was broken by particular men and choices. The system Augustus built lasted. In the 2nd century CE a run of emperors chosen by adoption ruled an empire from Britain to the Euphrates, a time Gibbon thought the happiest in human history. t: Jesus, Paul and the first Christians
s: Judea under Rome, c. 30 to 135 CE
x: A Jewish preacher was executed by a Roman governor in about 30 CE. Within a few decades his followers had communities across the eastern Mediterranean, and within a century Judea itself had been devastated by two failed revolts. Historians work here with an unusual mix of sources: letters, Gospels, a few Roman notices and a growing body of archaeology. Outside the New Testament, the firmest evidence is Roman. A stone from Caesarea names Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judea, and the historian Tacitus records that 'Christus' was executed under him. Josephus mentions Jesus twice, though one of the passages was later expanded by Christian copyists. Historians date Jesus' life to roughly 6-4 BCE to 30 CE, and almost all specialists, religious or not, accept that he existed. The earliest Christian writings are Paul's letters, from the 40s and 50s. Paul never met Jesus, but he knew his inner circle: he says he spent two weeks with Peter and met 'James the Lord's brother'. The Gospels came later, probably between about 70 and 95 CE, though a minority dates them earlier. From these sources most historians reconstruct a Jewish prophet who announced that God's kingdom was about to come; they disagree about much else. The first revolt against Rome broke out in 66 CE. In 70 the Romans took Jerusalem and burned the Temple, and its treasures were carried through Rome in triumph. The last rebels held out at Masada. Without the Temple, Judaism reorganised around the rabbis and the synagogue. A second revolt, under Simeon bar Kosiba (Bar Kokhba), ended in 135 with Jerusalem turned into a Roman colony that Jews could not enter. His own letters survive, and in 2023 a cave by the Dead Sea gave up Roman swords the rebels had hidden. Over these same decades, Christians and Jews drifted apart, more slowly than the traditional story says. Pilate inscription, Caesarea 26-36 CE Pilate's title: prefect of Judea Paul's letters 40s-50s CE earliest Christian writing; names James, Jesus' brother Gospel of Mark c. 70 CE (most scholars) the earliest Gospel Josephus, Antiquities 93/94 CE two passages on Jesus, one expanded by Christians Tacitus, Annals c. 115 CE execution of 'Christus' under Pilate Bar Kosiba letters 132-135 CE the leader of the second revolt, in his own words In Mark 13:2 Jesus looks at the Temple and says 'Not one stone will be left here upon another'. Most scholars read the chapter as written around the time of the destruction in 70 CE, one reason they date Mark then; those who date the Gospels earlier take it as a prediction made before the event.

s: how rich was Rome, and for whom?
x: Rome is the first economy that economists try to measure. There are no national accounts, so every number is built from proxies: census figures, wages, coins, shipwrecks, jars of olive oil, even lead in the Greenland ice. The answers range from 'nearly early-modern Holland' to 'bare subsistence'. Start with people. The empire probably held around 45 million under Augustus and 60 million by the 160s, but for Italy alone, scholars split between a low count of about 7 million and a high count of more than twice that. Enslaved people were a large minority, perhaps 10 percent across the empire and far more in Italy. Next, output. One widely cited reconstruction puts the 2nd-century economy at about 50 million tons of wheat-equivalent a year, very unequally shared. Whether ordinary people were comfortable or poor is one of the liveliest arguments in economic history. Trade left physical traces. Shipwreck counts peak around the 1st century CE, and on the banks of the Tiber, a hill of broken jars records some two and a half centuries of olive oil shipped from southern Spain to feed the capital. Lead in the Greenland ice rises with mining for silver; a 2025 study argues it also harmed Romans' health. Money tells a story of strain. The silver denarius was nearly pure under the Republic, and emperors short of cash quietly reduced its silver content. In 166 CE an epidemic came back with the armies from the east; it coincided with a cold spell, and how many it killed is now disputed again. By the 3rd century the wrecks, the lead and the coins all point downward, the story of Chapter 10. s: Parthia, Kush, Aksum, India, China and the Germans
x: Rome was never alone. Its armies were stopped in Mesopotamia and in Germany, its merchants sailed to India, its gold reached Han China only through middlemen, and an African kingdom kept the head of its first emperor buried under a temple step. To the east lay Parthia, an Iranian empire of horsemen that controlled the land routes between the Mediterranean and Asia. At Carrhae in 53 BCE Parthian archers destroyed a Roman army; for the next three centuries the two empires fought over Armenia and Mesopotamia without either winning for good. Beyond Parthia was Han China, the other great empire of the age (see Chapter 9). The two knew of each other only dimly. In 97 CE a Chinese envoy, sent west from the Tarim Basin by the general Ban Chao, reached the Persian Gulf and was talked out of going further by Parthian sailors; in 166 traders claiming to represent the Roman emperor reached China by sea. The sea was the open road. Ships left Egypt's Red Sea ports at midsummer and sailed home from India in December, out on one monsoon and back on the next (1.6). One papyrus prices a single returning cargo of pepper and ivory, and at Berenike excavators have found a statue of the Buddha. Up the Nile, the kingdom of Kush at Meroë traded with Rome and once raided it, and in the Ethiopian highlands Aksum was rising. In the north, Augustus tried to push the frontier from the Rhine to the Elbe. In 9 CE a German chief who had served in the Roman army lured three legions into a trap; after Germanicus' punitive campaigns of 14-16 CE, Rome gave up the plan and held the Rhine. Since the first finds in 1987, work at Kalkriese has probably located the battlefield, and new metal analysis ties finds there to one of the lost legions. t: India and China in the classical age
x: While Greeks, Persians and Romans fought over the Mediterranean, the two most populous regions on earth went through their own classical ages. China was unified for the first time and ruled by a bureaucracy whose model lasted two thousand years; India produced its first empire, its first royal inscriptions and the arithmetic the whole world now uses. In China, seven warring states became one in 221 BCE under Qin, and the Han dynasty that followed ruled for four centuries. In India, the Mauryas built an empire across most of the subcontinent, and their emperor Ashoka turned his regret for a war into a public creed. After a long age of foreign and regional dynasties came the Gupta kings, from about 320 CE. China has a historian to rival Herodotus: Sima Qian, whose Shiji became the model for every later dynastic history. But the most exciting evidence now comes out of the ground. Tombs and wells keep yielding bamboo and wooden slips: real laws, real accounts, lost books. Some of the most famous came from the antiquities market, which raises its own questions. For early India there is no Sima Qian. Historians use a Greek ambassador's lost book, known only in quotations, Ashoka's inscriptions, deciphered by a mint official in the 1830s, and coins, which are sometimes the only record that a king existed. s: iron, mass armies and the Hundred Schools, c. 476-221 BCE
x: For two and a half centuries a handful of Chinese kingdoms fought wars of a new scale and ferocity. The same pressure produced China's greatest age of philosophy, as thinkers competed to tell rulers how to survive, and lost books from that age keep coming out of the ground. War changed. Iron spread for tools and weapons, the crossbow let peasant conscripts fight like professionals, and armies grew to hundreds of thousands. Tradition records slaughter on an enormous scale. The states that survived were those that could count, tax and mobilise their people best. Thinkers offered rival answers. Mozi preached impartial care for all and condemned aggressive war. The Confucians split over human nature: Mencius thought it good, Xunzi thought it bad and in need of shaping. Others, later lumped together as 'Legalists', argued that only clear laws, rewards and punishments could make a state strong. Shang Yang put that into practice in Qin, and Han Fei turned it into theory. Qin's victory in 221 was, in part, a victory for their ideas. Archaeology has transformed this field. A tomb at Guodian held the oldest known Laozi, and other manuscripts preserve debates the classics forgot, such as whether a king should pass the throne to the worthiest man. Some of the most important, such as the Tsinghua slips, came from looters, but new scientific excavations keep adding more. Mozi c. 430 BCE impartial care; against aggressive war Shang Yang d. 338 BCE rank by merit in war and farming; harsh laws Mencius 4th century BCE human nature is good; rule by benevolence Xunzi c. 310-after 238 BCE human nature is bad; ritual and learning shape it Han Fei d. 233 BCE law, technique and power: the strong state

In 221 BCE the king of Qin finished conquering his rivals and called himself the First Emperor. His dynasty lasted only fifteen years, but the empire he built, with one script, one currency and one law, outlived him by two millennia. The Qin king Zheng took the last independent state in 221 BCE and invented a new title for himself. He replaced the old kingdoms with commanderies run by appointed officials and imposed a single script, coinage, system of weights and even axle width. Sima Qian remembers him as a tyrant who burned books and killed scholars, though historians now doubt parts of that story. His tomb is the most famous archaeological site in China: a buried city guarded by thousands of terracotta soldiers. Their weapons were made to standard patterns by small workshops working in parallel under central supervision. The emperor himself has not been disturbed, but mercury readings above the mound fit Sima Qian's story of a tomb with rivers of quicksilver. In 2025 an inscription on the Tibetan plateau was claimed to record his search for the elixir of life. The slips show what the history books cannot: a state that ran on paperwork. The tomb of a minor official held Qin's laws, down to rules on price tags; a well at Liye held a frontier county's daily records. They reveal a stretched administration, understaffed and run on forced labour. The First Emperor died in 210 BCE. Within four years rebels had destroyed his dynasty. Why it fell so fast is still argued over. Terracotta Army 1974 the scale and standardisation of the Qin state Shuihudi slips 1975 Qin statutes and an official's chronicle Liye well 2002 a frontier county's records Mercury survey 2016 readings above the mound fit Sima Qian's account Gyaring Lake inscription announced 2025 an expedition to collect 'yao' (disputed) Rome and Qin both standardised to rule: Rome its coins and roads, Qin its axles, weights and script. But Rome left Greek as the language of its eastern half and let many cities keep their own laws, while Qin imposed one script on everyone. Over the following centuries spoken Latin split into the Romance languages and spoken Chinese into many mutually unintelligible varieties, but the Chinese world kept a single written standard that people of every dialect could read.

The Han kept the Qin machine and gave it a softer face. For four centuries, with one interruption, it ruled through salaried officials who increasingly claimed to govern by Confucian principle, and the Chinese still call themselves 'the Han people'. Liu Bang, a commoner who had once been a minor Qin official, won the civil war that followed Qin's collapse. His dynasty kept Qin's centralised, salaried bureaucracy, and the numbers are impressive: one commandery alone had over two thousand officials on its books. Later Confucians told how Emperor Wu made their teaching the official ideology. Historians now think the change came more slowly and less cleanly. Wu's own reign is better remembered for war and monopolies (see 9.4 and 9.5), and for the historian Sima Qian, who was condemned for defending a disgraced general and castrated instead of being executed. In 2 CE the Han took China's oldest surviving census: almost 60 million registered people, and certainly more in reality. A few years later the regent Wang Mang took the throne, tried to remake society, and was swept away by floods and rebellion. The restored Eastern Han ruled from Luoyang, weakened by court factions and great landowners, until a religious rebellion and the warlords raised to fight it ended the dynasty in 220. In 81 BCE the Han court staged a debate over whether the state should run the salt and iron industries. The written record of it is one of the oldest surviving arguments about state ownership versus private enterprise, and the economist and the politician in you will recognise both sides. Emperor Wu's wars against the Xiongnu (see 9.5) were ruinously expensive. To pay for them, his ministers made salt, iron and liquor state monopolies and set up state trading offices to buy cheap and sell dear. They also replaced the coinage with the wuzhu, minted only by the state, which lasted in some form for seven centuries. After Wu's death the court called a debate. The Confucian literati argued that a government seeking profit corrupts its people; the minister Sang Hongyang answered that the frontier had to be paid for and that state trading kept prices steady. Critics added that state iron tools were poor and dear. The record we have was compiled later and is a literary reconstruction, not a transcript. The officials largely won, but the monopolies came and went for another century, and archaeology suggests they never reached everywhere. Most people were farmers who paid a light land tax and a heavy load of labour and military service. The census of 2 CE counted almost 60 million registered people. Over time, land concentrated in the hands of great families, who controlled local government and hid their tenants from the tax registers. Wang Mang, who usurped the throne in 9 CE, tried to stop this by nationalising land; his reforms collapsed, and so did he. The Han also gave the world paper. Tradition credits the court official Cai Lun in 105 CE, but older paper has been dug up in the north-west, including a fragment with a map on it whose status is still argued over. 118 BCE wuzhu coin introduced c. 119-110 BCE salt and iron monopolies set up 81 BCE the Debate on Salt and Iron 44-41 BCE monopolies abolished, then restored 2 CE 48 Iron Offices; census of 59.6 million 9-23 CE Wang Mang's land and coin reforms fail 85-88 CE monopolies revived, then dropped

s: the Xiongnu, Zhang Qian and the road west
x: China's greatest security problem for two thousand years was the steppe to its north. The Han first paid the nomad Xiongnu to stay away, then fought them for decades, and in doing so pushed Chinese power and Chinese envoys deep into Central Asia. The Xiongnu were a confederation of mounted herders who became a great power under Maodun at the same moment the Han was founded. For seventy years the Han emperors bought peace with silk, gold and brides. Ancient DNA shows the Xiongnu empire was itself a mosaic of peoples. Emperor Wu reversed the policy. From 133 BCE he sent huge armies onto the steppe; they drove the Xiongnu back but emptied the treasury, which is why his ministers turned to monopolies (see 9.4). Looking for allies, he sent Zhang Qian west to find the Yuezhi; Zhang was captured, escaped, and came home thirteen years later with the first Chinese reports of Ferghana, Bactria and lands beyond. Han armies later marched as far as Ferghana for its horses. The Xiongnu eventually split, and the eastern half submitted. To hold the road west, the Han built walls and beacon towers through the Hexi corridor to Dunhuang. At the relay station of Xuanquanzhi, archaeologists found tens of thousands of objects, including wooden slips that log the envoys, foreign delegations and officials who passed through. This network is what UNESCO now lists as the Silk Roads. The name itself is modern, and historians disagree about how much trade the routes actually carried. What the slips show most clearly is the state: soldiers, envoys and officials moving on government business, fed and housed at public expense. c. 209 Maodun leads the Xiongnu to c. 135 heqin: peace bought with silk and marriages 138 Zhang Qian sets out for the Yuezhi 133 Emperor Wu goes on the attack from 121 walls through the Hexi corridor 104 and 101 campaigns to Ferghana 65 envoy Chang Hui logged at Xuanquanzhi 51 the Xiongnu split; the eastern half submits

A few years after Alexander's army turned back at the Beas, a young adventurer named Chandragupta seized the throne of Magadha and built an empire across most of the subcontinent. We see it through a lost Greek travel book, a treatise on statecraft of uncertain date, and the ruins under modern Patna. Magadha, on the middle Ganges, had been the strongest kingdom of the Buddha's day (see 7.9). Under the Nanda kings it grew rich on land revenue. About 321 BCE Chandragupta Maurya overthrew them and went on to build the first empire to span most of India. When Alexander's successor Seleucus tried to recover the Indus lands, the two kings fought and then made a treaty: Seleucus gave up the territory in return for 500 elephants. Seleucus sent an ambassador, Megasthenes, whose book on India survives only in quotations. He describes Pataliputra as a vast walled city with 570 towers, run by boards of officials. Excavations in Patna have found part of a great hall of polished stone pillars, now being uncovered again. The other famous source is the Arthashastra, a manual on how a king should run a state: tax, trade, spies, law and war. Tradition makes its author Chandragupta's minister Kautilya, but scholars now think it was written by several hands and reworked over centuries. It is still one of the most hard-headed books on government ever written, and is often compared with Machiavelli. s: the emperor who said sorry, c. 268-232 BCE
x: Ashoka conquered Kalinga, an independent kingdom on India's east coast, counted the dead, and then had his regret carved into rock across his empire. His inscriptions are the first long texts from India that can be read, and the first time an Indian ruler speaks to us in his own words. Chandragupta's grandson Ashoka attacked Kalinga about eight years after he took the throne. In Rock Edict 13 he gives the toll in his own words and says he now prefers 'conquest by Dhamma'. That edict, however, was left out of the inscriptions set up in Kalinga itself. The edicts were carved on rocks at the edges of the empire and on polished pillars along its roads, at more than thirty sites. They speak in the local language and script: Prakrit in Brahmi across most of India, Kharosthi in the north-west, and Greek and Aramaic near Kandahar, where Greek settlers lived. One edict names the Greek kings to whom Ashoka sent envoys, which lets historians date his reign. Ashoka's form of the script was forgotten for well over a thousand years until James Prinsep deciphered it in 1837. A 2025 claim of much earlier Brahmi remains unconfirmed. What did Ashoka want? The edicts urge respect for parents, kindness to animals, tolerance of all sects and honest officials, enforced by special 'dhamma ministers'. Ashoka was a Buddhist, but scholars disagree about whether his dhamma was Buddhism, a civic morality for a diverse empire, or a tool of control. Within fifty years of his death the empire was gone. A general killed the last Maurya in about 185 BCE, and later Buddhist writers made him a persecutor. Why the empire collapsed so fast is one of the classic debates of Indian history. most of India Prakrit in Brahmi Girnar, Kalsi, Dhauli, Delhi-Topra pillar north-west (Pakistan) Prakrit in Kharosthi Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra Kandahar (Afghanistan) Greek and Aramaic bilingual edict, found 1958 Lumbini (Nepal) Prakrit in Brahmi pillar marking the Buddha's birthplace

s: Greeks, Kushans and the Tamil south, c. 185 BCE-300 CE
x: For five centuries after Ashoka no single power ruled India. Greek kings from Bactria, nomad Kushans from Central Asia and merchant kingdoms in the Deccan and the far south made the subcontinent a crossroads, and in this crowded world the first images of the Buddha were carved. The Greeks of Bactria (see 8.4) crossed the Hindu Kush as the Mauryas fell. Their best-known king, Menander, ruled the Punjab, and a Buddhist text remembers him debating a monk. Then came the Kushans, a nomad people from Central Asia, whose empire at its height ran from the Oxus to the Ganges. An inscription found in 1993 gave their royal line, but the date of their greatest king, Kanishka, has been argued about for a century. Under the Kushans the Buddha was first shown in human form, in Gandhara in a style borrowed from Greek and Roman sculpture and at Mathura in an Indian one. New Buddhist scriptures, the Mahayana sutras, were already being copied in Gandhara. Further south, the Satavahanas built an empire in the Deccan on the profits of trade with Rome. On the coasts, ports such as Arikamedu and Pattanam received Roman wine and oil jars, and the Tamil kingdoms produced the Sangam poems, among the finest early literature of India. How old Tamil urban culture is has become a political question. Under the Gupta kings northern India produced Kalidasa's poetry, Aryabhata's astronomy, the first stone temples and the decimal arithmetic that the whole world now uses. Whether to call it a golden age, and for whom, is another matter. The Guptas rose in the old Magadhan heartland and counted their era from 319/320 CE. Samudragupta's court poet boasted of his conquests on an Ashokan pillar, and his gold coins show a king who was warrior, priest and musician at once. His son Chandragupta II took western India from the Shakas, and was honoured at the cave temples of Udayagiri. Sanskrit literature reached a high point; Kalidasa may have written at his court. Aryabhata calculated with decimal place value and argued that the Earth spins. When the place-value system with zero began is hotly argued: the Bakhshali manuscript was announced as the oldest example, but its leaves date centuries apart, and the first known rules for calculating with zero are Brahmagupta's in 628. Hindu worship moved into permanent stone temples. Nationalist historians called this India's golden age; others answer that its glories belonged to a narrow elite while caste rules hardened. The great law book of caste, the Manusmriti, was probably already a few centuries old. Hun invaders from Central Asia took Gandhara around 440. Skandagupta drove back their first attack in the 450s, but around 500-530 their kings Toramana and Mihirakula overran much of the north-west and central India; Gupta power never recovered, and by the mid-6th century the dynasty had faded away. s: to Sri Lanka, Central Asia and China
x: Buddhism was one of the first religions to spread far beyond the culture that produced it. Carried by monks and merchants along the land and sea routes of 9.5 and 8.11, it reached China by the 1st century CE, and by 400 Chinese monks were walking to India to fetch better texts. Sri Lanka's chronicles credit Ashoka's own son with bringing Buddhism to the island, and it has been a Buddhist land ever since. In Central Asia, oasis cities on the routes north and south of the Taklamakan built monasteries and cave temples. In China the earliest firm record is an imperial edict of 65 CE about a prince who honoured the Buddha. The famous story of an emperor's dream and a mission to India is a later legend. Translation began in earnest with An Shigao, a Parthian, in Luoyang, and reached its peak with Kumarajiva, who arrived in Chang'an in 401. Some early 'Buddhist' carvings in China may be much later than once thought. In 399 the monk Faxian set out to find complete monastic rules. He crossed the deserts and mountains to India, stayed years in the Ganges valley and in Sri Lanka, and came home by sea. His record is one of our best descriptions of Gupta India. By the 5th century Chinese rulers were sponsoring vast cave temples at Dunhuang and Yungang. Mahinda (tradition) Ashoka's India Sri Lanka c. 250 BCE An Shigao Parthia Luoyang c. 148-170 CE Kumarajiva Central Asia Chang'an arrived 401 Faxian China India and Sri Lanka, and back 399-c. 412

s: two empires at the two ends of Eurasia
x: Around 100 CE two empires of similar size and population ruled the two ends of Eurasia. They knew almost nothing of each other. Comparing them is one of the liveliest fields in history, and the biggest question is not why they fell but why one came back and the other never did. The similarities are striking. Each covered about 4 million square kilometres and held some 60 million people. A 2025 study finds that income was about as unequally shared in both, though the Han elite took a larger share. Both, by modern standards, taxed lightly. The differences are in how they governed. The Han ran a bureaucracy of some 120,000-130,000 salaried officials, recorded in the dynastic history; Rome made do with about 600 senators and perhaps 20,000 knights, leaning on cities to govern themselves. One historian sums it up as soldiers versus scholar-officials. Rome spent far more on its standing army; the Han spent a much larger share of its defence budget paying foreign peoples to keep the peace. Even their money differed: China's coins were bronze tokens, Rome's were precious metal. Both empires broke up, the Han in 220 and the western Roman empire in the 5th century. China was briefly reunited under the Jin in 280 and lastingly under the Sui in 589, and again and again afterwards, while no one ever rebuilt the Roman world. Walter Scheidel argues that this 'First Great Divergence' shaped the whole later history of the world, because a Europe of competing states could innovate as no single empire would. Area about 4 million km² about 4 million km² People 57.7-59.6 million registered (census, 2 CE) about 60-75 million (estimates, 2nd century; see 8.10) Gini coefficient (estimate) 0.48 0.46 Top 1% share of income (estimate) 26% 19% Central officials about 120,000-130,000 (Han history) c. 600 senators, c. 20,000 equestrians Coinage cast bronze wuzhu struck gold, silver and bronze After the fall briefly reunited 280; lastingly 589 never reunified

Between the crises of the 3rd century and the Abbasid revolution of 750, the Roman empire became Christian and split in two, its western half broke into kingdoms, Persia had its last great dynasty, and a new faith from Arabia created an empire larger than Rome's. Historians call these centuries 'late antiquity', and they argue about whether to tell them as a fall or a new beginning. Five acts. In the 3rd century Rome nearly broke apart and Persia gained a new, aggressive dynasty. Diocletian and Constantine rebuilt the empire, and Constantine made it Christian. The West fragmented in the 5th century, while the East, under Justinian, codified Roman law and fought off plague. Then, from the 630s, Arab armies inspired by a new prophet took half the Roman empire and, by 651, all of Persia, and by 750 their caliphs ruled from Spain to Central Asia. For two centuries the period was told as Gibbon told it, as decline. Peter Brown taught historians to see a world of new religions, new art and new communities instead. The argument is still alive (see 10.4). New kinds of evidence are reshaping it. Papyri from Egyptian rubbish dumps show ordinary people's lives. Greenland ice and Alpine tree rings measure mining and climate year by year, and sediment cores tie epidemics to cold spells. Ancient DNA shows who moved where. Papyri Oxyrhynchus, Egypt taxes, prices, letters, early Bible copies Coins Roman antoniniani; Umayyad dinars state finances; public identity Ice cores Greenland lead record mining and smelting, year by year Tree rings Alps and Altai summer temperatures; the cold of the 530s-540s Sediment cores Gulf of Taranto regional climate Ancient DNA 1,500 genomes (2025); plague victims migration; the pathogens of epidemics

In the middle of the 3rd century the Roman empire nearly fell apart. Emperors came and went in quick succession, a new Persian dynasty captured one of them, and the silver coinage collapsed. Diocletian rebuilt the state by making it bigger, more bureaucratic and more expensive. In Iran, a new dynasty replaced the Parthians: the Sasanians, who claimed the heritage of the ancient Persian kings. Its second king, Shapur I, defeated three Roman emperors, by his own account, and in 260 took one of them, Valerian, prisoner. Christian writers turned Valerian's fate into a morality tale. Shapur settled Roman captives in Iran as builders and engineers. Rome's emperors paid their armies by putting less silver in each coin. By the 260s the main silver coin was mostly copper. Prices rose, the state took more of its taxes in kind, and plague returned in the 250s. Diocletian, a soldier from the Balkans, ended the crisis. He divided the empire among four rulers, rebuilt taxation on regular assessments of land and people, enlarged the army and reformed the coinage. He also tried to fix prices by law, and failed. In 303 he turned on the Christians in the last and fiercest persecution, which ended only in 311. c. 224 Ardashir founds the Sasanian dynasty 249-268 the silver coinage collapses 260 Shapur I captures the emperor Valerian 286-293 Diocletian's tetrarchy: four emperors 301 Edict on Maximum Prices 303-311 the Great Persecution Diocletian's Price Edict is the most famous price control of the ancient world: maximum prices and wages for about 1,000 items, enforced by the death penalty, issued after decades in which debased coinage had driven prices up. Britannica calls it unenforceable; it was later revoked. Our only account of its effects is by the hostile Christian writer Lactantius, who says that 'men were afraid to expose anything to sale' until the law was abandoned. Economists often cite it as a textbook case of price caps causing shortages, but the evidence for that is thin.

In 312 a Roman emperor fought under a Christian sign. Within eighty years Christianity had gone from persecuted sect to the empire's official religion, with its creed defined by imperial councils. How fast it grew, and why, are still argued about. Constantine won control of the West at the Milvian Bridge in 312. Christian writers tell of a sign from heaven before the battle, though their accounts differ, and a recent study questions one of them. In 313 he and his eastern colleague granted freedom of worship to all. Constantine poured money into churches and summoned the bishops to Nicaea in 325, where they defined Christ as 'of one substance' with the Father against the priest Arius. The creed they began is still recited, and in 2025 a pope and a patriarch prayed together at the site. He also founded a new capital, Constantinople. One later emperor, Julian, tried to revive the old gods and died after two years. Under Theodosius, Nicene Christianity became the official faith and pagan sacrifice was banned. How did a small sect become the majority? Rodney Stark argued that steady growth of about 40 percent a decade, through families and networks rather than mass conversions, would be enough. Critics point out that the same rate soon becomes impossible, so growth must have slowed, and they debate why. Archaeology occasionally adds a datapoint: in 2024 a tiny inscribed silver amulet showed a Christian buried in Germany before 270. 311 Galerius' edict of toleration 312 Milvian Bridge 313 freedom of religion ('Edict of Milan') 325 Council of Nicaea 330 Constantinople inaugurated 361-363 Julian tries to restore paganism 380 Nicene Christianity made the official faith 391-392 pagan sacrifice banned

Rome's great rival for four centuries was a sophisticated empire of many faiths: Zoroastrian kings, Christian bishops, Jewish rabbis who wrote the Babylonian Talmud, and a prophet, Mani, whose religion spread from North Africa to China. The Sasanian kings presented themselves as champions of the old Iranian religion of Zoroaster (see 7.8), and their great fire temples were royal shrines. One high priest boasted of persecuting other faiths, but Richard Payne argues that the empire mostly included religious minorities in a hierarchy rather than persecuting them. The prophet Mani preached a new universal religion at Shapur I's court before dying in prison under Bahram I; his faith spread across Eurasia. Mesopotamia was home to one of the largest and most important Jewish communities of the age. Under its own leader, the exilarch, it governed its own affairs, and its rabbis produced the Babylonian Talmud, still the central text of Jewish law. Christians, many descended from Roman prisoners, built a church across the empire, suffered a long persecution under Shapur II, and in 410-424 organised themselves as the independent Church of the East. The state rested on farming the rich lands of Iraq and on silver. Its drachms circulated from Arabia to Central Asia, and Khosrow I's cash land tax outlived the dynasty. The empire may have held some 13 million people in its last century, before war with Rome and then the Arab conquests destroyed it (10.8). Zoroastrian Kartir, high priest religion of the kings Manichaean Mani (216-c. 274/277) patronised, then its founder imprisoned; he died in prison Jewish the exilarch; rabbis of Sura and Pumbedita self-government; the Babylonian Talmud Christian the catholicos of the Church of the East persecuted from 339; organised as a recognised church from 410

In the 5th century the western half of the Roman empire broke up into kingdoms ruled by Goths, Vandals, Franks and others. Whether that was a catastrophe or a gradual transformation is one of the oldest arguments in history, and new evidence, from cattle bones to ancient DNA, keeps changing it. Gothic refugees fleeing the Huns were let into the empire, mistreated, and rebelled. At Adrianople in 378 they killed an emperor and destroyed his army. In 410 another Gothic army sacked Rome itself. Augustine, a bishop in North Africa, answered those who blamed the Christian God by writing the City of God. In 476 the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus, conventionally the last in the West, was quietly deposed. For a generation of historians led by Peter Brown, this was a 'transformation': Roman law, Latin, cities and the Church carried on under new rulers. Others answer that it was a collapse, measurable in the ground. In much of the West, pottery, roof tiles, coins and even the size of cattle shrank. Ancient DNA now shows that real migrations of people took place, though not how large or violent they were. In Spain the Visigoths built the most lasting of the successor kingdoms, with its capital at Toledo. They were Arian Christians ruling Catholic subjects until King Reccared converted in 589; councils of bishops at Toledo then became the kingdom's lawmakers. The same councils passed increasingly harsh laws against the kingdom's Jews. The kingdom lasted until 711 (see 10.9). 378 Battle of Adrianople; emperor Valens killed 410 Visigoths sack Rome 413 Augustine begins the City of God 476 Romulus Augustulus deposed 589 Third Council of Toledo: Visigothic Spain becomes Catholic

In Constantinople the Roman empire carried on. Its most ambitious ruler, Justinian, codified Roman law, built the greatest church in Christendom and won back Africa and Italy. Then the first great plague pandemic and a sudden cold snap struck, and historians are still arguing about how much damage they did. Justinian, a Latin speaker of peasant stock from the Balkans and nephew of the emperor Justin I, came to the throne in 527. His lawyers condensed centuries of Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis. Rediscovered in medieval Italy, it became the basis of legal study across Europe and a main root of the civil-law systems of continental Europe, which much of Latin America later adopted. In 532 a riot nearly toppled him; he rebuilt the burned city centre around the Hagia Sophia. His generals retook North Africa from the Vandals and, after twenty years of war, Italy from the Goths. In 541 plague arrived in Egypt and the next year in the capital. Procopius saw it and gives terrifying figures. Ancient DNA has identified the killer as Yersinia pestis, the bacterium of the Black Death, and in 2025 its genome was recovered from a mass grave in Jordan. But how many died is one of the hottest arguments in the field. Nature struck in another way too. Huge volcanic eruptions in 536 and 540 brought what was probably the coldest decade in two thousand years. Whether the cold, the plague and the wars together explain the shrinking of the empire in the 7th century, and the success of the Arab conquests (10.8), is still being tested. 527 Justinian becomes emperor 529-534 Code, Digest and Institutes 532 Nika riot; Hagia Sophia begun (finished 537) 533-534 Vandal Africa reconquered 536 and 540 great eruptions; probably the coldest decade in 2,000 years 541-542 plague reaches Egypt, then Constantinople 552 Totila defeated; Italy reconquered

Arabia was not cut off from the late antique world. Its southern kings turned to Judaism, its northern tribes served Rome and Persia as Christian allies, and the two empires fought over its edges. Into this world, by the account of Muslim tradition, Muhammad was born around 570. In Yemen, the kings of Himyar gave up their old gods in the 380s for a single 'Lord of the Sky', and a Jewish community appears in their inscriptions. In the 520s a Jewish king fought the Christian kingdom of Aksum across the Red Sea, and was defeated. In the north, Arab Christian dynasties guarded the frontiers of Persia and Rome. Mecca, in the Hijaz between them, was a shrine town whose trade is still debated. Muslim tradition gives a clear outline of Muhammad's life: born in Mecca, called as a prophet at about 40, driven to Medina in 622, victorious over Mecca in 630, dead in 632. That outline was written down a century and more after his death. A Christian text that may date from the 630s mentions a prophet among the Arabs, and historians disagree about how much of the traditional story can be checked. What is not in doubt is the result. Muhammad united much of Arabia behind a new faith and a single leadership in Medina. Within two years of his death his successors were attacking the two great empires (10.8). Traditional Muslim classical and modern Muslim scholarship the sira's outline is reliable Sceptical Crone and Cook (1977) rebuild early Islam from non-Muslim sources Apocalyptic Shoemaker (2012) Muhammad expected the end and led the first attacks Ecumenical Donner (2010) a 'Believers' movement' open to Jews and Christians Methodological Hoyland (2007) no reliable test of authenticity; weigh each report

For Muslims the Quran is the literal word of God. For historians it is the one text that almost certainly goes back to the earliest Muslim community. Both readings can be set side by side, together with what radiocarbon dating of the oldest manuscripts now shows. The Quran is about as long as the New Testament: 114 suras, arranged roughly from longest to shortest. Muslims hold it to be God's own speech, revealed to Muhammad, and the text claims divine protection for itself. Muslim tradition says the caliph Uthman fixed a single standard text and sent copies to the provinces. Manuscripts now let historians test this. Leaves in Birmingham and other early Qurans are written on parchment from the 7th century, and the Sanaa palimpsest preserves, under a later text, a version whose wording differs from the standard one. Most scholars think the evidence fits a standard text fixed in the mid-7th century; a minority argue for about 700. The Quran speaks to readers of the Bible. It tells of Abraham building the Kaaba with Ishmael, honours all the prophets from Abraham to Jesus, and names a sura after Mary. On Jesus' death it differs sharply from the Gospels. Believers and historians read these shared stories differently. Abraham builds the Kaaba with Ishmael (2:127) no link with Mecca (Genesis) Moses his story is retold in many suras the central figure of Exodus-Deuteronomy Mary chosen above all women (3:42); sura 19 named after her mother of Jesus (Gospels) Jesus messenger and Messiah; not crucified, 'it was made to appear' so (4:157) crucified and risen (Gospels)

Within a dozen years of Muhammad's death, Arab armies had taken Syria, Iraq and Egypt from the two great empires of the age. Within a century they ruled from Spain to Central Asia. It is one of the fastest and most lasting conquests in history, and how it happened is still argued over. The two empires were exhausted. Rome and Persia had just fought a quarter-century war in which Persia took Jerusalem and Egypt and Rome won them back. Both had been hit by plague and by a sharp cooling of the climate. Into this world came armies united, for the first time, under a single religious and political leadership from Medina. Syria fell after the battle of the Yarmuk in 636. Iraq was opened by al-Qadisiyya, whose battlefield was located in 2024 from Cold War spy-satellite photographs. The last Sasanian king was hunted across Iran and killed in 651. Egypt fell in 639-642, and North Africa, after long Berber resistance, by about 700. The conquerors ruled from new garrison towns and left most things as they were. In Egypt, Christian clerks went on collecting the old taxes and no one was pressed to convert. Jews, Christians and Zoroastrians became protected subjects who paid a poll tax, grounded in a verse of the Quran; over time the tax also marked a lower status. Some historians argue that the early movement was more open than later tradition remembered. Conversion was slow: in Iran most people became Muslim only after 750. 614-628 Persia takes Jerusalem and Egypt; Heraclius wins them back 634 Arab armies enter Syria 636 Yarmuk: Byzantine Syria lost c. 636-638 al-Qadisiyya: Iraq opened 639-642 conquest of Egypt 642, 651 Nahavand; Yazdegerd III killed at Merv 670-698 Kairouan founded; Carthage taken

The first dynasty of caliphs ruled from Damascus over an empire stretching from the Indus to the Atlantic. They gave it an Arabic administration, an Islamic coinage and its first great monument, and in 711 their armies crossed into Spain, beginning nearly eight centuries of Muslim rule in Iberia. After a civil war over the succession, Mu'awiya of the Umayyad clan made the caliphate a hereditary monarchy based in Damascus. Under Abd al-Malik the empire became recognisably Islamic in its public face: Arabic replaced Greek and Persian in government, and new coins carried no images, only words of faith. In Jerusalem he built the Dome of the Rock, whose purpose is still debated, and whose inscriptions speak directly to Christians about who Jesus was. In 711 a Berber general, Tariq ibn Ziyad, crossed the strait and landed below the rock that still bears his name (Gibraltar, from Jabal Tariq, 'Tariq's mountain'), and defeated the last Visigothic king. Within a few years almost all of Iberia was under Muslim rule. In the northern mountains a small Christian force held out at Covadonga, and in 732 a raid into France was turned back near Tours. In 750 the Umayyads were overthrown by the Abbasids, who moved the centre of the caliphate to Iraq. One Umayyad prince escaped to Spain and founded an independent emirate at Córdoba. Al-Andalus left a deep mark on Spanish, which has thousands of words from Arabic. aceite oil azzáyt, oil (ultimately from Aramaic) ojalá I hope so 'if God wills' alcalde mayor al-qadi, the judge arroz rice Andalusi arráwz, from ar-ruzz (ultimately from Greek) cero zero sifr, empty (via Italian zero) almohada pillow almukhádda (Andalusi Arabic) The Dome's inscriptions echo Quran 4:171, which tells the People of the Book not to go to excess in their religion and not to speak of a Trinity, and they quote sura 112, which in Abdel Haleem's translation says of God, 'He begot no one nor was He begotten' (112:3). Placed on the Temple Mount, close to the great churches of Christian Jerusalem, the building is read by many historians as a public argument with its Christian neighbours.

By 700 Christianity was not one church but several, divided by arguments over how Christ could be both God and man. Some of the oldest Christian nations, Armenia, Georgia and Ethiopia, lay outside the Roman world altogether, and Persian monks had carried the faith to China. Kingdoms on Rome's edges converted early, often from the top down. Armenia's king was baptised in the early 4th century, Georgia followed, and in Aksum King Ezana put the cross on his coins. Ethiopia later traced its kings to Solomon and the Queen of Sheba through a medieval epic. The Nubian kingdoms on the Nile converted in the 6th century and kept a treaty with Muslim Egypt for centuries. Within the empire, councils of bishops tried to define the faith. Ephesus (431) condemned Nestorius over what to call Mary; Chalcedon (451) defined Christ's two natures. Much of Egypt, Syria and Armenia rejected Chalcedon, and their churches remain separate today. The church of the Persian empire, the Church of the East, went its own way too. Some of these divisions have recently been called largely misunderstandings. At both ends of the world, monks carried the faith further. Monks of the Church of the East reached the Chinese capital in 635. In the far west, Ireland, never part of the empire, received bishops in the 5th century, and its monks went on to found Iona and evangelise northern Britain. Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Latin West, Greek East accept Oriental Orthodox Egypt, Ethiopia, Syria, Armenia, India reject Church of the East Persia, Central Asia, China outside the Roman councils after Ephesus In 1 Kings 10:1-13 the queen of Sheba comes to Solomon 'to test him with riddles', exchanges gifts with him and 'returned to her own land with her servants'. The Ethiopian epic adds a son, Menelik, and the Ark of the Covenant, neither of which is in the biblical text.

s: China reunited, the steppe Turks, Teotihuacan and the Maya
x: The centuries that saw Rome divided and Islam born were turning points elsewhere too. China was reunited and dug its Grand Canal, a Turkic empire spanned the steppe, and in the Americas the greatest city of the age declined while the Maya reached their peak. China, divided since the Han apart from a brief reunion under the Jin (280-c. 316), was reunited in 589 by the Sui. They joined older canals into a system linking north and south, and exhausted themselves doing it. The Tang dynasty that followed in 618 (see 11.4) would make Chang'an, with perhaps a million people, probably the largest city in the world. On the steppe, a Turkic empire stretched from China to the Caspian, and in India Harsha briefly rebuilt a northern empire. In the Americas, Teotihuacan, a planned city of perhaps 100,000 people or more in the valley of Mexico, declined after about 550, its centre burned. Whether its signs were true writing is now being argued again. As Teotihuacan's influence faded, the Maya cities of the southern lowlands reached their height between 600 and 900. Laser scanning from aircraft has revealed far more of their houses, fields and roads than anyone expected. China Sui reunification 589; Grand Canal 605-610; Tang from 618 Steppe Turkic empire from 552 India Harsha, 606-647 Mexico Teotihuacan declines from c. 550 Maya lowlands Late Classic peak, c. 600-900

Between the Abbasid revolution and the Mongol invasions there was no single centre of the world. Instead several large, connected regions, the Islamic world, China, Latin and Greek Christendom, India and Southeast Asia, Africa's trading states and the Americas, each grew rich in its own way, linked by trade, pilgrimage and the movement of books. The Islamic world had a new capital at Baghdad, whose wharves received ships from China, India and East Africa. Song China printed books (11.4). Latin Europe revived under Charlemagne (11.5), Byzantium converted the Slavs (11.7), Scandinavians crossed the Atlantic (11.6), and around 1100 crusaders and Iberian kings turned Christendom's energies against Islam (11.3, 11.8). This chapter can draw on new kinds of evidence. In Cairo, Jews kept their used papers rather than destroy them, and one synagogue's storeroom preserved centuries of business letters and contracts. Arab geographers described distant lands: al-Bakri, from Córdoba, wrote about the African kingdom of Ghana, and al-Idrisi drew a map of the world for a Christian king of Sicily. And archaeology can test legend: Norse sagas told of voyages to North America, and the ruins have been found. Cairo Genizah Fustat (Old Cairo) Jewish merchants' letters, contracts and accounts Arab geographers Córdoba, Sicily descriptions of Africa, Europe and Asia Printed books Song China cheap books and wider literacy Archaeology and sagas Newfoundland Norse voyages to America Ancient DNA across Europe who moved where (11.6)

The Abbasid caliphs built a new capital at Baghdad. It became famous for paper, books and the translation of Greek science, before their empire broke into pieces ruled by other dynasties in their name. In 762 the caliph al-Mansur founded a new capital on the Tigris, a round city whose wharves received ships from China, India and East Africa. One such ship, wrecked off Indonesia in the 830s, still held over 50,000 Chinese bowls. The caliphs struck gold dinars that carried only inscriptions, and silver dirhams that had begun as copies of Sasanian coins. Paper came from China by way of Central Asia, though not necessarily as the famous story tells it. Officials in Baghdad adopted it for records, and books multiplied. Scholars, many of them Christians, translated Greek philosophy, medicine and mathematics into Arabic, though historians now doubt that the 'House of Wisdom' was the great academy of legend. Al-Khwarizmi's work gave the world the words 'algebra' and 'algorithm'. The empire did not hold together. Rival caliphs ruled in Córdoba (11.2) and, from 969, in Cairo, and in Baghdad itself real power passed to Persian and then Turkish military dynasties. 762 Baghdad founded 813-833 al-Ma'mun: translation at its height 836-892 caliphs at Samarra 945-1055 the Buyids control Baghdad 969 Fatimids take Egypt and build Cairo 1055 Seljuk Turks enter Baghdad

Around the year 1000 Córdoba was probably the largest city in Europe and the capital of a caliphate. Its Muslims, Christians and Jews produced major works of philosophy, poetry and architecture, and how they lived together is still argued over, in Spain and beyond. Abd al-Rahman III declared himself caliph in 929. His capital may have held 100,000 people, with its Great Mosque, later a cathedral, and the palace city of Madinat al-Zahra outside it. Jews rose high in government: Hasdai ibn Shaprut served the caliph, and in the 11th century Samuel ha-Nagid became vizier of Granada, though the community suffered a massacre a generation later. After 1009 the caliphate split into rival 'taifa' kingdoms, several of which paid tribute to the king of Castile. When Castile took Toledo in 1085 they called in the Almoravids from North Africa, who swallowed them, to be followed by the stricter Almohads. Under the Almohads Córdoba's Jews were forced to convert or leave; Maimonides grew up in exile. His Muslim contemporary Ibn Rushd became the West's great interpreter of Aristotle. Was this a golden age of tolerance? Historians are sharply divided, and the debate carries political weight in modern Spain. Ancient DNA adds that North African ancestry became established under Islamic rule and outlasted it. 929 Abd al-Rahman III declares the caliphate 1009-1031 civil war; the caliphate breaks into taifas 1066 massacre of Granada's Jews 1086 Almoravids defeat Castile at al-Zallaqa 1148 Almohads take Córdoba 1212 Almohads defeated at Las Navas de Tolosa

From the mountains of the north, small Christian kingdoms pushed south over four centuries until, by 1248, only Granada remained under Muslim rule. Spain's national story was later built around this advance, and the name of that story is now itself a subject of debate. The kingdom that began at Covadonga (10.9) moved its capital south to León. Navarre briefly dominated the Christian north and its king divided his realms among his sons, creating kingdoms of Castile and Aragon. Portugal became a kingdom in 1139 and took Lisbon with crusaders' help. The decisive gains came after the caliphate's collapse. Castile took Toledo in 1085, guaranteeing its Muslims their property and faith. There, scholars translated Arabic science and philosophy into Latin, passing Greek learning preserved in Arabic to the rest of Europe. Aragon took Zaragoza; a Castilian lord, El Cid, carved out a principality at Valencia, and later became the hero of Spain's great epic. Pilgrims came from all over Europe to the shrine of St James at Santiago. In 1212 a crusading coalition of Christian kings broke the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa, and within a generation Córdoba, Valencia and Seville had fallen. Historians now argue whether 'Reconquista', 'reconquest', is the right word for all this. 1085 Toledo (Castile) 1118 Zaragoza (Aragon) 1147 Lisbon (Portugal) 1212 Las Navas de Tolosa 1236 Córdoba (Castile) 1238 Valencia (Aragon) 1248 Seville (Castile)

s: rebellion, rice, print and paper money, 755-1279
x: Between the 8th and the 13th centuries China was transformed. Its government came to run on written examinations, its printers produced books in large numbers, and its merchants and officials began to use paper money. The Tang dynasty (see 10.11) nearly died in 755, when its general An Lushan rebelled. The revolt was crushed after eight years, but regional warlords held power until the Song reunified the country in 960. One famous death toll is generally considered too high. Under the Song the empire was run by scholar-officials chosen by examination, and from 1313 those examinations followed the Confucian 'Four Books' as edited by Zhu Xi, a syllabus that lasted until 1905. Fast-ripening rice from Southeast Asia let farmers in the south grow two crops a year, and the population passed 100 million. China also pioneered two technologies. Printing from carved wooden blocks produced the oldest dated printed book, a Buddhist sutra of 868. And the Song state took over merchants' paper notes to issue the world's first government paper money. Some historians speak of a Song 'industrial revolution' in iron and coal; others doubt the numbers behind it. 755-763 An Lushan rebellion 868 the Diamond Sutra, earliest dated printed book 960 Song dynasty reunifies China 1024 state paper money (jiaozi) in Sichuan 1127 the north lost; Song continues in the south 1190 Zhu Xi's edition of the Four Books Movable type was invented in China by Bi Sheng (990-1051), yet carved woodblocks remained the usual way to print there.

On Christmas Day 800 a Frankish king was crowned Roman emperor in Rome. His reign shaped the script, the books and the Church of western Europe. Charlemagne ruled the Franks and greatly enlarged their kingdom; on Christmas Day 800 the pope crowned him emperor. His biographer insisted he had not wanted it, but Britannica judges that king and pope planned the coronation together. A new, clearer handwriting developed partly under his patronage, and most of our knowledge of classical literature comes from copies made at his court. Why did the centre of Europe move north, from the Mediterranean to the Rhineland? Henri Pirenne famously blamed the Arab conquests; archaeologists answer that Roman trade had collapsed before Islam began. Michael McCormick showed that by 800 trade with the eastern Mediterranean was reviving, much of it in enslaved people. Historians also argue whether 'feudalism' describes this society at all. The Church reformed itself from within. Monasteries such as Cluny answered only to the pope, and reforming popes then demanded that kings stop appointing bishops. The clash came to a head when the excommunicated German king Henry IV stood as a penitent at Canossa in 1077, and was settled by compromise in 1122. 800 Charlemagne crowned emperor in Rome 910 Cluny founded 1076-1077 Henry IV excommunicated; penance at Canossa 1122 Concordat of Worms

s: raiders, traders and settlers, 793 to c. 1050
x: For two and a half centuries Scandinavians sailed from Newfoundland to the rivers of eastern Europe. They raided monasteries, traded slaves and silver, founded towns and states, and settled islands in the North Atlantic. New dating methods and ancient DNA have transformed what we know about them. The sack of Lindisfarne in 793 sent a shockwave through Europe, though it was not the first Viking raid on England. But the Vikings were traders as much as raiders. On Gotland, one hoard alone holds about 76 kg of silver and bronze, mostly Arabic coins (dirhams). In the east, Scandinavians known as the Rus' ruled river towns; a chronicle has them invited to Novgorod in 862, and whether they founded the state of the Rus' has been argued for three centuries; in the Soviet Union, anti-Normanist views were officially sanctioned. In the North Atlantic they settled Iceland, where an open-air assembly met from about 930, and briefly reached North America. At L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, wood cut with metal tools has been dated to the exact year 1021, using the trace of a cosmic-ray burst in 993 preserved in the tree rings. Ancient DNA has added detail. Vikings in England came mostly from Denmark, those in Iceland mostly from Norway, and Scandinavia itself had absorbed people from central Europe. A famous warrior's grave at Birka turned out to hold a woman, and scholars still disagree about what that means. 793 Lindisfarne sacked 862 Rurik at Novgorod (tradition) c. 870 youngest coin in the Spillings hoard c. 930 Althing founded in Iceland 1021 trees felled at L'Anse aux Meadows

The eastern Roman empire survived the Arab conquests and fought a bitter internal war over religious images. Then it revived, converted the Slavs, and reached its medieval height, before a quarrel with Rome in 1054 and a defeat by the Turks in 1071, which cost it most of Anatolia. For over a century Byzantium argued about icons. Emperors banned them as idolatry; a council restored them in 787; the images were restored for good in 843. Under the Macedonian emperors from 867 learning revived and the empire expanded, though one famous story of Basil II's cruelty is probably exaggerated. Byzantium also sent missions to the Slavs. Two brothers, Cyril and Methodius, created an alphabet for the Slavs and translated scripture into their language. In about 988 Prince Vladimir of Kyiv was baptised as part of a marriage alliance. Relations with Rome soured over authority and ritual. In 1054 papal legates excommunicated the patriarch of Constantinople at the altar of Hagia Sophia, though contemporaries saw it as a minor quarrel. The excommunications were lifted in 1965, and in 2025 pope and patriarch renewed their hope of reunion. Seventeen years after 1054, at Manzikert, the Seljuk Turks captured the emperor, and most of Anatolia passed to the Turks. 730 religious images banned 787 Second Council of Nicaea restores icons 843 icons restored for good 863 Cyril and Methodius go to Moravia c. 988 Vladimir of Kyiv baptised 1054 mutual excommunications 1071 Manzikert 1965 excommunications lifted The commandment the iconoclasts cited:

In 1095 a pope called on western knights to march to the East. Over the next two centuries crusading armies took and lost Jerusalem, massacred Jews and Muslims, built states in Syria and Palestine, and sacked Constantinople, the Byzantine capital. Few subjects in medieval history are judged so differently. At Clermont in 1095 Urban II summoned knights to help the Christians of the East, promising them remission of their sins; what exactly he said is uncertain, since only differing accounts survive. The first victims were Jews in the Rhineland. In 1099 the crusaders took Jerusalem amid great killing, and founded four states along the eastern Mediterranean. Muslim leaders revived the idea of jihad against the invaders. In 1187 Saladin destroyed the kingdom's army at Hattin and retook Jerusalem; his reputation for generosity is now judged more coolly. In 1204 the Fourth Crusade, deep in debt to Venice, turned on Constantinople instead and sacked it, an act still judged harshly. What counts as a crusade? Most historians now include papally authorised wars in Spain and the Baltic as well as in the East, and the overall verdict has moved from Steven Runciman's condemnation to a closer study of crusaders' own religious motives. 1095 Council of Clermont 1096 massacres of Rhineland Jews 1099 Jerusalem taken 1144 Edessa falls 1187 Hattin; Saladin retakes Jerusalem 1204 Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople 1261 Byzantines retake Constantinople

Gold from West Africa crossed the Sahara to Mediterranean markets, ivory and gold from the south flowed to Indian Ocean ports, and Ethiopian Christians carved churches out of rock. Arabic writers, archaeology and now ancient DNA let us see these African worlds in more detail than ever. Gold from south of the Sahara was the main cargo of the camel caravans across the desert, and the trade encouraged the Berbers' conversion to Islam. A detailed early description of the kingdom of Ghana comes from al-Bakri, who never went there, and who describes a capital of two towns, one for Muslim merchants and one for the king, and a king who taxed salt in gold. Further east, the kingdom of Kanem took shape by Lake Chad. On the east coast, Swahili towns such as Kilwa traded with Arabia, India and China. Ancient DNA from burials on this coast shows that close to half the ancestry of the people studied came from Asian migrants, at first mostly Persian men who had children with African women, while their language stayed African. Inland, Mapungubwe controlled the gold and ivory trade, before power moved north to Great Zimbabwe. In the Ethiopian highlands, Christian kings carved churches from the living rock at Lalibela. In Fatimid Cairo, a synagogue storeroom preserved the everyday papers of a Jewish community, from which S. D. Goitein rebuilt the Mediterranean world of the 10th to 13th centuries. Ghana West African Sahel gold, salt taxes; al-Bakri's account (1068) Kanem Lake Chad Muslim ruler from the late 11th century Kilwa Swahili coast Indian Ocean trade; oldest standing mosque on the coast Mapungubwe Limpopo valley gold and ivory trade, c. 900-1300 Lalibela Ethiopian highlands eleven rock-cut churches Fustat (Cairo) Egypt the Genizah: merchants' letters

South India's Chola kings built great temples and sent a fleet across the Bay of Bengal. In Southeast Asia, Indian religions inspired the monuments of Borobudur and Angkor Wat. In the north-west, raids from Afghanistan were followed by Ghurid conquests that created the Delhi Sultanate, and how one of the raids is remembered is still a live political issue. The Cholas of Tamil Nadu built great temples at Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram, still in worship today, and in 1025 their navy struck Srivijaya, the Buddhist trading power that controlled the Strait of Malacca. Why they did it is unclear. In Java, the Sailendra kings built Borobudur, a Buddhist monument on a vast scale. In Cambodia, the Khmer king Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat for Vishnu, at the heart of a sprawling, low-density city mapped by laser surveys; one model puts Greater Angkor's population at 700,000 to 900,000. From Afghanistan, Mahmud of Ghazni raided India repeatedly and in 1026 plundered the temple of Somnath. Historians disagree about his motives, and the memory of Somnath has become a national symbol, commemorated by India's government in 2026 and analysed by historians as a story built over centuries. By 1206 the Ghurid conquests had produced the Delhi Sultanate. Borobudur Java 8th-9th centuries Brihadisvara temple Thanjavur 1009-1010 Chola raid on Srivijaya Sumatra and Malaya 1025 Somnath raided Gujarat 1026 Angkor Wat Cambodia 12th century Delhi Sultanate founded north India c. 1206

Beyond the reach of Eurasia's webs, the Americas had their own: great towns on the Mississippi and in the deserts of New Mexico, and Maya and Toltec cities in Mexico. In the Pacific, Polynesian navigators settled the remaining islands of East Polynesia, reaching Rapa Nui and New Zealand. Cahokia, on the Mississippi, was the largest town north of Mexico, and its decline after about 1150 is now debated. In the deserts of New Mexico, Chaco Canyon was the centre of a network of 'great houses' linked by roads. As the great Classic Maya cities declined, the lowlands suffered severe, repeated droughts, some of which can now be dated year by year, though how far drought caused the collapse is debated. In the north, Chichen Itza flourished, its buildings closely resembling those of Tula in central Mexico. After the Society Islands, Polynesians settled all the remaining islands of East Polynesia in a single pulse of about a century, reaching Aotearoa New Zealand around 1280. Rapa Nui (Easter Island) was once held up as a warning of ecological self-destruction; new evidence suggests that story is wrong. Chaco Canyon New Mexico 850-1250 Tula central Mexico grew c. 900-1200 Chichen Itza Yucatán 10th-15th centuries Cahokia Mississippi valley peak c. 1050-1150 Society Islands settled East Polynesia c. 1025-1120 Rapa Nui and New Zealand settled East Polynesia c. 1190-1300

t: The Mongols and the Black Death
x: In the 13th century the Mongols built the largest contiguous land empire in history. Their rule linked China, Iran, Russia and the Middle East, and in the 14th century a plague from the steppe killed a large part of the population from Europe to Egypt. This chapter follows both stories and the worlds that recovered afterwards. Chinggis Khan and his heirs conquered an empire of some 23 million square km. Janet Abu-Lughod argued that Mongol rule tied Eurasia into a single 'world system' of trade, and that plague and the Mongols' loss of China helped break it apart; Europe's later dominance, she argued, was no historical necessity. Our sources come from every side. The Secret History of the Mongols gives the Mongols' own view; Rashid al-Din, a convert from Judaism who served the Mongol rulers of Iran, wrote their history from within their court; and the traveller Ibn Battuta saw the plague at first hand in Syria. Science now adds evidence no chronicler could. Ancient DNA has identified the Black Death's cause, lead in Alpine ice shows mining stopping as the plague struck, and tree rings record the cold summers that came just before it. The Secret History the Mongols' own account (12.1) Rashid al-Din the Mongol court in Iran (12.2) Ibn Battuta a traveller's eyewitness view of the plague Ancient DNA the cause and origin of the Black Death (12.3) Ice cores and tree rings mining collapse; cold summers before the plague

A Mongol chief named Temüjin united the peoples of the steppe, took the title Chinggis Khan and led his armies into China and Central Asia. Within two decades he had destroyed some of the great cities of the Islamic world. How to weigh that destruction against what followed is still argued over. Temüjin's birth year is uncertain. In 1206 a great assembly proclaimed him Chinggis Khan, and he organised his army in units of tens. He attacked the Jin dynasty of northern China in 1211 and took Beijing in 1215. Then he turned west. When a governor of the Khwarazmian empire massacred a caravan sent under his protection, Chinggis invaded; Bukhara, Samarkand and Urgench were sacked, and Merv was destroyed and never recovered its old prosperity. He died in 1227. Chroniclers recorded enormous slaughter, but no one can count the dead, and historians disagree about how to balance the empire's destruction against the order it later imposed. 1155, 1162 or 1167 Temüjin born 1206 proclaimed Chinggis Khan 1211 war on the Jin begins 1215 Beijing taken 1220-21 Bukhara, Samarkand, Urgench, Merv 1227 death of Chinggis Khan

t: The khanates and the Pax Mongolica
x: Chinggis Khan's descendants divided his empire. One sacked Baghdad and killed its Abbasid caliph, another ruled the Russian lands from the steppe, and Khubilai Khan made himself emperor of China. Under Mongol rule merchants, monks and envoys crossed Eurasia, and some wrote about what they saw. In 1258 Hülegü sacked Baghdad and put to death al-Musta'sim, the last Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, but two years later the Mamluks of Egypt stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut. Hülegü's descendants ruled Iran, and one of them, Ghazan, became a Muslim in 1295. On the western steppe the Golden Horde ruled the Russian principalities through their own princes, who collected its tribute. Russian tradition remembers this as the 'Tatar yoke', a view historians have challenged, and the phrase itself appears in Slavic writing only in the later 17th century, although Latin writers used it as early as the 13th. In China, Khubilai founded the Yuan dynasty and completed the conquest of the Song, though his invasions of Japan failed. Travellers crossed the empire in both directions: the friar William of Rubruck reached Karakorum, the monk Rabban Sauma travelled to Europe for the Mongol ruler of Iran, and Marco Polo described the court of Khubilai, though whether he really went there is debated. Yuan China, Mongolia Khubilai; Dadu (Beijing); paper money Ilkhanate Iran, Iraq Baghdad 1258; Ghazan becomes Muslim 1295 Golden Horde western steppe, the Rus' tribute through Russian princes; Kulikovo 1380 Chagatai Central Asia between the Yuan and the Ilkhanate

In the 1340s a plague reached the Mediterranean from the steppe and spread across Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. Ancient DNA has confirmed its cause and probable origin, but how it travelled and how many it killed are still being worked out. Graves in Kyrgyzstan dated 1338-39 have yielded the strain of plague from which the pandemic's lineages branched out. How it reached the Black Sea is less clear: one Arabic account of its rapid spread may be literature rather than report, and the famous story of corpses hurled into besieged Caffa may not explain its arrival in Europe. A new hypothesis links its arrival to grain shipped to Italy after a volcanic eruption and failed harvests. Between 1347 and 1351 the plague killed a larger share of Europe's people than any earlier epidemic or war. Estimates of how large a share range from about a third to about 60 percent, and pollen evidence suggests some regions lost far more than others. The plague also struck the Islamic world. In Egypt and Syria it kept returning, and its recurrences slowed population growth for a century and a half. 1338-39 plague deaths in the Chüy valley, Kyrgyzstan c. 1345 probable volcanic eruption; cold summers 1345-47 1346 siege of Caffa 1347 Italian cities import grain from the Golden Horde 1347-51 the Black Death in Europe 1348 plague in Syria

The Black Death left behind terror and opportunity. Jews were massacred as scapegoats, penitents whipped themselves in the streets, and the survivors, now scarce, demanded higher wages. Economists still argue over whether the plague set western Europe on a different path from the rest of the world. Panic sought culprits. Jews were accused of poisoning the wells, and in town after town they were killed: in Strasbourg the chronicler wrote that 'the money was indeed the thing that killed the Jews'. The pope condemned the accusation, and one modern study suggests persecution was less likely where Jews were economically important. Bands of flagellants, too, alarmed the Church. With so many dead, labour was scarce and wages rose. England tried to freeze them by law, and resentment helped spark the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, whose preacher John Ball questioned the very idea of nobility. Over the following century serfdom faded in the West but hardened in the East. Did the plague make the West rich? Pamuk traces a wage gap between north-west Europe and the rest after 1450; Voigtländer and Voth argue high death rates kept incomes high; a recent survey finds the gains lasted only in some places, and the plague's effect on inequality is less simple than once thought. Ancient DNA suggests it may even have left a mark on our immune systems. Şevket Pamuk (2007) wages held up in England and the Low Countries; a gap opened after 1450 Voigtländer and Voth (2013) plague, war and cities kept death rates and incomes high Jedwab, Johnson and Koyama (2022) the wage rise lasted only in some parts of Europe Guido Alfani (2022) effects on inequality are 'much more complex' Robert Brenner economic models neglect 'class relationships and class conflicts'

England and France fought for over a century, the Church split between rival popes, and reformers challenged its teachings. In Italy, scholars hunted for lost classical texts and bankers grew rich, and in Mainz a new way of printing began. The Hundred Years' War ended with England almost expelled from France. In its course a young woman, Joan of Arc, raised the siege of Orléans, saying that saints had spoken to her. The papacy, long resident at Avignon, split between rival popes until the Council of Constance restored a single one in 1417. The same council condemned the English theologian John Wyclif, whose followers translated the Bible into English, and sentenced the Czech reformer Jan Hus, who had come on King Sigismund's promise of safe-conduct; he was burned at the stake. In Italy, Petrarch searched monasteries for lost classical texts, and in 1422 the Florentine banker Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici became banker to the papacy. Around 1455 Johannes Gutenberg printed the Bible at Mainz, the start of a revolution covered in Chapter 13. 1337 Hundred Years' War begins 1341 Petrarch crowned poet laureate 1378 Western Schism begins 1415 Hus burned at Constance 1417 Martin V ends the schism 1429-31 Joan of Arc: Orléans to Rouen 1453 England keeps only Calais c. 1455 Gutenberg Bible

After Las Navas de Tolosa (see 11.3), Castile and Aragon came to share one royal couple from 1479, though each kept its own government. Their Jews suffered mass violence and forced conversion in 1391. In 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella took Granada and expelled the Jews who would not be baptised, and Portugal had already begun to sail down the coast of Africa. Alfonso X of Castile began a law code, the Siete Partidas, that shaped law in Spain and later in some of its former colonies. In 1391 mobs in Seville and across the kingdoms killed thousands of Jews and forced others to convert, a turning point whose meaning historians now debate. Further pressure followed, as at the Disputation of Tortosa. The marriage of Isabella and Ferdinand in 1469 led to the union of the crowns of Castile and Aragon in 1479.
