Suspicion of the conversos led to the Spanish Inquisition, and in 1492, three months after Granada surrendered, the monarchs ordered the Jews to leave, blaming their influence on the conversos. How many left is uncertain, and modern Spain has revoked the decree and offered citizenship to descendants. Portugal, meanwhile, turned outward: its princes took Ceuta in Morocco in 1415 and explored the Atlantic coast of Africa. The voyages of 1492 and after belong to Chapter 13. 40,000-50,000 Gretchen Starr-LeBeau, drawing on Henry Kamen 100,000 Luis Suárez 150,000-200,000 'most contemporary historians', per a French university course

Timur, a conqueror from Central Asia, campaigned from India to Anatolia and strove to make Samarkand the most splendid city in Asia. At Ankara he captured the sultan of a rising Turkish dynasty, the Ottomans, and plunged it into civil war. The Ottomans recovered, and about half a century later took Constantinople, an event still contested in memory. Timur massacred whole cities in Iran and invaded India, while striving to make Samarkand, the capital of his realm, the most splendid city in Asia; its monuments of the Timurid age include the Bibi-Khanum mosque, the Gur-Emir mausoleum and Ulugh Beg's observatory. In 1402 he crushed the Ottomans at Ankara and captured their sultan. The Ottomans had grown from a small principality in north-western Anatolia into a power on both sides of the Dardanelles. Why they grew so fast is debated, but one institution was distinctive: the devshirme, which took Christian boys, converted them and trained them as soldiers and officials. On 29 May 1453 Mehmed II took Constantinople, ending the Roman empire in the east. He presented himself as heir to the Caesars as well as a champion of Islam. Hagia Sophia became a mosque, and in 2020 it became one again, to praise and protest. after 1293 Osman rules in north-western Anatolia 1324 or 1326 Bursa taken 1354 Gallipoli becomes a permanent Ottoman base in Europe 1398 Timur invades India 1402 Ankara: Bayezid I captured 1405 Timur dies at Otrar 1453 Constantinople taken 2020 Hagia Sophia a mosque again

Mali's kings grew rich on West African gold, and one of them astonished Cairo on his way to Mecca. Timbuktu became a city of scholars. In the south, Great Zimbabwe and Kilwa flourished on trade, and in Ethiopia a new dynasty claimed descent from Solomon. Mali was founded by Sundiata in the 13th century, though most of his story comes from an epic that historians use with care. Its most famous ruler, Mansa Musa, made his pilgrimage in 1324 and spent so much gold in Cairo that its price fell, and he built mosques at Gao and Timbuktu. His wealth became legendary. Timbuktu became one of Islam's great centres of learning. Its family libraries survived into the 21st century, and their manuscripts were moved south to Bamako around the time armed groups occupied the city in 2012-13. Mali's power passed in the 15th century to Songhay. In the south, Great Zimbabwe was an important trading centre of the interior, and Kilwa a prosperous port on the coast. In Ethiopia the Solomonic dynasty took power in 1270, its claims set out in the Kebra Nagast. On the Atlantic side, the kingdoms of Benin and Kongo were growing when the Portuguese arrived. Mali West African Sahel Sundiata; Mansa Musa's hajj, 1324 Timbuktu Niger bend mosques and manuscripts Songhay Niger bend succeeds Mali in the 15th century Great Zimbabwe Zimbabwe plateau stone city, 11th-15th centuries Kilwa Swahili coast height in the 13th-14th centuries Solomonic Ethiopia Ethiopian highlands from 1270; the Kebra Nagast Kongo west-central Africa king baptised 1491

A peasant rebel drove out the Mongols and founded the Ming dynasty. His son built the Forbidden City and sent great fleets across the Indian Ocean, and then China stopped sending them. In Korea a king invented an alphabet, and in Japan the shoguns' power weakened. The Red Turban rebellion against the Mongols was put down, but a rival rebel, the peasant-born Zhu Yuanzhang, toppled the Yuan dynasty and founded the Ming in 1368. His son, the Yongle emperor, seized the throne and moved the capital to Beijing. Yongle also sent the admiral Zheng He on the first of seven great voyages, to display Ming power and draw distant rulers into the tribute system. How large his ships were is still argued over. After 1433 the voyages stopped, criticised as too costly. In Korea, King Sejong created an alphabet so that ordinary people could write their own language. In Japan the Ashikaga shoguns' power was weak from the outset and weakened further; the Ōnin War broke out in 1467. 1368 Ming dynasty founded 1402 Yongle seizes the throne 1405 Zheng He's first voyage 1433 last voyage 1443/1446 Hangul completed and proclaimed 1467-77 Ōnin War in Japan

The Delhi Sultanate became an imperial power and then broke apart, its power in the north shattered by Timur. New states rose in the south, Hindu Vijayanagara and the Muslim Bahmani sultanate. Along the coasts, ports such as Calicut and Melaka flourished on Indian Ocean trade. The Khalji sultans made Delhi an imperial power. Muhammad bin Tughluq moved his capital south and experimented with token coins, and historians still argue over whether he was a visionary or a tyrant. In 1398 Timur's invasion broke the Sultanate's power in the north. In the Deccan and the south, Vijayanagara and the Bahmani sultanate fought for generations. The Indian Ocean linked them all to the wider world. Calicut traded pepper with Arab merchants and received the Chinese fleets, and Melaka, on the strait between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, became the region's greatest market. Delhi Sultanate (Khaljis) 1290-1320 imperial power Delhi Sultanate (Tughluqs) 1325-51 token coinage; capital moved Vijayanagara 1336 capital at Hampi Bahmani sultanate 1347 wars with Vijayanagara Calicut 15th century pepper; Chinese fleets Melaka c. 1400 leading emporium by the 1430s

s: the Mexica and the Inca, c. 1325 to 1500
x: In the 15th century two great empires rose in the Americas, the Mexica (Aztec) in central Mexico and the Inca in the Andes. Both grew rapidly in the 15th century, and both drew tribute from the peoples they conquered. The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on a lake in central Mexico, and after 1428 their Triple Alliance collected tribute across much of Mexico. Human sacrifice was commonly practised as part of their religion. The great skull rack found in Mexico City has confirmed it on a large scale, including women and children, though the numbers given by Spanish writers are still disputed. In the Andes, Pachacuti began the Inca expansion in the mid-15th century, knitting the empire together with roads and keeping records on knotted cords that are only beginning to be read. Among the peoples the Inca conquered were the Chimú of the Peruvian coast. How many people lived in the Americas on the eve of contact is uncertain, and what happened to them after 1492 is the story of Chapter 13. about 54 million William Denevan 60.5 million (middle range 44.8-78.2) Koch et al. (2019) 112 million Henry Dobyns

Between 1488 and 1498 Portuguese and Spanish voyages reached the Cape of Good Hope, the Caribbean and India, and within a few decades Spaniards had taken the Mexica capital and seized the Inca ruler. This chapter follows what came of those encounters down to about 1750, and the evidence, from Nahua testimony to Antarctic ice, by which we know it. In December 1488 Bartolomeu Dias returned to Portugal having rounded the Cape of Good Hope without seeing it. On 12 October 1492 Columbus's ships sighted land across the Atlantic. In 1494 Spain and Portugal agreed at Tordesillas on a line in the Atlantic dividing their claims, and on 20 May 1498 Vasco da Gama reached Calicut by sea. Within a few decades Spaniards had taken Tenochtitlan, in 1521, seized the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca, in 1532, and found silver at Potosí. The pages that follow take the story on: the Great Dying and the exchange of plants and animals (13.5), silver and world trade (13.6), the Atlantic slave trade (13.7), the Reformation and Habsburg Spain (13.8, 13.9), the Islamic empires and East Asia (13.10, 13.11), science (13.12), money and war in Europe (13.13) and North America (13.14). The evidence comes from many sides. The Mexica account of the conquest survives in Book 12 of the Florentine Codex, written in Nahuatl and Spanish under the Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagún and completed in 1575-77. Guaman Poma's illustrated Andean chronicle, with a prologue to King Philip III, is a critical account of Spanish rule in Peru. Numbers come from colonial records and modern science. Colonial counts let Livi Bacci trace the collapse of Hispaniola's people, while ancient DNA suggests that older estimates of the Caribbean's population were too high. The records of 34,948 voyages underlie the estimate that some 12.5 million Africans were forced aboard slave ships. And Lewis and Maslin have proposed that a dip in carbon dioxide in Antarctic ice, centred on 1610, records the deaths of about 50 million Indigenous Americans and the regrowth of forests that followed. Florentine Codex, Book 12 the Mexica account of the conquest, completed 1575-77 13.3 Guaman Poma, Nueva corónica an Andean critique of Spanish rule, 1612-15 13.4 Treaty of Tordesillas the Spanish-Portuguese line of 1494 13.1 Colonial counts (Livi Bacci) Hispaniola: 60,000 people in 1508, just over 26,000 in 1514 13.2 Ancient DNA a smaller pre-contact Caribbean population than older estimates 13.2 SlaveVoyages database 34,948 voyages; some 12.5 million Africans forced aboard 13.7 Antarctic ice cores a fall in carbon dioxide centred on 1610, the proposed 'Orbis Spike' 13.5

Between 1488 and 1511 Portuguese fleets rounded Africa, reached India by sea, touched Brazil and seized Goa and Melaka. A treaty with Spain in 1494 had already divided the two kingdoms' claims along a line in the Atlantic. Portugal's voyages down the African coast (12.6) led on to India. Bartolomeu Dias, who probably sailed in August 1487, rounded the Cape of Good Hope without seeing it and was home in December 1488. Who named the cape is uncertain: Barros says Dias called it the Cape of Storms and King John II renamed it, while Duarte Pacheco credits the name to Dias himself. In June 1494 Spain and Portugal agreed at Tordesillas to divide their claims along a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands, well beyond the pope's earlier line at 100 leagues; what lay east went to Portugal, what lay west to Spain. Vasco da Gama left Lisbon on 8 July 1497 and rounded the Cape that November. At Malindi he took on a Gujarati pilot who knew the route, and he reached Calicut (12.10) on 20 May 1498. The meeting went badly: in Britannica's words, the Zamorin's goodwill 'was dispelled by da Gama's insignificant gifts and rude behaviour.' Only 55 of his 170 men survived the voyage; he reached Lisbon in September 1499. In 1500 a fleet under Pedro Álvares Cabral sighted Brazil on 22 April, took formal possession, and sailed on to Calicut; Dias, sailing with it, was lost at sea near the Cape. Afonso de Albuquerque took Goa by assault in November 1510, putting its Muslim defenders to the sword, and Melaka (12.10) in July 1511. His aim was permanent fortresses with settled populations, though his first plan for a fort at Hormuz, in 1507, had to be dropped because of differences with his captains; in 1515 he returned and gained control of part of the island. Goa became the capital of the Portuguese Indies; UNESCO, calling it 'the former capital of the Portuguese Indies', says that its churches, one of which holds the tomb of Francis Xavier, 'illustrate the evangelization of Asia'. 1487-88 Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope 7 June 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas 1497-99 da Gama's voyage to Calicut and back 22 April 1500 Cabral sights Brazil November 1510 Albuquerque takes Goa July 1511 Albuquerque takes Melaka

Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492 and never gave up the belief that he had reached Asia. On Hispaniola the Taíno population collapsed within a generation, mostly before smallpox arrived. The friar Antonio de Montesinos and Bartolomé de las Casas challenged the colonists, and laws to restrain them had limited effect. Columbus's fleet sailed on 3 August 1492, and on 12 October land was sighted from the Pinta. Where he first landed, the island called Guanahani, is hotly disputed, though San Salvador in the Bahamas is generally preferred. He convinced himself that Cuba was the Asian mainland and never gave up the belief that he had reached Asia. His aims included religious ones: his Book of Prophecies, compiled after 1500, presents the voyages, in its modern publisher's words, as 'a first step toward the liberation of Jerusalem'. Carol Delaney argues that he wanted gold to launch a crusade, a reading one reviewer found thinly evidenced. When the Santa María ran aground on 25 December 1492, Columbus built a fort, La Navidad, on Hispaniola with help from the Taíno chief Guacanagarí and left 39 men there. The Taíno were an Arawakan-speaking people of the Greater Antilles. How many there were is disputed. Britannica says they may have numbered one or two million; Livi Bacci estimates 200,000-300,000 for Hispaniola; and a 2021 ancient-DNA study concludes that estimates of hundreds of thousands across the Caribbean are too large. Whatever the starting figure, the fall was steep. On Livi Bacci's figures 60,000 people remained in 1508 and just over 26,000 in 1514, and after the smallpox of 1518-19 only a few thousand. Because the Taíno were near extinction before smallpox struck, he argues that conquest itself explains the collapse: gold mining, the encomienda, displacement and falling fertility. On the fourth Sunday of Advent 1511 the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos preached against the colonists, asking, 'Are they not men? Do they not have rational souls?' The Laws of Burgos of December 1512 required encomenderos to feed, clothe and instruct the Indians and banned whipping, but in practice they did not improve conditions. Bartolomé de las Casas, who had sailed to the New World in 1502 and was later ordained a priest (accounts of the date range from 1507 to 1513), became the colonists' leading critic. The New Laws of 1542-43 banned the enslavement of Indians and stopped encomiendas passing to heirs; a revolt followed in Peru, in which the first viceroy was beheaded, and the ban on inheritance was repealed in 1545-46. At Valladolid in 1550-51 Las Casas and Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda debated whether Aristotle's idea of natural slavery applied to the Indians. A 2023 thesis argues that Spaniards then read the idea broadly, as an inferiority that education and faith could overcome. His writings, among them A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1552), became a major source of the 'Black Legend' of exceptional Spanish cruelty, and Spanish patriots condemned him for it. Critics say he exaggerated, though modern scholarship has largely supported his toll of Native deaths, while blaming most of them on disease rather than cruelty; and, one historian writes, whether or not he exaggerated, the Brief Account 'remains one of the most important documents ever written on human rights'. 3 Aug-12 Oct 1492 Columbus's first crossing 25 December 1492 Santa María aground; La Navidad built 1502 Las Casas sails to the New World Advent 1511 Montesinos's sermon on Hispaniola 27 December 1512 Laws of Burgos 1518-19 smallpox; a few thousand Taíno left on Hispaniola 1542-43 New Laws; inheritance ban repealed 1545-46 1550-51 debate at Valladolid

Between 1519 and 1521 Hernán Cortés, with a small Spanish force and Tlaxcalan allies, took Tenochtitlan as smallpox struck the city. Mexica memories written down in Nahuatl, and historians such as Matthew Restall, put Indigenous people at the centre of the story. Hernán Cortés landed at Tabasco in March 1519, founded Veracruz and sank his ships. Malintzin, also called Doña Marina, became his interpreter and mistress and bore him a son. Tlaxcala first fought him and then became his most faithful ally, and on 8 November 1519 he entered Tenochtitlan, the Mexica capital (12.11), with his small Spanish force and about 1,000 Tlaxcaltecs. Cortés soon seized Moctezuma, who died around 30 June 1520. In September or October 1520 smallpox reached Tenochtitlan. It killed Moctezuma's successor, and by one estimate a third to a half of the population died during the epidemic. The capture of the city was completed on 13 August 1521. The Mexica side of the story survives in Book 12 of the Florentine Codex, with chapters on the massacre at Cholula, Moctezuma's meeting with Cortés and the plague. It was set down in Nahuatl and Spanish under the Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagún and completed in 1575-77, more than 50 years after the events. The older, heroic story gave the decisive role to the Spaniards. Matthew Restall calls this a myth: the conquest, he argues, 'relied heavily on black and native allies', and Indigenous people saw it 'as a native civil war in which the Spaniards played an important but secondary role.' March 1519 Cortés lands at Tabasco 1519 Veracruz founded; the ships sunk 8 November 1519 Cortés enters Tenochtitlan with about 1,000 Tlaxcaltecs c. 30 June 1520 death of Moctezuma September-October 1520 smallpox reaches Tenochtitlan 13 August 1521 capture of Tenochtitlan completed 1575-77 Florentine Codex completed

Francisco Pizarro seized the Inca ruler Atahualpa in 1532, as the empire emerged from civil war, and within three years Spaniards held Cuzco and had founded Lima. The silver of Potosí was mined with forced labour whose long-run effects are still measured, and in Mexico the devotion to Our Lady of Guadalupe grew from a tradition whose early history is debated. The Inca empire (12.11) was divided against itself. After Huayna Capac died, his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa fought a civil war, by one account for seven years, and Atahualpa had won by 1532, just as Pizarro arrived. At Cajamarca on 16 November 1532 Pizarro's force of about 168 men seized Atahualpa. Atahualpa filled the room where he was held with gold and silver as ransom, but he was strangled in 1533; Britannica gives the date as 29 August, World History Encyclopedia as 26 July. Cuzco was occupied without a struggle in November 1533, and Pizarro founded Lima in 1535; he was killed by Almagro's former supporters in 1541. Between 1542 and 1545 silver was found at the Cerro Rico of Potosí, which UNESCO calls 'reputed to be the world's largest industrial complex in the 16th century'; workers were forced into its mines under the mita, a system of mandatory labour. Its silver's place in world trade is the subject of 13.6. The mining mita lasted from 1573 to 1812, and Melissa Dell has found that districts once subject to it today have household consumption about 25 percent lower, and child stunting about 6 percentage points higher, than districts just outside its old boundary. Andean voices survive. Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala's illustrated Nueva corónica y buen gobierno (1612-15), a critical account of Spanish rule in Peru, includes a prologue addressed to King Philip III. In Mexico, Catholic tradition holds that in December 1531 the Virgin Mary appeared to Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin at Tepeyac, and that her image appeared on his tilma before Bishop Zumárraga. In 2002 John Paul II canonized Juan Diego, praising him for 'accepting the Christian message without forgoing his indigenous identity'. The written record begins later, with Miguel Sánchez's account in 1648 and Luis Laso de la Vega's in Nahuatl in 1649. Stafford Poole judges that the story's symbolism 'does not rest on any objective historical basis', while those who uphold the tradition argue, or presume, that Sánchez drew on oral testimony or on an earlier unpublished account. Sánchez himself identified Tepeyac as a pre-Christian pilgrimage site of the goddess Tonantzin, whose place he believed Guadalupe had providentially taken, while Sahagún opposed the devotion as a thinly veiled continuation of Indigenous religion. 16 November 1532 Atahualpa seized at Cajamarca 26 July or 29 August 1533 Atahualpa executed November 1533 Cuzco occupied 1535 Lima founded 1542-45 silver found at Potosí 1573-1812 the mining mita 1612-15 Guaman Poma's Nueva corónica 1648-49 first published accounts of Guadalupe

t: The Great Dying and the Columbian exchange
x: After 1492 the Indigenous population of the Americas collapsed; one study puts the loss at 90 percent within a century. Historians still argue over how much was due to new diseases and how much to slavery, overwork and famine. Crops and animals crossed the ocean too, and some scientists think the die-off left a mark in the atmosphere. Chapter 12 set out the estimates of how many people lived in the Americas in 1492 (12.11); a 2019 synthesis by Koch and colleagues gives 60.5 million. The same team estimates that European epidemics removed 90 percent of them within a century, a 'Great Dying'. Britannica gives a range of 50 to 95 percent by 1650 across the Americas, and more than 99 percent on most Caribbean islands (13.2). Measles, smallpox, influenza, mumps, typhus and whooping cough were all new to the Americas. Was disease the whole story? Andrés Reséndez argues that slavery, overwork and famine also killed, and estimates that 2.5 to 5 million Native Americans were enslaved between Columbus's time and 1900. A 2026 study points out that no colonial-era mass grave has yet been shown to hold victims of smallpox, and proposes criteria for finding them. Ancient DNA can help: ten of 24 people sampled from a cemetery of the cocoliztli epidemic of 1545-50 at Teposcolula-Yucundaa, in Oaxaca, carried a Salmonella bacterium, a possible cause of that outbreak. Alfred Crosby named the traffic between the hemispheres 'the Columbian Exchange' in 1972. Maize, potatoes, cassava and sweet potatoes went to the Old World, where maize changed farming most, in Asia, Europe and Africa; cassava reached Africa in the 16th century. In the other direction, cattle and horses ran wild and multiplied on the Pampas and the Great Plains. The die-off may even show in the air. Lewis and Maslin proposed in 2015 that a dip in atmospheric carbon dioxide around 1610, which they called the 'Orbis Spike', marks the start of the Anthropocene. Koch and colleagues calculate that regrowth on abandoned land in the Americas took up the equivalent of 3.5 parts per million of CO2 directly, and that with carbon-cycle feedbacks and land-use change elsewhere the extra uptake came to about 5 ppm, 47-67 percent of an observed fall of 7-10 ppm. On their figures the fall cannot be explained without the regrowth, though the regrowth does not explain all of it. Geologists have not adopted an Anthropocene epoch: in 2024 they decisively rejected a proposal that would have started it in the mid-20th century. Population of the Americas before 1492 60.5 million Koch et al. (2019) Loss within a century 90% (87-92%) Koch et al. (2019) Loss across the Americas by 1650 50-95% Britannica Loss on most Caribbean islands more than 99% Britannica Native Americans enslaved, Columbus to 1900 2.5-5 million Reséndez Abandoned land regrown 55.8 million hectares Koch et al. (2019) CO2 fall from regrowth / observed fall 3.5 / 7-10 parts per million Koch et al. (2019) Extra land uptake with feedbacks about 5 ppm (47-67% of the fall) Koch et al. (2019)

t: Silver and the first global economy
x: Spanish America's silver went east to Europe and west across the Pacific to China. Dennis Flynn and Arturo Giráldez date the birth of global trade to the founding of Manila in 1571; others place it in the 19th century. Scholars also still debate how far American silver drove prices up in 16th-century Spain. At Potosí, in the Andes, silver was found between 1542 and 1545, and in the 16th century the site was regarded as the world's largest industrial complex (13.4). In New Spain, Zacatecas was founded in 1546 after a rich silver lode was found. By one estimate Spanish America produced about 150,000 tons of silver between 1500 and 1800, perhaps 80 percent of the world's output. Part of it went west, across the Pacific. Flynn and Giráldez argue that global trade began with the founding of Manila in 1571, and that silver flowed to China because it was worth twice as much there as in the rest of the world. Peter Coclanis, following Flynn and Giráldez, puts the galleons' cargo from Acapulco in the 17th century at an average of about two million pesos a year, more than fifty tons; Manila was little more than a way station for silver on its way to China. In 1581 the Ming promulgated throughout the empire the 'single whip', which turned land tax and labour service into one payment in silver; Britannica calls it 'little more than a bookkeeping change at best', while EBSCO's summary stresses that it depended on foreign silver. Kevin O'Rourke and Jeffrey Williamson use a different test, converging commodity prices. By that test they find no sign that the world economy was integrated by 1492 or 1498, and 'a very big globalization bang' in the 19th century, a much later start than Flynn and Giráldez propose. Did silver also drive up prices in Europe? In 1556 Martín de Azpilcueta, of the School of Salamanca, set out an early version of the quantity theory of money. In 1934 Earl Hamilton argued that American treasure was the principal cause of Spain's price revolution; John Munro notes that prices were already rising in 1516-20, before large silver imports. Isotopes in coins point both ways. In one study, Anne-Marie Desaulty and colleagues found that Mexican silver did not enter Spanish coinage before the early 17th century, which Desaulty said calls into question the link between American metal and the price revolution. In another, they found Mexican silver in English coins from the mid-1550s, though Potosí's appeared only nearly a century later, and Science News reported that this study adds 'hard data' to theories linking American silver to inflation. Potosí silver found 1542-45 regarded as the world's largest industrial complex Zacatecas founded 1546 silver town of New Spain Acapulco to Manila Manila founded 1571 about 2 million pesos of silver a year (17th century) Ming China single whip, 1581 land tax and labour service paid in silver Azpilcueta (Navarrus) Comentario, 1556 early quantity theory of money Earl Hamilton 1934 American treasure the principal cause of Spain's price revolution

Between the 16th and the 19th centuries about 12.5 million Africans were shipped to the Americas, and about 10.7 million survived the crossing. Most were taken to the Caribbean and Brazil. African rulers responded to the trade in different ways, and economists still debate its long-term effects on Africa. The SlaveVoyages database estimates that about 12.5 million Africans were shipped to the Americas and about 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage; Britannica gives a lower total of 10 to 12 million. Many died before the ships sailed: an estimated 10 to 15 percent of captives died on the way to the coast. The trade grew over time: about 278,000 people were embarked in the 16th century and about 6.5 million in the 18th, more than half of the total. Demand for enslaved labour rose sharply with the growth of sugar plantations in the Caribbean, which received about 52 percent of those landed; Brazil took about 39 percent, and North America under 4 percent (about 388,000 people, on Gates's figures). Spain supplied its American colonies through asientos, monopoly contracts granted by the crown; the last went to Britain's South Sea Company in 1713, for 4,800 slaves a year for 30 years. African rulers responded in different ways. In 1526 Afonso I, the Christian king of Kongo (12.8), protested to João III of Portugal that 'our country is being completely depopulated'. Two centuries later Agaja of Dahomey conquered Allada and the coastal state of Ouidah, and in time accepted the trade, on condition that it be a royal monopoly. Economists still argue over the long-term cost: Nathan Nunn finds that the countries from which the most slaves were taken are poorer today, while Margherita Bottero and Björn Wallace reply that the relationship 'did not become significantly negative until 1970'. Embarked for the Americas about 12.5 million (12,521,336) Landed in the Americas about 10.7 million (10,702,656) Died on the way to the African coast 10-15% of captives Share of arrivals: Caribbean 51.9% Share of arrivals: Brazil 38.9% Share of arrivals: North America 3.8% (Gates: about 388,000 people) Share of arrivals: Spanish American mainland 3.3%

Within a quarter-century of Martin Luther's 95 Theses of 1517, Anabaptist and Reformed churches had formed and Henry VIII had made himself head of the Church of England. The Catholic Church answered at the Council of Trent. Settlements at Augsburg in 1555 and Westphalia in 1648 followed, and historians still debate how religious the Thirty Years' War was and what Westphalia founded. On 31 October 1517, by the traditional account, Martin Luther posted 95 Theses at the castle church in Wittenberg. Whether he nailed them to the door is debated: the historian Erwin Iserloh argued in 1961 that he never did, though it is certain that Luther sent them to Archbishop Albrecht. Print may have helped: Jared Rubin finds that cities with a press by 1500 (12.5) were at least 29 percentage points more likely to be Protestant by 1600. In 1543, in On the Jews and Their Lies, Luther urged that synagogues be set on fire; in 1994 the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America rejected 'this violent invective'. Eric Gritsch judged that Luther's arguments against Jews were 'theological, not biological', though he notes that the National Socialists used Luther to support their racist antisemitism, and the ELCA deplores 'the appropriation of Luther's words by modern anti-Semites'. Reform soon took many forms. In January 1525, at Felix Manz's house in Zurich, radicals who had broken with Ulrich Zwingli baptized each other, the start of the Anabaptist movement; in Geneva, John Calvin's Ecclesiastical Ordinances of 1541 organised a Reformed church; in England, the Act of Supremacy of 1534 made Henry VIII supreme head of the Church of England. Pope Paul III approved the Society of Jesus in 1540, and the Council of Trent (1545-63) defined virtually every doctrine Protestants contested. The Peace of Augsburg (1555) let each ruler in the Empire choose Catholicism or Lutheranism for his lands, but made no provision for Calvinists. The Thirty Years' War killed, by Peter Wilson's estimate, about 1.8 million soldiers and at least 3.2 million civilians, cutting the Empire's population by at least a fifth, though Wilson denies that it was a religious conflict. The Peace of Westphalia (1648) extended toleration to Calvinists and confirmed the Dutch and Swiss republics as independent. Whether it founded a modern system of sovereign states is disputed: Andreas Osiander calls that picture 'a past that is largely imaginary'. 1517 Luther's 95 Theses, Wittenberg 1525 first Anabaptist baptisms, Zurich 1534 Act of Supremacy, England 1540 the Jesuits recognised by Paul III 1541 Calvin's Ecclesiastical Ordinances, Geneva 1545-63 Council of Trent 1555 Peace of Augsburg 1648 Peace of Westphalia

Philip II governed his empire from his desk in Spain, yet his state was declared bankrupt in 1557 and he stopped paying his lenders four times. In 1588 only about 65 of the Armada's 130 to 150 ships returned to Spain, and in 1609-14 some 300,000 Moriscos were expelled. Historians still debate whether, and how, Spain then 'declined'. In 1555 Philip II took over his father's dominions. He made Madrid his capital, built the Escorial as his residence and the centre of his empire, and ruled from his desk. In 1557 the state was declared bankrupt, and not for the last time. Yet the bankers kept lending. Philip stopped all payments to his lenders four times, and Mauricio Drelichman and Hans-Joachim Voth argue that a 'cheat the cheater' mechanism kept the lending going and profitable overall. In 1588 Philip sent the Armada against England: some 130 to 150 ships and 18,000 men. After an English fireship attack off Calais and the fiercest fighting of the campaign at Gravelines, only about 65 ships made it back to Spain; Medina Sidonia himself reached Santander. Between 1609 and 1614 about 300,000 Moriscos, converts from Islam, were expelled from Spain (on 1492, see 12.6), some 120,000 of them from Valencia; most settled in North Africa and Constantinople. Teresa of Ávila (1515-82) originated the Carmelite Reform; canonised in 1622, she became in 1970 the first woman named a Doctor of the Church. Miguel de Cervantes, Alcalá de Henares's 'great son', published Don Quixote in two parts, in 1605 and 1615. Was this the start of a decline? Contemporaries already wrote tracts asking why Spanish power had diminished. J. H. Elliott's 1961 essay 'The Decline of Spain' remains one of the best introductions to the question, and his work examined how Spain's leaders tried to avert decline; Henry Kamen argues that 19th- and 20th-century politicians and historians built 'a fictitious image' of 16th-century Spain, and examines 'the persistent obsession with the notion of national decline'. 1555 Philip II takes over his father's dominions 1557 the state declared bankrupt 1588 the Armada: about 65 ships return to Spain 1605 Don Quixote, Part I 1609-14 about 300,000 Moriscos expelled 1615 Don Quixote, Part II 1622 Teresa of Ávila canonised

The Ottomans twice besieged Vienna, the Safavids made Shi'ism the religion of their state, and in India the Mughal emperor Akbar abolished a tax on non-Muslims, while Aurangzeb later reimposed the jizya. Historians still argue over the label 'gunpowder empires' that was given to all three. Süleyman, known in Turkish as Kanuni, 'the Lawgiver', ruled from 1520 to 1566 (on the Ottoman rise, see 12.7). In 1529 he besieged Vienna, but the siege was lifted. A second Ottoman siege, in 1683, was broken by a relief army under Charles of Lorraine and the Polish king Jan III Sobieski, a defeat Britannica sees as the beginning of the end of Ottoman domination in eastern Europe. At Smyrna (Izmir) in 1665, Jews acclaimed Sabbatai Zevi as the messiah; his movement spread as far as Amsterdam and London and threatened the authority of the rabbis. In 1666, at Adrianople, he converted to Islam. In July 1501 Ismail was enthroned as shah, ruling at first only Azerbaijan, and proclaimed Shi'ism the religion of his state, enforcing its creed and prayers in the mosques; he had taken the city of Tabriz that year. In 1514 his Sunni rival, the Ottoman sultan Selim I, defeated him heavily at Chaldiran. Abbas I, who came to the throne in 1588, moved the capital to Isfahan and made it the centre of Safavid architecture; the city fell to Afghan invaders in 1722. In India, Akbar (r. 1556-1605) made marriage alliances with Rajput rulers and abolished the tax on pilgrims and the tax non-Muslims paid in place of military service. In 1575 work began on a hall for religious debate, the Ibadat Khana, at Fatehpur Sikri; at first only Muslim scholars debated there, but from 1578 Akbar brought Hindus, Parsis and Christians into the discussions. He never renounced Islam. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal at Agra in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Under Aurangzeb (r. 1658-1707) the empire reached its greatest extent, but in 1679 he reimposed the jizya on non-Muslims, and Hindu temples were often destroyed. Audrey Truschke argues that he acted for political rather than religious ends; a reviewer finds parts of her case debatable. William McNeill and Marshall Hodgson called these states 'gunpowder empires'. Recent historians answer that most of their armies still relied mainly on swords, spears and bows, and that their rulers' power may have rested more on governance. Gábor Ágoston stresses how pragmatically the Ottomans adapted firearms, but also points to intelligence, leadership and large, disciplined armies, while Douglas Streusand keeps the label but treats the three empires as parts of one international system, and as complex polities in which Islam was one component among many. Ismail I Safavid shah from 1501 Shi'ism made the state religion Süleyman Ottoman 1520-66 siege of Vienna, 1529 Akbar Mughal 1556-1605 religious debates; taxes on pilgrims and non-Muslims abolished Abbas I Safavid 1588-1629 capital moved to Isfahan Aurangzeb Mughal 1658-1707 greatest extent; jizya reimposed, 1679

In 1644 a rebel army took Beijing and was driven out by Ming and Manchu troops; the Qing emperor Kangxi later sent troops to Taiwan and made a treaty with Russia. Catholic missionaries quarrelled over Chinese rites, Japan's Tokugawa shoguns banned Christianity, and a Japanese invasion in the 1590s killed at least 125,000 Koreans. In 1644 the rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing with ease; a combined force of former Ming and Manchu troops then drove him out (on the Ming, see 12.9). The Manchus had founded their Qing dynasty in 1636, and under Qing rule China's territory grew to three times its size and its population from some 150 million to 450 million. Tree rings studied in 2024 show long megadroughts in northern China in 1576-93 and 1628-44, which the researchers argue contributed to the Ming collapse. The Kangxi emperor (r. 1661-1722) put down the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, begun by Wu Sangui, sent troops across the Taiwan Strait in 1683 and made the Treaty of Nerchinsk with Russia in 1689. He also encouraged Western learning and Roman Catholicism. The Jesuit Matteo Ricci had reached Macau in 1582, taken to dressing as a Chinese scholar, and settled in Beijing in 1601. The Jesuits held that Chinese ceremonies honouring Confucius and ancestors could be tolerated within limits; Dominicans and Franciscans disagreed and appealed to Rome, which banned the rites in 1704, 1715 and 1742 and allowed Catholics to join ceremonies for Confucius only in 1939. In 1592 Toyotomi Hideyoshi invaded Korea as part of a plan to invade China through Korea, and his army took Seoul on 12 June. Ming China sent armies to Korea's aid, Admiral Yi Sun-sin's navy hampered the Japanese at sea, and the invasion was abandoned after Hideyoshi died in 1598. At least 125,000 Koreans died, and many Korean potters were carried off to Japan; relations were restored in 1607. In Japan the Tokugawa shoguns governed from Edo from 1603 to 1867, a period of internal peace and economic growth. Three decrees of the 1630s banned Christianity completely. Portuguese ships were excluded in 1639, and from 1641 the Dutch traded from Dejima, off Nagasaki, where Chinese merchants also came; relations with Korea, the Ryukyus and the Ainu ran through the domains of Tsushima, Satsuma and Matsumae. Historians long called this sakoku, the 'closed country', but Ronald Toby showed that the shogunate kept up an active network for gathering information abroad. (On Christian missions elsewhere, see 13.8.) 1582 Matteo Ricci reaches Macau 1592 Japan invades Korea; Seoul taken 1598 Hideyoshi dies; invasion abandoned 1603 Tokugawa shogunate begins 1630s exclusion decrees; Christianity banned in Japan 1644 Li Zicheng takes Beijing and is driven out 1683 Kangxi's troops cross to Taiwan 1704-1742 papal bans on the Chinese rites

Between Copernicus's book of 1543 and Newton's Principia of 1687, astronomers put the Sun at the centre of the planets' motions, and the Church tried Galileo for defending the idea. Historians now argue over whether this was one 'Scientific Revolution' and over what printing did, while observatories at Samarkand and Jaipur belonged to other traditions. The Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus proposed that the planets move around the Sun as a fixed point. His De revolutionibus was printed at Nuremberg in 1543, the year he died, with an unsigned letter by Andreas Osiander and a subtly altered title that made the book look less like a claim about the real world. Tradition says Copernicus first saw the printed book on his deathbed. Working from Tycho Brahe's precise observations, Johannes Kepler found that Mars moves in an ellipse, published in Astronomia Nova (1609), and set out three laws of planetary motion. In January 1610 Galileo found four moons circling Jupiter. In 1616 the Congregation of the Index declared false any theory that the Earth moved around the Sun and suspended Copernicus's book until it was corrected (the corrections followed in 1620). After Galileo's Dialogue (1632), he was tried in Rome, found guilty of 'vehement suspicion of heresy', made to abjure, and confined to his house for the rest of his life. In 1992 Pope John Paul II spoke about the affair, but there was no retrial or pardon. Newton's Principia (1687), written at Edmond Halley's urging while Newton was a professor at Cambridge, set out three laws of motion and universal gravitation. Steven Shapin opens his history, 'There was no such thing as the Scientific Revolution, and this is a book about it', and sees instead a diverse array of practices; H. Floris Cohen keeps the concept, rebuilt as six linked transformations, and asks why modern science arose in Europe rather than in Greece, China or the Islamic world. Printing (12.5) is argued over too: Elizabeth Eisenstein held that books made learning stable and fixed, while Adrian Johns stresses competing cultures of print and rampant piracy. Astronomers outside Europe worked in other traditions. Ulugh Beg's observatory at Samarkand, built in the 1420s, produced a star catalogue that became the standard throughout the Islamic world and reached Latin in 1665. In the early 18th century Jai Singh II built the Jantar Mantar at Jaipur, about twenty fixed instruments for naked-eye observation in a tradition of Ptolemaic astronomy shared by many civilizations. 1543 De revolutionibus Copernicus 1609 Astronomia Nova: the elliptical orbit of Mars Kepler 1610 four moons of Jupiter Galileo 1627 Rudolphine Tables Kepler 1632-33 Dialogue; trial in Rome Galileo 1665 Latin translation of Ulugh Beg's star catalogue Thomas Hyde 1687 Principia Newton

t: Money, states and war in Europe
x: Historians have long argued over how war, money and the state shaped one another in early modern Europe. Shares in the Dutch East India Company traded in Amsterdam from 1602, and England, after its civil wars and the Revolution of 1688-89, founded the Bank of England to pay for war with France. Whether that Revolution made the Crown's promises credible is still debated. The phrase 'military revolution' appeared, little noticed, in 1956; in the view associated with Michael Roberts, costly gunpowder warfare forced states to become more efficient. Geoffrey Parker revived the debate in 1988, arguing that the military revolution marks the 16th century as much as the Renaissance and the Reformation do. Critics questioned both the timing and the direction of cause: Jeremy Black placed the decisive changes in the later 17th century and argued that the state's own development came first; Bert Hall found that artillery spread slowly; and John Lynn found that France's army only really took off later. The Dutch East India Company (VOC), launched in 1602, introduced shares that could be easily transferred, and buyers were trading them within days; Lodewijk Petram sees this as the start of Amsterdam's transformation. The company held a monopoly of Dutch trade from the Cape of Good Hope to the Strait of Magellan, renamed Jacatra (now Jakarta) Batavia in 1619 and lasted until 1799. In the same city, in 1656, the Portuguese-Jewish community (on Iberia's Jews, see 12.6) placed Baruch Spinoza under its harshest ban, which was never lifted. Its reasons are uncertain; Steven Nadler suspects the ideas Spinoza later published, such as his denial that the soul is immortal. England's civil wars lasted from 1642 to 1651; in Ireland, rebels sought to restore the Catholic Church to its pre-Reformation position (on the Reformation, see 13.8). In the Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 the Catholic James II was replaced by Mary II and William III, prince of Orange. In 1694 the Bank of England was founded as a private bank to be the government's banker, chiefly to pay for the war against France; William and Mary were among its first stockholders. Douglass North and Barry Weingast (1989) argued that the new institutions after 1688 let the government commit credibly to upholding property rights, and pointed to evidence from capital markets. Gary Cox (2012) agrees that the Revolution was a watershed but a narrower one, working through Parliament's control of taxes and new borrowing and through ministerial responsibility, while property rights at home were little affected. Steven Pincus and James Robinson argue that the Revolution created very few new formal rules, and that its most significant changes were de facto rather than written into law. Michael Roberts costly gunpowder warfare forced states to become more efficient Geoffrey Parker (1988) it marks the 16th century as much as the Renaissance does Jeremy Black decisive changes after 1650; the state's development came first Bert Hall artillery was adopted slowly, its effect long uncertain John Lynn France's early war effort outran its administration; the take-off came later

s: New Mexico, New France, Virginia and New England
x: Between 1607 and 1610 England, France and Spain founded Jamestown, Quebec and Santa Fe. Native nations made treaties and fought wars, from Plymouth's treaty with Massasoit to King Philip's War and the Pueblo Revolt, and in 1619 captive Africans reached Virginia, a date whose place in the American story is still argued over. Pedro de Peralta founded Santa Fe as the capital of New Mexico in 1610. Spanish missionaries burned the Pueblos' kivas, masks and other sacred objects, and on 10 August 1680 Popé led a full-scale revolt; the Spaniards sheltered in the Palace of the Governors and then fled, leaving about 400 dead, among them 21 priests. The Pueblos stayed free until 1692, when the Spanish reconquest of New Mexico began. Santa Fe itself was retaken by force in December 1693. Samuel de Champlain began the settlement of Quebec in 1608, and in New France the fur trade remained everyone's chief concern except the missionaries'. The Haudenosaunee, 'the people of the longhouse', were a confederacy of five nations that the English called the Six Nations after the Tuscarora joined in 1722. When the League was founded is disputed, and proposed dates vary widely, among them Lewis Henry Morgan's 1400-1450 and W. M. Beauchamp's 1600. Barbara Mann and Jerry Fields dated it by a solar eclipse to 31 August 1142, but David Henige finds 'no serious evidence' for that date. Jamestown, settled in May 1607, was the first permanent English settlement in North America; it lived through the 'Starving Time' of 1609-10, and in July 1619 its governor called the first representative assembly. That year the '20 and odd' Africans arrived, captives seized by the English warship White Lion from a Portuguese slave ship (on the Atlantic slave trade, see 13.7). Virginia recognised slavery in statute law in 1662 and codified its slave laws in 1705. In December 2019 five historians asked the New York Times to correct the 1619 Project's claim that protecting slavery was a main reason for the American Revolution. The Times defended it, but in March 2020 it changed the passage to say that this was a primary motivation for 'some of the colonists'. Adam Serwer argues that the quarrel is really about national identity. At Plymouth, founded in 1620, in the first winter half the Mayflower's passengers and crew died of disease and malnutrition; the treaty with the Wampanoag leader Massasoit, signed in March 1621, held until after his death in 1661. In 1675 war broke out between Native Americans and the English settlers and their Indian allies; named after his son Metacom, whom the English called Philip, King Philip's War was per capita one of the bloodiest conflicts in American history. Some 800 English died and a third of New England's English towns were burned and abandoned; among Native people about 2,000 died of wounds, 3,000 of disease or starvation, and 1,000 were sold into slavery. 1607 Jamestown settled 1608 Quebec begun 1610 Santa Fe founded 1619 Virginia's first representative assembly; the '20 and odd' Africans arrive 1620 Plymouth founded 1662 slavery recognised in Virginia's statute law 1675-76 King Philip's War 1680 the Pueblo Revolt

Between 1776 and 1804 revolutions in North America, France and Haiti declared equal rights or independence. By the Maddison Project's estimates the world economy began to accelerate only after 1820, and GDP per person in Britain and the United States pulled away from those in China and India. This chapter follows both revolutions, and the evidence historians use to measure them. In 1776 the American Declaration of Independence held 'that all men are created equal' (14.2). In 1789 the French Assembly abolished 'the feudal system' and declared that men are 'born and remain free and equal in rights' (14.3). In Saint-Domingue the enslaved rose in 1791, and in 1804 their leaders declared the independence of Haiti (14.4). The other revolution was economic (14.6). The 2023 update of the Maddison Project finds 'pockets of economic growth' before 1820, but a world economy that 'only started to accelerate after that year'. On its figures, GDP per person in the United Kingdom rose from 3,306 international dollars in 1820 to 8,212 in 1913, and in the United States from 2,674 to 10,108, while China's went from 882 to 985 and India's from 937 to 1,073. In 1800 the Netherlands, at 4,184, stood above the United Kingdom, at 3,343. How do we know? Partly from censuses. The United States held its first census in 1790, a simple headcount used to share out seats in the House of Representatives. Britain's first census, in 1801, found 8.9 million people in England and Wales, leaving out those at sea, in the military and in prison. Output is harder to count. For most of this period no official statistics fully cover GDP, so economic historians reconstruct it, often indirectly from real wages and urbanization. The Maddison Project now covers 169 countries, but its comparisons depend on the benchmark year used to compare prices, which Bolt and van Zanden defend keeping at 1990, with adjustments, and Rafael Guthmann argues that its methods differ between countries and periods. US census, 1790 a headcount to apportion House seats a count of people, not of output British census, 1801 8.9 million in England and Wales sailors, soldiers and prisoners left out Founding documents the texts of 1776, 1787 and 1789 the Constitution counted enslaved people as three fifths (14.2) Maddison Project 2023 GDP per person, 169 countries, to 2022 early figures reconstructed from wages and urbanization Price benchmarks a common yardstick across countries results shift with the benchmark year

In 1784 Kant defined enlightenment as humanity's emergence from a 'self-imposed nonage'. Writers from Montesquieu and Rousseau to Adam Smith and Moses Mendelssohn argued about government, trade and freedom of conscience. Historians still dispute how radical the Enlightenment was, and how it regarded race and empire. Kant, writing in 1784, called enlightenment 'man's emergence from his self-imposed nonage' and gave it a motto: Sapere aude, dare to know. Its political thought built on Locke, whose Second Treatise is the classical source of modern liberal theory. Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) argued, in Britannica's summary, that the three powers 'must be confided to different individuals or bodies, acting independently', a scheme that shaped James Madison. In William Bristow's summary, Rousseau held that only direct democracy could realize human freedom. Scotland produced its own Enlightenment, with Hutcheson, Adam Smith, Hume and Reid. Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776) opens with a pin factory in which ten workers, each specializing in a task, turn out 48,000 pins a day, and it attacks the restrictions of what Smith called the 'mercantile system'. Moses Mendelssohn (1729-1786) translated the Pentateuch and the Psalms into German. In Jerusalem (1783), as Daniel Dahlstrom puts it, he argued that 'neither the state nor religion can legitimately coerce human conscience', and in 1784 he wrote his own essay on what it means to enlighten. Historians argue over what the Enlightenment was. Jonathan Israel divides it into a 'radical' camp, following Spinoza, and a 'moderate' one; Anthony La Vopa calls this an 'oversimplified classification' and Israel's method 'fundamentally unhistorical'. Its record on race and empire is also disputed. William Bristow writes that its writings are 'rife with rank ethno- and Eurocentrism, often explicit', yet Sankar Muthu argues that Diderot, Kant and Herder defended the freedom of non-European peoples to order their own societies, and Pauline Kleingeld argues that Kant himself 'radically changed his mind' about race in the 1790s. Locke Second Treatise classical source of liberal political theory Montesquieu The Spirit of the Laws (1748) the three powers held by separate bodies Rousseau political writings only direct democracy realizes freedom (in Bristow's summary) Adam Smith The Wealth of Nations (1776) division of labour; against the 'mercantile system' Moses Mendelssohn Jerusalem (1783) no coercion of conscience by state or religion Kant 'What is Enlightenment?' (1784) emergence from self-imposed nonage

After 1763 colonial dissent grew, and in 1776 the Declaration of Independence held that 'all men are created equal'. The Constitution of 1787 counted enslaved people as 'three fifths of all other Persons' and barred a ban on the slave trade before 1808; the Bill of Rights followed in 1791. Historians still dispute what the Revolution was about. The Proclamation of 7 October 1763 stopped grants of land west of the Appalachians; Max Edelson sees it as the beginning of 'escalating colonial dissent'. The Declaration of Independence, dated 4 July 1776, held 'that all men are created equal', and accused the King of inciting 'the merciless Indian Savages'. The Constitution, signed on 17 September 1787, counted 'three fifths of all other Persons', that is, enslaved people, in apportioning representatives and direct taxes, and left out 'Indians not taxed'. It barred Congress from banning the slave trade before 1808 and required escaped people 'held to Service or Labour' to be returned. Sean Wilentz argues that the framers chose to abide slavery without legitimizing it; David Waldstreicher, that slavery mattered as much to the Constitution as the Constitution did to slavery's survival. The Bill of Rights was ratified on 15 December 1791; its First Amendment forbids Congress to make any law 'respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof'. Not everyone stayed for the new republic: by Maya Jasanoff's estimate some 60,000 loyalists fled, taking 15,000 slaves with them. Interpretations differ. Bernard Bailyn (1967) argued that the Revolutionary leaders' fears of 'slavery' and conspiracy were sincere, drawn from British opposition thought. In its publisher's words, Gordon Wood's The Radicalism of the American Revolution argues that the Revolution 'transformed an almost feudal society into a democratic one'. R. R. Palmer placed it in a wider Western age of democratic revolution (14.3). The 1619 Project's lead essay, as the Times later summarised it, gave protecting slavery as 'one primary reason' the colonists fought the Revolution. Five historians, including Wilentz and Wood, read this as a claim that independence was declared to ensure slavery would continue and called it 'not true'; the New York Times narrowed the wording to 'a primary motivation for some of the colonists'. 7 October 1763 Proclamation stops land grants west of the Appalachians 4 July 1776 Declaration of Independence 17 September 1787 Constitution signed 15 December 1791 Bill of Rights ratified 1808 first year in which Congress could ban the slave trade after the war some 60,000 loyalists leave, with 15,000 enslaved people

In August 1789 the Assembly abolished the feudal system and declared that men are 'born and remain free and equal in rights', and in 1791 it removed the last exceptions to the rights of Jews. In 1793-94 the Terror officially executed about 17,000 people. Historians still argue over the death toll in the Vendée and over what kind of revolution this was. After the night of 4 August 1789, the Assembly's decree of 11 August declared that it 'completely abolishes the feudal system'. The first article of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (26 August) declared that 'Men are born and remain free and equal in rights', and its tenth article protected religious opinions. Did those rights include Jews? On 23 December 1789 Clermont-Tonnerre answered: 'We must refuse everything to the Jews as a nation and accord everything to Jews as individuals.' On 27 September 1791 the Assembly revoked every remaining exception relating to Jews who swore the civic oath. In 1794 the Convention also abolished slavery in the colonies (14.4). Under the Terror, from September 1793 to July 1794, about 17,000 people were officially executed, perhaps 10,000 more died in prison or without trial, and at least 300,000 were arrested; it ended with Robespierre's fall on 9 Thermidor. In the Vendée, estimates vary widely: Jean-Clément Martin's runs to up to 250,000 insurgents and 200,000 republicans, while Peter McPhee rejects Pierre Chaunu's 500,000 rebel deaths and calls Reynald Secher's own estimate 'far lower, if still massive'. Secher calls the repression genocide; McPhee replies that huge numbers were killed, but that 'It was not a genocide'. What kind of revolution was it? Georges Lefebvre (1939) divided 1789 into four revolutions, aristocratic, bourgeois, popular and peasant, and, as his publisher puts it, wrote history 'from below'. Alfred Cobban (1964) challenged such social explanations, and François Furet (English edition, 1981) distinguished between commemorative and conceptual history. 4-11 August 1789 the feudal system abolished 26 August 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen 23 December 1789 Clermont-Tonnerre's speech on the Jews 27 September 1791 last exceptions to Jews' rights revoked 5 September 1793 the Terror begins 4 February 1794 slavery abolished in the colonies (14.4) 27 July 1794 (9 Thermidor) fall of Robespierre; the Terror ends

In 1791 the enslaved of Saint-Domingue rose, and in 1804 their leaders declared the independence of Haiti. In 1825 Haiti was charged an indemnity of 150 million francs, whose cost is still disputed. Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 and slavery from 1834, and historians argue over the part economics played. In 1789 Saint-Domingue held roughly 465,000 to 500,000 enslaved people, about 30,000 whites and a similar number of free people of colour. In August 1791 thousands of the enslaved rose in rebellion. On 4 February 1794 the National Convention abolished slavery in all the French colonies. Toussaint Louverture made himself governor-general for life in 1801; seized by the French, he died in April 1803. Leclerc's expedition of about 40,000 men was ruined by fighting and yellow fever, Dessalines won at Vertières, and on 1 January 1804 he declared Haiti independent; the French failure contributed to the Louisiana Purchase. Philippe Girard writes that the victors then 'eradicated Haiti's white population', calls this genocide, and asks that it be read in its Haitian context. In 1825 Haiti was charged an indemnity of 150 million francs, later cut to 90 million; combined with loans, it became a double debt. Haiti made its last payment on the indemnity in 1878, partly with a loan raised in France in 1875, and the loans of the double debt were paid off in 1888; Britannica gives 1887 as the year the payments were scheduled to end. The New York Times (2022) estimated that the payments cost Haiti between $21 billion and $115 billion in lost growth; two economists and two legal scholars, who put the initial debt at nearly 280% of GDP, estimate its cost at between $3 billion and $50 billion; their scenarios run from about $1.6 billion to $1.1 trillion, and they give reasons why their figures may overstate the cost and others why they may understate it. Some critics said the story was already known. In 2025 President Macron said that the decision of 1825 placed a price on freedom and set up a joint commission of historians, without offering reparations. Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 and slavery itself from 1 August 1834, with apprenticeship until 1838 and £20 million paid to slave-owners. Why? Eric Williams argued that slavery's profits fed British industry and that abolition followed its decline. Seymour Drescher replied that abolition came while slavery was still valuable and harmed Britain's economic interests. Heblich, Redding and Voth (2022) find that slave wealth raised British income by about a decade's growth, reviving the first half of Williams's thesis. August 1791 rising of the enslaved in Saint-Domingue 4 February 1794 France abolishes slavery in its colonies 1802-1803 Leclerc's expedition; Vertières, November 1803 1 January 1804 Dessalines declares Haiti independent 1807 Britain abolishes its slave trade 1825 indemnity of 150 million francs (cut to 90 million in 1838) 1834-1838 British abolition takes effect; apprenticeship ends 1878; 1888 last indemnity payment (BnF; NYT data); double debt paid off (NYT data)

In 1808 Napoleon forced Spain's kings to abdicate and chose his brother Joseph to rule Spain. Between 1808 and 1826 all of Latin America except Cuba and Puerto Rico broke away from Spain and Portugal, and Brazil crowned an emperor of its own. Economists still disagree about whether the decades that followed were 'lost'. Napoleon's Civil Code of 1804 swept away hereditary nobility and the privileges of class, but it subordinated women to their fathers and husbands. In the 19th century a number of European and Latin American countries adopted it of their own accord. (For the Revolution that came before Napoleon, see 14.3.) In 1808 Napoleon turned on Spain. The people of Madrid rose against the French on 2 May; three days later, at Bayonne, Napoleon forced Ferdinand VII and his father Charles IV to give up the crown, and chose his brother Joseph to rule. Spaniards free of French rule adopted a liberal constitution at Cádiz in 1812, which declared Spain's American possessions full members of the kingdom, not mere colonies. Yet Creoles in the Cortes were denied equal representation, and on his return in 1814 Ferdinand abolished the Cortes and all its works. In New Spain, Miguel Hidalgo called for revolt at Dolores on 16 September 1810 and raised a large popular army; he was executed the next July. In November 1813 José María Morelos's Congress of Chilpancingo declared Mexico independent, but Morelos too was captured and shot. In the south, San Martín crossed the Andes and won at Chacabuco in 1817, Bolívar freed New Granada at Boyacá in 1819, and Sucre's victory at Ayacucho in 1824 secured the independence of the South American republics. By 1826 Spain kept only Cuba and Puerto Rico in the Americas. Brazil followed a different path. The Portuguese court had moved to Rio in 1808, and in 1822 Pedro proclaimed independence and was crowned emperor. What did independence do to the economy? Bates, Coatsworth and Williamson argue that in Latin America, as later in Africa, it brought about half a century of instability, violent conflict and stagnation. Prados de la Escosura replies that per capita income grew, and that the region fell behind the US and Western Europe but not the rest of the world. In his view, 'lost decades' is an unwarranted description of 1820-1870. (For Latin America's later export economies, see 14.13.) 1804 the Civil Code in France 1808 abdications at Bayonne; the Portuguese court reaches Rio 1810 Hidalgo's call to revolt at Dolores 1812 the Constitution of Cádiz (abolished 1814) 1813 the Congress of Chilpancingo declares Mexico independent 1817-1819 Chacabuco (1817), Boyacá (1819) 1822 Pedro proclaims Brazil independent 1824-1826 Ayacucho; by 1826 Spain keeps only Cuba and Puerto Rico in the Americas

The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the 18th century. Economists have revised its growth rates downward, and they still argue about why it happened there first, whether it raised workers' living standards, and when Europe pulled ahead of China. Arnold Toynbee used the term 'Industrial Revolution' for Britain's economic development between 1760 and 1840. In 1769 the Scottish engineer James Watt patented his separate condenser, which vastly improved the efficiency of the steam engine. How fast did the economy grow? Antràs and Voth's table of estimates shows Feinstein (1981) putting output growth in England at 1.1% a year in 1760-1800 and 2.7% in 1801-31. Crafts and Harley (1992) put it at about 1% and 1.9%. Their revision made the revolution look more gradual, but they still call it an important discontinuity. Why Britain? Robert Allen argues that high wages and cheap capital and energy made labour-saving machines uniquely profitable to invent and use there. Jane Humphries and Benjamin Schneider find no high-wage economy in spinning, a leading sector, and Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda find that industry grew where wages were low but mechanical skills were high. Allen, answering an earlier critique by Humphries, has presented new evidence that women and children took part in the high-wage economy. Emma Griffin, reviewing his book, finds that he has 'convincingly argued' that high wages and cheap fuel deserve 'a central place', though she doubts that any single explanation will do. Did workers gain? Charles Feinstein found that the average working-class family's standard of living rose by less than 15% between the 1780s and 1850s. Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda find that real wages rose sharply in the industrial north but fell in the south. Kenneth Pomeranz argues that coal and American imports let Britain escape the limits of its land, and he now concedes that his claim of rough parity with the Yangzi delta is stronger for 1750 than for 1800. Broadberry, Guan and Li date the divergence between his view and older Eurocentric ones. Robert Allen (2009) high wages and cheap capital and energy made machines pay in Britain Humphries and Schneider (2019) no high-wage economy in spinning Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2023) industry grew where wages were low and mechanical skills high Charles Feinstein (1998) living standards rose by less than 15%, 1780s-1850s Kenneth Pomeranz (2000) coal and American imports eased Britain's land constraint Broadberry, Guan and Li (2018) divergence earlier than the California School says, later than Eurocentric writers said

t: Industry spreads and the social question
x: Steam railways opened in England in 1825 and in Belgium by 1835, and Belgium, Germany, the United States and Meiji Japan built industries of their own. Britain extended its limits on child labour and appointed factory inspectors, Marx and Engels published their Manifesto in the year of Europe's revolutions, and Bismarck's Germany created the first old-age social insurance. The Stockton and Darlington, a steam-hauled public railway, opened in 1825, and the Liverpool and Manchester, the world's first inter-city line, followed in 1830. Belgium, where machine shops were growing at Liège from about 1807, became the first country in continental Europe to be transformed economically, and in 1835 a train ran from Brussels to Mechelen. In Britannica's account, France industrialised more slowly and Germany expanded after unification (1870-71), though the economic historian John Munro sees 'much more rapid growth and discernible industrialization' from the 1850s; the United States later far outstripped Europe. In Japan the Meiji government founded the Tomioka silk mill in 1872 with French machinery, and by the beginning of the 20th century Japan was the world's leading exporter of raw silk. (On Meiji Japan, see 14.10.) Britain's Factory Act of 1833 barred children under nine from factories, limited the hours of older children, required schooling for those under 13, and created a four-man inspectorate to enforce the rules. In February 1848 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published the Manifesto of the Communist Party, which opens: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.' That same year revolution began in Sicily in January, spread across Europe after the revolution of 24 February in France, and, in Britannica's judgement, 'ended in failure and repression', although some reforms lasted, among them the emancipation of the peasants in Austria and the end of absolute monarchy in Denmark. In the 1880s Bismarck's Germany introduced sickness insurance, workers' compensation and, in 1889, the world's first old-age insurance, with a pension age of 70. The Social Security Administration's history says Bismarck wanted both to promote workers' well-being and to head off more radical socialist demands. c. 1807 machine shops at Liège 1825 Stockton and Darlington railway opens 1830 Liverpool and Manchester, the first inter-city line 1833 British Factory Act 1835 train from Brussels to Mechelen 1848 the Communist Manifesto; revolutions from Sicily to Paris 1872 Tomioka silk mill 1883-1889 German sickness, accident and old-age insurance

Italy became a kingdom in 1861, and the German Empire was proclaimed in 1871. In the same decades racial antisemitism took shape, pogroms struck the Jews of the Russian empire, the Jewish officer Alfred Dreyfus was convicted of treason in France, and in 1897 the First Zionist Congress met at Basel. Scholars still debate whether nations are modern creations or have older roots. The Kingdom of Italy was established in 1861, and it annexed Venetia in 1866 and papal Rome in 1870. On 18 January 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. Where do nations come from? For the modernist Ernest Gellner, 'the world was created round about the end of the eighteenth century'. Anthony Smith stressed ethnic roots, and when the two debated at Warwick in 1995 Gellner called such continuity 'inessential'. Benedict Anderson called the nation 'imagined', because its members never meet most of their fellow-members, and Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger argued that many supposedly ancient traditions had been invented recently. In the 1870s Wilhelm Marr is credited with coining the word 'antisemitism', and racial antisemitism took shape in the late 19th century. In the Russian empire pogroms began at Yelizavetgrad in 1881, and the restrictive May Laws followed in 1882. At Kishinev in 1903 a pogrom left about 45 to 49 Jews dead (45 by the Encyclopaedia Judaica's count, 49 in the description of Steven Zipperstein's study) and hundreds wounded. In France the army captain Alfred Dreyfus, who was Jewish, was convicted of treason in 1894. Émile Zola took up his case, but the army did not publicly declare him innocent until 1995. In 1896 Theodor Herzl called for 'the restoration of the Jewish State'. Herzl later said the Dreyfus affair had made him a Zionist; Shlomo Avineri points instead to his long analysis of the failure of emancipation. The First Zionist Congress met at Basel in 1897 and sought a home for the Jewish people secured by public law. For those who identify as Zionists, as the description of Derek Penslar's study puts it, the word connotes liberation; for others it is a source of distaste. Britannica notes that under the British Mandate, in the 1920s and 1930s, Palestine's Arab population feared that the land would eventually become a Jewish state, and Penslar's study of 2023 offers a new take on the movement's relationship to colonialism. (See 14.12.) Ernest Gellner modern, from about 1800 ethnic continuity 'inessential' Anthony Smith built on older ethnic roots modernism 'only tells half the story' (as Gellner reports him) Benedict Anderson an imagined community members never know most of the others Hobsbawm and Ranger traditions often recent 'invented comparatively recently'

Between 1861 and 1888 Russia freed its serfs, and the United States, Cuba and Brazil abolished slavery. Freedom often came with conditions, and in 1877 federal troops left three Southern states, ending Reconstruction there. Economists and historians still argue about what slavery meant for economic growth. By Alexander II's Emancipation Manifesto of 3 March 1861, Russia's serfs were freed. They were organised in village communities and were to repay the state over 49 years for the land they received. Emancipation freed roughly 40 percent of the population from bondage, but the reforms left the empire's political structure unchanged. In the United States, Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 did not end slavery in the nation. The Thirteenth Amendment, passed at the end of the Civil War and ratified in December 1865, did. After the disputed election of 1876, what 64 Parishes calls an unwritten deal, the Compromise of 1877, though some historians doubt that a bargain was struck, secured the presidency for Rutherford B. Hayes, and federal troops were removed from Florida, Louisiana and South Carolina, effectively ending Reconstruction there. Cuba replaced slavery in 1880 with the patronato, a transition meant to last eight years, and ended it early in 1886. Brazil abolished slavery outright in 1888, without compensation to the owners. (On Haiti and British abolition, see 14.4.) Was slavery economically doomed? Robert Fogel and Stanley Engerman argued in 1974 that slavery, 'in spite of its inhumanity', had been efficient, and that it ended because of political decisions rather than economic weakness. Their book provoked bitter controversy. Herbert Gutman, Paul David and others attacked it from several directions. More recently, historians of the 'new history of capitalism' have tied industrial capitalism to slave-grown cotton. Alan Olmstead and Paul Rhode reply that they mishandle the evidence. Russia, 1861 Emancipation Manifesto land repaid over 49 years; village communities United States, 1865 Thirteenth Amendment slavery abolished, except as punishment for crime United States, 1877 troops withdrawn from three states Reconstruction effectively ended there Cuba, 1880 and 1886 law of 1880; Royal Decree of 1886 patronato of up to eight years, ended two years early Brazil, 1888 decree of 13 May complete emancipation, no compensation to owners

Britain fought China over the opium trade in 1839-42, and Britain and France fought it again in 1856-60, while the Taiping rebellion cost tens of millions of lives. Japan's new imperial government abolished the feudal domains and brought in conscription, and Japan went on to defeat China in 1894-95 and Russia in 1904-05. Foreign traders, mainly British, had been exporting opium illegally from India to China since the 18th century. When the Chinese government confiscated and destroyed more than 20,000 chests of it at Canton, Britain went to war: the first Opium War lasted from 1839 to 1842, and Britain and France fought a second from 1856 to 1860. The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) made China pay Britain a large indemnity, cede Hong Kong Island and open five treaty ports to British trade and residence instead of one. In 1858 the importation of opium was legalized, and in 1860 British and French troops captured Beijing and plundered and burned the Yuanming Garden, the emperor's summer palace. (On the Qing to 1722, see 13.11.) Meanwhile the Taiping rebellion (1850-64) was led by Hong Xiuquan, a disappointed candidate in the civil-service examinations who believed himself the son of God and the younger brother of Jesus Christ. In 1853 his followers took Nanjing and renamed it Tianjing, 'Heavenly Capital'; it fell in July 1864. Forces organised under the Qing official Zeng Guofan fought the Taipings, as did a Western-trained 'Ever-Victorious Army', led first by the American Frederick Townsend Ward and then by the British officer Charles Gordon. Estimates of the dead vary. Britannica gives an estimated 20 million and a page on Tobie Meyer-Fong's study of the war's aftermath some 30 million; a popular history says conservative estimates start at 20 to 30 million and that much of the mortality came from disease and famine rather than fighting. From 1861 Zeng Guofan, Li Hongzhang and Zuo Zongtang tried to consolidate Qing power by introducing Western technology. Britannica credits this Self-Strengthening movement with some notable gains but judges its overall success limited. In Japan, the Meiji Restoration brought down the Tokugawa shogunate and restored direct imperial rule. The new government declared feudalism abolished in 1871, turning nearly 300 fiefs into 72 prefectures and 3 metropolitan districts; it introduced nationwide conscription in 1873 and set the land tax at 3 percent of the land's assessed value. (On Japan's industrial drive, see 14.7.) Rivalry over Korea brought war between China and Japan in 1894. At Shimonoseki in 1895 China recognized Korea's independence, ceded Taiwan, the Pescadores and the Liaodong Peninsula, and agreed to pay a large indemnity, but Russia, France and Germany forced Japan to hand Liaodong back. Three years later Russia pressed China into leasing it Port Arthur, at the peninsula's tip. In 1900 the Boxers, a secret society encouraged by the empress dowager Cixi, attacked Chinese Christians and Western missionaries and besieged the foreign legations in Beijing until an international force of some 19,000 troops took the city on 14 August. The protocol of 1901 imposed an indemnity of 450 million Haikwan taels at 4 percent interest, to be paid off by the end of 1940. In 1904-05 Japan fought Russia over Korea and Manchuria and became, in Britannica's words, 'the first Asian power in modern times to defeat a European power'. 1839-42 first Opium War; Treaty of Nanjing, 1842 1850-64 Taiping rebellion; Nanjing its capital from 1853 1856-60 second Opium War; Beijing taken, 1860 1861-95 Self-Strengthening movement 1871-73 Japan: fiefs abolished, conscription, land tax 1894-95 Sino-Japanese War; Treaty of Shimonoseki 1900-01 Boxer rising; Boxer Protocol 1904-05 Russo-Japanese War

After the rising of 1857-58 the British Crown took over the East India Company's rule in India, and in 1876-78 famine killed an estimated 5.5 million people in the south, on Mike Davis's figures. In Africa, Leopold II's Congo Free State ran on forced labour, and Germany waged a war on the Herero and Nama that it recognised as genocide in 2021. Scholars still argue over how many died under British rule in India and over who gained from empire. The rising of 1857-58 began among the East India Company's Indian troops, the sepoys, at Meerut, and spread to Delhi, Agra, Kanpur and Lucknow. Its name is disputed: Britannica files it under 'Indian Mutiny', but in India it is often called the First War of Independence, and Britannica itself warns that 'To regard the rebellion merely as a sepoy mutiny is to underestimate the root causes leading to it'. In August 1858 Parliament transferred British power over India from the Company to the Crown, beginning the Raj, which lasted until 1947; in 1876 Queen Victoria took the title Empress of India.
