In 1790 Alexander Hamilton reported on the debts left by the Revolution and urged the Union to assume the states' debts; in 1791 Congress chartered a national bank, and Hamilton argued for government aid to manufactures. The bank divided Jefferson and Hamilton over how to read the Constitution, a federal whiskey tax met armed resistance in western Pennsylvania, and in 1796 Washington warned the nation against the spirit of party. In January 1790 Hamilton reported that the federal debt, foreign and domestic, came to '54,124,464 dollars, and 56 cents', and that for the states' debts 'the total amount may be safely stated at 25 millions of dollars'. The debt, he wrote, 'was the price of liberty', and he concluded that 'it is expedient, there should be an assumption of the state debts by the Union.' How assumption passed is told in Jefferson's own later account, which the editors of his papers date '[1792?]'. He writes that he invited Hamilton and Madison to dinner ('I immediately wrote to each to come and dine with me the next day'), and that 'It ended in Mr. Madison's acquiescence in a proposition that the question should be again brought before the house': Madison would not vote for assumption but 'should not be strenuous' against it, two members whose districts lay on the Potomac, White and Lee, would change their votes, and the capital would move to the Potomac, with 'an intermediate residence at Philadelphia' to win Pennsylvania. Washington signed the bill for a Bank of the United States in February 1791. It had $10 million in capital, $2 million of it owned by the government, and opened in Philadelphia on 12 December 1791 with a twenty-year charter. Jefferson and Hamilton disagreed over it. Jefferson argued that 'the constitution allows only the means which are "necessary" not those which are merely "convenient"'; Hamilton answered that 'necessary often means no more than needful, requisite, incidental, useful, or conducive to.' (For the Supreme Court's later answer, see US2.2.) When the charter came up for renewal in 1811, the House rejected it by one vote, and Vice President George Clinton broke a tie in the Senate against it. Hamilton's Report on Manufactures of 5 December 1791 argued that for new industries 'the interference and aid of their own government are indispensible' (his spelling). The whiskey excise of 1791, the first national internal revenue tax, met armed resistance: in July 1794 about 500 armed men burned the home of the regional tax inspector, Washington sent some 13,000 troops into western Pennsylvania, 'the opposition melted away', and the two men convicted of treason were later pardoned. In his Farewell Address of 19 September 1796 Washington warned of 'the baneful effects of the Spirit of Party', advised the nation 'to steer clear of permanent Alliances', and wrote that 'Religion and morality are indispensable supports.' Economists still weigh Hamilton's system. Peter Rousseau and Richard Sylla argue that the financial system built in the 1790s 'was central to the nation's early growth and modernization', and a 2021 study by Hall, Payne, Sargent and Szőke measures how long Hamilton's policy took to work 'by building a reputation for servicing debts as promised'. Historians also stress what the founding era cost ordinary people: Terry Bouton's Taming Democracy (2007), a study of Pennsylvania, argues, in a reviewer's words, that the American gentry from 1776 to roughly 1800 succeeded at 'stunting the meaning and practice of democracy for ordinary white men.' January 1790 Report on Public Credit federal debt $54.1 million; states' debts about $25 million account dated [1792?] assumption bargain Madison agrees not to be 'strenuous'; capital to the Potomac February 1791 Bank of the United States signed; $10 million capital, $2 million federal 1791 whiskey excise the first national internal revenue tax 5 December 1791 Report on Manufactures government 'aid' for new industries 1794 Whiskey Rebellion some 13,000 troops; no battle; two pardoned 19 September 1796 Farewell Address against 'the Spirit of Party' 1811 Bank renewal lost by one House vote and the Vice President's tie-break

Jefferson and Hamilton had already clashed over the Bank (US3.1). The French Revolution 'exacerbated pre-existing political divisions' and aligned the political elite along pro-French and pro-British lines, behind Hamilton's Federalists and Jefferson's Democratic-Republicans. A Federalist Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts in 1798, Jefferson and Madison, keeping their authorship secret, answered with the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, and the tied election of 1800 led to the Twelfth Amendment. The French Revolution deepened existing divisions in American politics. Jefferson led the pro-French Democratic-Republicans, and Hamilton the Federalists, who viewed the Revolution with skepticism. John Jay's treaty with Britain was 'immensely unpopular with the American public', but it 'squeaked through the Senate on a 20 to 10 vote on June 24, 1795.' In 1798 a Federalist-controlled Congress passed four laws known together as the Alien and Sedition Acts. They raised the residency requirement for citizenship from 5 to 14 years, and the Sedition Act made it a crime to publish any 'false, scandalous, and malicious writing' about the government. The only journalists prosecuted under it were editors of Democratic-Republican newspapers. The Sedition Act was to last 'until the third day of March, one thousand eight hundred and one, and no longer.' Jefferson and Madison drafted the reply, and kept their authorship secret because they feared arrest for sedition. Their resolutions treated the Union as 'a compact among individual states'; Kentucky passed Jefferson's in 1798, and Virginia its 'more temperate resolution' on Christmas Eve. Virginia's declared that the states 'have the right, and are in duty bound, to interpose'. A further Kentucky resolution, of December 1799, declared that 'a nullification, by those sovereignties, of all unauthorized acts done under colour of that instrument, is the rightful remedy'. What these words meant is still argued. In the early 1830s John Calhoun and Robert Hayne cited the resolutions as precedents for nullification; Madison denied that a single state could nullify federal law within its borders (US3.7). In 1800 Jefferson and Aaron Burr tied in the electoral college, because electors could not say which of their votes was for president. The House chose Jefferson on 17 February 1801, after 36 ballots, and Hamilton tried to 'engineer support for Jefferson' over Burr. The Twelfth Amendment, ratified on 15 June 1804, requires electors to vote for the vice president 'in distinct ballots'. Jefferson later called his election 'as real a revolution in the principles of our government as that of 76.' 24 June 1795 Jay Treaty passes the Senate, 20 to 10 1798 Alien and Sedition Acts 1798 Kentucky Resolutions (Jefferson) 24 December 1798 Virginia Resolution (Madison) 3 December 1799 Kentucky's 'nullification' resolution 17 February 1801 House elects Jefferson on the 36th ballot 3 March 1801 Sedition Act expires 15 June 1804 Twelfth Amendment ratified

In 1803 the United States bought Louisiana from France for $15 million, though Jefferson doubted that the Constitution allowed it, and Lewis and Clark crossed the continent to the Pacific. The embargo of 1807-09 cost about 8 percent of GNP by Douglas Irwin's estimate, the war with Britain that began in 1812 ended in a peace that restored the prewar boundaries, and the Hartford Convention helped bring down the Federalist Party. Napoleon gave up his plans for Louisiana when his army in St. Domingue 'was being decimated by yellow fever, and war between France and England still threatened'. Jefferson had sent James Monroe to join Robert Livingston in France, and in 1803 the United States bought Louisiana, about 828,000 square miles, for $15 million, roughly 4 cents an acre, doubling the country's size. Jefferson wrote to John Breckinridge that 'the constitution has made no provision for our holding foreign territory', and that the Executive had 'done an act beyond the constitution.' Robert J. Miller argues, in his publisher's summary, that Jefferson used the Doctrine of Discovery 'to exert American authority in the Louisiana Territory' and to 'conquer' the Indian nations; the official histories describe a purchase of territory from France. On 14 May 1804 William Clark and the Corps of Discovery, more than 45 strong, left Camp River Dubois. They reached the Pacific by November 1805 and were back in St. Louis on 23 September 1806. Among them were Sacagawea, the Shoshone wife of the interpreter Toussaint Charbonneau, with her newborn son, and York, 'who had been enslaved by William Clark since his childhood.' From December 1807 to March 1809 the United States imposed an embargo on its own international shipping. Douglas Irwin estimates its cost at about 8 percent of 1807 GNP, when trade was roughly 13 percent of output: some trade continued, and 'domestic producers successfully shifted production toward previously imported manufactured goods'. On 1 June 1812 Madison asked Congress to declare war on Great Britain. The causes included British impressment of American seamen and restrictions on neutral trade, but also 'western expansion, relations with American Indians, and territorial control of North America.' By 1814 neither side could claim a clear victory; the British blockaded the east coast and burned the White House and other government buildings in Washington. On Christmas Eve 1814 the Treaty of Ghent restored the 'status quo ante bellum'. Federalists from five New England states met at Hartford from 15 December 1814 to 5 January 1815. Some raised the possibility of secession; the convention instead proposed amendments: to apportion representatives and direct taxes by 'free persons', to require two-thirds of both Houses to declare war unless the country was 'actually invaded', to limit embargoes to sixty days, and to bar a president 'from the same State two terms in succession'. Counting free persons alone would have ended the Constitution's count of 'three fifths of all other Persons' (US2.1). Even as the convention finished, a British ship was still crossing the Atlantic with the terms of the Treaty of Ghent. As its emissaries approached Washington they 'were met by the news of Gen. Andrew Jackson's unexpected victory in the Battle of New Orleans', and 'its unpopularity was a factor in the demise of the Federalist Party.' 1803 Louisiana bought for $15 million 14 May 1804 Corps of Discovery leaves Camp River Dubois November 1805 the Corps reaches the Pacific 23 September 1806 the Corps returns to St. Louis December 1807 to March 1809 embargo: about 8 percent of GNP lost (Irwin) 1 June 1812 Madison asks Congress for war 24 December 1814 Treaty of Ghent 15 December 1814 to 5 January 1815 Hartford Convention

The First Amendment bound Congress, but some states still kept established churches: Virginia guaranteed religious freedom by statute in 1786, and Massachusetts was the last of the original states to disestablish, in 1833. Revivals spread through the Methodist and Baptist churches and fed reforms from temperance to women's rights, while new movements such as the Latter-day Saints appeared beside older communities such as the Jews of Newport. Virginia's Statute for Religious Freedom, written by Jefferson in 1777, was adopted on 16 January 1786, after James Madison's anonymous Memorial and Remonstrance opposed a General Assessment, a tax to support all Christian sects that Patrick Henry had championed. It provides that 'no man shall be compelled to frequent or support any religious worship, place, or ministry whatsoever.' The First Amendment's words, 'Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion', named Congress (US2.9), and Massachusetts was the last of the original 13 states to disestablish its churches, in 1833. On 1 January 1802 Jefferson answered the Baptists of Danbury, Connecticut, with a phrase about 'a wall of separation between Church & State.' In 1998 the FBI made his erased draft legible. It shows that on Levi Lincoln's advice he cut a section on fasts and thanksgivings, which Lincoln feared would hurt him among New England Republicans; Federalist preachers had used such days to revile Jefferson. James Hutson of the Library of Congress concludes that 'it was meant to be a political manifesto, nothing more', whereas the Supreme Court in Reynolds v. United States (1878) said Jefferson's words might be accepted 'almost as an authoritative declaration of the scope and effect of the [first] amendment'. The Second Great Awakening, roughly 1795 to 1835, grew 'particularly among Methodist and Baptist churches' and 'stimulated several moral and philanthropic reforms, including temperance and the emancipation of women.' Crowd estimates for the camp meeting at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, in August 1801 'range from 10,000 to 30,000.' In Philadelphia, where 'blacks had been confined to the gallery' of St. George's church, Richard Allen and more than forty others left St. George's, and in 1816 Allen was consecrated bishop of the new African Methodist Episcopal Church. In one influential interpretation, Nathan Hatch argues that in these years 'American Christianity was democratized and common people became powerful actors on the religious scene.' Latter-day Saints hold that an angel, Moroni, told Joseph Smith of engraved golden plates; the Book of Mormon appeared in 1830, the church was organized on 6 April 1830, at Fayette or Manchester, New York (firsthand accounts by those present disagree), and Smith was killed by a mob at Carthage, Illinois, in 1844. Newport's synagogue, dedicated in 1763, is the oldest synagogue building in the United States. In 1790 Washington wrote to its congregation that 'It is now no more that toleration is spoken of', praised a government 'which gives to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance', and used the words 'every one shall sit in safety under his own vine and figtree, and there shall be none to make him afraid.' They closely follow Micah 4:4: 'they shall all sit under their own vines and under their own fig trees, and no one shall make them afraid'. The Jewish population, about 3,000 in 1820, 'ballooned from 15,000 to 150,000' between 1840 and 1860. The earliest temperance societies seem to have been those founded at Saratoga, New York, in 1808 and in Massachusetts in 1813; by 1833 there were 6,000 local societies. At Seneca Falls on 19-20 July 1848, 68 women and 32 men signed a Declaration of Sentiments, drafted by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and the M'Clintock family, which held that 'all men and women are created equal'; eleven resolutions passed unanimously, but the suffrage resolution was only 'narrowly approved', after Frederick Douglass 'stood with Stanton' for it. 1786 Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom 1790 Newport Washington: 'to bigotry no sanction' 1801 Cane Ridge, Kentucky camp meeting; 10,000 to 30,000 people 1802 Danbury, Connecticut Jefferson's 'wall of separation' 1808 Saratoga, New York one of the earliest temperance societies 1830 Fayette or Manchester, New York church organized; Book of Mormon 1833 Massachusetts the last original state to disestablish 1848 Seneca Falls, New York Declaration of Sentiments

From Fulton's steamboat of 1807 to some 30,000 miles of railroad track by 1860, Americans built new ways to move goods, and the Erie Canal cut freight rates from upstate New York to the Atlantic by about 90 percent. Mills at Lowell spun cotton picked by enslaved people, and a Second Bank of the United States first fed and then tightened the credit boom that ended in the Panic of 1819. Historians still disagree over whether to call these changes a 'market revolution'. Robert Fulton's steamboat ran 150 miles up the Hudson from New York to Albany in August 1807, a trip of 32 hours. Ten years later work began on the Erie Canal, which was completed in 1825; it ran 363 miles, and New York State authorized $7 million in loans to build it. By the round figures of the historian Justin Nordstrom, freight rates from upstate New York to the Atlantic then fell by about 90 percent, and hauling time from 30 days to 10. About 3,000 miles of railroad track had been laid by 1840, and about 30,000 by 1860. George Rogers Taylor called the years 1815 to 1860 'the transportation revolution' in the title of his book of 1951, and a retrospective a quarter-century later made 'the case for the permanent impact' of the book. The Merrimack Manufacturing Company, incorporated in 1822, produced its first textiles in 1823 as the first mill in what became Lowell; it was funded and planned by the Boston Associates, a group of Boston financiers who incorporated the town of Lowell in 1826 (on the Industrial Revolution in Britain, see 14.6). Lowell had 18,000 people by 1836 and 30,000 by 1850, and its cotton came from the South, 'picked and processed by enslaved men and women'. Its mill women walked out twice: in 1834, when 800 of them left work against a 12.5 percent wage cut, and in 1836, when between 1,500 and 2,000 workers turned out. Lowell National Historical Park, citing Edward Baptist, now says that the Merrimack company's cotton 'took slaves a combined 100,000 days of labor per year to produce' (US3.6). Credit expanded too. Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States in April 1816 with $35 million in capital, and it opened in January 1817 (for its constitutionality, McCulloch v. Maryland, see US2.2). Three economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, James Narron, David Skeie and Donald Morgan, tell the story of what followed: farmers and speculators bid up land on easy credit from state banks, which the Second Bank did little to restrain and even fed in its western branches; then cotton prices 'plummeted in January 1819 after British investors substituted to Indian cotton', and the Bank's deflationary tightening brought down prices and land values. Federal Reserve History calls the result 'a financial panic that drove the economy into a steep recession'. Was all this a 'market revolution'? Charles Sellers, in The Market Revolution (1991), his most widely debated book, described a shift 'from an agrarian to a capitalist society' that carried real costs. Daniel Walker Howe, in What Hath God Wrought (2007), dates the change earlier, judges it less harmful and argues that 'most American family farmers welcomed the chance to buy and sell in larger markets'; he refuses the term and writes of a 'communications revolution' instead. Daniel Feller warned that 'a monograph that presupposes a market revolution will certainly discover one'. 1807 Fulton's steamboat, New York to Albany: 150 miles in 32 hours 1816-17 Second Bank chartered with $35 million; opens in January 1817 1817 work begins on the Erie Canal 1819 cotton prices fall in January; panic and recession 1825 Erie Canal completed: 363 miles 1826 Lowell incorporated by the Boston Associates 1834, 1836 Lowell mill women walk out 1840 and 1860 about 3,000 and about 30,000 miles of railroad track

Congress banned the import of enslaved people from 1808, but slavery and the trade within the country went on: between the Constitution and the Civil War about a million people were moved from the Upper South to the Lower South, and cotton output rose from about 3,000 bales in 1790 to about 2 million a year by the mid-1840s. Historians and economic historians disagree sharply over how slavery and capitalism were linked. Virginia tightened its laws after Nat Turner's revolt of 1831, the year in which William Lloyd Garrison launched The Liberator. Jefferson signed the act banning the import of enslaved people on 2 March 1807 (for the Constitution's 1808 clause, see US1.12). It took effect on 1 January 1808 and imposed heavy penalties on international traders, but it did not end slavery itself or the domestic sale of enslaved people, though it required manifests for those shipped along the coast. As Henry Louis Gates Jr. reports, drawing on the historian Walter Johnson, in the seven decades between the ratification of the Constitution and the Civil War about one million enslaved people were moved from the Upper South to the Lower South, roughly two-thirds of them through the domestic slave trade. Cotton output rose from 3,135 bales in 1790 to 731,452 in 1830 by L. C. Gray's figures, and by Fogel and Engerman's rounded figures to about 2 million a year by the mid-1840s and about 4 million on the eve of the Civil War. Edward Baptist, in The Half Has Never Been Told (2014), argues that violence drove the rise in productivity: as Eric Foner summarises him, 'Violence, Baptist contends, explains the remarkable increase of labor productivity'. Sven Beckert's idea of 'war capitalism' holds, in a University of Cape Town report of 2014, that early capitalism 'depended not on free wage labour, but on slavery and other unfree forms of labour'. The economic historians Alan Olmstead and Paul Rhode reply that Baptist, Beckert and Walter Johnson 'mishandle historical evidence and mis-characterize important events' (2018); their own research found that picking rates 'increased about fourfold between 1801 and 1862', driven by 'new cotton varieties' (2008). Northern mills such as Lowell's drew on this cotton (US3.5). On the night of 21-22 August 1831, in Southampton County, Virginia, Nat Turner's rebels killed 'fifty-five white men, women, and children'. White people then killed 'roughly three dozen Black people without trials', and Turner was executed on 11 November. The Virginia legislature judged ending slavery 'inexpedient' and passed restrictions 'aimed at further suppressing Black religion and limiting the rights of free Blacks'. In Philadelphia, Richard Allen had built Bethel church, and in 1816 he 'united other African Methodist congregations' into the African Methodist Episcopal Church and became its bishop. On 1 January 1831 William Lloyd Garrison began The Liberator, promising that he would 'not equivocate', would 'not retreat a single inch' and would 'be heard'. Frederick Douglass escaped from slavery on 3 September 1838, 'dressed as a sailor', and in 1845 published his first autobiography. Edward Baptist (2014) violence explains the rise in enslaved people's productivity Sven Beckert 'war capitalism': early capitalism rested on slavery, not free wage labour Olmstead and Rhode (2008) picking rates rose about fourfold, 1801-1862, driven by new cotton varieties Olmstead and Rhode (2018) Baptist, Beckert and Johnson 'mishandle historical evidence' Lowell National Historical Park, citing Baptist the Merrimack company's cotton took 100,000 days of enslaved labor a year

Most states reduced or dropped property tests for voting, and turnout among those entitled to vote, by the American Presidency Project's figures, rose from 57.6 percent in 1828 to 80.2 percent in 1840, but New York and Pennsylvania shut most Black men out. Andrew Jackson won the presidency in 1828, vetoed the recharter of the Second Bank, and ended South Carolina's nullification of the tariff with a Compromise Tariff and a Force Bill. His opponents organised as the Whigs, and historians still disagree over what his democracy meant. 'Suffrage was expanded as property and other restrictions on voting were reduced or abandoned in most states,' in Britannica's summary. The gain was for white men. New York's constitution of 1821 dropped the property test for white men but required 'm[e]n of colour' to own a freehold worth $250; in 1825 only 298 of nearly 6,000 free adult Black New Yorkers qualified. In 1838 Pennsylvania restricted the vote 'to "white freemen" only'. By the American Presidency Project's figures, which before 1920 are 'adjusted for the shifting definition of citizens with voting rights' (women, for example, are excluded), turnout among those entitled to vote rose from 57.6 percent in 1828 to 80.2 percent in 1840. In 1828 Jackson beat John Quincy Adams by 642,553 popular votes (56 percent) to 500,897 (43.6 percent), and by 178 electoral votes to 83; in South Carolina and Delaware the legislatures chose the electors. Vetoing the Bank's recharter on 10 July 1832, he wrote: 'It is to be regretted that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes.' In 1833 he ordered the federal deposits removed from the Bank, and its federal charter ended in 1836. What caused the Panic of 1837 is debated. Peter Temin (1969) argued that the boom before it 'did not have its origins in the Bank Wars' and pointed to Mexican silver and 'the money-tightening policies of the Bank of England'; Peter Rousseau (2002) blames the Treasury's transfers of government balances between banks and 'a policy-induced increase in the demand for coin in the Western states'. On 24 November 1832 a South Carolina convention at Columbia declared the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 'null, void, and no law, nor binding upon this State, its officers or citizens'. Jackson's proclamation of 10 December replied that 'disunion, by armed force, is TREASON'. On 2 March 1833 he signed both a Compromise Tariff and a Force Bill; South Carolina then rescinded its nullification of the tariffs and nullified the Force Bill instead. Jackson's opponents 'formally organized' the Whig party in 1834 against 'King Andrew'. They favoured 'a protective tariff and federally financed internal improvements', and in 1840 they elected William Henry Harrison. Historians have judged Jacksonian democracy in very different ways. Arthur Schlesinger Jr. (1945) saw an effort to 'control the power of the capitalist groups'; Edward Pessen saw democratic rhetoric that hid inequality; Robert Remini called Jackson a genuine 'man of the people'; Daniel Walker Howe calls the Jacksonians champions of white male supremacy. Daniel Feller notes that Schlesinger gave Indian affairs two sentences: 'Indian removal simply didn't seem that important to [Schlesinger]' (US3.8). 1821 New York drops the property test for white men; $250 freehold for men of colour 1828 Jackson defeats Adams, 178 electoral votes to 83 10 July 1832 Bank veto 24 November 1832 South Carolina nullifies the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 2 March 1833 Compromise Tariff and Force Bill 1833-36 federal deposits removed; the Bank's federal charter ends 1834 Whig party formally organised 1838-40 Pennsylvania limits the vote to 'white freemen'; Harrison elected

Under the Indian Removal Act of 1830, Jackson's government signed almost 70 removal treaties and relocated nearly 50,000 people to Indian Territory, by the National Archives' count. The Supreme Court held in 1832 that Georgia's laws had no force in the Cherokee nation, yet after a minority faction signed a treaty more than 16,000 Cherokee were forcibly evicted in 1838-39, and at least a thousand died. The Seminoles fought removal in Florida, and historians still disagree over how to judge it. Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act on 28 May 1830. It 'authorized the President to negotiate removal treaties with Indian tribes living east of the Mississippi River'. In his message to Congress of 6 December 1830 he presented removal as part of 'the benevolent policy of the Government'. By the end of his presidency, the National Archives counts, almost 70 removal treaties had been signed, nearly 50,000 eastern Indians had been relocated to Indian Territory, and 25 million acres had been opened to white settlement. The Cherokee defended their land with their own laws. In 1829 Womankiller supported the death penalty for unauthorised sales of Cherokee land: 'It is a good law -- it will not kill the innocent but the guilty.' On 3 March 1832, in Worcester v. Georgia, Chief Justice Marshall wrote that 'The Cherokee nation, then, is a distinct community occupying its own territory, with boundaries accurately described, in which the laws of Georgia can have no force'. The retort often put in Jackson's mouth, beginning 'John Marshall has made his decision', is in Daniel Feller's judgement 'dubious at best'. In late 1835 a 'small, rump faction' signed the Treaty of New Echota, and the Senate ratified it in May 1836. That year Principal Chief John Ross told the Senate: 'Our cause is your own. It is the cause of liberty and justice.' Removal began in May 1838 and was completed by the end of March 1839: more than 16,000 Cherokee were forcibly evicted and sent to Indian Territory, in present-day Oklahoma. How many died is uncertain. The National Park Service says more than a thousand Cherokee died on the journey and 'perhaps several thousand' more from its consequences; the National Archives says about 4,000 of 16,000 died; a 2017 blog post of the National Museum of the American Indian says that about a quarter of 'more than 20,000' died. In Florida the Seminoles fought three wars, in 1817-18, 1835-42 and 1855-58. The first began over attempts to recapture 'runaway Black slaves living among Seminole bands'; the second followed most Seminoles' refusal to leave their reservation and, by the Seminole Nation Museum's account, began with 'Dade's Massacre in December 1835'. Its cost is disputed: Britannica gives $40-60 million and up to 2,000 U.S. soldiers killed, the Seminole Nation Museum about $15 million and more than 1,500. By 1842 about 3,000 Seminoles had been removed; the museum counts about 3,500 Seminoles in Florida today, descended from those who stayed or returned. How to judge removal is debated. Francis Paul Prucha (1969) rejected a 'devil theory': 'To call Jackson an Indian-hater... is to speak in terms that had little meaning to Jackson'; 'To Jackson this seemed the only answer.' Claudio Saunt (2020) calls removal 'not an inevitable chapter' but 'a fiercely contested political act designed to secure new lands for the expansion of slavery', which deported '80,000 men, women and children'. At the Society for Historians of the Early American Republic's 2020 plenary session, Daniel Feller dismissed the view that removal was 'deliberately vicious and inhuman, if not overtly genocidal'; in The Panorama, the society's blog, Jeffrey Ostler replied that the United States 'bears responsibility for this and other genocidal policies'. Theda Perdue and Michael Green call removal 'ethnic cleansing', and Gary Clayton Anderson, in Ostler's summary, argues that it was ethnic cleansing and explicitly not genocide. Cherokee deaths more than 1,000 on the journey; perhaps several thousand more afterwards National Park Service Cherokee deaths about 4,000 of 16,000 National Archives Cherokee deaths about one-fourth of more than 20,000 National Museum of the American Indian (blog, 2017) People removed nearly 50,000 under Jackson National Archives People removed 80,000 Claudio Saunt (2020) Second Seminole War $40-60 million; up to 2,000 U.S. soldiers killed Britannica Second Seminole War about $15 million; more than 1,500 U.S. soldiers killed Seminole Nation Museum

t: The Monroe Doctrine and Latin America
x: In 1819 Spain ceded East and West Florida to the United States by treaty, and in 1822 President Monroe told Congress that the new American states ought to be recognised. In December 1823 he declared the Americas closed to future European colonisation, a principle the United States could enforce only in the late 1800s. The doctrine has been reread ever since, from the Roosevelt Corollary of 1904 to a 'Trump Corollary' in 2025. In 1818, in a raid against the Seminoles and escaped slaves (US3.8), Andrew Jackson 'seized the Spanish forts at Pensacola and St. Marks'. The Adams-Onís, or Transcontinental, Treaty was signed at Washington on 22 February 1819. Its Article II reads: 'His Catholic Majesty cedes to the United States, in full property and sovereignty, all the territories which belong to him, situated to the eastward of the Mississippi, known by the name of East and West Florida.' The United States took on liability for '$5 million in damage done by American citizens who rebelled against Spain', Spain gave up its claims to the Pacific Northwest, the United States recognised Spanish sovereignty over Texas (US3.10), and the treaty was ratified in 1821. On 8 March 1822 Monroe told Congress that 'the Provinces which have declared their independence and are in the enjoyment of it ought to be recognized' (on the wars of independence, see 14.5). In August 1823 the British foreign minister, George Canning, suggested a joint Anglo-American declaration, but Secretary of State John Quincy Adams 'vigorously opposed cooperation with Great Britain'. In his message to Congress of 2 December 1823 Monroe declared that the American continents 'are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers', and that the United States would consider any attempt by the European powers 'to extend their system to any portion of this hemisphere as dangerous to our peace and safety'. He added: 'With the existing colonies or dependencies of any European power we have not interfered and shall not interfere.' The Office of the Historian sums up the doctrine as 'separate spheres of influence for the Americas and Europe, non-colonization, and non-intervention', and notes that only 'In the late 1800s' did U.S. economic and military power enable it to enforce it. Simón Bolívar distrusted the United States: in a letter of August 1829 to Colonel Patrick Campbell, the British chargé d'affaires, he wrote that it seemed 'destined to plague America with miseries in the name of Freedom'. Later readings changed the doctrine's meaning. The Roosevelt Corollary of 1904 envisioned the United States as 'an international police power', and the Office of the Historian says it 'inverted the original meaning of the doctrine'. The historian Jay Sexton, in Kirkus's summary of his argument, sees in the doctrine 'a fusion of anti-colonialism and interventionism'. On 18 November 2013 Secretary of State John Kerry told the Organization of American States: 'The era of the Monroe Doctrine is over.' The National Security Strategy released in early December 2025 states that the United States 'will reassert and enforce the Monroe Doctrine to restore American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere', under what it calls a 'Trump Corollary', which Global News reports prioritises American-led cooperative efforts against mass migration, drug trafficking and 'hostile foreign incursion or ownership of key assets'. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said: 'Past administrations perpetuated the belief that the Monroe Doctrine had expired. They were wrong'; the political scientist Max Cameron of the University of British Columbia said that recent U.S. military operations in the region had created 'a sense of horror in many places that this is a return to gunboat diplomacy'. 1819 Adams-Onís Treaty Spain 'cedes' East and West Florida 1822 Monroe to Congress the new states 'ought to be recognized' 1823 Monroe's message no 'future colonization'; no interference with 'existing colonies' 1829 Bolívar to Campbell the United States seemed 'destined to plague America with miseries' 1904 Roosevelt Corollary the United States as 'an international police power' 2013 Kerry at the OAS 'The era of the Monroe Doctrine is over.' 2025 National Security Strategy 'reassert and enforce the Monroe Doctrine'; a 'Trump Corollary'

t: Texas and the war with Mexico
x: Texas broke away from Mexico in 1836 and joined the United States in 1845. A quarrel over its border led to war in 1846, and in 1848 Mexico ceded 55 percent of its territory. Americans such as Lincoln, Thoreau and Douglass opposed the war, and Mexican writers blamed it on American ambition. Mexico's Law of April 6, 1830 tried to stop Anglo-American immigration into Texas and further imports of slaves, but in the Handbook of Texas's words it 'only slowed immigration and the Peculiar Institution, but did not curb them.' By 1834 the non-Indian population was about 21,000, by Almonte's estimate. The Handbook describes the centralist government of the Siete Leyes, which replaced the federal Constitution of 1824, and notes that slavery 'has also been cited as an underlying cause' of the revolt that followed, because of 'slaveowners' concern with protecting their peculiar institution'. Texas declared independence on 2 March 1836, under a constitution that guaranteed the protection of slavery, and the Alamo fell four days later. About 350 prisoners were killed at Goliad. At San Jacinto on 21 April a battle of eighteen minutes cost the Mexican army 630 dead and 730 captured. On slavery in the wider republic, see US3.6. Annexation took nine more years. Congress passed the annexation resolution on 28 February 1845, and Texas legally entered the Union on 29 December; antislavery sentiment had been the chief obstacle. That summer an unsigned article in the Democratic Review, usually credited to its editor John L. O'Sullivan (Linda Hudson credits Jane McManus Storm Cazneau), spoke of 'our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence', and said of annexation: 'Slavery had nothing to do with it.' Historians read the phrase differently. In its publisher's summary, Reginald Horsman's Race and Manifest Destiny (1981) shows that 'the belief in white American superiority was firmly ensconced in the nation's ideology by 1850'; Frederick Merk (1963), in John Mack Faragher's words, 'rejected inevitability in favor of a more contingent interpretation of American expansionism in the 1840s'. The appeal to Providence states the writer's faith; it is evidence of how expansionists spoke, not of what Providence intended. The immediate quarrel was the border. Mexico held that Texas ended at the Nueces River, the United States that it ran to the Rio Grande, and Slidell was sent to Mexico to negotiate the purchase of the disputed areas. The first major battle was fought at Palo Alto on 8 May 1846, and the United States declared war on 13 May. Some Americans opposed the war. On 22 December 1847 Abraham Lincoln, in his Spot Resolutions, asked 'Whether the spot on which the blood of our citizens was shed, as in his messages declared,' was really American soil; the House never acted on them. Henry David Thoreau spent a night in jail rather than pay his poll tax to a government that, in Britannica's summary of his view, endorsed slavery and waged an imperialist war against Mexico, and his essay of 1849 came to be called 'Civil Disobedience'. Frederick Douglass wrote in The North Star: 'Slavery, treachery and mad ambition, are at the head of the government, in the person of James K. Polk'. Historians still divide. Amy S. Greenberg presents a war waged against an unoffending neighbor, while Robert W. Merry judges that Polk fulfilled the vision of those who elected him. Of 78,718 Americans who served, 1,733 died in battle and 11,550 died of other causes, more than six times as many. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed on 2 February 1848, made the Rio Grande the border. Mexico ceded 55 percent of its territory, more than 500,000 square miles, and the United States paid 'the sum of fifteen millions of dollars' and took over claims against Mexico up to 'three and one-quarter millions of dollars'. Mexicans in the ceded lands could stay or leave with their property. Those who stayed could 'retain the title and rights of Mexican citizens' by saying so within a year; the rest 'shall be incorporated into the Union of the United States', with full citizenship when Congress judged proper. The Senate approved the treaty on 10 March 1848, by 38 votes to 14, but rewrote Article IX and deleted Article X, which guaranteed the protection of Mexican land grants. Mexican writers, among them Alcaraz, Payno and Ramírez, concluded that 'the insatiable ambition of the United States, favored by our weakness, caused it.' Mexicans call the conflict the Guerra de 1847 or the Guerra de Estados Unidos a México, and in Mexico 'the loss of battles and territories was a national trauma', followed by turmoil, civil war and foreign intervention. Why Mexico lost is argued. Peter Guardino puts economics first, rather than disunity, while Brian DeLay points to years of raids by Native warriors that had left northern Mexico 'too divided, exhausted, and distracted to resist'. 6 April 1830 Mexican law to stop Anglo-American immigration and slave imports 2 March 1836 Texas declares independence; the Alamo falls on 6 March 21 April 1836 San Jacinto 28 February 1845 Congress passes the annexation resolution 8-13 May 1846 Palo Alto; the United States declares war 22 December 1847 Lincoln's Spot Resolutions 2 February 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo signed 10 March 1848 Senate approves the treaty, 38 to 14, rewriting Article IX and deleting Article X

Recorded immigration rose from about 129,000 in the 1820s to over 1.4 million in the 1840s, most of it from Ireland and Germany. Arrivals jumped after the Irish Famine began in 1845, the port cities grew, and nativists turned on Catholic newcomers. In January 1848 gold was found in California, where the Indian population collapsed in the decades that followed. Recorded arrivals in the United States rose from 128,502 in the 1820s to 538,381 in the 1830s and 1,427,337 in the 1840s, and then to 2,814,554 in the 1850s. Ireland and Germany supplied about seven in ten of them: 656,145 Irish and 385,434 Germans in the 1840s, and 1,029,486 Irish and 976,072 Germans in the 1850s. The Irish surge followed the potato blight. From 1845 late blight, Phytophthora infestans, caused the potato crop to fail, and the Great Famine lasted until 1849, or 1851 by some reckonings. About a million people died of starvation and disease, and over a million emigrated. The American figures show the jump: 114,371 arrivals in 1845, 154,416 in 1846 and 234,968 in 1847, then 369,980 in 1850 and 427,833 in 1854. The cities grew fast. New York had 123,706 people in 1820, 312,710 in 1840 and 515,547 in 1850; Baltimore, Boston and New Orleans had all passed 100,000 by 1850, Cincinnati more than doubled in the 1840s, to 115,435, and St. Louis grew from 16,469 to 77,860. In Philadelphia in May and July 1844, Catholic objections to reading the Protestant King James Bible in the public schools led to 'some of the bloodiest rioting of the antebellum period', and rioters burned St. Michael's and St. Augustine's Catholic churches. In 1849 the secret Order of the Star-Spangled Banner formed in New York City; it grew into the anti-Catholic, anti-immigrant Know-Nothing movement, and by late 1855, 43 members of the House were avowed members. On religion in the young republic, see US3.4. On 24 January 1848 James W. Marshall found flakes of gold at Sutter's sawmill on the South Fork of the American River, in the valley the Nisenan called Cullumah, 'beautiful valley'. Within a year about 80,000 'forty-niners' had arrived. Between 1846 and 1873 California's Indian population fell from perhaps 150,000 to 30,000. Benjamin Madley argues that the killing in these years was genocide; Newsweek reports his estimate that 'between 9,000 and 16,000 Indians, though probably many more, were killed'. Gary Clayton Anderson calls it ethnic cleansing, not genocide, and puts the number killed at no more than 2,000. On the removal of Native nations in the East, see US3.8. New York 123,706 312,710 515,547 Baltimore 62,738 102,313 169,054 Boston 43,298 93,383 136,881 New Orleans 27,176 102,193 116,375 Cincinnati 9,642 46,338 115,435 St. Louis not listed 16,469 77,860

t: The Supreme Court and the nation
x: Under John Marshall the Supreme Court protected corporate charters from the states and reaffirmed its power to review state courts. Roger Taney's Court read charters more narrowly. In the Amistad case of 1841 the Court freed Africans who had taken over the ship carrying them as slaves. Marbury, McCulloch and Gibbons are treated as doctrine in US2.6 and US2.2; this page turns to other rulings. In Dartmouth College v. Woodward (1819) the Court held that the college's charter of 1769 was a contract, which New Hampshire could not alter, because the Constitution forbids states to impair the obligation of contracts. Marshall wrote that 'this is a contract the obligation of which cannot be impaired without violating the Constitution'. He also defined a corporation: 'A corporation is an artificial being, invisible, intangible, and existing only in contemplation of law.' Daniel Webster argued for the trustees, and the decision had far-reaching impact on business charters. Two years later, in Cohens v. Virginia, the Court reaffirmed that it could review state-court judgments that raised federal questions, since 'a case arising under the Constitution or laws of the United States is cognizable in the Courts of the Union'. The opinion observed that 'In many States, the judges are dependent for office and for salary on the will of the legislature.' The Cohens themselves lost; their conviction stood. Roger B. Taney succeeded Marshall as Chief Justice. In Charles River Bridge v. Warren Bridge, decided on 14 February 1837, the owners of a bridge chartered by Massachusetts in 1785 argued that their charter barred a rival bridge chartered in 1828. The Court disagreed. In the words of the case as printed in the United States Reports, 'in grants by the public, nothing passes by implication', and 'The object and the end of all Government is to promote the happiness and prosperity of the community'; and the same report adds that 'we must not forget, that the community also have rights'. In the judgment of the Supreme Court Historical Society, Taney 'interpreted corporation charters more strictly, state powers more generously, than Marshall had.' His reputation has been contested from the start. At his appointment a New York journal called him 'that political hack', while Edward Bates, Lincoln's Attorney General, hoped that his 'great error' in the Dred Scott case, which belongs to a later chapter, would not forever 'tarnish his otherwise well earned fame'. Two Spanish planters, Pedro Montes and José Ruiz, bought 53 Africans and put them aboard the Cuban schooner Amistad. On the night of 1-2 July 1839 the Africans, led by Sengbe Pieh (Joseph Cinqué), seized the ship and killed the captain and the cook. In August the USS Washington took the Amistad off Long Island. President Van Buren favored extraditing the Africans to Cuba. Before the Supreme Court they were represented by the former president John Quincy Adams. On 9 March 1841 Justice Joseph Story delivered the decision: 'The negroes were never the lawful slaves of Ruiz or Montez, or of any other Spanish subject.' They had been kidnapped in Africa and unlawfully transported to Cuba, and so 'by the laws of Spain itself, were entitled to their freedom.' In November 1841 thirty-five survivors sailed for Africa, reaching Sierra Leone in January 1842, and the Amistad Committee went on to found the Mende Mission 'to expand Christianity in Africa'. On slavery and the early abolitionists, see US3.6. Dartmouth College v. Woodward 1819 a college charter is a contract that the state cannot impair Cohens v. Virginia 1821 the Supreme Court may review state-court judgments on federal questions Charles River Bridge v. Warren Bridge 1837 'in grants by the public, nothing passes by implication' United States v. The Amistad 1841 the Africans were kidnapped, never lawful slaves, and were free

In 1820 the Missouri Compromise drew a line across the Louisiana Territory between slavery and freedom. In the House a gag on antislavery petitions lasted from 1836 to 1844. The war with Mexico revived the question of slavery in new territory, and by 1848 the Wilmot Proviso, popular sovereignty and the Free Soil Party offered rival answers. In 1819 the Tallmadge amendment called for 'the gradual extinction of slavery in Missouri'; the House passed it and the Senate refused it. Under the compromise of 1820, whose Missouri act was approved on 6 March, Maine entered the Union as a free state and Missouri was allowed to enter with slavery, and slavery was outlawed above the 36°30' line in the remainder of the Louisiana Territory (US3.3). It stood until the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, and in 1857 the Supreme Court ruled it unconstitutional. Thomas Jefferson wrote to John Holmes that 'this momentous question, like a fire bell in the night, awakened and filled me with terror', and added: 'we have the wolf by the ear, and we can neither hold him, nor safely let him go.' In 1836 a resolution introduced by Henry Laurens Pinckney of South Carolina provided that antislavery petitions be tabled without consideration. The House renewed the gag; its version of December 1837 began 'Resolved, that all petitions, memorials, and papers touching the abolition of slavery'. John Quincy Adams led an eight-year struggle against it, as an infringement of the First Amendment right of petition, and in 1837 he presented a petition from 22 slaves for emancipation. In 1844 his motion to repeal the standing rule carried by 108 votes to 80. On the abolitionists themselves, see US3.6. The war with Mexico (US3.10) reopened the question of slavery in the territories. On 8 August 1846 David Wilmot, a Democratic congressman from Pennsylvania, moved to attach to Polk's $2 million appropriation a proviso that 'as an express and fundamental condition to the acquisition of any territory from the Republic of Mexico' slavery should be prohibited there. The House passed it in a vote that split almost entirely along sectional lines, but the Senate never voted on it. In February 1847 the House passed it again, but the Senate passed the bill without it, and the House then accepted that version. The proviso never passed both houses, but the Republican Party, founded in 1854, later took up its principle. By 1848 the parties gave different answers. The Democrat Lewis Cass supported popular sovereignty, under which each territory would decide whether slavery was legal. A Free Soil convention at Buffalo on 9 August 1848 nominated Martin Van Buren on a platform of 'no more Slave States and no more Slave Territory' and 'Free Soil, Free Speech, Free Labor, and Free Men', and Frederick Douglass endorsed him. Zachary Taylor won the presidency, and Van Buren took 10 percent of the popular vote. 1819 Tallmadge amendment passed by the House, refused by the Senate 6 March 1820 Missouri Compromise Maine free; Missouri may enter with slavery; no slavery above 36°30' in the rest of the Louisiana Territory 1836 gag rule (Pinckney) antislavery petitions tabled 1844 gag rule repealed carried by 108 to 80 8 August 1846 Wilmot Proviso passed by the House; the Senate never voted February 1847 Wilmot Proviso again passed by the House; the bill passed without it 9 August 1848 Free Soil platform, Buffalo Van Buren wins 10 percent of the popular vote

The census of 1860 counted 3,953,760 enslaved people among 31,443,321 Americans, and in Mississippi and South Carolina they were a majority. This page sets out how far slaveholding reached and introduces three bodies of evidence for the era: the armies' Official Records, the files of the Freedmen's Bureau, and the interviews with formerly enslaved people collected in the 1930s, whose limits the Library of Congress itself spells out. The Eighth Census, taken in 1860, counted 31,443,321 people, of whom 3,953,760 were enslaved. By a University of Maryland tabulation of its returns, enslaved people made up 39 percent of the population of the eleven states that formed the Confederacy and 13 percent of the slave states, with the District of Columbia, that stayed in the Union. They were a majority in South Carolina (57 percent) and Mississippi (55 percent); Virginia held the most, 490,865 people. On cotton, the domestic slave trade and the South before 1848, see US3.6. How many white Southerners owned slaves depends on what is counted. The historian Joseph T. Glatthaar, working from census data, calculated that 4.9 percent of people in the slaveholding states owned slaves, but that 19.9 percent of family units did; in Mississippi the share was 49 percent of families, and in South Carolina 46 percent. PolitiFact, reporting his figures in 2017, rated false a viral claim that only 1.4 percent of Americans owned slaves at slavery's peak. Two archives document the war and its aftermath. The War of the Rebellion: A Compilation of the Official Records of the Union and Confederate Armies prints the 'battle reports for both Union and Confederate armies' and correspondence. The Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, created by Congress on 3 March 1865 and in operation until 1872, left labor contracts, lists of rations issued, indentures of apprenticeship and marriage certificates that hold 'the names of hundreds of thousands of formerly enslaved individuals'. Volunteers working with the Smithsonian have transcribed more than 1.7 million images of these records. Between 1936 and 1938 the Federal Writers' Project sent out-of-work writers in seventeen states to interview formerly enslaved people; the Library of Congress holds more than 2,300 of their accounts. The Library itself warns that 'Those interviewed were extremely old', that most had known slavery 'only as children or adolescents', that most were living in abject poverty during the Depression, that 'The relative absence of black interviewers introduced an important source of bias', and that fewer than two percent of the formerly enslaved people available were interviewed. The chapter follows the crisis of the 1850s (US4.1-US4.4), the war (US4.5-US4.8), Reconstruction (US4.9-US4.11), the West (US4.12) and memory (US4.13); on emancipations worldwide see 14.9. The 1860 census counts of free and enslaved people by state the Maryland tabulation is marked preliminary Glatthaar's calculations slaveholding by person and by family 4.9 percent of people, but 19.9 percent of families The Official Records Union and Confederate battle reports and correspondence given as 127 volumes plus index and atlas, or as 128 Freedmen's Bureau records, 1865-1872 contracts, ration lists, marriage certificates more than 1.7 million images transcribed by volunteers WPA narratives, 1936-1938 more than 2,300 first-person accounts very old informants; few Black interviewers; under 2 percent interviewed

t: The Compromise of 1850 and the Fugitive Slave Act
x: In September 1850 Congress passed a series of separate laws that admitted California as a free state, created the territories of New Mexico and Utah, and enacted a new Fugitive Slave Act. The act barred accused people from testifying and commanded citizens to help enforce it. Uncle Tom's Cabin sold 300,000 copies in its first year, and attempts to seize people under the act led to deaths at Christiana, Pennsylvania, and in Boston. On 29 January 1850 Henry Clay introduced resolutions meant to 'adjust amicably all existing questions of controversy' arising out of slavery. The Senate debated them for seven months and at first voted the package down; Stephen A. Douglas of Illinois then 'stepped forward with substitute bills, which passed both Houses.' Acts approved on 9 September admitted California as a free state, set the boundary of Texas and offered it ten million dollars, and created the territories of New Mexico and Utah; a new Fugitive Slave Act followed on 18 September, and on 20 September Congress made it unlawful to bring slaves into the District of Columbia for sale. On the war with Mexico and the Wilmot Proviso, see US3.10 and US3.13. The Fugitive Slave Act gave the accused no voice: 'In no trial or hearing under this act shall the testimony of such alleged fugitive be admitted in evidence'. The commissioner who heard a case received ten dollars if he issued a certificate for the person's removal and five if he did not. The act declared that 'all good citizens are hereby commanded to aid and assist' in enforcing it, and anyone who obstructed an arrest or helped a fugitive escape faced 'a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars, and imprisonment not exceeding six months'. Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin ran in instalments in The National Era, an abolitionist newspaper, from 1851, and appeared as a two-volume book in 1852. By the Stowe Center's figures it sold 10,000 copies in the United States in its first week and 300,000 in its first year, and in the 19th century only the Bible outsold it. Resistance turned deadly. On 11 September 1851 Edward Gorsuch of Maryland and a search party came to William Parker's house at Christiana, in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania; dozens of members of the local Black community arrived to help Parker, and Gorsuch was killed. Forty-one people, 'both Black and white', were indicted, and the jury acquitted Castner Hanway, tried for treason, on 11 December. In Boston on 24 May 1854 a federal marshal arrested Anthony Burns. An attack on the courthouse to free him failed, though a marshal was shot dead, and on 2 June hundreds of soldiers marched Burns down State Street to Long Wharf and back into slavery. A Boston minister, Leonard Grimes, bought his freedom in February 1855. One prominent businessman wrote: 'we went to bed…compromise conservative Union Whigs and waked up stark mad abolitionists.' 29 January 1850 Clay's resolutions proposed a package to settle the disputes over slavery; at first voted down 9 September 1850 California act admitted California as a free state 9 September 1850 Texas and New Mexico act set Texas's boundary, offered it $10 million, created New Mexico Territory 9 September 1850 Utah act created Utah Territory 18 September 1850 Fugitive Slave Act no testimony from the accused; $10 or $5 fees; citizens commanded to assist 20 September 1850 District of Columbia act barred bringing slaves into the District for sale

In 1854 the Kansas-Nebraska Act repealed the Missouri Compromise's ban on slavery north of 36°30' and left the question to settlers. Its opponents helped found the Republican Party, which soon displaced the Whigs, while the nativist Know-Nothings drew more than a fifth of the presidential vote in 1856. In Kansas about 56 people were killed in the fighting over slavery before it became a state in 1861. Senator Stephen Douglas of Illinois introduced a bill dividing the land west of Missouri into the territories of Kansas and Nebraska, and argued for popular sovereignty, under which settlers would decide whether slavery was legal. Signed into law on 30 May 1854, the act 'repealed the Missouri Compromise', which had barred slavery north of 36°30' in the Louisiana territories (US3.13). 'Anti-slavery supporters were outraged', and opponents of the act 'helped found the Republican Party', which opposed slavery's expansion into the territories. Pro- and antislavery settlers rushed into Kansas to influence its first election. Lawrence, founded by New England settlers in July 1854, became 'the focal point of abolitionist activity'. Between 1854 and 1861 about 56 people on both sides were killed in what came to be called Bleeding Kansas. On 25 May 1856, at Pottawatomie in Franklin County, five proslavery men were killed. Three days earlier, on 22 May, the violence had reached the Capitol. After Senator Charles Sumner's speech 'The Crime Against Kansas', Representative Preston Brooks of South Carolina, a kinsman of Senator Andrew Butler, found Sumner in the Senate chamber, franking copies of his speech, and beat him unconscious with a cane; 'both men became heroes in their respective regions.' Kansas entered the Union in January 1861. The old party system broke apart. The Republican Party grew out of meetings at Ripon, Wisconsin, in May 1854 and Jackson, Michigan, in July; it drew antislavery leaders who had been Democrats, Whigs and Free-Soilers, and within four years it 'rapidly displaced the Whigs' as the main opposition to the Democrats. At the same time the Know-Nothing or American Party, which grew out of 'anti-immigrant and especially anti-Roman Catholic sentiment' and a secret order founded in New York City in 1849, flourished. Its native-born Protestant supporters feared immigrants, mainly Germans in the Midwest and Irish in the East (US3.11). In the presidential election of 1856 the Democrat James Buchanan won with 174 electoral votes and 45.3 percent of the popular vote. The Republican John C. Frémont won 114 electoral votes and 33.1 percent, carrying 11 Northern states. Millard Fillmore, on the Whig-American ticket, took 873,053 votes, 21.5 percent, but carried only Maryland. 1849 the secret Order of the Star-Spangled Banner forms in New York City 30 May 1854 Kansas-Nebraska Act approved; the Missouri Compromise repealed May and July 1854 Republican meetings at Ripon and Jackson July 1854 New England settlers found Lawrence 22 May 1856 Brooks beats Sumner in the Senate chamber 25 May 1856 five proslavery men killed at Pottawatomie 1856 Buchanan 174 electoral votes, Frémont 114, Fillmore 8 January 1861 Kansas enters the Union

t: Dred Scott, Lincoln and Douglas, and John Brown
x: In 1857 the Supreme Court ruled that Congress could not ban slavery from a federal territory and that Black Americans descended from enslaved people could not be citizens. In 1858 Abraham Lincoln met Stephen Douglas in seven debates across Illinois; he lost the election but became nationally prominent. In October 1859 John Brown led a raid on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry and was hanged that December. Dred Scott had been held as a slave by an army surgeon, Dr. Emerson, at Rock Island in Illinois and at Fort Snelling, then in the free Territory of Wisconsin, and claimed his freedom on the ground of that residence. On 6 March 1857 Chief Justice Roger B. Taney read the Court's opinion. It held that enslaved people, and the free descendants of Africans brought to the country as slaves, were not citizens, and that Congress 'had no authority to ban slavery from a Federal territory'. The vote was 7-2; the Missouri Compromise was held unconstitutional, and Justices McLean and Curtis dissented. Writing of the founding era, Taney said that Black people 'had for more than a century before been regarded as beings of an inferior order', 'so far inferior that they had no rights which the white man was bound to respect'. The National Archives notes that many legal scholars consider the decision 'the worst ever rendered by the Supreme Court'; the 13th and 14th Amendments overturned it (US2.11). In a speech at Springfield on 16 June 1858, Lincoln said: 'A house divided against itself cannot stand. I believe this government cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free.' The words echo Mark 3:25, which in the NRSVUE reads: 'And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand.' He and Douglas then held seven debates, from Ottawa on 21 August to Alton on 15 October. At Freeport Douglas said that, whatever the Supreme Court might decide, 'the people have the lawful means to introduce it or exclude it as they please, for the reason that slavery cannot exist a day or an hour anywhere, unless it is supported by local police regulations.' At Ottawa Lincoln said of the Black man that 'in the right to eat the bread, without the leave of anybody else, which his own hand earns, he is my equal and the equal of Judge Douglas, and the equal of every living man.' At Charleston he said he was not 'in favor of bringing about in any way the social and political equality of the white and black races', nor of 'making voters or jurors of negroes', and that, since he believed a physical difference would 'forever forbid the two races living together on terms of social and political equality', 'I as much as any other man am in favor of having the superior position assigned to the white race.' How to weigh these statements is taken up in US4.7. Lincoln lost the election, but 'these debates launched him into national prominence.' On 16 October 1859 John Brown and twenty-one men attacked the U.S. Armory and Arsenal at Harpers Ferry. Colonel Robert E. Lee arrived with 90 Marines, and sixteen people were killed, ten of them Brown's men. Brown was convicted of murder, of conspiring with enslaved people to rebel and of 'treason against the state of Virginia', and was hanged on 2 December 1859. Words dated that day and attributed to him read: 'the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood.' 6 March 1857 Chief Justice Taney 'no rights which the white man was bound to respect' 16 June 1858 Lincoln, Springfield 'A house divided against itself cannot stand.' 21 August 1858 Lincoln, Ottawa 'he is my equal ... and the equal of every living man' 27 August 1858 Douglas, Freeport slavery needs 'local police regulations' 18 September 1858 Lincoln, Charleston 'the superior position assigned to the white race' 2 December 1859 John Brown 'never be purged away but with blood'

Abraham Lincoln won the presidency in 1860 with 39.8 percent of the popular vote and no recorded votes in nine slave states. Eleven states seceded between December 1860 and June 1861; the declarations of South Carolina, Mississippi, Georgia and Texas named slavery, and the Confederate Constitution protected it. Historians now broadly agree that slavery was at the centre of the crisis. The postwar Lost Cause claim that secession, not slavery, caused the war has lost much of its academic support, though polls show Americans still divided. In 1860 Lincoln won 180 electoral votes with 39.8 percent of 4,692,538 popular votes; Stephen Douglas won 29.4 percent, John C. Breckinridge 18.2 and John Bell 12.6. The American Presidency Project records no votes for Lincoln in nine slave states, and in South Carolina the legislature chose the electors. Computed state by state from its returns, Lincoln won 53.9 percent of the vote in the free states and all his electoral votes there, while Breckinridge took 56.0 percent in the Lower South and Bell led in the border slave states. South Carolina seceded on 20 December 1860, and six more states of the Lower South followed by 1 February 1861. South Carolina's declaration of causes cited 'an increasing hostility on the part of the non-slaveholding States to the institution of slavery' and the election of a President 'whose opinions and purposes are hostile to slavery'. It complained that Northern states, in resisting the return of fugitives (US4.1), 'have enacted laws which either nullify the Acts of Congress or render useless any attempt to execute them.' Mississippi declared: 'Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery-- the greatest material interest of the world.' Georgia complained of 'numerous and serious causes of complaint against our non-slave-holding confederate States with reference to the subject of African slavery', and Texas held that Africans had been 'rightfully held and regarded as an inferior and dependent race'. The Confederate Constitution invoked 'the favor and guidance of Almighty God', forbade any 'law denying or impairing the right of property in negro slaves', and required that slavery in the territories 'shall be recognized and protected'. At Savannah on 21 March 1861 the Confederate Vice President, Alexander H. Stephens, said that the new government's 'corner-stone rests, upon the great truth that the negro is not equal to the white man'. At 4:30 a.m. on 12 April a mortar at Fort Johnson fired a shell that burst almost directly over Fort Sumter. After a 34-hour bombardment a surrender was agreed on 13 April, and Major Anderson's garrison marched out on 14 April; during the salute, an accidental explosion killed Private Daniel Hough. On 15 April Lincoln called for 75,000 militia, and between 17 April and 8 June Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina and Tennessee seceded. Historians now broadly agree that slavery was at the centre of secession and the war: the National Park Service says that 'most professional historians agree' that slavery and the status of African Americans 'were at the heart of the crisis', and PolitiFact, reporting their views in 2024, quoted Michael Burlingame calling it the 'central cause' and Paul Finkelman saying: 'It's all about slavery.' In the Lost Cause, an interpretation popularised by Edward Pollard and Jubal Early, 'Secession, not slavery, caused the Civil War', enslaved people were 'faithful slaves', and the Confederacy lost only to the Union's 'overwhelming advantages in men and resources'. Caroline Janney writes that it 'has lost much of its academic support' but remains important in how the war is commemorated in the South and remembered in popular culture. Alan Nolan called the denial of slavery's role 'outrageous and disingenuous'. What historians have argued over is how slavery led to war, and whether the war could have been avoided. Revisionist historians held that 'the Civil War could and should have been avoided': James G. Randall blamed a 'blundering generation' of politicians, and Avery Craven the 'work of politicians and pious cranks', a view that, Robert Dietle notes, 'began to be revised' by the early 1950s. Charles Dew, from the speeches of the states' secession commissioners, finds slavery and race 'absolutely critical factors at the heart of our great national crisis'. In 2011 a Pew poll found 48 percent of Americans calling the war mainly about states' rights and 38 percent mainly about slavery; a YouGov poll in 2023, with different wording, found 56 percent naming slavery and 28 percent states' rights. 18 free states 3,411,201 53.9% 35.6% 8.2% 2.2% Lower South (AL, FL, GA, LA, MS, TX) 394,114 0% 9.3% 56.0% 34.8% Upper South (AR, NC, TN, VA) 466,158 0.4% 7.6% 46.8% 45.2% Border slave states (DE, KY, MD, MO) 421,065 6.0% 21.7% 31.9% 40.4% Whole country 4,692,538 39.8% 29.4% 18.2% 12.6%

The Union's 'Anaconda' plan aimed to blockade the Confederate coast and push down the Mississippi. Its turning points included Antietam, the deadliest one-day battle in American military history, Gettysburg and Vicksburg in July 1863, and the fall of Atlanta in 1864, before Lee's surrender at Appomattox in April 1865. How many died is still debated: the traditional figure is about 620,000, and a census-based estimate of 2011 puts it near 750,000. Winfield Scott's 'Anaconda' plan called for a naval blockade of the Confederate coast and a thrust down the Mississippi. In the East the armies of George McClellan and Robert E. Lee met at Antietam in Maryland on 17 September 1862, in what the American Battlefield Trust calls 'the deadliest one-day battle in American military history'. It ended in a tactical draw; Lee withdrew into Virginia, and five days later Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation (US4.6). In July 1863 the Union won twice in two days. At Gettysburg, on 1-3 July, George Meade's army defeated Lee and ended his second invasion of the North, at an estimated cost of 51,112 casualties; the Trust calls the battle 'the turning point of the Civil War'. On 4 July, after a 47-day siege, John Pemberton surrendered Vicksburg to Ulysses S. Grant, which ensured Union control of the Mississippi and, in the Trust's words, 'cleaved the South in two'. In 1864 William T. Sherman's campaign forced John Bell Hood to abandon Atlanta on 1 September, which helped ensure Lincoln's re-election that November, and on 9 April 1865 Lee surrendered his army to Grant at Appomattox Court House. The traditional count of the dead, about 620,000, rests on research by the Union veterans William F. Fox and Thomas Leonard Livermore; its often-cited form is 618,222, with 360,222 Union and 258,000 Confederate deaths. In 2011 the historian J. David Hacker estimated instead 650,000 to 850,000, 'with 750,000 as the central figure'. He compared the native-born men and women missing from the 1870 census; his census samples covered only the white population, so for Black deaths he relied on existing estimates, which he and others suspect are too low. By his figures, white men aged 10 to 44 who were born in the South died at a rate of 13.1 percent, against 6.1 percent for those born in the free states and territories. James McPherson has said: 'I have always been convinced that the consensus figure of 620,000 is too low.' Hacker himself notes 'huge problems estimating mortality with census data', which his method was designed in part to get around, and his range, the release notes, 'spans a wide margin'. The American Battlefield Trust still uses 620,000 and calls Hacker's range 'very broad', saying it 'includes civilian casualties, and is not directly linked to the war years of 1861-1865'. On the traditional count, disease killed more soldiers than battle did: 'For every three soldiers killed in battle, five more died of disease.' On the home fronts, civilians organised. In the North the US Sanitary Commission, a private relief group founded in May 1861 and inspired by women's groups such as the Women's Central Relief Association, supported an army Medical Bureau that the National Park Service calls 'unprepared and undersized'; sanitary fairs organised and run by women raised $2,736,868.84 for it. In the Confederate capital, food shortages spawned the Richmond bread riot of 2 April 1863, 'the largest civil disturbance in the Confederacy during the war'.
