The demand for the vote made at Seneca Falls in 1848 divided the movement in 1869 over the Fifteenth Amendment, and it was first won in the West, where Wyoming Territory enfranchised women in 1869. By 1919, by the Bill of Rights Institute's count, women had full suffrage in 15 states, and it lists 12 more where they could vote for federal offices (in Ohio and Indiana the 1917 laws were soon overturned); in August 1920 the Nineteenth Amendment barred denial of the vote on account of sex. Many women still could not vote because of discriminatory state laws, and Black women in the Jim Crow South met the same disfranchising tactics used against Black men. The Declaration of Sentiments adopted at Seneca Falls in 1848 (US3.4) began from the claim that 'all men and women are created equal' and listed among man's wrongs that 'He has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise.' After the Civil War the question was whose vote came first. At the American Equal Rights Association's meeting of 12 May 1869 the movement broke apart over the Fifteenth Amendment, which covered race but not sex. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony, for whom any amendment without women's suffrage was unacceptable, founded the National Woman Suffrage Association to seek a constitutional amendment, while Lucy Stone and Julia Ward Howe's American Woman Suffrage Association worked for suffrage laws state by state. Frederick Douglass supported the Fifteenth Amendment, arguing that the ballot was more urgent for Black men than for women. In that fight Stanton argued that African Americans were ignorant of the country's laws and customs, and said it was 'a serious question whether we had better stand aside and see "Sambo" walk into the kingdom [of civil rights] first.' The vote was won first in the West. 'The territory of Wyoming granted women the vote in 1869.' Utah Territory followed in 1870 and Washington Territory in 1883, then the states of Colorado in 1893 and Idaho in 1896, and by 1912, the National Archives notes, nine western states had adopted woman suffrage. Not every early grant was full or lasting: Washington's territorial supreme court overturned its law in 1887, Congress rescinded the vote of Utah's women the same year, and Montana Territory's grant of 1887 covered school elections only. On the Bill of Rights Institute's list, New York in 1917 was the first state east of the Mississippi where women won the vote in state elections. By 1919, the Institute says, they had full suffrage in 15 states, and it lists 12 more where they could vote for federal offices, from Illinois in 1913 to Tennessee in 1919, though Ohio's law of 1917 was repealed by referendum that November and Indiana's struck down by its supreme court that October; in the other 21, all in the South or the East except New Mexico, women could be denied the vote until the Nineteenth Amendment. The movement's divisions over race did not end in 1869. Sharon Harley writes that the mainstream movement 'even condoned white supremacist ideologies in order to garner southern support for white women's voting rights'. Black women organized on their own: the National Association of Colored Women, founded in 1896, elected Mary Church Terrell its first national president. At the 1913 suffrage parade in Washington, Ida B. Wells-Barnett, who had organized the Chicago-based Alpha Suffrage Club that year, 'refused to join her fellow Black suffragists at the rear', while Terrell marched with the all-Black delegation. Martha S. Jones's Vanguard (2020) tells how Black women, in its publisher's words, 'defied both racism and sexism to fight for the ballot'. The House passed the Nineteenth Amendment on 21 May 1919 and the Senate two weeks later, and Tennessee became the 36th state to ratify it, on 18 August 1920. It reads: 'The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex. Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation.' Yet, the National Archives notes, 'Many women remained unable to vote long into the 20th century because of discriminatory state voting laws', and Black women in the Jim Crow South 'encountered the very same disfranchisement strategies' used against Black men (US5.7). Paid work changed more slowly. Claudia Goldin, who received the economics prize in 2023, showed that women's participation in the labor force traced a U-shaped curve over two centuries. At the beginning of the twentieth century, in the prize committee's words, 'While around twenty per cent of all women worked for pay, only five per cent of married women did so', and the records often listed women only as wives, though they worked on family farms and in businesses or produced goods at home. 1848 Declaration of Sentiments, Seneca Falls 1869 movement splits over the Fifteenth Amendment; Wyoming Territory grants women the vote 1896 National Association of Colored Women founded; Terrell president by 1912 nine western states have woman suffrage 1913 Wells-Barnett refuses the rear of the Washington parade; Illinois grants the vote for federal offices 1917 New York grants women the vote 1919 House (21 May) and Senate pass the Nineteenth Amendment 18 Aug 1920 Tennessee becomes the 36th state to ratify

t: The United States in the First World War
x: The United States entered the war in April 1917, after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare and a decoded German telegram proposed an alliance with Mexico, with Mexico to reconquer territory in Texas, New Mexico and Arizona. About 24 million men registered for the draft, and the Espionage Act brought prosecutions for speech that the Supreme Court upheld in Schenck (1919). Influenza killed about 675,000 Americans, the Justice Department raided suspected radicals after the war, and the Senate never ratified the Treaty of Versailles. The sinking of the British liners Lusitania and Arabic had killed 131 American citizens. On 31 January 1917 the German ambassador, Count Johann von Bernstorff, told Secretary of State Robert Lansing that Germany would restart unrestricted submarine warfare the next day; Wilson still left open the possibility of negotiating with Germany if its submarines refrained from attacking American shipping. In January British cryptographers had deciphered a telegram from the German foreign minister, Arthur Zimmermann, to the German ambassador in Mexico City; Britain passed it to Wilson on 24 February, and it was published widely in the American press on 1 March. In the National Archives' transcript it reads: 'We intend to begin on the first of February unrestricted submarine warfare. We shall endeavor in spite of this to keep the United States of America neutral. In the event of this not succeeding, we make Mexico a proposal or [sic] alliance on the following basis: make war together, make peace together, generous financial support and an understanding on our part that Mexico is to reconquer the lost territory in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. The settlement in detail is left to you. You will inform the President of the above most secretly as soon as the outbreak of war with the United States of America is certain and add the suggestion that he should, on his own initiative, invite Japan to immediate adherence and at the same time mediate between Japan and ourselves. Please call the President's attention to the fact that the ruthless employment of our submarines now offers the prospect of compelling England in a few months to make peace. Signed, ZIMMERMANN.' On 2 April 1917 Wilson asked Congress for war: 'The world must be made safe for democracy.' The Senate voted for war by 82 to 6 on 4 April, and the House concurred two days later, by 373 to 50. Jeannette Rankin of Montana, elected in 1916 as the first woman member of Congress, voted no: 'I want to stand by my country, but I cannot vote for war.' Six weeks after the declaration only 73,000 men had enlisted, against a hoped-for army of 1 million volunteers. The Selective Service Act, passed on 18 May 1917, required men aged 21 to 30, and later up to 45, to register, and about 24 million did. The National Archives says that '4.8 million went to war', 2.8 million of them drafted and 2 million volunteers. The Department of Veterans Affairs counts 4,734,991 servicemembers worldwide, with 53,402 battle deaths, 63,114 other deaths in service and 204,002 wounded. The Espionage Act of 15 June 1917 allowed the prosecution of anyone who 'interfered with or attempted to undermine the United States' war effort', with up to 20 years in prison and a $10,000 fine, and the Sedition Act of 1918 made it a crime to 'speak ill of or criticize the American government', the Constitution or the flag; it was repealed three years later. The defendants in Schenck v. United States were convicted under the Espionage Act for a document that 'intimated that conscription was despotism in its worst form'. On 3 March 1919 Justice Holmes, for a unanimous Court, upheld the convictions: 'The most stringent protection of free speech would not protect a man in falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic.' He set out a test: 'The question in every case is whether the words used are used in such circumstances and are of such a nature as to create a clear and present danger that they will bring about the substantive evils that Congress has a right to prevent.' (For the standard the Court adopted in 1969, see US2.9.) Eugene V. Debs, a leading Socialist, was indicted under the same act for an anti-war speech at Canton, Ohio, on 16 June 1918; the Supreme Court upheld the verdict in 1919, and he was sentenced to ten years in prison; President Harding commuted the sentence to time served in December 1921. In the United States the influenza of 1918 was first identified among military personnel that spring, and it killed about 675,000 Americans, out of at least 50 million deaths worldwide (15.1). After the war came bombings and raids. On 2 June 1919 the anarchist Carlo Valdinoci blew up the front of the home of the new Attorney General, A. Mitchell Palmer, one of a series of coordinated attacks that day. A young Justice Department lawyer, J. Edgar Hoover, was put in charge of gathering intelligence; in December radicals including Emma Goldman and Alexander Berkman were put on a ship dubbed the 'Red Ark'; and in January 1920 simultaneous raids in major cities called on local police to arrest thousands of suspected anarchists. The operation's constitutionality was questioned, and Palmer and Hoover were roundly criticized. The peace failed in the Senate. Reservationists led by Henry Cabot Lodge, and Irreconcilables, opposed the Treaty of Versailles, citing Article 10 on collective security and the League of Nations; on 19 March 1920 it 'fell short of ratification by seven votes', and the United States signed a separate Treaty of Berlin on 25 August 1921 (15.3). 31 Jan 1917 Germany announces unrestricted submarine warfare from the next day 1 Mar 1917 Zimmermann telegram published in the American press 2 Apr 1917 Wilson asks Congress for war 4 Apr 1917 Senate votes 82-6 for war; House concurs two days later, 373-50 18 May 1917 Selective Service Act 15 Jun 1917 Espionage Act 3 Mar 1919 Schenck v. United States 19 Mar 1920 Treaty of Versailles falls seven votes short in the Senate

Real output fell by about a quarter between 1929 and 1933, when unemployment reached 24.9 percent in the series Stanley Lebergott published in 1957, which for 1929-39 uses the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimates of 1948. By 1944 output was more than twice its 1929 level and unemployment was 1.2 percent, while federal outlays had risen from about 3 percent of GDP in 1929 to about 41 percent. The 1920s began with a slump. A 'sharp deflation in 1920' lasted 'about one year', and on Stanley Lebergott's estimates unemployment was 11.9 percent in 1921 but only 1.9 percent in 1926. The Bureau of Economic Analysis's GDP series begins only in 1929. For earlier years MeasuringWorth's reconstruction puts real GDP at $822.1 billion in 1921 and $1,127.1 billion in 1928, in 2017 dollars, a rise of about 37 percent. Because it is a different series, it is not strictly comparable with BEA's figures from 1929 on, and the chart on this page does not join the two. In BEA's series real GDP fell from $1,191.1 billion in 1929 to $877.4 billion in 1933, about 26 percent, in chained 2017 dollars. Unemployment rose from 3.2 percent in 1929 to 24.9 percent in 1933. These figures are reconstructions: in 1948 the Monthly Labor Review explained that 'Estimates for the period 1929-39 were prepared by the Bureau of Labor Statistics', which put the number unemployed in 1933 at 12,830,000. Output was back above its 1929 level in 1936, yet unemployment was still 17.0 percent that year, and it rose again from 14.3 percent in 1937 to 19.0 percent in 1938. On the Depression worldwide, see 15.4; on its causes, US6.5. War transformed the figures. Federal net outlays, $3,127 million in fiscal 1929 and $9,468 million in 1940, reached $92,712 million in 1945. As a share of GDP they were about 3.0 percent in 1929, 9.8 percent in 1934 and 40.7 percent in 1944; the series divides fiscal-year outlays by calendar-year GDP. Real GDP peaked in 1944 at $2,524.8 billion, more than twice its 1929 level, and unemployment fell to 1.2 percent. On the Second World War in global terms, see 15.6. This chapter takes the 1920s first: the economy (US6.1), the culture wars (US6.2), immigration restriction (US6.3) and Black America (US6.4). It then turns to the Crash and the Depression (US6.5), the New Deal and the debates over it (US6.6-US6.8), the Dust Bowl and the politics of faith (US6.9), and the road to war, the home front and the war itself (US6.10-US6.13). On the First World War at home and the Red Scare, see US5.13; on the Commerce Clause, US2.2. Ford built more than 15 million Model Ts between 1908 and 1927 as the price fell from $850 to as little as $260, and by 1932 two-thirds of American dwellings had electricity, though only 11 percent of farm dwellings did. Households bought most durables on instalments while farm prices collapsed, the top income-tax rate fell from 73 to 25 percent, and the Dow closed at its peak of 381.17 on 3 September 1929. 'From 1908-1927, Ford Motor Company produced over 15 million Model T cars', and 'the price dropped from $850 to as little as $260.' Ford began building magnetos on 'a crude moving assembly line in April 1913' at Highland Park. The moving line turned out 'a finished Model T every 93 minutes', against 12½ hours per car under stationary assembly. Electricity reached most homes in these years. 'In 1907, only 8 percent of all dwellings were using electricity; by 1932, this figure had risen to 67 percent.' But by 1932 more than 80 percent of urban dwellings had service, against only 11 percent of farm dwellings. KDKA in Pittsburgh broadcast the Harding-Cox election returns on 2 November 1920, and within four years 600 stations existed in the United States. Martha Olney's notes put 70 to 90 percent of consumer durables in the 1920s as bought on instalments, and the ratio of consumer debt to income doubled. Olney argues that this debt mattered when the economy turned down: households cut other spending to avoid default, and 'Consumer spending collapsed in 1930, turning a minor recession into the Great Depression.' Hers is one explanation among several (US6.5). Farm prices fell. 'From 1919 to 1920, corn tumbled from $1.30 per bushel to forty-seven cents' in Minnesota, by MNopedia's figures. Harding took office during a 'sharp deflation in 1920, which lasted for about one year', and signed the Budget and Accounting Act of 1921, which 'allowed the President to present a unified budget for the first time.' Congress twice passed the McNary-Haugen farm relief bill, and Coolidge vetoed it both times. Under Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon the top income-tax rate fell from 73 percent to 58 percent under the Revenue Act of 1921, then to 46 percent in 1924 and 25 percent in 1926. Christopher Frenze's 1982 staff study for the Joint Economic Committee argues that the cuts raised revenue from the rich: between 1921 and 1922, after the first cut, income taxes paid by those reporting incomes of $50,000 or more rose from $318 million to $446 million. The Miller Center's essay on Coolidge says the cuts favoured the rich and that Coolidge's policies 'contributed to the stock market crash of 1929'. Gene Smiley and Richard Keehn (1995) argue that a primary motive for the cuts was to reduce tax avoidance by wealthier people, and that the cuts did reduce it. The Dow Jones average rose from 63 in August 1921 until 'the index peaked on September 3, 1929, closing at 381.17'. Buyers on margin put down 'typically 10 percent, and borrowed the rest.' The crash itself is the subject of US6.5. The Eighteenth Amendment banned the manufacture, sale and transport of intoxicating liquors for drinking; one study estimates that consumption fell to about 30 percent of its earlier level and recovered to 60-70 percent, and the Twenty-first Amendment ended Prohibition in December 1933. In 1925 a Tennessee jury convicted Scopes under a law against teaching any theory that denied the Bible's account of creation, while estimates of the Klan's peak membership run from about one million to several million. The Eighteenth Amendment, ratified on 16 January 1919, prohibited 'the manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors … for beverage purposes', to take effect 'After one year from the ratification of this article'. The Volstead Act of October 1919 enforced it and defined intoxicating liquor as anything above 0.5 percent alcohol; Congress passed it over President Wilson's veto. Did people stop drinking? Jeffrey Miron and Jeffrey Zwiebel estimate, from mortality, mental-health and crime statistics, that consumption 'fell sharply at the beginning of Prohibition, to approximately 30 percent' of its earlier level, then recovered 'to about 60-70 percent of its pre-prohibition level'. In the ABA Journal's account, 'The rise of organized crime syndicates, spurred by a flourishing bootlegging industry' fed the movement for repeal. The Twenty-first Amendment repealed the Eighteenth, ratified through conventions in the states; on 5 December 1933 Utah became the 36th state to approve it. In his sermon of 21 May 1922, 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?' (printed in The Christian Work on 10 June), Harry Emerson Fosdick attacked the demand that believers accept the virgin birth and a Bible God had 'inerrantly dictated to men a good deal as a man might dictate to a stenographer.' Tennessee's Butler Act made it unlawful 'to teach any theory that denies the story of divine creation as taught by the Bible'. Scopes's trial opened in Dayton on 10 July 1925, and on 21 July the jury found him guilty after 10 minutes. Clarence Darrow questioned William Jennings Bryan about Jonah and the whale and about Joshua making the sun stand still; the verse reads, in the NRSVUE, 'And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped until the nation took vengeance on their enemies.' Bryan died days after the trial. On appeal, in January 1927, the Tennessee Supreme Court upheld the law but set aside the conviction because of the way the fine had been set. How big was the second Ku Klux Klan? 'At its peak, the Klan claimed to have four to six million members or more', Scott McLemee notes. Linda Gordon, the author of The Second Coming of the KKK, told TIME in 2017 that 'At its peak, the Klan numbered between 3 million and 5 million people in the North'. McLemee argues that the claim is credible only if it includes four or five million who signed up and soon quit, which 'would leave a million members'. In Indiana, the publisher's description of Leonard Moore's Citizen Klansmen says more than 25 percent of native-born men joined; the History Museum in South Bend gives 250,000 white men, about 30 percent of the state's native-born white men. Grand Dragon D. C. Stephenson was convicted of second-degree murder in the death of Madge Oberholtzer. On the Klan of Reconstruction, see US4.11. 16 January 1919 Eighteenth Amendment ratified prohibition to take effect one year later October 1919 Volstead Act liquor defined as above 0.5 percent alcohol; passed over Wilson's veto 21 May 1922 Fosdick, 'Shall the Fundamentalists Win?' attacked demands for belief in the virgin birth and a dictated Bible 10-21 July 1925 Scopes trial, Dayton guilty verdict after 10 minutes January 1927 Tennessee Supreme Court law upheld; conviction set aside over the fine 1920s the Klan in Indiana more than 25 percent of native-born men, by Moore's publisher's account 5 December 1933 Utah ratifies the Twenty-first Amendment the 36th state; Prohibition repealed

Quota laws in 1921 and 1924 cut the annual cap on quota immigration from about 350,000 to 164,667, set by nationality, and the 1924 act excluded immigrants from Asia. In the 1930s Mexicans and Americans of Mexican descent were repatriated to Mexico in numbers that scholars estimate at about 400,000 to one million, and that California's legislature, in a statute of 2005, put at two million. 'On May 19, 1921, President Warren Harding signed the Quota Act of 1921.' It admitted each year 3 percent of the foreign-born of each nationality counted in the 1910 census, about 350,000 people, and it 'did not, however, establish quotas of any kind for residents of the Western Hemisphere'. On the literacy test of 1917 and the immigration that came before, see US5.4. The Johnson-Reed Act of 1924 cut the quota to 2 percent and 'pushed back the year on which quota calculations were based from 1910 to 1890'. It 'capped quota immigration at 164,667 people per year', and under the national-origins system, from 1929, the cap was 153,879. By barring aliens ineligible for citizenship, the act 'completely excluded immigrants from Asia'. 'The Japanese government protested, but the law remained.' Sacco and Vanzetti were tried in 1921 for a payroll robbery and murder and executed on 23 August 1927. In 1977 Governor Michael Dukakis of Massachusetts proclaimed that 'any stigma and disgrace' should be removed from their names, declaring that 'The atmosphere of their trial and appeals was permeated by prejudice against foreigners'. Whether they were guilty is a separate question and still disputed: Douglas Linder's account reports that a ballistics test in 1961 gave 'strong evidence that Sacco did indeed fire a fatal bullet', and that some argue one man may have been guilty and the other innocent. How many people of Mexican descent were sent or went to Mexico in the 1930s? As summarised by Lee, Peri and Yasenov, Hoffman (1974) put the number at 400,000 to 500,000, Gratton and Merchant (2013), with Hoffman, at about 400,000, and Balderrama and Rodríguez (2006) at up to one million. Lee, Peri and Yasenov (2022), who write that the lower figures fit the census data better, describe an episode in which 'at least 400,000 Mexicans returned to Mexico between 1929 and 1934'. California's legislature, in a statute of 2005, states that 'it is estimated that two million people of Mexican ancestry were forcibly relocated', 'approximately 1.2 million of whom had been born in the United States'; that is the legislature's figure, not a scholarly estimate. Did their departure help native workers? Lee, Peri and Yasenov find that it did not: 'Mexican repatriations resulted in reduced employment and occupational downgrading for U.S. natives.' 19 May 1921 Quota Act 3 percent of each nationality's foreign-born in 1910; about 350,000 a year 1924 Johnson-Reed Act 2 percent, on the 1890 census; cap of 164,667 1924 exclusion of aliens ineligible for citizenship immigrants from Asia excluded; Japan protested 1929 national-origins quotas cap of 153,879 23 August 1927 Sacco and Vanzetti executed tried in 1921; guilt still disputed 1977 Dukakis proclamation trial 'permeated by prejudice against foreigners' 1929-1934 Mexican repatriation at least 400,000 returned, as Lee, Peri and Yasenov write 2005 California Apology Act states two million, about 1.2 million of them US-born

About 2 million Black people left the South from the First World War to the Second. In Tulsa in 1921 a mob destroyed 35 blocks of Greenwood; Oklahoma's commission judged in 2001 that the dead likely numbered between 100 and 300, and a federal review of January 2025 called it 'a coordinated, military-style attack on Greenwood'. In the Scottsboro case the Supreme Court held in 1932 and 1935 that the Fourteenth Amendment required effective counsel in capital cases and barred the exclusion of Black citizens from juries. According to the National Archives, 'From World War I until World War II, it is estimated that about 2 million Black people left the South', and the Census Bureau estimates 6 million between 1910 and 1970. The Metropolitan Museum of Art treats the Harlem Renaissance as part of 'the new Black cities that took shape in the 1920s–40s'; its artists included Aaron Douglas, Augusta Savage and James Van Der Zee. Marcus Garvey co-founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association in 1914 and arrived in Harlem in 1916. His trial for mail fraud began on 18 May 1923, and on 21 June he was sentenced to five years in prison; his sentence was commuted, and in 1927 he was deported, 'never to return'. He died in London in 1940, and President Biden pardoned him posthumously on 19 January 2025. On 31 May and 1 June 1921 a mob destroyed 35 blocks of Tulsa's Greenwood district and about 1,256 homes. How many died is uncertain. Oklahoma's commission, reporting on 28 February 2001, judged that the dead likely numbered between 100 and 300, and reported that its forensic anthropologist, Clyde Snow, could identify 38 victims 'By the most conservative of all possible methods'. The Justice Department's review, announced on 10 January 2025, called the massacre 'a coordinated, military-style attack on Greenwood' in which some police took part in 'murder, arson and looting', but found 'no living perpetrator' who could be prosecuted. The survivors went to court. In June 2024 the Oklahoma Supreme Court dismissed their suit, brought under Oklahoma's public nuisance law; as Lessie Benningfield Randle's lawyer said on 30 May 2026, 'Unfortunately our litigation was ended back in 2024'. Viola Fletcher died at 111, as KGOU reported on 24 November 2025. As of 6 October 2026, Lessie Benningfield Randle was alive at 111. On 1 June 2025 Tulsa's mayor, Monroe Nichols, announced a plan, the Road to Repair, under which a Greenwood Trust would be created with the goal of securing $105 million in assets, most of it secured or committed by 1 June 2026. This book has not confirmed how much had been raised by that date. On 25 March 1931 nine Black youths, aged 13 to 19 by Prologue's account, were seized at Paint Rock, Alabama, and first tried at Scottsboro, the Jackson County seat, in April 1931. The International Labor Defense, 'the legal arm of the Communist Party', ran their defence, and one accuser, Ruby Bates, recanted and testified for the defence at Haywood Patterson's second trial in 1933 that there had been no rape. In Powell v. Alabama (1932) the Supreme Court held that the failure to provide effective counsel in a capital case was 'a denial of due process within the meaning of the Fourteenth Amendment'; in Norris v. Alabama (1935) it held that evidence that no Black citizen had been called for jury service 'for a generation or longer' 'established the discrimination which the Constitution forbids', a denial of equal protection. On 21 November 2013 Alabama posthumously pardoned Charles Weems, Andy Wright and Haywood Patterson. On the Fourteenth Amendment, see US2.11. 31 May-1 June 1921 Tulsa massacre 35 blocks and about 1,256 homes destroyed 28 February 2001 Oklahoma commission's report dead likely 100-300; 38 victims identifiable June 2024 Oklahoma Supreme Court survivors' public-nuisance suit dismissed 10 January 2025 Justice Department review 'no living perpetrator' to prosecute November 2025 Viola Fletcher died at 111 (KGOU, 24 November 2025) 6 October 2026 Lessie Benningfield Randle alive at 111 (KTUL) 1 June 2025 Greenwood Trust announced by the city goal: $105 million in assets, mostly secured or committed by 1 June 2026 1932 and 1935 Powell v. Alabama; Norris v. Alabama effective counsel; no exclusion of Black citizens from juries 21 November 2013 Alabama pardons Weems, Wright and Patterson, posthumously

t: The Crash and the Great Depression
x: A recession had already begun when the stock market crashed in October 1929; by the summer of 1932 the Dow stood 89 percent below its peak. Real output fell by about a quarter to 30 percent, depending on the measure, and about 9,000 banks failed. Economists still weigh the Federal Reserve, spending, the gold standard and the collapse of credit as causes. The Dow Jones Industrial Average peaked at 381.17 on 3 September 1929. On Black Monday, 28 October, it fell nearly 13 percent, and the next day nearly 12 percent more; it bottomed at 41.22 in the summer of 1932, 89 percent below its peak, and did not regain its 1929 high until November 1954. The crash did not start the downturn: a recession had begun in the summer of 1929. Christina Romer argues that the crash deepened it by cutting purchases of durable goods: 'The stock market crash is the prime source for the collapse in durable goods purchases starting in November 1929.' For the Depression outside the United States, see 15.4. In the Bureau of Economic Analysis series, real GDP fell from $1,191 billion in 1929 to $877 billion in 1933 (in chained 2017 dollars), about 26 percent between the annual averages; Britannica, measuring from the peak to the trough of the downturn, gives 30 percent. Britannica puts the fall in industrial production at 47 percent, and Romer finds that producer prices fell by slightly over 40 percent from July 1929 to July 1932. In the standard series of Lebergott and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which for 1929-39 are the same, unemployment peaked in 1933 at 24.9 percent, about a quarter of the labor force; how to count the jobless from 1933 on is disputed (US6.7). The banks failed in waves: the Caldwell banks of Nashville in November 1930; on 11 December the Bank of United States, the fourth-largest bank in New York City; and banks in Chicago in June 1931 (map, US6.6). From the fall of 1930 to the winter of 1933 the money supply fell by nearly 30 percent. The FDIC counts about 9,000 bank suspensions, with losses to depositors of about $1.3 billion; the Social Security Administration says the failed banks took 'with them $7 billion in depositors' assets'. The figures measure different things: the first is what depositors lost, the second the deposits held in banks that failed. Why was the slump so deep? Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz blamed the Federal Reserve, which, as their publisher summarises the argument, failed to manage the monetary system and to counter the banking panics. Peter Temin (1976) answered, as Kirkus Reviews reported, that 'there is no evidence that the banking panic of 1930 had a deflationary effect on the economy' and that the data were consistent with the spending hypothesis, the view that a fall in spending caused the slump. Barry Eichengreen and Temin point to 'the mentality of the gold standard', and Eichengreen and Jeffrey Sachs found that 'currency depreciation was beneficial for the initiating countries.' Ben Bernanke (1983) argued that 'the financial disruptions of 1930-33 reduced the efficiency of the credit allocation process'; the Nobel committee cited this work in 2022. Historians also debate whether the Tariff Act of 1930 (Smoot-Hawley) provoked foreign retaliation that deepened the Depression. Dow Jones average, Sept. 1929 to summer 1932 down 89% Federal Reserve History Real GDP, 1929-1933 down about 26% (annual averages); down 30% (peak to trough) BEA; Britannica Industrial production, peak to trough down 47% Britannica Producer prices, July 1929 to July 1932 down slightly over 40% Romer (1993) Money supply, fall 1930 to winter 1933 down nearly 30% Federal Reserve History Banks suspended or failed about 9,000 FDIC; SSA Depositors' losses; deposits in failed banks about $1.3 billion; $7 billion FDIC; SSA Unemployment, 1933 24.9% (Lebergott and BLS); 24.3% (Darby, 1975) Darby, NBER working paper (1975)

t: Hoover and the first New Deal
x: In January 1932 Hoover signed the act creating the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, which lent to banks and other financial institutions, insurance companies and railroads. Roosevelt's first months in office, from 4 March 1933, brought a bank holiday, the law creating deposit insurance, the suspension of the gold standard, the AAA, the NIRA and the Civilian Conservation Corps. Banking panics had struck Nashville and New York in 1930 and Chicago in 1931 (US6.5). On 22 January 1932 President Hoover signed the Reconstruction Finance Corporation Act. With $500 million in capital, the RFC lent to banks and other financial institutions, insurance companies and railroads, and from July 1932 to states and cities. Franklin D. Roosevelt was inaugurated on 4 March 1933. In the American Presidency Project's transcript of the speech as delivered, he said: 'So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance.' He declared that 'the money changers have fled from their high seats in the temple of our civilization', that 'Our greatest primary task is to put people to work', and asked for 'broad Executive power to wage a war against the emergency'. Two days later Proclamation 2039 closed the banks. Congress passed the Emergency Banking Act on 9 March, banks began to reopen on 13 March, and by 15 March banks holding 90 percent of the system's resources were open again; 'some 4,000 banks would remain closed forever.' The Banking Act of 1933, known as Glass-Steagall and signed on 16 June, created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and 'effectively separated commercial banking from investment banking'; its limits on affiliations between the two were repealed by the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999. On 20 April 1933 the gold standard was suspended, and in June gold clauses in contracts were abrogated. Under the Gold Reserve Act of 30 January 1934, Roosevelt fixed gold at $35 an ounce by proclamation the next day, up from $20.67. 'Scholars believe', in the words of Federal Reserve History, 'Roosevelt's reflation accelerated America's recovery from the Great Depression.' On the Federal Reserve and the money power, see US2.13. The Agricultural Adjustment Act of May 1933 paid farmers to grow less, aiming to restore farm purchasing power to its level of 1909-14; the Supreme Court struck it down in 1936. The National Industrial Recovery Act of 16 June set up industry codes of fair competition and funded public works. Its Section 7(a) declared that 'employees shall have the right to organize and bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing'. The Civilian Conservation Corps, created on 5 April, paid enrollees $30 a month, $25 of it sent home, and had 1,433 camps by July 1933. Minorities were enrolled 'at far lower rates than the legislation allowed'. 22 January 1932 Reconstruction Finance Corporation Act (Hoover) loans to banks, insurance companies, railroads, and later states and cities 6-9 March 1933 bank holiday; Emergency Banking Act banks closed, then reopened from 13 March 5 April 1933 Civilian Conservation Corps $30 a month, $25 sent home 20 April 1933 gold standard suspended gold clauses abrogated in June May 1933 Agricultural Adjustment Act paid farmers to cut output; struck down 1936 16 June 1933 National Industrial Recovery Act industry codes; Section 7(a); public works 16 June 1933 Banking Act (Glass-Steagall) created the FDIC; separated commercial and investment banking 30 January 1934 Gold Reserve Act president to fix the gold value of the dollar; $35 an ounce from the next day

t: The second New Deal and the Court
x: From 1935 the WPA put some 8.5 million people to work, the Social Security Act left about half of workers outside it, and the Wagner Act protected the right to join unions. The Supreme Court struck down the NIRA's code system in 1935; Roosevelt's plan to enlarge the Court failed in 1937, but that spring the Court upheld a minimum-wage law. The Works Progress Administration, created in 1935, put some 8.5 million people to work at a cost of about $11 billion before it ended in 1943. Whether such relief workers count as employed changes the record of the decade. Lebergott and the Bureau of Labor Statistics counted them as unemployed; Michael Darby, in an NBER working paper of 1975, called this 'A major conceptual error', and in that paper counting them as employed brings unemployment in 1936 down from 17.0 to 10.1 percent. The two series are identical until 1932 and diverge from 1933 (chart); in the version Darby published in 1976, as Robert Margo tabulates it, the rate for 1936 is 9.9 percent. The Social Security Act of 1935, writes Larry DeWitt of the Social Security Administration, 'excluded from coverage about half the workers in the American economy', among them agricultural and domestic workers; 65 percent of African American workers fell outside it, and '27 percent of the white workforce was likewise excluded from coverage.' Why is debated. Ira Katznelson stresses the power of southern members of Congress, and, as a Columbia Magazine review summarises his argument, holds that the New Deal in effect traded away Black Americans' interests to win major benefits for whites; Robert Lieberman and Linda Gordon also see a racial motive. DeWitt, answering Lieberman, Gordon and others, concludes that 'the racial-bias thesis is both conceptually flawed and unsupported', and that the exclusion 'was due to considerations of administrative feasibility involving tax-collection procedures.' The Wagner Act of 5 July 1935 gave employees the right to form and join unions, required employers to bargain with unions chosen by a majority, and created the National Labor Relations Board. The Fair Labor Standards Act, signed on 25 June 1938, set a minimum wage of 25 cents an hour and a 44-hour week at first, and banned oppressive child labor; it covered industries employing only about one-fifth of the labor force. On 27 May 1935 a unanimous Supreme Court ruled against the NIRA's code system in Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States: 'Extraordinary conditions do not create or enlarge constitutional power'. For the commerce power and judicial review, see US2.2 and US2.6. On 5 February 1937 Roosevelt proposed to add a justice for each sitting justice over 70, up to six. The Senate Judiciary Committee called it 'an invasion of judicial power such as has never before been attempted in this country', and the plan was shelved by July. Meanwhile, on 29 March 1937, the Court upheld a minimum-wage law by 5 to 4 in West Coast Hotel v. Parrish, overruling Adkins (1923): 'The Constitution does not speak of freedom of contract.' Whether Justice Owen Roberts changed his vote because of the plan is debated. The legal historian G. Edward White notes that the justices had first voted on the case at their conference of 19 December 1936, where Roberts voted to sustain the Washington law, before the plan was introduced in February 1937. The 'switch in time' reading, which William Leuchtenburg describes as the view of contemporaries, ties the decision to the plan; White concludes that Roberts's switch 'had nothing to do with the introduction of the Court-packing plan'. 27 May 1935 Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States NIRA codes struck down, unanimously 5 July 1935 Wagner Act right to join unions; NLRB 1935 Works Progress Administration some 8.5 million put to work, 1935-43 1935 Social Security Act about half of workers excluded 5 February 1937 court-packing plan shelved by July 1937 29 March 1937 West Coast Hotel v. Parrish minimum wage upheld, 5 to 4; Adkins overruled 25 June 1938 Fair Labor Standards Act 25 cents an hour; about one-fifth of the labor force covered

Real GDP grew about 43 percent from 1933 to 1937 and passed its 1929 level in 1936, before the recession of 1937-38. Economists disagree over what drove the recovery and what held it back: Romer credits gold inflows and money, Cole and Ohanian blame cartelization, Eggertsson disputes them, and Fishback has measured the programmes one by one. The effects of the HOLC's redlining maps are also disputed. In the BEA series real GDP rose from $877 billion in 1933 to $1,257 billion in 1937 (chained 2017 dollars), about 43 percent, passing its 1929 level in 1936; Britannica gives growth of 9 percent a year from 1933 to 1937. Then a recession ran from May 1937 to June 1938: real GDP fell 10 percent from peak to trough and unemployment rose back to 20 percent. Federal Reserve History notes that 'Fed policymakers doubled reserve requirement ratios', and also lists the Treasury's sterilization of gold, the new Social Security payroll tax and tighter fiscal policy. On how unemployment is counted, see US6.7. What drove the recovery? Christina Romer argues that 'nearly all of the observed recovery of the U.S. economy prior to 1942 was due to monetary expansion', fed by 'Huge gold inflows'. Harold Cole and Lee Ohanian (2004) conclude that 'New Deal cartelization policies are an important factor in accounting for the failure of the economy to recover back to trend.' Gauti Eggertsson (2012) replies that with zero interest rates and falling prices, conditions he finds 'satisfied during the Great Depression', such policies were expansionary in his model. Price Fishback has measured the programmes one by one. With Valentina Kachanovskaya he finds that a federal dollar raised state income per person 'by between 40 and 96 cents', with 'no positive effects on private employment.' In his survey, relief and public works had income multipliers 'of around one' and 'reduced crime rates, and lowered several types of mortality'; the farm programs 'typically aided large farm owners but eliminated opportunities for share croppers, tenants, and farm workers'; and the Home Owners' Loan Corporation 'staved off drops in housing prices and home ownership rates'. The HOLC's maps of the 1930s, which marked some neighborhoods in red, are disputed. Daniel Aaronson, Daniel Hartley and Bhashkar Mazumder (2021) find that 'The maps led to reduced home ownership rates, house values, and rents' and 'increased racial segregation in later decades.' Fishback, Jonathan Rose, Kenneth Snowden and Thomas Storrs (2021; 2024) argue that the Federal Housing Administration redlined first, that 'the HOLC itself broadly loaned to such neighborhoods and to Black homeowners', and that 'the HOLC's redlining maps had little effect on the geographic distribution of either program's mortgage market activity'. In a Chicago Fed brief (2022), Rose, one of the co-authors, concluded that the FHA's red lines were 'likely far more impactful than the HOLC's.' Christina Romer NBER WP 3829 recovery before 1942 'due to monetary expansion' Harold Cole and Lee Ohanian JPE, 2004 cartelization slowed the return to trend Gauti Eggertsson AER, 2012 at zero rates and deflation such policies were expansionary Fishback and Kachanovskaya JEH, 2015 income per person up 40-96 cents per dollar; no private employment effects Price Fishback survey, 2017 relief cut crime and mortality; farm programmes cut sharecroppers' opportunities Aaronson, Hartley and Mazumder AEJ: Policy, 2021 HOLC maps cut home ownership, raised segregation Fishback, Rose, Snowden and Storrs NBER 2021; JUE 2024 FHA redlined first; HOLC maps had little effect on where either agency lent

Drought and the plowing of marginal land produced the Dust Bowl, and 300,000 to 400,000 people from Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas and Missouri settled in California, few of them from the Dust Bowl itself. Huey Long proposed to cap fortunes, and the priest and broadcaster Charles Coughlin turned to antisemitism. Pius XI taught a family wage and subsidiarity, while the Catholic Worker and Black churches offered hospitality and food to the poor. Strictly, the Dust Bowl covered western Kansas, southeastern Colorado and the Oklahoma Panhandle, with adjoining areas. Droughts struck in 1930-31, 1934, 1936 and 1939-40. Low crop prices, pushed lower by a record wheat crop in 1931, and high machinery costs led farmers to put more submarginal land into production, while the one-way disc plow 'greatly increased the risk of blowing soil'. On Black Sunday, 14 April 1935, a dust storm hit Boise City, Oklahoma, at about 5:15 pm; the name 'Dust Bowl' is generally traced to an Associated Press report about it published the next day. James Gregory estimates that 300,000 to 400,000 people from Oklahoma, Texas, Arkansas and Missouri settled in California in the 1930s, but 'The actual Dust Bowl counties were sparsely populated and contributed few refugees.' Huey Long's Share Our Wealth plan, set out in the Congressional Record in 1934-35, would have limited fortunes to 'not more than $3 to 4 million', let every family 'possess not less than $5,000 free of debt' and an income 'of not less than $2,500 per year', and paid 'Old-age pensions of $30 per month to persons over 60 years of age'. Charles Coughlin, a priest at the Shrine of the Little Flower in Royal Oak, Michigan, reached a regular radio audience that the US Holocaust Memorial Museum puts at 30 million. In 1933 he hailed the New Deal as Christ's Deal, while, by the museum's account, already attacking bankers as 'modern Shylocks', a phrase that drew on antisemitic stereotypes. Ten days after Kristallnacht, in November 1938, he claimed that Jews controlled the radio and the press, and that year his magazine Social Justice serialized the antisemitic Protocols of the Elders of Zion. His archbishop ordered him to stop broadcasting in 1941, and on 1 May 1942 told him to stop all non-pastoral activities or risk being defrocked. On the Holocaust, see 15.7. In Quadragesimo Anno (15 May 1931) Pope Pius XI taught that 'the worker must be paid a wage sufficient to support him and his family', and stated the principle of subsidiarity: 'Just as it is gravely wrong to take from individuals what they can accomplish by their own initiative and industry and give it to the community, so also it is an injustice and at the same time a grave evil and disturbance of right order to assign to a greater and higher association what lesser and subordinate organizations can do.' He also declared that 'no one can be at the same time a good Catholic and a true socialist'. Compare Rerum Novarum (US5.9). The Catholic Worker, founded in New York City in 1933 by Dorothy Day and Peter Maurin, ran houses of hospitality that welcomed the poor as guests rather than as clients. In Chicago, the historian Wallace Best finds, Black migrants flocked to storefront churches. Elder Lucy Smith's church fed as many as about 90 people a day, and Best found no mainline Black church giving such relief. Father Divine's Peace Mission Movement served food at very low prices and was racially integrated. On the Great Migration, see US6.4. Quadragesimo Anno (Pius XI) 15 May 1931 a family wage; subsidiarity; socialism rejected Share Our Wealth (Huey Long) 1934-35 fortunes capped at $3 to 4 million; $30 pensions over 60 Black Sunday, Boise City 14 April 1935 the storm that named the Dust Bowl Migration to California 1930s 300,000-400,000, few from the Dust Bowl proper Charles Coughlin 1933 to 1942 radio audience put at 30 million; antisemitism; off the air 1941, curbed 1942

From 1935 Congress passed Neutrality Acts that banned arms exports and loans to nations at war, and in 1939 it let belligerents buy arms for cash and carry them away. In 1939 the United States refused the refugees of the St. Louis and let a bill to admit 20,000 refugee children die in committee, while about 118,000 German quota places went unused between 1933 and 1941. Lend-Lease and the Atlantic Charter followed in 1941, and on 8 December Roosevelt asked Congress to declare war on Japan. 'On August 31, 1935, Congress passed the first Neutrality Act', which banned the export of arms to nations at war. A law of 1936 added a ban on loans to belligerents, and one of 1937 let the president allow them to buy goods other than arms on a 'cash-and-carry' basis. The Neutrality Act of November 1939 lifted the arms embargo and put all trade with belligerents on cash-and-carry terms. American ships were barred from belligerent ports, and 'The ban on loans remained in effect.' Outside Congress, the America First Committee opposed entry into the war and claimed 800,000 members. At its rally in Des Moines on 11 September 1941, Charles Lindbergh accused Great Britain, Jews and the Roosevelt administration of leading the United States into war. (On the quota laws, see US6.3; on the Holocaust, 15.7.) The St. Louis left Hamburg on 13 May 1939 with 937 passengers. Cuba, the United States and Canada all refused them, and in the end 254 of the passengers were killed in the Holocaust. The Wagner-Rogers bill, introduced on 9 February 1939, would have admitted 20,000 refugee children aged 14 and under over two years. It died in the Senate Immigration Committee in the first week of July. The quotas were treated as ceilings. The German quota was 25,957 a year, yet between 1933 and 1941, by the Holocaust Museum's estimate, roughly 118,000 German places that could have been used went unfilled. From July 1941 visa control was centralized in Washington. Lend-Lease, 'An Act to Promote the Defense of the United States', was approved on 11 March 1941, and the program eventually dispensed some $50 billion in assistance. On 9-10 August Roosevelt and Churchill met aboard USS Augusta in Placentia Bay, and on 14 August they released a joint declaration of eight principles, the Atlantic Charter. Its first principle reads: 'First, their countries seek no aggrandizement, territorial or other'. Its third reads: 'Third, they respect the right of all peoples to choose the form of government under which they will live'. On 8 December 1941 Roosevelt went before a joint session of Congress: 'Yesterday, December 7, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan.' He closed: 'I ask that the Congress declare that since the unprovoked and dastardly attack by Japan on Sunday, December 7, 1941, a state of war has existed between the United States and the Japanese Empire.' His draft had read 'a date which will live in world history'. The America First Committee dissolved after Pearl Harbor. For the war in Europe and Asia as a whole, see 15.6. 31 Aug 1935 first Neutrality Act: no arms exports to nations at war 1936; 1937 ban on loans; cash-and-carry for goods other than arms 13 May 1939 the St. Louis leaves Hamburg with 937 passengers Jul 1939 Wagner-Rogers bill dies in the Senate Immigration Committee Nov 1939 arms embargo lifted; all trade on cash-and-carry 11 Mar 1941 Lend-Lease approved 14 Aug 1941 Atlantic Charter released 8 Dec 1941 Roosevelt asks Congress to declare war on Japan

Real GDP rose by about 92 percent between 1939 and 1944, federal outlays climbed from under a tenth of GDP to about two-fifths, and by 1945 the debt held by the public exceeded GDP. Women's employment rose almost 60 percent, a Black worker proposed a 'double victory', and the Bracero Program brought Mexican workers on labor contracts. Executive Order 9066 led to the removal of about 122,000 people of Japanese ancestry; the Court upheld the exclusion in 1944, Congress apologized in 1988, and in 2018 the Chief Justice called Korematsu 'gravely wrong the day it was decided'. Measured in chained 2017 dollars, real GDP rose from $1,312 billion in 1939 to $2,525 billion in 1944, about 92 percent, before slipping to $2,500 billion in 1945 and $2,210 billion in 1946. Federal net outlays rose from 9.8 percent of GDP in fiscal 1939 to 40.7 percent in 1944 and 1945. Federal debt held by the public, 44.3 percent of GDP in 1939, reached 103.2 percent in 1945. The Women's Bureau reported in 1946 that women's employment had 'increased almost 60 percent between 1940 and 1945'. Using new data on wartime employment and job placements, the economist Evan K. Rose argues that where women took wartime jobs was driven mainly by industrial mobilization rather than by drafted men leaving local labor markets, and that the areas most exposed to wartime work show 'limited overall effects on female labor force participation in 1950'. In a letter to the Pittsburgh Courier dated 31 January 1942, James G. Thompson proposed: 'let we colored Americans adopt the double VV for a double victory'. 'Locked out of jobs on the factory floor', as the National Park Service puts it, Thompson worked in the cafeteria at Cessna. The Bracero Program brought Mexican workers to the United States on labor contracts; from 1942 to 1964, 4.6 million contracts were signed. That is a count of contracts, not of individual workers. In the Zoot Suit Riots in Los Angeles, 3-10 June 1943, 'Many zoot-suiters were beaten by servicemen and stripped of their zoot suits on the spot.' Executive Order 9066, signed on 19 February 1942, 'authorized the forced removal of all persons deemed a threat to national security'. About 122,000 people of Japanese ancestry were removed, nearly 70,000 of them American citizens, and held in ten incarceration centers. On 18 December 1944, in Korematsu v. United States, the Court upheld the exclusion order by six votes to three. Writing for the Court, Justice Hugo Black said that courts 'must subject them to the most rigid scrutiny', meaning legal restrictions on a single racial group. Dissenting, Justice Frank Murphy called the decision 'this legalization of racism', and Justice Robert Jackson warned that its principle 'lies about like a loaded weapon'. The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 found that the incarceration had been 'motivated largely by racial prejudice, wartime hysteria, and a failure of political leadership', apologized, and provided 'a $20,000 cash payment to each person who was incarcerated'. In Trump v. Hawaii (2018), in an opinion upholding the president's travel proclamation, Chief Justice John Roberts wrote: 'Korematsu was gravely wrong the day it was decided, has been overruled in the court of history'. In June 2025, under the executive order 'Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History', the Interior Department and the Park Service put up signs at Manzanar and Minidoka inviting visitors to report negative content. The Japanese American National Museum said it was 'deeply disturbed by this new directive'. On 20 September 2025 The Washington Post reported that a sign about the detention of Japanese Americans had been removed at at least one more park. In June 2026 a federal district judge, Angel Kelley, ordered the administration to restore park signage removed in 2025, and KQED reported that at Manzanar QR codes had been posted asking the public what should be taken down. On 2 July 2026 the First Circuit Court of Appeals stayed that order, finding the Interior Department likely to succeed in its appeal. That is the status as of July 2026; the appeal continues. 31 Jan 1942 James G. United States, 6-3 1988 Civil Liberties Act: apology and $20,000 to each person incarcerated 2018 Trump v. Hawaii: Korematsu 'gravely wrong' Jun 2025 signs at Manzanar and Minidoka invite reports of negative content Jun-Jul 2026 district court orders removed signage restored; First Circuit stays the order on 2 July

At Midway in June 1942 the United States lost one carrier and Japan four, and on D-Day, 6 June 1944, nearly 160,000 Allied troops landed in Normandy. The VA counts 16,112,566 Americans who served and 291,557 battle deaths, in armed forces whose segregation was not banned until 1948. In 1944 the government created the War Refugee Board but refused requests to bomb Auschwitz, and whether bombing could have saved lives is still debated. At the Battle of Midway, 4-7 June 1942, the Navy's historians write, 'Against the loss of one U.S. carrier, the Japanese lost four—all of which had participated in the Pearl Harbor attack.' The American carrier lost was Yorktown. In Europe, on D-Day, 6 June 1944, nearly 160,000 Allied troops landed by sea and air in Normandy, on beaches that included Utah and Omaha. For the global course of the war, see 15.6. The Department of Veterans Affairs counts 16,112,566 Americans who served in the Second World War. It lists 291,557 battle deaths, 113,842 other deaths in service and 670,846 wounded. The National WWII Museum gives slightly different totals: 407,316 killed and 671,278 wounded, plus 5,662 merchant mariners dead. Those who served did so in segregated forces. More than one million Black men were inducted, from 2.5 million who registered, and segregation in the armed forces was not banned until President Truman's executive order of 26 July 1948. On the Holocaust itself, see 15.7. After a Treasury memorandum titled 'The Acquiescence of this Government in the Murder of the Jews', Roosevelt issued Executive Order 9417 on 22 January 1944. It created the War Refugee Board and made it government policy to take 'all measures within its power to rescue the victims of enemy oppression'. (The Treasury's draft had spoken of the 'immediate rescue and relief of the Jews of Europe'.) The Board itself claimed to have saved 'tens of thousands of lives'. On 14 August 1944 Assistant Secretary of War John J. McCloy refused requests to bomb Auschwitz. Such an operation, he wrote, 'would in any case be of such doubtful efficacy that it would not warrant the use of our resources'. Yet the IG Farben industrial complex next to the camp was bombed four times in the last year of the war. Historians disagree about what more could have been done. David S. Wyman (1984) argues, as his publisher summarizes the book, that a serious rescue effort could almost certainly have saved several hundred thousand Jews. William D. Rubinstein (1997) answers, as his publisher summarizes it, that few of the Jews who perished could have been saved by any Allied action. On the bombing itself, the Jewish Virtual Library notes that 'Several recent studies have suggested that it was not possible to bomb the camp', citing those of James Kitchens and Richard Levy. The same article cites Stuart Erdheim's study, which argues that bombing would have been 'no more complex than numerous other missions.' Richard Breitman and Allan J. Lichtman (2013) look at Roosevelt's record as a whole. As American University's news release summarizes them, they conclude that he did far more to help European Jews than any other world leader of his time. t: The atomic bomb and the end of the war
x: The Army Corps of Engineers set up the Manhattan Engineer District in 1942; the project employed 130,000 workers at its peak and tested its first bomb on 16 July 1945. Roosevelt died on 12 April; on 6 August Truman announced the bombing of Hiroshima, and Nagasaki was bombed on 9 August, with death tolls that differ by source and by the period counted. Whether the bombs were needed is still debated, and in June 1945 the United Nations Charter was signed in San Francisco. 'In August, the Corps set up the Manhattan Engineer District (MED) to manage the project'. Leslie Groves took charge in September 1942, and Roosevelt gave his final authorization that December. The project's main sites were Oak Ridge in Tennessee, Hanford in Washington and Los Alamos in New Mexico. At its peak it employed 130,000 workers, and it cost about $2.2 billion. Its first bomb was exploded in the Trinity test on 16 July 1945. Roosevelt did not live to see it: he died at Warm Springs, Georgia, on 12 April 1945. On 6 August 1945 President Truman announced: 'Sixteen hours ago an American airplane dropped one bomb on Hiroshima, an important Japanese Army base.' And: 'It is an atomic bomb.' A second bomb fell on Nagasaki on 9 August. How many died depends on who counts and over what period. The U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey of 1946 put the dead at between 70,000 and 80,000 in Hiroshima and over 35,000 in Nagasaki. The Radiation Effects Research Foundation estimates 90,000 to 166,000 deaths in Hiroshima and 60,000 to 80,000 in Nagasaki within two to four months, and says the total is 'not known precisely'. The City of Hiroshima's long-term estimate is that 237,000 people were killed directly or indirectly. Was the bomb needed? Gar Alperovitz, writing in 2015, argues that American military leaders and intelligence judged Japan to be on the verge of surrender, and that the Japanese moved to surrender only after the Soviet Union entered the war: 'By and large, the top generals and admirals who managed World War II knew better.' Robert P. Newman (1995) holds, as the description of his book summarizes it, that Truman used the bomb to end the war as quickly and with as few casualties as possible. Richard B. Frank, the author of Downfall, wrote in an H-Diplo roundtable on Hasegawa's book that anyone who could conceivably have been president in 1945 would have authorized the bombs. Tsuyoshi Hasegawa (2005) writes, in a passage Frank quotes: 'The evidence is compelling that Soviet entry into the war had a strong impact on the peace party. Indeed, the Soviet attack, not the Hiroshima bomb, convinced political leaders to end the war by accepting the Potsdam Proclamation.' At the San Francisco conference, from 25 April to 26 June 1945, representatives of 50 countries met. The Charter of the United Nations was signed on 26 June and came into force on 24 October 1945. U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey (1946) Hiroshima 70,000-80,000 early American estimate U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey (1946) Nagasaki over 35,000 early American estimate Radiation Effects Research Foundation Hiroshima 90,000-166,000 deaths within 2-4 months Radiation Effects Research Foundation Nagasaki 60,000-80,000 deaths within 2-4 months City of Hiroshima Hiroshima 237,000 killed directly or indirectly

In the Bureau of Economic Analysis's series real GDP roughly tripled between 1950 and 1980, while the population grew from about 140 million in 1945 to about 228 million in 1980. Real median family income rose about 74 percent from 1953 to 1973 and then changed little to 1980, and the official poverty rate fell from 22.4 percent in 1959 to 11.1 percent in 1973 before rising to 13.0 percent in 1980. In the Bureau of Economic Analysis's series real GDP was $2,458.5 billion in 1950 and $7,257.3 billion in 1980, in chained 2017 dollars: it roughly tripled. The figure for 1945, $2,500.1 billion, is higher than that for 1950; on the wartime economy, see US6.0. The population, also from BEA, rose from 139,928 thousand in 1945 to 227,726 thousand in 1980, from about 140 million to about 228 million. Dividing one series by the other, real GDP per person was about $16,200 in 1950 and about $31,900 in 1980: it roughly doubled, while the population grew by about half. The Census Bureau's real median family income, measured in 2025 C-CPI-U dollars, was $41,880 in 1953, the series' first year, and $73,000 in 1973, a rise of about 74 percent. It was $69,850 in 1975 and $73,230 in 1980. The official poverty rate was 22.4 percent in 1959, the first year measured, fell by about half to 11.1 percent in 1973, and was 13.0 percent in 1980. Both series turned after 1973: income stopped rising and poverty rose. On the 1970s, see US7.12. Each measure on this page comes from a single series, and each has its own units. The income series is now expressed in C-CPI-U dollars (R-CPI-U-RS before 2000), a changed deflator, so its levels differ from those in older printed tables, and it begins only in 1953; chained-dollar GDP levels change with each BEA revision. On the postwar world economy and Bretton Woods, see 15.13; on the Cold War worldwide, 15.9; on rights movements and religion worldwide, 15.14. This chapter begins with containment (US7.1), the Red Scare (US7.2), Korea and the Eisenhower years (US7.3) and the postwar boom (US7.4). It then follows civil rights from 1945 to 1965 (US7.5-US7.6), Kennedy, Johnson and the Great Society (US7.7), Vietnam (US7.8), 1968 and the new movements (US7.9) and the women's movement (US7.10), and ends with Nixon (US7.11), the 1970s (US7.12) and religion and the rise of the religious right (US7.13). On the atomic bomb and the end of the war, see US6.13; on Brown v. Board and voting-rights doctrine, see US2. In February 1946 George Kennan's Long Telegram from Moscow described Soviet power as 'highly sensitive to logic of force'; in March 1947 the Truman Doctrine pledged to 'support free peoples', and the Marshall Plan's funding eventually rose to over $12 billion. The Berlin airlift, the North Atlantic Treaty of April 1949 and NSC-68 followed, while historians disagree about who began the Cold War. On 22 February 1946 George Kennan, the American chargé d'affaires in the Soviet Union, sent the Secretary of State the message known as the Long Telegram. He described Soviet power as 'a political force committed fanatically to the belief that with US there can be no permanent modus vivendi', and as 'Impervious to logic of reason, and it is highly sensitive to logic of force.' His views also appeared in what the Office of the Historian calls 'an anonymous contribution to the journal Foreign Affairs, the so-called "X-Article."' On the Cold War worldwide, see 15.9. The Truman Doctrine of 12 March 1947 declared: 'I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.' Truman requested $400,000,000 for Greece and Turkey. George Marshall announced the plan that bears his name in a speech to Harvard's graduating class on 5 June 1947, and Congress approved funding that would eventually rise to over $12 billion. The Berlin crisis, a Soviet blockade of West Berlin, began on 24 June 1948. In the American airlift that answered it, 'one plane landed every 45 seconds at Tempelhof Airport', and the blockade ended on 12 May 1949; the same Office of the Historian page also gives 11 May. The North Atlantic Treaty was signed in Washington on 4 April 1949, and its members 'agreed to consider attack against one an attack against all.' NSC-68, 'completed by the U.S. Department of State's Policy Planning Staff on April 7, 1950', called for a massive build-up. After the Korean War began, defense spending 'almost tripled', from 5 to 14.2 percent of GDP between 1950 and 1953. On Korea, see US7.3. Who began the Cold War? The orthodox historians, in Seth Center's summary, 'place primary responsibility for the Cold War on the Soviet Union'; many of them were 'former Roosevelt or Truman administration officials'. Center names Herbert Feis, among whose books is From Trust to Terror: The Onset of the Cold War, 1945-1950, and writes that these works 'emphasize Stalin's "ruthlessness," "spirit of mistrust," and revolutionary goals.' Revisionist historians, among them William Appleman Williams in The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959), argued, as Verso's online encyclopedia summarises them, that the United States had long had imperial ambitions. In 1983 John Lewis Gaddis described 'The Emerging Post-Revisionist Synthesis on the Origins of the Cold War'. Seth Center calls Gaddis that synthesis's 'first and foremost proponent' and writes that he 'concludes that the conflict grew out of external and internal conflict in both the Soviet Union and the United States.' For We Now Know (1997) Gaddis drew on newly opened Soviet archives. Reviewing it, Neal Ascherson described Gaddis as convinced that Stalin, more than anyone or anything else, brought about the Cold War, and wrote that the archives settled that Kim Il Sung had attacked South Korea first, in 1950. 22 February 1946 Kennan's Long Telegram Soviet power 'highly sensitive to logic of force' 12 March 1947 Truman Doctrine 'support free peoples'; $400,000,000 for Greece and Turkey 5 June 1947 Marshall's speech at Harvard funding eventually over $12 billion 24 June 1948 to 12 May 1949 Berlin blockade and airlift one plane every 45 seconds at Tempelhof 4 April 1949 North Atlantic Treaty attack against one an attack against all 7 April 1950 NSC-68 a massive build-up; defense 5 to 14.2 percent of GDP, 1950-53

A loyalty order of March 1947, the Hollywood Ten's contempt citations, Alger Hiss's conviction for perjury and the Rosenbergs' execution in June 1953 ran alongside Senator Joseph McCarthy's campaign, from his Wheeling speech of February 1950 to his censure by the Senate, 67 to 22, in December 1954. The Venona translations, made public from 1995, feed an argument between Haynes and Klehr, who stress Soviet espionage, and Ellen Schrecker, who stresses the harm of the anticommunist crusade. Executive Order 9835, of 21 March 1947, provided: 'There shall be a loyalty investigation of every person entering the civilian employment of any department or agency' of the federal executive. In October 1947 the Hollywood Ten refused to answer the questions of the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), sitting in Washington. They were 'voted in contempt of Congress on November 24, 1947', received 'sentences of six months to one year in prison', and were blacklisted. On the Red Scare after the First World War, see US5.13. Whittaker Chambers accused Alger Hiss in 1948. On 21 January 1950 Hiss was found 'Guilty on two counts of perjury' and sentenced to five years. In what the FBI calls the atom spy case, 'On March 29, 1951, the jury rendered a verdict of guilty' against Julius and Ethel Rosenberg. Both were executed on 19 June 1953. At Wheeling, West Virginia, on 9 February 1950, Senator Joseph McCarthy said, in the text printed by History Matters: 'I have here in my hand a list of 205 . . . a list of names that were made known to the Secretary of State'. The number is disputed: History Matters notes that advance copies of the speech given to the press 'record the number as 205', but that in a letter to Truman the next day and in the transcript McCarthy submitted to the Congressional Record ten days later 'he uses the number 57.' The televised Army-McCarthy hearings, which began on 22 April 1954, 'showed McCarthy in an increasingly unattractive light', and on 2 December 1954 the Senate, 'on a vote of 67 to 22, censured Joseph McCarthy.' The United States 'began a secret program in February 1943 later codenamed VENONA' to break Soviet cables. It ran until 1980. The first of six public releases, in July 1995, 'included 49 messages', and over five more releases 'all of the approximately 3,000 VENONA translations were made public.' The Department of Energy's history of the Manhattan Project names 'Julius Rosenberg, and Rosenberg's wife Ethel' among the spies Venona uncovered. Ethel's own part is disputed. A memo of 22 August 1950 by the codebreaker Meredith Gardner, which the Associated Press described in 2024 as recently declassified, concluded that she knew of her husband's work 'but that due to illness she did not engage in the work herself'; the historian Harvey Klehr, as the AP reports, has written that she 'was an active participant in her husband's spy network.' Haynes and Klehr, authors of Venona and In Denial (2003), argue that Soviet espionage was extensive; their publisher's description says In Denial charges revisionist scholars with ignoring or distorting new evidence from Russian archives. The publisher's description of Ellen Schrecker's Many Are the Crimes (1998), reproduced by the National Humanities Center, calls it 'the first post-Cold War exploration of the anticommunist witch-hunt and its devastating impact'. Reviewing it, Alan Wald quotes her asking whether 'the espionage, which unquestionably occurred' required 'a politically repressive internal security system', and reports that her answer is no. 21 March 1947 Executive Order 9835 loyalty investigation of every new federal civilian employee October-November 1947 the Hollywood Ten before HUAC contempt of Congress; six months to one year in prison 21 January 1950 Alger Hiss guilty on two counts of perjury; five years 9 February 1950 McCarthy at Wheeling 'a list of 205' (57 in his later transcript) 29 March 1951 the Rosenbergs convicted executed 19 June 1953 22 April 1954 Army-McCarthy hearings begin televised 2 December 1954 Senate vote McCarthy censured, 67 to 22 July 1995 Venona first of six releases (49 messages); about 3,000 translations public in all

The Department of Veterans Affairs counts 36,574 American deaths in the Korean theater, 33,739 of them in battle, and 17,672 more in service outside it; the National Park Service writes of 'over 50,000'. Truman relieved MacArthur in April 1951 and the armistice was signed on 27 July 1953; in 1956 Congress enlarged and funded the Interstate System, after Sputnik it passed the National Defense Education Act, and in 1961 Eisenhower warned against the 'military-industrial complex'. How many Americans died in Korea? The Department of Veterans Affairs counts 33,739 battle deaths and 2,835 other deaths in theater: 36,574 in all. The National Park Service writes of 'over 50,000 American deaths'. The gap is mostly a matter of what is counted. The same VA fact sheet also lists 17,672 'Other Deaths in Service (Non-Theater)', and the three VA figures together come to 54,246. The historian Allan R. Millett explains that the Defense Department's older figures for 'other deaths' appear to have 'included all noncombat deaths throughout the armed forces, worldwide, during the entire Korean War era (1950–57)'. On who attacked first, see US7.1; on the Cold War worldwide, 15.9. 'On April 11, 1951, President Truman officially relieved Douglas MacArthur of his command'; as the Truman Library puts Truman's reasoning, he felt the general had 'overstepped his authority, defied direct orders from his superior'. In 1952 Eisenhower pledged that 'he would personally go to Korea'. Armistice negotiations had gone on at Panmunjom for two years when, 'Finally, on July 27, 1953', the armistice was signed. The Federal-Aid Highway Act, signed on 29 June 1956, enlarged the Interstate System to 41,000 miles, from the 40,000 miles authorized in 1944, and paid for it. It 'authorizes $25 billion over the period 1957-1969 as the Federal share (90 percent)' and 'establishes the Highway Trust Fund.' The Senate's history of the act ties the roads to defense: 'transporting troops and for evacuating cities in case of nuclear attack'. Of Sputnik's launch on 4 October 1957 the Office of the Historian writes: 'The successful launch came as a shock to experts and citizens in the United States'. Congress answered with the National Defense Education Act, which 'made substantial funds available for low-cost student loans' and supported science, mathematics and foreign languages. In his farewell address of 17 January 1961 Eisenhower said: 'In the councils of government, we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex. The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist.' He also warned that public policy 'could itself become the captive of a scientific-technological elite.' 11 April 1951 Truman relieves MacArthur Truman felt he had 'defied direct orders' 1952 Eisenhower's pledge 'he would personally go to Korea' 27 July 1953 armistice signed after two years of talks at Panmunjom 29 June 1956 Federal-Aid Highway Act 41,000 miles; $25 billion, 1957-69; 90 percent federal share 4 October 1957 Sputnik 'a shock to experts and citizens' after Sputnik National Defense Education Act low-cost student loans; science, mathematics, languages 17 January 1961 farewell address the 'military-industrial complex'

By 1956, 7.8 million of 16 million Second World War veterans had taken part in education or training under the GI Bill, but scholars disagree about its racial effects, and Levittown, begun in 1947, barred Black families. About 76 million births came in the baby boom of 1946-1964, union membership peaked at about a third of workers, 'under God' entered the Pledge in 1954, and 'In God we trust' became the national motto in 1956. The GI Bill was signed on 22 June 1944. By 1956 '7.8 million of 16 million World War II veterans had participated in an education or training program', and from 1944 to 1952 the Veterans Administration (today's Department of Veterans Affairs) backed nearly 2.4 million home loans. On the postwar world economy, see 15.13. Who gained? Publishers Weekly's review summarises Katznelson's argument in When Affirmative Action Was White (2005): the bill unfairly favoured white veterans by turning the administration of benefits over to local governments. Turner and Bound (2002) find 'a substantial and positive impact on the educational attainment of white men and black men born outside the South', but that 'for those black veterans likely to be limited to the South in their educational choices, the G.I. Bill had little effect on collegiate outcomes', widening the educational gap between Black and white men from southern states. The description of Mettler's Soldiers to Citizens by her literary agency presents the bill's benefits as reaching across lines of class and race. Two new studies find widening racial gaps. Agbai, in a peer-reviewed article in the American Journal of Sociology (2025) on the bill's home-loan guaranty, finds that 'the GI Bill is linked with increased homeownership and home value for Black and White veterans', but that 'the policy exacerbated extant racial inequalities' in housing; Althoff and Szerman, in a working paper of June 2026 that has not yet been peer reviewed, estimate 'a 5-percentage-point (47 percent) widening of the racial college gap'. Levittown, on Long Island, begun in 1947, barred Black families. Its Clause 25 read: 'No dwelling shall be used or occupied by members of other than the Caucasian race'. It had 17,447 homes by November 1951, and in the Searchable Museum's words, 'Levittown refused to house Black veterans and their families.' On civil rights, see US7.5. Pew Research Center counts 'a total of 76 million births during the boom' of 1946-1964, with annual births 'surpassing 4 million in 1954 and remaining above that level until 1965.' Union membership peaked at about a third of workers: the Congressional Research Service cites 'a peak of 34.2% in 1945' in one series and 'its post-World War II peak of 33.5% in 1954' in another, against 10.1 percent of wage and salary workers in 2022 (9.4 percent on the measure behind the 1945 peak). 'Under God' entered the Pledge of Allegiance on 14 June 1954. Signing the bill, Eisenhower said that 'the millions of our school children will daily proclaim ... the dedication of our nation and our people to the Almighty.' 'In God we trust' became the national motto under a law 'approved by the President on July 30, 1956', and was 'first used on paper money in 1957'. Gallup found church membership at 73 percent in 1937; it 'remained near 70% for the next six decades', and was 47 percent in 2020 (membership of a church, synagogue or mosque). On religion and the rise of the religious right, see US7.13.
