s: The armed forces, Till, Montgomery and Little Rock
x: In 1948 Truman ordered equal treatment in the armed services, and in 1956 southern members of Congress urged 'lawful means' of resistance to Brown v. Board of Education. Emmett Till was lynched in 1955, Montgomery's buses were boycotted for more than a year, and in 1957 Eisenhower sent paratroopers to Little Rock. Martin Luther King Jr. wrote that 'Christ furnished the spirit and motivation while Gandhi furnished the method.' On 26 July 1948 President Truman issued Executive Order 9981, which declared 'equality of treatment and opportunity for all persons in the armed services'. In the National Archives' words, 'by the end of the Korean conflict, almost all of the military was integrated' (on Korea, see US7.3). On 17 May 1954 the Supreme Court ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that segregated schools were 'inherently unequal'; for the case as doctrine, see US2.11. On 12 March 1956 the Southern Manifesto, signed by 19 senators and 82 representatives, all from former Confederate states, was introduced in the House. It 'attacked Brown as an abuse of judicial power that trespassed upon states' rights' and urged southerners to exhaust all 'lawful means' of resistance. Emmett Till, a 14-year-old visiting relatives in Mississippi, was lynched on 28 August 1955. At the courthouse in Sumner an all-white, all-male jury acquitted Roy Bryant and J. W. Milam, who later confessed in a paid interview. His open-casket visitation and funeral were held at Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ in Chicago. On 25 July 2023 President Biden made that church, the Sumner courthouse and Graball Landing near Glendora, where Till's body is believed to have been recovered from the Tallahatchie River, into the Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument, which the Park Service calls America's 425th national park. PBS NewsHour reports that Congress had failed to act against lynching 'more than 200 times' since 1900. The Emmett Till Antilynching Act, passed by the House 422 to 3, became law on 29 March 2022 and sets a maximum sentence of 30 years. In Montgomery, Rosa Parks was arrested on 1 December 1955. The bus boycott ran from 5 December 1955 to 20 December 1956, and the new Montgomery Improvement Association elected Martin Luther King Jr. its president. In Browder v. Gayle bus segregation was found unconstitutional, and the Supreme Court affirmed the ruling in November 1956. In September 1957 Governor Faubus called out the state's National Guard to surround Little Rock Central High School, and on 4 September nine Black students, known as the Little Rock Nine, attempted to enter. Eisenhower's Executive Order 10730 (the National Archives dates it 23 September; its transcript is signed 24 September) placed the Arkansas National Guard under federal control and sent 1,000 paratroopers of the 101st Airborne Division. The Southern Christian Leadership Conference, founded in January 1957 at Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, 'drew on the power and independence of black churches' in its aim to redeem 'the soul of America.' King had studied personalism at Boston University under Brightman and DeWolf, a philosophy that, in the King Institute's words, 'emphasizes the necessity of personal religious experience in understanding God', and received his PhD in June 1955. In 'Pilgrimage to Nonviolence' (1960) he wrote that Rauschenbusch's Christianity and the Social Crisis was a book that 'left an indelible imprint on my thinking', that 'Christ furnished the spirit and motivation while Gandhi furnished the method', and that Niebuhr 'made me aware of the complexity of human motives.' On rights movements and religion worldwide, see 15.14. 26 July 1948 Executive Order 9981: equal treatment in the armed services Washington 17 May 1954 Brown v. s: Sit-ins to the Voting Rights Act
x: The sit-ins of 1960, the Freedom Rides of 1961 and the Birmingham campaign of 1963, where King wrote that 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere', were followed by the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Black voter registration in Mississippi rose from 6.7 percent in 1965 to 74.2 percent in 1988. On 1 February 1960 four students from North Carolina A&T sat in at the Woolworth's store in Greensboro. By the end of April 'over 50,000 students had participated', and the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) was founded on 15-17 April. The Freedom Riders left Washington on 4 May 1961. Near Anniston, Alabama, 'one of the buses was firebombed', and in Birmingham 'Bull' Connor's police 'offered no protection.' The Interstate Commerce Commission's ban on segregation took effect on 1 November 1961. The Birmingham campaign began on 3 April 1963, and King was arrested on Good Friday, 12 April. In his Letter from Birmingham Jail, dated 16 April, he wrote: 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.' He wrote that 'This "Wait" has almost always meant "Never."' And he asked: 'Was not Amos an extremist for justice: "Let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever flowing stream."' He went on to ask the same of Paul. King's wording closely follows the Revised Standard Version: 'But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an everflowing stream.' The NRSVUE renders Amos 5:24 'But let justice roll down like water and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.' On 3 May 'Commissioner Connor directed local police and fire departments to use force', and on 15 September Klansmen bombed the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church, 'killing four young girls.' On 28 August 1963 the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, with Bayard Rustin as march organiser, drew 'more than 200,000 demonstrators.' A. Philip Randolph had first called for a march on Washington in 1941, and on 26 March 1963 he telegraphed King that the Negro American Labor Council had begun planning a June march 'for Negro job rights'. The House passed the civil rights bill on 10 February 1964 by 290 to 130. Democrats voted 152 to 96 for it, Northern Democrats 141 to 4 and Southern Democrats 11 to 92; Republicans voted 138 to 34. The Senate debated the bill for sixty days. On 10 June it voted 71 to 29 for cloture, with 27 Republicans and 44 Democrats in the majority, and it passed the bill nine days later; Johnson signed it on 2 July 1964. On the filibuster and cloture, see US2.3. In the Freedom Summer of 1964 Michael Schwerner, James Chaney and Andrew Goodman disappeared in Mississippi on 21 June; their bodies were found on 4 August '14 feet below an earthen dam.' In 1967 seven men were convicted, 'none on murder charges', and Edgar Ray Killen was 'convicted of manslaughter on June 21, 2005.' At the 1964 Democratic convention Fannie Lou Hamer of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party told the credentials committee: 'If the Freedom Democratic Party is not seated now, I question America.' Offered a compromise of two at-large seats, Hamer replied: 'We didn't come all this way for no two seats.' In Alabama, Jimmie Lee Jackson was shot on 18 February 1965, and 'Bloody Sunday' at the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma followed on 7 March. The march of 21-25 March swelled to 25,000 at Montgomery, and Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act on 6 August 1965. Black registration rose: in Mississippi from 6.7 percent in March 1965 to 74.2 percent in November 1988, and in Alabama from 19.3 to 68.4 percent (chart). For the Act in the courts, from Shelby County (2013) to Louisiana v. Callais (2026), see US2.5. 1 Feb. 1960 Greensboro sit-in over 50,000 students taking part by the end of April 4 May 1961 Freedom Riders leave Washington a bus firebombed near Anniston; ICC ban from 1 Nov. 1961 3 April 1963 Birmingham campaign begins King arrested 12 April; Letter dated 16 April 28 Aug. 1963 March on Washington more than 200,000 demonstrators 21 June 1964 Schwerner, Chaney and Goodman disappear bodies found 4 August 2 July 1964 Civil Rights Act signed House 290-130; Senate cloture 71-29 7 March 1965 Bloody Sunday, Edmund Pettus Bridge march to Montgomery, 21-25 March 6 Aug. 1965 Voting Rights Act signed Black registration rises (chart)

t: Kennedy, Johnson and the Great Society
x: Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles from Cuba in October 1962, and Kennedy was killed in Dallas in November 1963. Johnson declared 'unconditional war on poverty' in January 1964 and in 1965 signed Medicare, Medicaid and an end to national-origins immigration quotas. The official poverty rate fell from 19.0 percent in 1964 to 11.1 percent in 1973; how much the programmes achieved is still argued over. A U-2 flight on 14 October 1962 photographed missile sites in Cuba. Kennedy announced a 'quarantine' on 22 October, and on 28 October Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles. The United States pledged not to invade Cuba. Robert Kennedy told the Soviet ambassador, Anatoly Dobrynin, that the United States planned to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey soon, but 'this could not be part of any public resolution of the missile crisis'; the Office of the Historian records that the missiles were removed in April 1963. On the Cold War worldwide, see 15.9. Kennedy was killed in Dealey Plaza, Dallas, on 22 November 1963, and the Warren Commission concluded that 'Oswald acted alone.' Under Executive Order 14176 the National Archives released 31,419 and then 37,127 pages of assassination records on 18 March 2025, smaller batches through 3 April 2025, and 11,022 more pages on 30 January 2026. In his State of the Union message of 8 January 1964 Johnson said: 'This administration today, here and now, declares unconditional war on poverty in America.' On 30 July 1965, at the Truman Library in Independence, Missouri, he signed the Social Security Amendments of 1965, which created Medicare and, under Title XIX, Medicaid; Harry and Bess Truman received the first Medicare insurance cards. The Census Bureau's official poverty rate, which begins in 1959 at 22.4 percent, fell to 19.0 percent in 1964, 14.7 in 1966 and 11.1 in 1973 (chart). For the aged it fell from 35.2 percent in 1959 to 16.3 percent in 1973. On 3 October 1965, on Liberty Island, Johnson signed the immigration bill known as Hart-Celler. 'This bill that we will sign today is not a revolutionary bill,' he said, while condemning 'the harsh injustice of the national origins quota system'. The Act abolished that system and set caps of 120,000 for the Western Hemisphere and 170,000 for the rest of the world. Pew Research Center (2015) estimates that 'roughly 59 million immigrants' arrived from 1965 to 2015, that the foreign-born share rose 'from 5% in 1965 to 14%', and that of these immigrants 'half (51%) are from Latin America and one-quarter are from Asia.' Did the programmes work? Charles Murray's Losing Ground (1984), as the Manhattan Institute describes it, argues that the social programmes of the 1960s and 1970s made matters worse for their supposed beneficiaries, the poor and minorities. The contributors to Legacies of the War on Poverty (2013), edited by Martha J. Bailey and Sheldon Danziger, judge that popular view too negative, as their publisher summarises the book. Christopher Wimer and his co-authors (2016), using an anchored Supplemental Poverty Measure, find that from 1967 to 2012 'poverty rates have dropped by 40 %' and that 'government policies, not market incomes, are driving the declines.' Richard Burkhauser and his co-authors, using an absolute full-income measure, report that 'our absolute FPM rate fell from 19.5 to 1.6 percent' from 1963 to 2019, but that relative poverty fell only 'from 19.5 to 16.0 percent'. Census Bureau official poverty rate 22.4% (1959); 19.0% (1964); 11.1% (1973) Charles Murray Losing Ground, 1984 the programmes made matters worse for the poor (Manhattan Institute's summary) Martha J. Bailey and Sheldon Danziger, eds. Legacies of the War on Poverty, 2013 the popular view is too negative (publisher's summary) Christopher Wimer and others Demography, 2016 anchored SPM poverty down 40% (1967-2012), driven by government policies Burkhauser, Corinth, Elwell and Larrimore NBER Working Paper 26532, 2019, revised 2021 full-income poverty 19.5% to 1.6% (1963-2019); relative poverty 19.5% to 16.0%

In August 1964 Congress approved the president's determination 'to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack' against American forces. American troops in Vietnam numbered 537,000 at the end of 1968, the year 16,899 Americans died there, before Saigon fell on 30 April 1975. At home came the draft lottery, the Moratorium and the shootings at Kent State and Jackson State; historians still divide over whether the war was necessary and winnable. The Tonkin Gulf Resolution, passed on 7 August 1964, approved the president's determination 'to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States'. The Senate passed it 88 to 2, with Senators Morse and Gruening against. The House vote is recorded as 416 to 0 in the State Department's documentary history, Foreign Relations of the United States, and in the Voteview roll-call record, as James M. Lindsay of the Council on Foreign Relations also gives it; Britannica and the Defense Department's Vietnam War commemoration give 414 to 0. A National Security Agency report of 2002, made available in 2007, confirmed an attack on 2 August but 'concluded the August 4 attack never happened.' The resolution was repealed in January 1971, in the National Archives' words 'in an attempt to curtail President Nixon's power to continue the war.' On war powers and the War Powers Resolution, see US2.12. By Edwin Moïse's tabulation, American military personnel in Vietnam numbered 23,300 at the end of 1964, 184,000 at the end of 1965 and 537,000 at the end of 1968, and 539,000 at mid-1969, falling to 24,000 at the end of 1972 (chart). The National Archives lists 58,220 American military fatal casualties, 47,434 from hostile and 10,786 from non-hostile causes; the highest yearly toll was 16,899, in 1968. The Tet offensive began on 30 January 1968, when about 84,000 troops attacked 36 provincial capitals and 64 district towns. In the Defense Department commemoration's words, 'The offensive shocks the American public.' At home, 'A lottery drawing – the first since 1942 – was held on December 1, 1969' for men born from 1944 to 1950; the first date drawn was 14 September. The last draft call came on 7 December 1972, and the authority to induct ended on 30 June 1973. On 15 October 1969 'Over two million people across the United States' joined the Moratorium to End the War in Vietnam. At Kent State University on 4 May 1970 the Ohio National Guard fired 'between 61 and 67 shots' in 'a 13-second period', 'killing four and wounding nine.' At Jackson State on 14-15 May, city police and highway patrolmen fired 'nearly 400 rounds of bullets and buckshot over 28 seconds in every direction', and they 'turned on Alexander Hall, a women's dormitory.' Phillip Gibbs and James Green were killed, and 'Twelve people were shot by the police and survived.' In June 1971 the Pentagon Papers, a study of about 7,000 pages commissioned by McNamara in 1967, were leaked. In New York Times Co. v. United States, on 30 June, the Court stated that 'Any system of prior restraints of expression comes to this Court bearing a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity.' The full report was released in 2011. On the press clause, see US2.9. The peace agreement was signed on 27 January 1973. On 29 April 1975 Operation Frequent Wind took 'over 7,000 personnel—primarily Americans and Vietnamese' out of Saigon, and the next day 'NVA tanks rolled through the gate of the Presidential Palace in Saigon, effectively ending the war.' The historian Michael G. Kort, who himself argues that the war 'could and should have been won at far less cost than the United States, South Vietnam, and their allies suffered in defeat', frames the debate as two questions: was the war necessary and wise, and, once the United States was involved, 'was that war winnable?' The orthodox narrative, whose proponents he says include the journalists David Halberstam, Frances FitzGerald, Stanley Karnow and Neil Sheehan, and which he says 'also became the prevailing viewpoint among American academics', 'answers both questions firmly in the negative'; the revisionist narrative answers both in the affirmative, holding that the United States went to war 'without first developing a strategy for victory'. Against the revisionists, Fredrik Logevall, author of Choosing War (1999), said: 'The Vietnam tragedy, which we are still living with in so many ways, which led to deaths of millions, was an unnecessary war'. Mark Moyar's Triumph Forsaken (2006), which James McAllister, as Moyar quotes him, said 'can rightfully claim to be the most consequential revisionist book ever produced on the Vietnam War', shows, in Moyar's own description, 'how Diem consolidated control over a badly fractured country' and 'how the removal of Diem crippled South Vietnam's ability to fight the Communists.' Critics answered in the same H-Diplo roundtable: Jessica Chapman, as Moyar quotes her, found 'a disturbing lack of critical analysis throughout the book', and Lloyd Gardner, discussing an American invasion of North Vietnam, wrote that 'a more likely scenario would find the Americans without support among the populace.' 7 Aug. 1964 Tonkin Gulf Resolution Senate 88-2; House 416-0 (some sources 414-0) 30 Jan. 1968 Tet offensive begins about 84,000 troops; 36 provincial capitals 15 Oct. 1969 Moratorium over two million people 1 Dec. 1969 first draft lottery since 1942 first date drawn: 14 September 4 May 1970 Kent State four killed, nine wounded 14-15 May 1970 Jackson State Gibbs and Green killed; twelve wounded by gunfire June 1971 Pentagon Papers leaked Court: 'heavy presumption' against prior restraint, 30 June 30 April 1975 fall of Saigon over 7,000 evacuated on 29 April

In 1968 King and Robert Kennedy were shot, the Kerner Report concluded that the nation was 'moving toward two societies', police and protesters clashed during the Democratic convention in Chicago, and Nixon won the presidency with 43.4 percent of the vote. Farmworkers struck in Delano, Chicano students walked out in Los Angeles, American Indian activists held Alcatraz and Wounded Knee, and a riot followed a police raid on the Stonewall Inn. King was shot 'At 6:05 P.M. on Thursday, 4 April 1968' at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, where he had come in support of 'striking Memphis sanitation workers.' News of his death 'prompted major outbreaks of racial violence, resulting in more than 40 deaths nationwide.' James Earl Ray pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 99 years. On the night of 4 June, the day of the California primary, Robert Kennedy declared victory to his supporters at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles. Around 12:15 a.m. on 5 June, as he left through the hotel kitchen, he was shot; he was pronounced dead at 1:44 a.m. on 6 June, and Sirhan Sirhan was convicted of his murder. The Report of the National Advisory Commission on Civil Disorders, the Kerner Report, stated in 1968: 'This is our basic conclusion: Our nation is moving toward two societies, one black, one white—separate and unequal.' It also stated: 'White racism is essentially responsible for the explosive mixture which has been accumulating in our cities since the end of World War II.' The Democratic convention in Chicago, 26-29 August, nominated Hubert Humphrey. 'The largest clash between police and protesters occurred on August 28 in Grant Park', and the Walker Report found 'unrestrained and indiscriminate police violence.' Richard Nixon won 43.4 percent of the popular vote and 301 electoral votes, Humphrey 42.7 percent and 191, and George Wallace 13.5 percent and 46. 'On September 8, 1965, hundreds of Filipino American farmworkers walked off' the vineyards of Delano, California, under Larry Itliong's Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee; 'A week into the Delano Grape Strike, the NFWA joined.' The two later merged into the United Farm Workers, and the strike lasted five years. Dolores Huerta 'was the lead negotiator in getting the final contracts.' In March 1968 'approximately 15,000 high school students walked out' of schools in East Los Angeles, and the Chicano Moratorium of 29 August 1970 drew '20,000 to 30,000 participants'; that day the journalist Rubén Salazar was killed by a deputy's tear-gas projectile. On 18 March 2026 NPR reported that 'a New York Times investigation out today reveals Chavez's alleged history of sexual assault'; NPR said it had not independently investigated the allegations, and Texas Public Radio that it 'has not independently verified any of the claims.' Huerta's statement, reported on 18 March, began: 'I am nearly 96 years old, and for the last 60 years have kept a secret because I believed that exposing the truth would hurt the farmworker movement I have spent my entire life fighting for.' The United Farm Workers said in a statement of 17 March that it had 'learned of deeply troubling allegations' that Chávez 'behaved in ways that are incompatible with our organization's values', and that it would not take part in Cesar Chavez Day activities on 31 March. The Cesar Chavez Foundation said the same day: 'We are deeply shocked and saddened by what we are hearing.' Chávez's family said: 'Our family is devastated by today's New York Times article about our father, Cesar Chavez', and 'We wish peace and healing to the survivors and commend their courage to come forward'. In its obituary of Huerta on 28 October 2026, the Associated Press wrote that she had revealed that year that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by César Chávez, the farmworker movement's co-founder, and reported that she had died at home at 96. Indians of All Tribes occupied Alcatraz Island from 20 November 1969 until 11 June 1971. Afterwards, in the National Park Service's words, 'a policy of Indian self-determination became the official US government policy.' On 27 February 1973 about 200 Oglala Lakota and members of the American Indian Movement took Wounded Knee, South Dakota, and held it for 71 days, until 8 May; 'two protestors were shot and killed', and a U.S. Marshal was paralysed. In New York, 'In the early morning hours of June 28, 1969, a riot broke out in response to a police raid on the Stonewall Inn', and demonstrations followed over the next days; the Stonewall National Monument was proclaimed on 24 June 2016. On 14 February 2025 the Associated Press reported that the words 'transgender' and 'queer' had been deleted from the monument's National Park Service website, and that the Park Service had not responded to a request for comment. The homepage, last updated on 9 July 2026, begins: 'Before the 1960s, almost everything about living authentically as a lesbian, a bisexual person or a gay man was illegal.' On the women's movement, see US7.10. 8 Sept. 1965 Filipino American farmworkers strike; the NFWA joins a week later Delano, California March 1968 about 15,000 high school students walk out East Los Angeles 4 April 1968 King shot Memphis 5 June 1968 Robert Kennedy shot; dies 6 June Los Angeles 28 Aug. 1968 largest clash between police and protesters Grant Park, Chicago 28 June 1969 riot after a police raid on the Stonewall Inn New York 20 Nov. 1969 to 11 June 1971 occupation by Indians of All Tribes Alcatraz Island 27 Feb. to 8 May 1973 occupation by the Oglala Lakota and AIM Wounded Knee, South Dakota

Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963) wrote of 'the problem that has no name'; in 1964 the House added 'sex' to Title VII, and in 1966 NOW set out to bring women into 'full participation' in American life. In 1972 the Senate passed the Equal Rights Amendment and Nixon signed Title IX, while women's labor force participation rose from about 34 percent in 1950 to about 51 percent in 1980. Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA fought ratification, and as of November 2026 the amendment has not been published as part of the Constitution. Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique was published in 1963 and became an immediate best seller; Britannica notes that Friedan called the discontent of American housewives 'the problem that has no name'. On 8 February 1964 Representative Howard Smith, a Virginia Democrat, offered an amendment in the House adding 'sex' to Title VII of the civil rights bill, and it carried by a teller vote of 168 to 133. (On the Civil Rights Act as a whole, see US7.6.) It has often been assumed that Smith meant to sink the bill. Jo Freeman (1991) argues that the addition was 'not as thoughtless, or as devious, as has previously been assumed', and finds the pattern of the vote 'not consistent with' a plot to kill the bill. On 29 October 1966 the National Organization for Women adopted a Statement of Purpose written by Friedan: 'The purpose of NOW is to take action to bring women into full participation in the mainstream of American society now'. On 22 March 1972 the Senate passed the Equal Rights Amendment: '84 senators voted aye; eight, including Ervin, voted nay.' Its first section reads: 'Equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex.' Hawaii ratified it two hours later. On 23 June 1972 Nixon signed the Education Amendments of 1972, whose Title IX begins: 'No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in'. A resolution introduced in the Senate in June 2022 states that only 1 in 27 girls took part in school sports before Title IX, against 2 in 5 when it was written. On 22 January 1973 the Court decided Roe v. Wade, Justice Blackmun writing; for the doctrine and Dobbs, see US2.11. Congress sent the ERA to the states with a seven-year deadline, later extended to 1982. By the end of 1972, 22 states had ratified, and by 1977, 35; five of them, Nebraska, Tennessee, Idaho, Kentucky and South Dakota, voted to rescind their ratifications. In 1972 Phyllis Schlafly announced her opposition to the ERA and then founded STOP ERA; she founded the Eagle Forum in 1975. In Britannica's summary, she believed that women enjoyed 'unique privileges that the amendment would abolish' and contended that it 'would lead to military conscription for mothers'; whether the amendment would have had those effects was the heart of the dispute with its supporters. Meanwhile women's labor force participation, averaged from monthly BLS data, rose from about 34 percent in 1950 to about 43 percent in 1970 and about 51 percent in 1980. Nevada ratified in 2017, the first state to do so since 1977; Illinois followed in 2018 and Virginia on 15 January 2020. With the five states that voted to rescind, that makes 38, the three-quarters threshold, and whether rescissions and ratifications after the deadline count is the legal question. On 17 December 2024 the Archivist, Colleen Shogan, and her deputy stated that the ERA 'cannot be certified as part of the Constitution', citing the Office of Legal Counsel's opinions of 2020 and 2022 and court decisions, and concluded that 'the Archivist of the United States cannot legally publish the Equal Rights Amendment.' In January 2025 President Biden declared it 'the 28th amendment to the Constitution', but the White House said he would not order the Archivist to certify and publish it. On 4 November 2025 the Ninth Circuit held, in Valame v. Trump, that 'The ERA was not ratified by three-fourths of the States prior to the deadline set by Congress, June 30, 1982'; the plaintiff petitioned the Supreme Court on 9 March 2026. On 21 April 2026 Judge William G. Young in Massachusetts rejected Equal Means Equal's argument about the deadline. On 22 June 2026 the Supreme Court denied review in Valame. On 3 August 2026, by its own account, Equal Means Equal filed its opening brief in the First Circuit. Supporters argue, in the Brennan Center's words, that 'just as Congress had the power to set a deadline, they have the power to lift one'; the Office of Legal Counsel, the Archives and the courts so far hold the deadline binding. As of November 2026 the ERA has not been published as part of the Constitution (see US2.8). 22 Mar 1972 Senate passes the ERA, 84-8; Hawaii ratifies Senate Historical Office end of 1972 22 states have ratified CAWP, Rutgers 1977 35 states have ratified; five of them have voted, at various dates, to rescind Brennan Center 2017-2020 Nevada, Illinois and Virginia ratify Brennan Center 17 Dec 2024 Archivist: the ERA 'cannot be certified' National Archives Jan 2025 Biden calls it 'the 28th amendment'; publication not ordered NPR 4 Nov 2025 Ninth Circuit: not ratified before the 1982 deadline National Constitution Center 21 Apr 2026 Massachusetts district court rejects the deadline argument Equal Means Equal 22 Jun 2026 Supreme Court denies review in Valame Supreme Court docket 3 Aug 2026 Equal Means Equal files its opening brief in the First Circuit Equal Means Equal

s: Détente, the dollar and Watergate, 1969 to 1974
x: In 1972 Nixon became the first president to visit mainland China while in office and signed the ABM Treaty and SALT I in Moscow; at home the EPA opened in 1970, and in August 1971 he suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold. The Watergate break-in of June 1972 led to Senate hearings, the public disclosure of the White House taping system and, on 24 July 1974, an 8-0 ruling that a generalized claim of privilege must yield to the needs of a criminal trial. Nixon announced his resignation on 8 August 1974, and a month later Ford pardoned him. Nixon travelled to China from 21 to 28 February 1972, the first American president to visit mainland China while in office. In the Shanghai Communiqué the United States 'acknowledges that all Chinese on either side of the Taiwan Strait maintain that there is but one China'. In Moscow on 26 May 1972 he and Brezhnev signed the ABM Treaty, which 'limited strategic missile defenses to 200 interceptors each and allowed each side to construct two missile defense sites', together with the Interim Agreement of SALT I. The State Department's historians write that SALT I 'is considered the crowning achievement of the Nixon-Kissinger strategy of détente'. For the Cold War as a whole, see 15.9. The Environmental Protection Agency, set up under Reorganization Plan No. 3 of 9 July 1970, opened its doors on 2 December 1970, with William Ruckelshaus as its first administrator. The Clean Air Act of 1970 created national ambient air quality standards and, in the EPA's words, 'resulted in a major shift in the federal government's role in air pollution control.' On 15 August 1971 Nixon told the nation: 'I have directed Secretary Connally to suspend temporarily the convertibility of the dollar into gold or other reserve assets'. He also announced 'a freeze on all prices and wages' for 90 days and 'an additional tax of 10 percent on goods imported'. The fixed-rate system did not survive. The Smithsonian Agreement of December 1971 set 'a new set of fixed exchange rates centered on a devalued dollar', but in March 1973 six European Community currencies began a joint float against the dollar, which, in the Office of the Historian's words, 'effectively signaled the abandonment of the Bretton Woods fixed exchange rate system.' On Bretton Woods, see 15.13. Watergate began 'Early on the morning of June 17, 1972,' when 'five men broke into the Democratic National Committee headquarters.' The Senate voted unanimously on 7 February 1973 to create a select committee, whose hearings were televised from May 1973. On 16 July 1973 Alexander Butterfield made the White House taping system public: he 'repeated the disclosure in open committee testimony before live television cameras.' On 20 October 1973, in the 'Saturday Night Massacre', Attorney General Elliot Richardson resigned and his deputy William Ruckelshaus was fired; Robert Bork then 'was ordered to fire special prosecutor Cox. He did.' The House Judiciary Committee adopted three articles of impeachment, the first by 27 votes to 11. On 24 July 1974, in United States v. Nixon, the Supreme Court ruled 8-0, with Justice Rehnquist not taking part. Chief Justice Burger wrote: 'The generalized assertion of privilege must yield to the demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a pending criminal trial.' Neither the separation of powers nor the need for confidentiality, 'without more', he held, could 'sustain an absolute, unqualified Presidential privilege of immunity from judicial process under all circumstances.' (On presidential immunity and impeachment as doctrine, see US2.4.) On 8 August 1974 Nixon told the nation: 'I shall resign the Presidency effective at noon tomorrow.' On 8 September President Ford's Proclamation 4311 granted a 'full, free, and absolute pardon unto Richard Nixon for all offenses against the United States' for the period from 20 January 1969 to 9 August 1974. 17 Jun 1972 five men break into the Democratic National Committee headquarters 7 Feb 1973 Senate creates a select committee, unanimously May 1973 televised hearings begin 16 Jul 1973 Butterfield discloses the taping system in open testimony 20 Oct 1973 'Saturday Night Massacre': Bork fires Cox 24 Jul 1974 United States v. Nixon, 8-0 8 Aug 1974 Nixon announces his resignation, effective at noon the next day 8 Sep 1974 Ford's Proclamation 4311 pardons Nixon

The oil embargo of 1973-74 nearly quadrupled the price of oil, and after Iranian output fell, prices more than doubled between April 1979 and April 1980; consumer prices rose 11.1 percent in 1974 and 13.5 percent in 1980, while unemployment averaged about 8.5 percent in 1975. Carter, Sadat and Begin produced the Camp David frameworks in 1978, Carter signed airline deregulation, and in July 1979 he spoke of 'a crisis of confidence'. That autumn the Federal Reserve under Volcker turned to managing bank reserves, and the embassy in Tehran was seized, its 52 American hostages held for 444 days. The oil embargo of the Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries (OAPEC) began in October 1973. Its cuts 'nearly quadrupled the price of oil from $2.90 a barrel before the embargo to $11.65 a barrel in January 1974', and the embargo was lifted in March 1974. In the second shock Iranian output fell by '4.8 million barrels per day (7 percent of world production at the time) by January 1979', and oil prices were 'more than doubling between April 1979 and April 1980.' Graefe, writing in Federal Reserve History, says the loss of supply 'may not have been the most important factor', pointing instead to 'a fear of further disruptions' and 'widespread speculative hoarding'. On oil and the world economy, see 15.13. Consumer prices (CPI-U) rose 5.5 percent in 1969, 11.1 percent in 1974, 9.1 percent in 1975 and 13.5 percent in 1980; they rose in every year from 1969 to 1982. Unemployment, averaged from the monthly BLS figures, went from about 3.5 percent in 1969 and 4.9 percent in 1973 to about 8.5 percent in 1975 and 9.7 percent in 1982. In 1975, then, prices rose 9.1 percent while unemployment averaged about 8.5 percent. At Camp David from 5 to 17 September 1978, Carter, Sadat and Begin produced 'two "Framework" documents', and Egypt and Israel signed a peace treaty in March 1979. Signing the Airline Deregulation Act on 24 October 1978, Carter said: 'For the first time in decades, we have deregulated a major industry'; the act meant 'phasing out all activities of the Civil Aeronautics Board by 1985'. In his address to the nation of 15 July 1979 he said: 'It is a crisis of confidence. It is a crisis that strikes at the very heart and soul and spirit of our national will.' He also said that 'too many of us now tend to worship self-indulgence and consumption.' The American Presidency Project titles it 'The Malaise Speech'. On 6 October 1979 the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker shifted 'to managing the volume of bank reserves', and the federal funds rate 'reached a record high of 20 percent in late 1980'. By the measure the Federal Reserve History essay uses, 'Inflation peaked at 11.6 percent in March' 1980; by the annual CPI-U measure, prices rose 13.5 percent that year. On 4 November 1979 the American embassy in Tehran was seized, and '52 United States citizens were held hostage for 444 days until January 20, 1981'. A rescue attempt, Operation Eagle Claw, on 24-25 April 1980, killed eight American servicemen. Oct 1973 - Mar 1974 OAPEC embargo; oil from $2.90 to $11.65 a barrel 5-17 Sep 1978 Camp David: two framework documents 24 Oct 1978 Airline Deregulation Act signed Mar 1979 Egypt-Israel peace treaty 15 Jul 1979 Carter: 'a crisis of confidence' 6 Oct 1979 Federal Reserve turns to managing bank reserves 4 Nov 1979 - 20 Jan 1981 52 Americans held hostage for 444 days 24-25 Apr 1980 Operation Eagle Claw; eight servicemen killed

t: Religion and the rise of the religious right
x: In 1957 Billy Graham preached for 16 weeks at Madison Square Garden. In 1962 and 1963 the Supreme Court struck down an official school prayer and required Bible reading, while Vatican II allowed the vernacular in the liturgy, and in 1965 Nostra Aetate declared that what happened in Christ's passion cannot be charged against all the Jews. In the week of the Six-Day War of 1967 the New York-area United Jewish Appeal raised more than $20 million, and in 1983 the Court upheld the IRS's denial of tax exemption to Bob Jones University. Historians disagree about what launched the religious right, whose Moral Majority Jerry Falwell founded in 1979: Randall Balmer points to the fight over segregated schools, Daniel K. Williams to issues of gender, sexuality and nationalism. On 25 June 1962, in Engel v. Vitale, the Supreme Court struck down, by 6 votes to 1, New York's Regents' prayer, which began 'Almighty God, we acknowledge our dependence upon Thee'. Justice Black wrote that 'it is no part of the business of government to compose official prayers'. On 17 June 1963, in School District of Abington Township v. Schempp, decided with Murray v. Curlett, the Court ruled 8-1 against required Bible reading under the rule that 'At least ten verses from the Holy Bible shall be read, without comment'. Yet Justice Clark wrote that 'the Bible is worthy of study for its literary and historic qualities.' Justice Stewart dissented in both cases. For the doctrine, see US2.9. Billy Graham's 1949 revival in Los Angeles was extended to eight weeks. In 1953 at Chattanooga he removed the ropes separating Black and white listeners, and in 1957 he preached at Madison Square Garden for 16 weeks and welcomed Martin Luther King Jr., who prayed at the crusade on 18 July 1957. Britannica notes Graham's friendship with numerous presidents. The Second Vatican Council (1962-65) allowed the vernacular in the liturgy: in Sacrosanctum Concilium (4 December 1963) it ruled that 'the limits of its employment may be extended'. Its declaration Nostra Aetate (28 October 1965) taught that what happened in Christ's passion 'cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today', and that 'the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God'. In the week of the Six-Day War in June 1967, the United Jewish Appeal in the New York area raised more than $20 million, JTA reported. Eric Alterman writes that 'June 1967 transformed American Jews' relationship not only to Israel, but also to themselves.' From 1970 the IRS denied tax exemption to racially discriminatory private schools. In Bob Jones University v. United States (24 May 1983) the Court, 8-1, upheld its denial to a university whose rule was 'There is to be no interracial dating', holding that the government has 'a fundamental, overriding interest in eradicating racial discrimination in education'. Jerry Falwell founded the Moral Majority in 1979. It opposed 'abortion, pornography, the ERA, and gay rights', was 'credited with helping' elect Ronald Reagan in 1980, and dissolved in 1989. What set off the religious right is debated. Randall Balmer points to Green v. Connally, a ruling of the federal district court for the District of Columbia of 30 June 1971, which, as he quotes it, held that 'racially discriminatory private schools are not entitled to the Federal tax exemption'. 'Green v. Connally served as the catalyst, not Roe v. Wade,' he writes, and he quotes Paul Weyrich: 'It wasn't the abortion issue; that wasn't sufficient'. Daniel K. Williams holds instead that the IRS issue 'was simply one factor among many in the formation of a conservative Republican evangelical coalition', and that 'issues of gender, sexuality, and nationalism played a much greater role than race in the mobilization of Christian conservatives.' In a 2015 article he traces the pro-life movement to Catholic founders of the late 1960s, many of them liberal Democrats, and argues that evangelicals who joined in the late 1970s recast it as a conservative cause. Roe v. Wade itself was decided on 22 January 1973 (see US7.10). 25 Jun 1962 Engel v. In the Bureau of Economic Analysis's series real GDP grew about 3.3 times between 1980 and 2025 while the population grew by about half, so real GDP per person rose about 2.2 times. Real median household income was about 41 percent higher in 2025 than in 1984, with falls after 2007 and after 2019, and federal debt held by the public rose from 24.9 percent of GDP in 1980 to 97.8 percent in 2025. In the Bureau of Economic Analysis's series real GDP was $7,257.3 billion in 1980 and $23,943.3 billion in 2025, in chained 2017 dollars: about 3.3 times as large. It dipped in 2020, to $20,284.5 billion from $20,715.7 billion in 2019. The population, also from BEA, rose from 227,726 thousand to 341,944 thousand, from about 228 million to about 342 million. Computed from BEA data, real GDP per person was about $31,900 in 1980 and about $70,000 in 2025, about 2.2 times as much. The Census Bureau's real median household income, in what the series labels '2025 C-CPI-U Dollars', was $61,910 in 1984, the series' first year, and $87,460 in 2025, about 41 percent higher. Its path was uneven: $74,810 in 2007, $69,070 in 2012, $85,320 in 2019 and $81,460 in 2022. On the Great Recession, see US8.6; on inflation in 2021-2024, US8.10; on inequality and wages, US8.12. Federal debt held by the public, in the Office of Management and Budget's fiscal-year series, was 24.9 percent of GDP in 1980, 40.4 percent in 1990 and 47.2 percent in 1995. It fell to 31.4 percent in 2001, after the budget ran surpluses in fiscal 1998-2001 (US8.3), and then rose to 52.1 percent in 2009, 98.3 percent in 2020 and 97.8 percent in 2025. On the federal purse and the Federal Reserve, see US2.13. This chapter follows Reagan and the economy (US8.1), the American side of the end of the Cold War (US8.2), Bush and Clinton (US8.3) and immigration and a changing population (US8.4); then 9/11 at home (US8.5), the Great Recession at home (US8.6), Obama (US8.7), Trump's first term (US8.8), January 6 and its aftermath (US8.9), Biden (US8.10), Trump's second term to November 2026 (US8.11), the economy since 1980 (US8.12) and faith and polarization (US8.13). On the end of the Cold War worldwide, see 15.14 and 16.1; on 9/11 and the wars, 16.3; on the financial crisis, 16.4; on parties, money and polarization, US2.14. Ronald Reagan won the 1980 election with 489 electoral votes, and the top income-tax rate fell from 70 percent in 1981 to 28 percent in 1988 while debt held by the public rose from 24.9 percent of GDP in 1980 to 40.4 percent in 1990. After the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker changed course in 1979, the federal funds rate peaked at 19.10 percent in June 1981, recession began in July 1981 and inflation, in William Niskanen's figures, fell from 10.4 percent in 1980 to 4.2 percent in 1988; economists such as Niskanen, who served on Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers, and Paul Krugman have disagreed about what Reaganomics achieved. In the 1980 election Ronald Reagan won 489 electoral votes and 50.7 percent of the popular vote; Jimmy Carter won 49 electoral votes and 41.0 percent, and John Anderson (independent) 6.6 percent. The top federal income-tax rate was 70 percent in 1981, 50 percent in 1982, 38.5 percent in 1987 and 28 percent in 1988; it rose again to 31 percent in 1991 and 39.6 percent in 1993. From 1988 to 1990 a 33 percent 'rate bubble' also applied to part of the income range. In the Treasury's estimates, the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 cut revenue by 1.21 percent of GDP in its year of enactment and by 4.15 percent in the third year after enactment; the 1982 act raised revenue by an average of about 1 percent of GDP a year over four years, and the Tax Reform Act of 1986 was close to revenue-neutral, with an average of 0.01 percent. Signing the 1986 act on 22 October, Reagan said: 'Millions of working poor will be dropped from the tax rolls altogether'. Under Paul Volcker the Federal Reserve had changed course in October 1979, choosing to 'target reserve growth rather than the fed funds rate as its policy instrument.' The federal funds rate peaked at 19.10 percent in June 1981; the economy 'entered recession again in July 1981', and unemployment reached 10.8 percent in November and December 1982; it was 5.3 percent in December 1988. In Niskanen's figures inflation 'declined from 10.4 percent in 1980 to 4.2 percent in 1988', and Federal Reserve History gives an average of 'only 3.5 percent in the latter half of the 1980s.' On the inflation of the 1970s, see US7.12; on the Federal Reserve, US2.13. Federal debt held by the public rose from 24.9 percent of GDP in fiscal 1980 to 38.8 percent in fiscal 1989 and 40.4 percent in 1990; Niskanen, measuring privately held debt, gives a rise 'from 22.3 percent of GDP to 38.1 percent.' When the air traffic controllers struck in 1981, Reagan said on 3 August that those who failed to report for duty 'are in violation of the law, and if they do not report for work within 48 hours, they have forfeited their jobs', and on 5 August he fired 'the 11,345 union employees who ignored his presidential order'. What did Reaganomics achieve? William Niskanen, a member of Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers, wrote that 'the major achievements of Reaganomics were the sharp reductions in marginal tax rates and in inflation', while finding that on federal spending there was 'no "Reagan revolution"'. Paul Krugman, in Peddling Prosperity (1994), wrote, as Niskanen's review of the book quotes him, that 'There was no sign of an acceleration of long-term growth rates at any point during the twelve years of conservative rule' under Reagan and Bush. Benjamin Friedman of Harvard, author of Day of Reckoning (1988), drew lessons from the Reagan deficits in a 1992 paper, among them that 'Across-the-board cuts in personal income tax rates reduced the government's tax revenues', that 'Reducing tax revenues did not restrain government spending, at least not by enough to avoid the emergence of historically large deficits', and that 'Greater deficits did result in reduced private investment'. 1980 presidential election Reagan 489 electoral votes, 50.7 percent; Carter 49, 41.0 percent 1981 Economic Recovery Tax Act revenue effect -1.21 percent of GDP in the year of enactment, -4.15 percent three years later (Treasury estimate) June 1981 federal funds rate peaks 19.10 percent August 1981 air traffic controllers fired 11,345 November-December 1982 unemployment 10.8 percent (5.3 percent in December 1988) 22 October 1986 Tax Reform Act signed top rate 28 percent from 1988 1988 inflation (Niskanen) 4.2 percent, from 10.4 in 1980 fiscal 1989 and 1990 debt held by the public 38.8 and 40.4 percent of GDP, from 24.9 in 1980

The Reagan administration modernized American forces and in 1983 proposed missile defence; computed from BEA data, defence spending rose from about 6.4 percent of GDP in the third quarter of 1980 to about 7.9 percent in the third quarter of 1986. Reagan also negotiated: the INF Treaty of December 1987 eliminated 2,692 missiles, while the Iran-Contra affair led to 14 people being charged. Scholars disagree about how far American policy, material pressures or new ideas ended the Cold War. The Reagan administration 'pursued a comprehensive modernization of U.S. nuclear and conventional forces.' Computed from BEA data, national defense spending was about 6.4 percent of GDP in the third quarter of 1980, about 7.9 percent in the third quarter of 1986 and about 6.7 percent in the third quarter of 1991. On 23 March 1983 Reagan proposed a missile defence aimed at 'rendering these nuclear weapons impotent and obsolete'; the Office of the Historian describes the Strategic Defense Initiative as a programme 'which Soviet leaders found highly threatening'. At Reykjavik in October 1986 Reagan and Gorbachev 'discussed the prospect of abolishing all nuclear weapons.' At the Brandenburg Gate on 12 June 1987 Reagan said: 'General Secretary Gorbachev, if you seek peace, if you seek prosperity for the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, if you seek liberalization: Come here to this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!' Peter Robinson, the speechwriter, writes that the State Department and the National Security Council 'submitted their own alternate drafts', and that 'In each, the call to tear down the wall was missing.' The INF Treaty, signed on 8 December 1987, banned ground-launched missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 kilometres; it entered into force on 1 June 1988, and 'A total of 2,692 missiles was eliminated'. In Moscow in 1988 Reagan said that the term 'evil empire' belonged to 'another era.' In the Iran-Contra affair, in Britannica's description, the National Security Council 'became involved in secret weapons transactions and other activities that either were prohibited by the U.S. Congress or violated the stated public policy of the government.' The Boland Amendment of 1984 'banned direct or indirect U.S. military aid to the Contras'. On 13 November 1986 Reagan told the nation: 'We did not—repeat—did not trade weapons or anything else for hostages, nor will we.' On 4 March 1987 he said: 'A few months ago I told the American people I did not trade arms for hostages. My heart and my best intentions still tell me that's true, but the facts and the evidence tell me it is not.' Independent Counsel Walsh reported that '14 persons were charged'; 11 were convicted, 'two convictions were overturned on appeal', those of North and Poindexter, and President George H. W. Bush pardoned six people on 24 December 1992. On presidential power and impeachment as doctrine, see US2.4. Who ended the Cold War? Gorbachev received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1990 'for the leading role he played in the radical changes in East-West relations'. Francis Sempa, asking whether Reagan was a crusader or a conciliator, answers: 'The answer, I believe, is that he was both'. In his account 'Reagan the crusader launched a political, military, psychological, and economic offensive designed to undermine Soviet power', while 'Reagan the conciliator engaged in summitry and arms control negotiations with a reform-oriented Mikhail Gorbachev'. He cites John Lewis Gaddis, who, Sempa writes, held that Reagan ended the Cold War by 'changing rather than containing' the Soviet Union. Stephen Brooks and William Wohlforth argue, in the Belfer Center's summary of their article, that shifting material pressures 'had a much greater influence on Soviet foreign policy in the 1980s than previously thought.' Robert English, replying, faults them, in the same centre's summary, for privileging materialist explanations 'to the exclusion of other possible causes—in particular, the influence of "new thinkers" led by Mikhail Gorbachev'. On the end of the Cold War worldwide, see 15.14 and 16.1. 23 March 1983 missile defence proposed 'impotent and obsolete' October 1986 Reykjavik abolishing all nuclear weapons discussed 13 November 1986 Reagan's address on Iran 'did not trade weapons or anything else for hostages' 4 March 1987 Reagan's second address on Iran 'the facts and the evidence tell me it is not' 12 June 1987 Brandenburg Gate speech 'tear down this wall' 8 December 1987 INF Treaty signed ranges of 500 to 5,500 km banned 1 June 1988 INF Treaty in force 2,692 missiles eliminated 24 December 1992 Bush pardons six of 14 charged by Walsh

In January 1991 Congress voted on the use of force against Iraq, 52 to 47 in the Senate and 250 to 183 in the House, and in November 1993 NAFTA passed the House with more Republican than Democratic votes. Republicans' Contract with America (1994), welfare reform (1996) and budget surpluses in fiscal 1998-2001 followed, and in December 1998 the House impeached Clinton on two articles, by 228 to 206 and 221 to 212, on which the Senate voted 45 to 55 and 50 to 50 in February 1999. Economists still disagree about NAFTA's effects and about welfare reform's results. Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990. A coalition 'Comprising forces from thirty-four countries' began the air war on 16 January 1991 and the ground war on 24 February, and the war ended on 28 February. On 12 January 1991 the Senate passed a joint resolution to authorize the use of American forces under UN Security Council Resolution 678 by 52 to 47, Republicans voting 42 to 2 and Democrats 10 to 45; the House passed its resolution by 250 to 183, Democrats 86 to 179 and Republicans 164 to 3. The House passed NAFTA on 17 November 1993 by 234 to 200, Democrats 102 to 156 and Republicans 132 to 43, and the Senate on 20 November by 61 to 38. What did NAFTA do? Caliendo and Parro estimate that the 'U.S.'s welfare increases by 0.08%' and that trade within the bloc rose by 41 percent for the United States. Hakobyan and McLaren find NAFTA 'dramatically lowering wage growth for blue-collar workers in the most affected industries and localities'. The two findings measure different things: a small national average, and losses concentrated in particular places. On the China shock, see US8.12. The Republicans' Contract with America was 'signed Sept. 27, 1994, on the Capitol steps'; among its pledges was to 'require all laws that apply to the rest of the country also apply equally to the Congress'. Apart from term limits, all its parts passed the House, and Newt Gingrich became 'the first Republican in 40 years to serve as speaker'. Welfare reform, which President Clinton signed as Public Law 104-193 on 22 August 1996, replaced AFDC with TANF, which now provides 'approximately $16.5 billion to states'. Ron Haskins of Brookings, who had spent 14 years on the staff of the House Ways and Means Committee and wrote an inside history of the 1996 law, told Congress in 2006 that 'Between 1994 and 2005, the caseload declined about 60 percent' and that 'child poverty fell every year' from 1994 to 2000. Shaefer and Edin find that the 'prevalence of extreme poverty has risen sharply since 1996, particularly among those most affected by the 1996 welfare reform.' Meyer, Wu, Mooers and Medalia, linking 2011 survey data to administrative records, reply that of the 3.6 million non-homeless households reporting cash income below $2 a person a day 'more than 90% are not in extreme poverty once we include in-kind transfers, replace survey reports of earnings and transfer receipt with administrative records, and account for the ownership of substantial assets', and conclude that extreme poverty 'cannot be substantially higher now due to welfare reform'. The federal budget, in deficit by 4.45 percent of GDP in fiscal 1992 and 0.26 percent in 1997, ran surpluses of 0.76 percent in 1998, 1.30 in 1999, 2.30 in 2000 and 1.21 in 2001, before returning to deficit in 2002. The top income-tax rate rose to 31 percent in 1991, under President George H. W. Bush, and to 39.6 percent under the 1993 budget act. The Treasury estimated that the 1990 budget act raised revenue by 0.41 percent of GDP in its year of enactment and by about 0.5 percent a year on average, and that the 1993 act raised it by 0.36 percent in its year of enactment and by about 0.6 percent a year on average. On 19 December 1998 the House adopted two of four articles of impeachment against Clinton: the first by 228 to 206 (Republicans 223 to 5, Democrats 5 to 200) and the third by 221 to 212 (Republicans 216 to 12, Democrats 5 to 199); the second and fourth failed. At the Senate trial, on 12 February 1999, the Senate voted 45 to 55 on Article I (perjury), all 45 guilty votes being Republican, and 50 to 50 on Article II (obstruction), with five Republicans voting not guilty. On impeachment as doctrine and the two-thirds rule, see US2.4. Under IRCA (1986) nearly 2.7 million people became lawful permanent residents, and the Immigration Act of 1990 raised employment visas from 54,000 to 140,000 a year. Between the 2010 and 2020 censuses the Hispanic population grew 23 percent and the Asian-alone population 35.5 percent; estimates of the unauthorized population run from DHS's 11 million (January 2022) to Pew's 14 million (2023). USCIS still processes DACA renewals, though with a growing backlog, and official and independent counts of departures since January 2025 differ widely. Reagan signed the Immigration Reform and Control Act on 6 November 1986, writing: 'The employer sanctions program is the keystone and major element.' Applicants for legalization had to show 'that they entered the United States before January 1, 1982', farmworkers had a separate route, and employers who hired unauthorized workers faced 'civil penalties of $250 to $10,000'. In the figures of DHS's Office of Immigration Statistics, nearly 2.7 million people became lawful permanent residents under IRCA: about 1.6 million who had lived in the country since before 1982 and 1.1 million special agricultural workers. Signing the Immigration Act of 1990, George H. W. Bush said: 'This bill is good for families, good for business, good for crime fighting, and good for America.' The act set 'a flexible cap of 700,000 until 1995 and 675,000 thereafter', created 40,000 diversity visas, raised employment visas from 54,000 to 140,000 and created Temporary Protected Status. Between the 2010 and 2020 censuses the Hispanic population grew 23 percent, from 50.5 million to 62.1 million (18.7 percent of the whole); the Asian-alone population grew 35.5 percent, to 19.9 million, and the White-alone population fell 8.6 percent. The Census Bureau warns that comparisons of the 2020 and 2010 race data 'should be made with caution', and that differences in the overall racial distributions are 'largely due to improvements in the design of the two separate questions for race data collection and processing as well as some demographic changes over the past 10 years.' Population growth 'slowed to 0.5%' between July 2024 and July 2025 as net international migration declined, and the Congressional Budget Office 'reduced its projections of net immigration from 2025 to 2029'. Estimates of the unauthorized population differ by source and date. DHS's statistics office estimated 11 million on 1 January 2022, as USAFacts reports it; the Migration Policy Institute estimates 13.7 million as of mid-2023; and Pew estimates 14 million in 2023, above its 2007 high of 12.2 million, with a likely fall of up to 1 million in the first half of 2025. Economists disagree about effects on wages: studying the 1980 Mariel boatlift, George Borjas finds that the wage of high-school dropouts in Miami 'dropped dramatically, by 10 to 30 percent', while Giovanni Peri and Vasil Yasenov, using 'a sample of non-Cuban high-school dropouts', 'find no significant difference in the wages of workers in Miami relative to its control after 1980.' DACA, announced on 15 June 2012, covered people 'under the age of 31 as of June 15, 2012' who had come before their 16th birthday and 'continuously resided in the United States since June 15, 2007'. On 17 January 2025 the Fifth Circuit largely affirmed a ruling that DACA was unlawful but 'narrowed the ruling to apply only to Texas'. CBS News reported that more than 525,000 people were enrolled at the end of June 2025, nearly 88,000 of them in Texas, and that under the administration's plan Texas residents would get deportation deferrals but not work authorization. As consulted on 4 November 2026, USCIS was processing renewals and accepting, but not processing, initial requests; the latest reports found for this book, from the Texas Tribune (October 2025) and FWD.us (May 2026), describe Judge Hanen's implementing directions as still awaited. CBS News reported on 8 October 2026, citing federal data, that active DACA holders had fallen 14 percent, to 436,350, between September 2025 and 30 June 2026, while the backlog of pending renewal applications had more than quadrupled, to over 125,000. Enforcement figures for 2025-26 come from different counters. ICE's budget document, as the Washington Times reported in April 2026, gave 442,637 removals in fiscal 2025 (Newsweek reported the same figure) and a target of '1,000,000 returns and removals' a year. DHS said, as Fox News reported in May 2026, that more than 3 million people had left, 'including an estimated 2.2 million "self-deportations"'. A DHS spokesperson told Newsweek in October 2026 that nearly 1.1 million had been deported as of September. Marc Rosenblum of the Migration Policy Institute counts 'about 980,000' deportations from 20 January 2025 to 31 July 2026, 'a figure in line with the department's public statements'. He estimates between 1.3 million and 2.4 million total departures, deportations and self-departures together, of which 790,000 to 1.9 million were of immigrants with at least a year's residence. He judges it 'highly unlikely that 3 million immigrants have departed'. AP reported that the administration's own count was 1.2 million deported or removed, and wrote that 'The discrepancy could not immediately be reconciled.' White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: 'President Trump has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history.' TRAC counted 65,765 people in ICE detention on 11 July 2026, 70.6 percent of them with no criminal conviction; ICE, as ABC News reported on 21 July 2026, said that 60 percent of them had a criminal record. On the second term's immigration policy, see US8.11. fiscal 2025 (to 30 September 2025) 442,637 removals; 166,939 of people with criminal records ICE budget document, as reported by the Washington Times (15 April 2026) first year back in office; deportations to 17 May 2026 more than 3 million departures, including an estimated 2.2 million self-deportations; nearly 900,000 deported DHS, as reported by Fox News (21 May 2026) to September 2026 nearly 1.1 million deported a DHS spokesperson, as reported by Newsweek (13 October 2026) 20 January 2025 to 31 July 2026 about 980,000 deportations; 1.3 million to 2.4 million total departures (790,000 to 1.9 million of immigrants resident at least a year) Migration Policy Institute (Rosenblum, October 2026) second term, to October 2026 1.2 million deported or removed the administration, as reported by AP (22 October 2026) 11 July 2026 65,765 in ICE detention; 70.6 percent with no criminal conviction (TRAC); 60 percent with a criminal record (ICE) TRAC; ICE, as reported by ABC News (21 July 2026) future years target of 1,000,000 returns and removals a year ICE, as reported by the Washington Times

s: The AUMF, the Patriot Act, Homeland Security, Iraq and Guantánamo
x: The attacks of 11 September 2001 killed 2,977 people. Within weeks Congress authorised force against those responsible, 98 to 0 in the Senate and 420 to 1 in the House, and passed the USA PATRIOT Act; a Department of Homeland Security opened in 2003, and in October 2002 Congress authorised force against Iraq. Estimates of what the wars cost depend on what is counted, and in September 2026 fifteen wartime detainees remained at Guantánamo. The attacks of 11 September 2001 'killed 2,977 people from 90 nations': 2,753 in New York, 184 at the Pentagon and 40 on Flight 93. For the attackers and the wars abroad, see 16.3. Congress passed an Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF), approved on 18 September. Its operative clause reads: 'That the President is authorized to use all necessary and appropriate force against those nations, organizations, or persons he determines planned, authorized, committed, or aided the terrorist attacks that occurred on September 11, 2001, or harbored such organizations or persons, in order to prevent any future acts of international terrorism against the United States by such nations, organizations or persons.' The Senate passed it 98 to 0 on 14 September, and the House 420 to 1, Republicans 214 to 0 and Democrats 204 to 1, the one vote against cast by Lee, a California Democrat. The text leaves it to the President to determine who 'planned, authorized, committed, or aided' the attacks; on presidential power as doctrine, see US2.4. The USA PATRIOT Act passed the House 357 to 66 on 24 October 2001, Republicans 211 to 3 and Democrats 145 to 62, and the Senate 98 to 1 the next day, Feingold, a Wisconsin Democrat, casting the one vote against. Approved on 26 October, it included a Title II headed 'ENHANCED SURVEILLANCE PROCEDURES', and its section 215 dealt with 'ACCESS TO RECORDS AND OTHER ITEMS UNDER THE FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE SURVEILLANCE ACT.' After Congress passed the Homeland Security Act in November 2002, the new Department of Homeland Security combined 'all or part of 22 different federal departments and agencies', opening its doors on 1 March 2003. In October 2002 Congress authorised force against Iraq. The resolution, approved on 16 October, provides: 'The President is authorized to use the Armed Forces of the United States as he determines to be necessary and appropriate in order to-- (1) defend the national security of the United States against the continuing threat posed by Iraq; and (2) enforce all relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions regarding Iraq.' The House passed it 296 to 133 on 10 October, Republicans 215 to 6 and Democrats 81 to 126; the Senate passed it 77 to 23 the next day, Republicans 48 to 1 and Democrats 29 to 21. Most House Democrats voted no, and most Senate Democrats yes. For the war itself and the dispute over the prewar intelligence, see 16.3. What the wars cost depends on what is counted. The Congressional Research Service counted $1.6 trillion appropriated for war operations through fiscal 2014, $815 billion for Iraq and $686 billion for Afghanistan and other counterterrorism operations. Neta C. Crawford of Boston University, a co-director of the Costs of War project at Brown University's Watson Institute, estimates 'about $8 trillion in current dollars': $5.8 trillion spent from fiscal 2001 to 2022, counting interest on war borrowing, increases in the base defence budget, homeland security and veterans' care as well as $2.1 trillion in the Defense Department's overseas contingency appropriations, plus about $2.2 trillion in veterans' care owed to 2050. The prison at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, opened on 11 January 2002 with the arrival of 20 detainees. The military has held about 780 men and boys there; fifteen wartime prisoners remained in January 2026 and were still there in September. In 2025 the base also held migrants, about 775 of them 'for days or weeks', and 54 men as of 9 January 2026. The case against Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and three co-defendants, Walid bin Attash, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali and Mustafa al-Hawsawi, goes on. On 11 July 2025 the D.C. Circuit voted 2 to 1 to throw out plea deals that would have given Mohammed and two of them life sentences without parole, and on 19 October 2026 the Supreme Court declined to review former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin's decision to cancel the deals, Justice Kavanaugh recusing himself. In August 2026 a military judge set the trial to begin on 5 June 2028. Steve Vladeck of Georgetown University Law Center, a CNN legal analyst who had filed a brief urging the justices to take up the appeals, said that 'even the current summer 2028 trial date is entirely unrealistic' (CNN, republished by Scripps News). 11 Sept. 2001 the attacks 2,977 killed 14-18 Sept. 2001 AUMF passed and approved Senate 98-0; House 420-1 24-26 Oct. 2001 USA PATRIOT Act passed and approved House 357-66; Senate 98-1 11 Jan. 2002 Guantánamo prison opens 20 detainees; 15 left in Sept. 2026 10-16 Oct. 2002 Iraq resolution passed and approved House 296-133; Senate 77-23 1 March 2003 Department of Homeland Security opens all or part of 22 agencies 19 Oct. 2026 Supreme Court declines the plea-deal case trial date of 5 June 2028, set in August 2026

s: 2007 to 2012: TARP, the stimulus and Dodd-Frank
x: The recession that began in December 2007 lasted until June 2009; real GDP fell 4.3 percent, and unemployment peaked at 10 percent in October 2009. The House rejected the bank rescue, TARP, once and then passed it; the 2009 stimulus passed with three Republican votes, all in the Senate, and Dodd-Frank followed in 2010. Economists still differ over how much the rescue and the stimulus achieved. The Great Recession 'began in December 2007 and ended in June 2009, which makes it the longest recession since World War II.' Real GDP 'fell 4.3 percent from its peak in 2007Q4 to its trough in 2009Q2'; home prices fell about 30 percent on average from their mid-2006 peak to mid-2009; the net worth of households and nonprofit organisations fell from about $69 trillion in 2007 to $55 trillion in 2009; and the unemployment rate 'peaked at 10 percent in October 2009'. In September 2008 Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy with 'a reported $639 billion in assets', the largest bankruptcy in American history at that time. For the crisis worldwide, see 16.4. Annual unemployment rose from 4.6 percent in 2007 to 9.6 percent in 2010 and was still 8.1 percent in 2012 (chart). RealtyTrac, counting properties with any foreclosure filing rather than completed foreclosures, found 2,824,674 such properties in 2009, 'a 120 percent increase' on 2007; in 2010 'A record 2.9 million properties received foreclosure filings.' On 29 September 2008 the House rejected the bill carrying the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), 205 to 228: Democrats voted 140 to 95 for it and Republicans 65 to 133 against. The Senate passed a revised bill 74 to 25 on 1 October, Democrats 39 to 9 and Republicans 34 to 15, and on 3 October the House passed it 263 to 171, Democrats 172 to 63 and Republicans 91 to 108. In its final report, in April 2024, the Congressional Budget Office found that '$444 billion of the $700 billion initially authorized was disbursed' and that 'the government's total subsidy cost was $31 billion'; mortgage programmes cost about $31 billion and aid to the auto industry about $12 billion, while purchases of bank capital gained about $9 billion and investment partnerships for securitization markets about $3 billion. Pietro Veronesi and Luigi Zingales estimate that the intervention of October 2008 'increased the value of banks' financial claims by $130 billion' at 'a taxpayers' cost of $21-$44 billion', and also conclude: 'The big winners of the plan were the bondholders of the three former investment banks and Citigroup, while the losers were JP Morgan shareholders and the US taxpayers.' The stimulus, the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, passed both houses on 13 February 2009: the House by 246 to 183, with Democrats 246 to 7 and Republicans 0 to 176, and the Senate by 60 to 38, with three Republicans, Collins, Snowe and Specter, voting yes. The Congressional Budget Office later put its total budgetary impact over 2009-2019 at 'nearly $840 billion' and estimated that its effects on output 'peaked in the first half of 2010.' Dodd-Frank passed the House 237 to 192 on 30 June 2010, Democrats 234 to 19 and Republicans 3 to 173, and the Senate 60 to 39 on 15 July, with three Republicans (Brown, Collins and Snowe) voting yes and one Democrat (Feingold) voting no. How much did the stimulus do? Before it passed, Christina Romer of the Council of Economic Advisers and Jared Bernstein of the Vice-President's office estimated that a package of about $775 billion 'is expected to create between three and four million jobs by the end of 2010', while warning that such estimates 'are subject to significant margins of error.' John B. Taylor, studying the stimulus packages of the 2000s, found that they 'had little if any direct impact on consumption or government purchases' and that 'Households largely saved the transfers and tax rebates.' Gabriel Chodorow-Reich, reviewing evidence from differences between places, puts the cross-sectional spending multiplier at about 1.8 and concludes that the evidence points to 'a national no-monetary-policy-response multiplier of 1.7 or above.' In a 2014 survey of the Clark Center's IGM panel, 36 economists agreed or strongly agreed and 1 disagreed that the act had lowered unemployment at the end of 2010; on whether its benefits would exceed its costs, 25 agreed, 10 were uncertain and 2 disagreed. Dec. 2007 recession begins ends June 2009; real GDP down 4.3% Sept. 2008 Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy $639 billion in assets 29 Sept. 2008 House rejects TARP 205-228 1-3 Oct. 2008 TARP passes Senate 74-25; House 263-171 13 Feb. 2009 stimulus (ARRA) passes House 246-183; Senate 60-38 Oct. 2009 unemployment peaks 10 percent (monthly) 30 June and 15 July 2010 Dodd-Frank passes House 237-192; Senate 60-39 April 2024 CBO's final TARP report $444 billion disbursed; cost $31 billion

s: 2008 to 2016: the ACA, the midterms and Obergefell
x: Barack Obama won the 2008 election with 52.93 percent of the popular vote and 365 electoral votes, and was re-elected in 2012 with 51.06 percent and 332. The Affordable Care Act passed in 2009-10 without a Republican vote, and the share of Americans without health insurance fell; Republicans won the House in 2010 and enlarged their majority in 2014. In Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) the Supreme Court held, 5 to 4, that same-sex couples may exercise the fundamental right to marry, and in November 2025 it declined to hear a petition asking it to overrule that decision. In 2008, by the Federal Election Commission's count, Barack Obama won 69,498,516 votes (52.93 percent) and 365 electoral votes, and John McCain 59,948,323 (45.65 percent) and 173. The Affordable Care Act (H.R. 3590) passed the Senate 60 to 39 on 24 December 2009, every Republican present voting no; on 21 March 2010 the House concurred 219 to 212, Democrats 219 to 34 and Republicans 0 to 178. The Congressional Budget Office and the Joint Committee on Taxation estimated that the law and its companion reconciliation act together 'would produce a net reduction in federal deficits of $143 billion over the 2010–2019 period'. By the Census Bureau's Current Population Survey, 13.3 percent of Americans, 41.8 million people, lacked health insurance in 2013, 10.4 percent in 2014 and 8.8 percent, 28.1 million, in 2016; in 2024, 92.0 percent had coverage (chart). The CDC's National Health Interview Survey, which counts people uninsured at the time of interview, gives 9.7 percent in 2020, 7.6 percent in 2023, 8.2 percent in 2024 and 8.3 percent, 28.0 million people, in 2025. Studies of the law's effects ask different questions. Sarah Miller, Norman Johnson and Laura Wherry, comparing near-elderly adults 'most likely to benefit', identified by socioeconomic status, in states that expanded Medicaid under the ACA and in states that did not, find that mortality had 'trended similarly' before the expansions and that afterwards those in expansion states 'experienced a 0.132 percentage point decline in annual mortality, a 9.4 percent reduction over the sample mean'. In 2014 the Congressional Budget Office projected that the law would reduce hours worked 'by about 1.5 percent to 2.0 percent' from 2017 to 2024, equal to about 2.0 million full-time-equivalent workers in 2017 and 2.5 million in 2024, 'almost entirely because workers will choose to supply less labor.' Theda Skocpol and Vanessa Williamson, as their book on the Tea Party (2011) is summarised on a page of Harvard's Weatherhead Center, describe the movement as joining grassroots activists with national elites and funders, who used grassroots energy to further long-standing goals. The organisation Tea Party Patriots names, on its current website, 'our three core values of fiscal responsibility, constitutionally limited government, and free markets.' At the start of the 111th Congress Democrats held 257 House seats and Republicans 178; at the start of the 112th, after the 2010 midterm, Republicans held 242 and Democrats 193. After the 2014 midterm Republicans held 247 seats to the Democrats' 188. In 2012 Obama was re-elected with 65,915,795 votes (51.06 percent) and 332 electoral votes to Mitt Romney's 60,933,504 (47.20 percent) and 206. Unemployment was 7.8 percent in January 2009, peaked at 10.0 percent in October 2009 and was 4.7 percent in January 2017 (BLS). On parties and polarisation, see US2.14 and US8.13. On 26 June 2015, in Obergefell v. Hodges, the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4. Justice Kennedy wrote for the Court: 'The Court now holds that same-sex couples may exercise the fundamental right to marry', and added that there is 'no lawful basis for a State to refuse to recognize a lawful same-sex marriage performed in another State'. Of the petitioners he wrote: 'They ask for equal dignity in the eyes of the law.' Chief Justice Roberts, joined by Justices Scalia and Thomas, wrote the lead dissent, and Scalia, Thomas and Alito each wrote one too. Roberts wrote: 'But this Court is not a legislature. Whether same-sex marriage is a good idea should be of no concern to us.' And: 'Under the Constitution, judges have power to say what the law is, not what it should be.' On 10 November 2025 the Court denied Kim Davis's petition asking it to overrule Obergefell, with no noted dissent.
