Hodges 5-4 10 Nov. 2025 Davis petition denied no noted dissent 2025 uninsured (CDC survey) 8.3%, 28.0 million

Donald Trump won the presidency in 2016 with 304 electoral votes, while Hillary Clinton led the popular vote by 2,868,686. His first term brought the 2017 tax law, a 25 percent tariff on steel and a Section 301 case against China, 226 or 234 new federal judges depending on the count, and two impeachments that ended in acquittal; Democrats won the House in the 2018 midterm. In 2020 the CDC counted 350,831 deaths with COVID-19 as the underlying cause, the first COVID-19 vaccine was authorised for emergency use in December, and Joe Biden won the election by 306 electoral votes to 232. In 2016, by the Federal Election Commission's count, Hillary Clinton won 65,853,514 votes (48.18 percent) and Donald Trump 62,984,828 (46.09 percent), a margin of 2,868,686 for Clinton; the electors cast 304 votes for Trump and 227 for Clinton. Seven electors voted for others, among them two in Texas, one for John Kasich and one for Ron Paul. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act passed the Senate 51 to 48 in the early hours of 20 December 2017, every Republican present voting yes and no Democrat or independent doing so, and the House 224 to 201 later that day, Republicans 224 to 12 and Democrats 0 to 189. The Congressional Budget Office and the Joint Committee on Taxation estimated that it would 'increase the deficit by $1,455 billion over the next 10 years, excluding effects from macroeconomic feedback'; in September 2025 CBO found its estimates 'consistent with observed outcomes in 2018 and 2019'. Gabriel Chodorow-Reich, Matthew Smith, Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick (2024) find that domestic investment by firms with the average tax change rose '20% versus a no-change baseline', but that for the corporate provisions the revenue feedback from growth 'offsets only 2p.p. of the direct cost of 41% of pre-TCJA corporate revenue'. Proclamation 9705 of 8 March 2018 imposed 'a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on steel articles'. On 22 March 2018 the U.S. Trade Representative found under Section 301 that China's technology-transfer practices were 'unreasonable and burdens or restricts U.S. commerce'. Economists have measured the tariffs' effects. Amiti, Redding and Weinstein (2019) find that 'the full incidence of the tariffs has fallen on domestic consumers and importers so far'. Autor, Beck, Dorn and Hanson (2024) find that 'The trade-war has not to date provided economic help to the US heartland', and also that exposed regions 'became less likely to identify as Democrats'. The U.S. International Trade Commission (2023) found that the Section 232 tariffs 'increased U.S. production of steel products by 1.9 percent', while the steel and aluminum tariffs together 'decreased production in downstream industries 0.6 percent on average'; Michael Stumo of the Coalition for a Prosperous America, an advocacy group that says it represents 'domestic producers and workers', said that 'tariffs are a critical reshoring tool to stimulate domestic production'. On tariffs and the courts in 2025-26, see US2.13; on trade with China, see US8.12. Pew Research Center counts 226 judges appointed in Trump's single term, against 320 for Obama and 322 for George W. Bush over two terms each, including 3 Supreme Court justices and 54 appellate judges, 'one short of the 55 Obama appointed'. Pew counts only the Supreme Court, the appeals courts and the district courts; Ballotpedia counts '234 Article III federal judges through December 31, 2020', among them 174 district judges, and includes the Court of International Trade, which Pew leaves out; neither source reconciles the two totals. In the 2018 midterm Democrats won the House: at the start of the 116th Congress they held 235 seats to the Republicans' 199, with one seat vacant, against 194 to 241 two years earlier. On 18 December 2019 the House impeached Trump: Article I (abuse of power) passed 230 to 197, with no Republican voting yes and Democrats 229 to 2, and Article II (obstruction of Congress) 229 to 198. On 5 February 2020 the Senate acquitted him, 48 to 52 on Article I, Romney the only Republican voting guilty, and 47 to 53 on Article II. After the events of 6 January 2021 (US8.9) the House impeached him again on 13 January, on an article headed 'incitement of insurrection', 232 to 197, with 10 Republicans voting yes. On 13 February the Senate voted 57 to 43 to convict, short of the two-thirds required; the seven Republicans voting guilty were Burr, Cassidy, Collins, Murkowski, Romney, Sasse and Toomey. For impeachment as doctrine, see US2.4. Unemployment, 4.7 percent in January 2017, was 3.5 percent in February 2020, rose to 14.8 percent in April 2020 and was 6.4 percent in January 2021; real GDP grew 2.5 percent in 2017, 3.0 in 2018 and 2.6 in 2019 and fell 2.1 percent in 2020 (BLS; BEA, current estimates). The CARES Act passed the Senate 96 to 0 on 25 March 2020 and was signed into law on 27 March; the Congressional Budget Office and the Joint Committee on Taxation estimated that it would 'increase federal deficits by about $1.7 trillion over the 2020-2030 period'. On 11 December 2020 the Food and Drug Administration issued the first emergency use authorization for a COVID-19 vaccine. The CDC counted 350,831 deaths in 2020 with COVID-19 as the underlying cause; counting it as underlying or contributing cause, the toll was 384,536 in 2020 and, provisionally, 460,513 in 2021. For the pandemic worldwide, see 16.11. In the 2020 election Joe Biden won 81,283,501 votes (51.31 percent) to Trump's 74,223,975 (46.85 percent), a margin of 7,059,526, and 306 electoral votes to 232. 2016 presidential election popular vote Clinton 48.18%, Trump 46.09%; electoral votes Trump 304, Clinton 227 20 Dec. 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act passes Senate 51-48; House 224-201 8 March 2018 Proclamation 9705 25 percent tariff on steel after the 2018 midterm 116th Congress opens House: Democrats 235, Republicans 199 18 Dec. 2019 first impeachment Article I 230-197; Article II 229-198 5 Feb. 2020 Senate acquits 48-52 and 47-53 25-27 March 2020 CARES Act passes and is signed Senate 96-0 11 Dec. 2020 first COVID-19 vaccine authorised for emergency use FDA 2020 presidential election Biden 51.31%, Trump 46.85%; electoral votes 306-232 13 Jan. and 13 Feb. 2021 second impeachment and acquittal House 232-197; Senate 57-43 to convict

On 6 January 2021, when Congress was scheduled to count the electoral votes, rioters broke into the Capitol; a report of a bipartisan Senate investigation called it 'a violent and unprecedented attack on the U.S. Capitol', found that about 140 officers reported injuries and that seven people, three of them officers, 'ultimately lost their lives', and recorded that Congress affirmed the electoral result at 3:42 a.m. on 7 January. The Justice Department charged about 1,583 people, and on 20 January 2025 President Trump commuted 14 sentences and pardoned all others convicted. The two parties describe the day, the pardons and the investigations in their own and opposing terms, and polls in January 2025 found majorities against the pardons. On 6 January 2021, in the words of the report of the Senate Homeland Security and Rules committees (released 8 June 2021), 'Members of Congress were scheduled to perform their constitutional obligation to count the electoral votes' (for the 2020 result, see US8.8). 'Most demonstrators headed to the Ellipse, near the White House, for the "Save America" rally'. 'At approximately 12:53 p.m.', the report records, individuals in a crowd at the Capitol 'picked up one of the metal bike racks'. 'Rioters, attempting to disrupt the Joint Session of Congress, broke into the Capitol building', and 'Vice President Pence and congressional leaders were evacuated to secure locations.' The D.C. National Guard 'began arriving at the Capitol Complex at 5:20 p.m.', 'more than four hours after the barriers at the Capitol were first breached.' Congress reconvened that evening, and 'the Joint Session of Congress officially affirmed the results of the Electoral College at 3:42 a.m. on January 7.' 'Approximately 140 law enforcement officers reported injuries suffered during the attack', and 'seven individuals, including three law enforcement officers, ultimately lost their lives.' The report, which called the day 'a violent and unprecedented attack on the U.S. Capitol', examined 'the security, planning, and response failures' behind it. The House select committee on the January 6th attack issued its final report (H. Rept. 117-663) on 22 December 2022. It states that 'the central cause of January 6th was one man, former President Donald Trump, whom many others followed. None of the events of January 6th would have happened without him.' The House had impeached Trump a second time on 13 January 2021, and the Senate's 57 votes to convict fell short of two-thirds (US8.8); on impeachment and presidential immunity as doctrine, see US2.4. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia reported that about 1,583 people had been federally charged 'with crimes associated with the attack of the U.S. Capitol', about 608 of them with 'assaulting resisting, or impeding law enforcement agents or officers'; about 1,100 had been sentenced, and 170 more had pleaded guilty or been found guilty and awaited sentencing. ABC News reported the charge figures on 6 January 2025. On 20 January 2025 President Trump issued a proclamation that states: 'This proclamation ends a grave national injustice that has been perpetrated upon the American people over the last four years and begins a process of national reconciliation.' It commuted the sentences of fourteen named people 'to time served as of January 20, 2025'; granted 'a full, complete and unconditional pardon to all other individuals convicted of offenses related to events that occurred at or near the United States Capitol on January 6, 2021'; and directed the Attorney General to 'pursue dismissal with prejudice to the government of all pending indictments.' In May 2025 the Justice Department agreed in principle to pay 'a little under $5 million' to the family of Ashli Babbitt, who was shot by a Capitol Police lieutenant. The Capitol Police chief, J. Thomas Manger, wrote to his officers that he 'completely disagree[d] with the Department of Justice's decision', adding: 'In 2021, the DOJ said that there was no evidence to show that law enforcement broke the law.' A Republican-led House subcommittee chaired by Barry Loudermilk is reinvestigating the attack. Its first hearing was titled 'Examining the Investigation into the DNC and RNC Pipe Bombs'. NPR, checking claims made at the hearing, noted that 'The president has direct control of the D.C. National Guard', and that a Justice Department inspector general had found no evidence 'showing or suggesting that the FBI had undercover employees in the various protest crowds, or at the Capitol, on January 6.' Brian Cole Jr., charged with placing the two pipe bombs, 'which never exploded', pleaded not guilty; a grand jury returned a new, eight-count indictment on 30 September 2026, and his trial, set in July, is scheduled for 16 February 2027. Each side describes these events in its own words. On the fifth anniversary Loudermilk said: 'True accountability requires focusing on facts, not selective storytelling for partisan gain.' A December 2024 interim report by a House Administration subcommittee he chaired said that 'The January 6 Select Committee was improperly constituted and lacked authority.' A White House website blamed the Capitol Police for turning a 'peaceful demonstration into chaos.' Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, said: 'Donald Trump and far-right extremists in Congress have repeatedly attempted to rewrite history.' On the pardons, Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, said on 21 January 2025: 'There is no other way to describe President Trump's pardon of Jan. 6 offenders than un-American.' In a Marist poll of 7-9 January 2025, before the proclamation, 62 percent disapproved and 35 percent approved of pardoning people 'convicted of attacking the Capitol'; Republicans approved, 64 to 30 percent, and 89 percent of Democrats disapproved. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll of 20-21 January, 58 percent said Trump should not pardon all people convicted. Washington Post-University of Maryland polls, as reported by the Christian Science Monitor, found that the share saying punishments were 'not harsh enough' fell from more than half in 2021 to 38 percent in 2023, and that in December 2024 90 percent of Democrats and 40 percent of Republicans opposed pardons. s: Rescue, inflation and the 2024 election, 2021 to 2025
x: The American Rescue Plan passed in March 2021 with no Republican votes, and consumer prices rose 4.7 percent in 2021 and 8.0 percent in 2022; Bernanke and Blanchard trace most of the surge to price shocks, while San Francisco Fed economists estimate that fiscal support added about 3 points by the end of 2021. The infrastructure and CHIPS laws drew Republican votes in both chambers, while the Inflation Reduction Act passed on party lines. In the certified 2024 result Donald Trump won 312 electoral votes to Kamala Harris's 226. The Senate passed the American Rescue Plan on 6 March 2021 by 50 votes to 49, with no Republican voting yes; the House agreed on 10 March by 220 to 211, Democrats voting 220-1 and Republicans 0-210. CBO estimated that the Senate-passed bill would add about $1.86 trillion to deficits over 2021-2030. For COVID-19 worldwide, see 16.11. Consumer prices, which had risen 1.2 percent in 2020, rose 4.7 percent in 2021, 8.0 percent in 2022, 4.1 percent in 2023 and 2.9 percent in 2024, on the BLS CPI-U annual averages. Over the twelve months to June 2022 they rose 9.1 percent, which the BLS called 'the largest 12-month increase since the period ending November 1981'; over the twelve months to December 2024 the rise was 2.9 percent. Unemployment, 6.4 percent in January 2021, fell to 3.4 percent in April 2023 and was 4.0 percent in January 2025; real GDP grew 6.3 percent in 2021, 2.4 percent in 2022, 2.9 percent in 2023 and 3.0 percent in 2024 (BEA, current estimates). Economists differ on the causes. Ben Bernanke and Olivier Blanchard (2025) conclude that, 'contrary to early concerns that inflation would be spurred by overheated labor markets, most of the inflation surge resulted from shocks to prices given wages', though they add that tight labor markets have had a more persistent effect on wages and inflation. Economists at the San Francisco Fed, comparing the United States with other rich countries in March 2022, estimated that American fiscal support 'may have contributed to this divergence by raising inflation about 3 percentage points by the end of 2021', while warning that the estimate carried 'considerable uncertainty' and placing it in the upper range of other research. The two findings measure different things and need not conflict. The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act passed the Senate 69-30 in August 2021, with 19 Republicans in favour, and the House 228-206 in November, with 13 Republicans voting yes and 6 Democrats no. NBC News reported CBO's estimate that it would add $256 billion to projected deficits over ten years. The CHIPS and Science bill passed in July 2022 with 17 Republican votes in the Senate and 24 in the House, and CBO estimated that it would add $79 billion to deficits through 2031. The Inflation Reduction Act passed the Senate 51-50 on the Vice President's tie-breaking vote and the House 220-207, on party lines in both; CBO's estimate of the enacted law was a net deficit reduction of $58.1 billion over 2022-2031; under scorekeeping rules that figure leaves out an estimated $180 billion of added revenue from the law's IRS enforcement funding, which CBO reported separately. On 26 August 2021 an ISIS-K bombing at Abbey Gate, Kabul, killed at least 160 Afghan civilians and 13 American service members. On 31 August Biden said that 'more than 120,000 people' had been evacuated, spoke of 'The extraordinary success of this mission', and declared: 'I was not going to extend this forever war, and I was not extending a forever exit.' The State Department's after-action review, released in June 2023, found that 'during both administrations' there was 'insufficient senior-level consideration of worst-case scenarios and how quickly those might follow'; it treated the decisions of both presidents to end the mission as beyond its scope, while saying they 'had serious consequences'. (The wars themselves are in 16.3.) In April 2024 the House passed aid for Ukraine 311-112, with Republicans splitting 101 to 112, and the Senate cleared the combined package 79-18 (see 16.5). In the certified 2024 result Trump received 77,302,580 votes (49.80 percent) and 312 electoral votes; Harris received 75,017,613 (48.32 percent) and 226. Trump signed 225 executive orders in 2025; in February 2026 the Supreme Court held 6-3 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, and other trade statutes were used instead; economists and the administration dispute who bears the tariffs' cost. CBO estimated that the 2025 reconciliation act adds $3.4 trillion to deficits over ten years, which the White House's economists contest; Pew and GAO measured a federal workforce about a tenth smaller, and MPI's count of about 980,000 deportations stands beside DHS officials' claim of more than 3 million departures. In the third quarter of 2026 output grew at a 3.4 percent annual rate, unemployment was 4.2 percent and consumer prices were 3.7 percent higher than a year earlier; the midterm elections were held on 3 November 2026, and this book's status line is 'as of 2 November 2026'. According to the Federal Register, President Trump signed 225 executive orders in 2025, numbered EO 14147 to EO 14371. The tariffs are told in depth in US2.13. In brief: on 20 February 2026, in Learning Resources v. Trump, the Supreme Court held 6-3 that 'IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs'; Justice Kavanaugh, joined by Thomas and Alito, dissented, arguing that text, history and precedent show that it does. The President then imposed a 10% surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows up to 15% for 150 days. It was collected from 24 February 2026; an increase to 15% that he announced on 21 February was never put into effect. The surcharge expired on 24 July 2026, a 2-1 trade-court ruling against it having been stayed on appeal. That day Section 301 tariffs of 10% or 12.5% on imports from 60 trading partners took effect; as of 12 October 2026 a challenge had been argued but not decided. CBO estimates that about $130 billion of IEEPA tariffs was refunded in fiscal 2026. Economists differ on who pays. Mary Amiti and colleagues at the New York Fed found that 'nearly 90 percent of the tariffs' economic burden fell on U.S. firms and consumers' in 2025; the National Economic Council director, Kevin Hassett, called it 'the worst paper I've ever seen in the history of the Federal Reserve System', saying its authors were 'basically only looking at changes in prices'. Caroline Freund, as summarised by the Tax Foundation, estimates that 'foreigners have absorbed 47 percent of the tariff burden while US importers paid 53 percent'. The White House Council of Economic Advisers reported in July 2025 that tariffs 'have not reduced the disinflationary impulse from imported goods as of May', while noting that its analysis did not identify what prices would have done without tariffs. Looking ahead, the Yale Budget Lab estimated in July 2026 that current tariffs would raise consumer prices by about 0.7 percent, about $1,100 a household a year, and the Tax Foundation that they raise taxes by an average of $820 a household in 2026 and lower long-run GDP by 0.4 percent. Immigration enforcement is treated in US8.4. The Migration Policy Institute counts about 980,000 deportations by ICE and CBP between 20 January 2025 and 31 July 2026; DHS officials have claimed more than 3 million total departures, including about 2 million self-departures, which MPI says is about double its own estimate. US8.4 also gives the administration's own count of deportations, as AP reported it. On the civil service, Pew's analysis of OPM data found that the civilian federal workforce shrank by 10.3 percent in 2025, from 2,312,301 to 2,074,649. GAO, covering 22 agencies to January 2026, found a fall of nearly 256,000, more than 11 percent, as agencies offered incentives to resign or retire, carried out reductions in force and restricted hiring. GAO also estimated, as OPM quoted it, that agencies spent about $9.5 billion on paid administrative leave in 2025, about $6.7 billion of it under the deferred resignation program; OPM replied that for 'a one-time expense of at most $9.5 billion, taxpayers save more than $40 billion each year', a figure it computed itself. The Partnership for Public Service, a good-government group, put their cost to the economy at 'more than $165.6 billion', mostly modelled from cancelled science grants and disengaged staff; its data director called it 'a conservative estimate'. In November 2025 the Washington Examiner reported that DOGE had closed eight months early. CBO estimated on 21 July 2025 that the 2025 reconciliation act (Public Law 119-21) increases deficits by $3.4 trillion over 2025-2034, as revenues fall by $4.5 trillion and direct spending by $1.1 trillion. The White House Council of Economic Advisers, assuming growth about 1.1 to 1.2 percent higher a year on average over the law's first four years, projected in June 2025 '$2.1 to $2.3 trillion in offsetting deficit reduction due to higher growth from the OBBB tax provisions', and the White House said that, counting projected growth, the bill meant 'deficit reduction of $755 billion relative to the CBO's tax hike baseline'. As reported by Georgetown's Center for Children and Families, CBO projected 10 million more uninsured people in 2034, 5.3 million of them from the Medicaid work requirement before interactions. Christopher Jacobs of The Federalist disputed one provision, which accounted for about 100,000 of that total: it 'didn't take anything away from anyone, or any state, now', he wrote, calling its supposed effect 'highly speculative'. He did not contest CBO's figures for the work requirement or the limits on immigrants' eligibility, and wrote that 'a community engagement requirement for program recipients seems reasonable.' A 43-day shutdown, which CBS News called the longest in history, ended on 12 November 2025: Democrats had demanded an extension of the expiring Affordable Care Act tax credits, Republicans had insisted that health care be negotiated separately, and the deal promised a vote on the tax credits in December. On 11 December 2025 the Senate rejected both a Democratic three-year extension and a Republican alternative, each 51-48, short of the 60 votes needed; the House passed a three-year extension 230-196 on 8 January 2026, with 17 Republicans in favour; and KFF reported in October 2026 that the enhanced credits had expired in 2026. Piketty, Saez and Zucman find that the bottom half's pretax income stagnated while top incomes boomed; Auten and Splinter, adjusting tax data differently, find top shares lower and after-tax top shares little changed. Economists likewise differ on whether pay has kept up with productivity and on how many manufacturing jobs Chinese imports cost. Manufacturing employment fell from about 19.6 million in June 1979 to about 12.7 million in September 2026, and union membership from 20.1 percent of wage and salary workers in 1983 to 10.0 percent in 2025. How far inequality has risen depends on how income is measured. Thomas Piketty, Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman (2018), combining tax, survey and national-accounts data, find that pretax income 'has stagnated for the bottom 50% of the distribution at about $16,000 a year', while 'Income has boomed at the top.' Gerald Auten and David Splinter (2024) argue that estimates built only on tax returns 'are biased by tax-base changes', 'social changes, and missing income sources'. Adjusting for these, they find top shares 'lower' and rising 'less since 1980 than other studies using tax data', with 'little change in aftertax top income shares', and conclude that 'increasing government transfers and tax progressivity have resulted in rising real incomes for all income groups.' A second debate concerns pay. The Economic Policy Institute reports that from 1979 to 2020 net productivity rose 61.8 percent while the hourly pay of typical workers, production and nonsupervisory employees, rose 17.5 percent. Martin Feldstein (2008) found that 'total compensation per hour' rose at about the same rate as productivity from 1970 to 2006, once both are adjusted for prices in the same way. Anna Stansbury and Lawrence Summers (2017) take a middle position: a point of extra productivity growth has gone with 0.7 to 1 point of extra median compensation growth, but 'other factors orthogonal to productivity have been acting to suppress typical compensation'. On trade, David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson (2013) find that, between 1990 and 2007, Chinese 'import competition explains one-quarter of the contemporaneous aggregate decline in US manufacturing employment', and in 2021 that its effects 'are present out to 2019'. Lorenzo Caliendo, Maximiliano Dvorkin and Fernando Parro (2019), modelling the whole economy, estimate a loss of about 0.55 million manufacturing jobs, about 16 percent of the decline from 2000 to 2007, and find that 'The U.S. gains in the aggregate'. Nicholas Bloom and colleagues (2019) find the losses concentrated in 'large, importing firms that simultaneously expand employment in non-manufacturing.' For China's rise, see 16.2. Manufacturing employment reached its all-time peak, 19.6 million, in June 1979, according to the BLS. In the BLS series it was about 17.3 million in January 2000, 11.4 million in February 2010 and 12.7 million in September 2026. Union membership fell from 20.1 percent of wage and salary workers (17.7 million) in 1983 to 10.0 percent (14.7 million) in 2025, when the public-sector rate was 32.9 percent and the private-sector rate 5.9 percent. National health spending grew 7.2 percent in 2024 to $5.3 trillion, or $15,474 a person and 18.0 percent of GDP. The share of Americans with consistently liberal or conservative views doubled in the two decades to 2014, and by 2022 most Republicans and most Democrats called members of the other party more immoral than other Americans. Pew's 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study found 62 percent of adults Christian, down from 78 percent in 2007, and 29 percent unaffiliated, a rise that has levelled off, at least for now. Anti-Jewish incidents made up most religion-based hate crimes in the FBI figures for 2024 and 2025, as reported by the ADL, and Gallup's average confidence in institutions stood at 27 percent in 2026. Pew found in 2014 that the share of Americans holding consistently liberal or consistently conservative views 'has doubled over the past two decades from 10% to 21%.' In 2022, 72 percent of Republicans said Democrats were more immoral than other Americans, and 63 percent of Democrats said the same of Republicans, up from 47 and 35 percent in 2016. In Congress, Pew's analysis of DW-NOMINATE scores, which place lawmakers by their roll-call votes, found the parties 'farther apart ideologically today than at any time in the past 50 years', with both having 'shifted further away from the center, but Republicans more so.' Parties, money and polarization are treated in US2.14. Pew's 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study, of 36,908 adults, found 62 percent Christian, against 78 percent in 2007 and 71 percent in 2014, and 29 percent unaffiliated, against 16 and 23 percent; since 2019 the Christian share has hovered between 60 and 64 percent. In Pew's words the unaffiliated population 'has leveled off – at least temporarily.' Evangelical Protestants are 23 percent of adults, down from 26 percent in 2007, and mainline Protestants 11 percent, down from 18; Catholics are 19 percent, Jews 2 percent and Muslims 1 percent. American Catholics are 36 percent Hispanic. Among validated voters in 2024, 81 percent of white evangelical Protestants and 55 percent of Catholics voted for Trump, while the unaffiliated voted 70 percent for Harris. The rise of the religious right to 1979 is in US7.13, and religion worldwide in 16.9. Pew estimated about 7.5 million Jewish Americans in 2020, 2.4 percent of adults; 71 percent of Jewish adults were Democrats or leaned Democratic, while 75 percent of Orthodox Jews were Republicans or leaned Republican. FBI figures as reported by the ADL counted 1,938 anti-Jewish hate crime incidents in 2024, nearly 70 percent of religion-based hate crimes and the most since the FBI began collecting such data in 1991. FBI figures as reported by the ADL counted 1,528 anti-Jewish incidents in 2025, 63 percent of 2,408 religion-based incidents, and, as reported by the Algemeiner, 205 against Muslims. The FBI's own summary shows all reported hate-crime incidents falling from 11,679 to 10,881; among agencies that reported at least six common months in both years the fall was 7.0 percent. The ADL's own audit, which includes non-criminal harassment, counted 6,274 antisemitic incidents in 2025, down a third from 9,354 in 2024, though assaults rose from 196 to 203. AP reported that some critics find the ADL's criteria too broad, while Aryeh Tuchman, who formerly led the ADL's Center on Extremism and now directs the Nexus Center for Antisemitism, which AP says 'promotes a more nuanced definition of antisemitism than the ADL uses', said the ADL's approach reflects a genuine concern that anti-Zionism threatens the safety of American Jews. For Israel and the Palestinians, see 16.6. Gallup reported in July 2026 that average confidence in the institutions it tracks was 27 percent, one point above the record low of 2023, with Republicans 13 points more confident than Democrats (36 percent against 23). Small business stood at 67 percent and the military at 61; the police at 45, organized religion at 33, the Supreme Court and the presidency at 27 each, and Congress at 9.
